lessons.plain: Every AWS account starts with one all-powerful login called the root user. It is tied to the email address used to sign up, and it can do anything, including closing the account and changing billing. Your own permission rules cannot limit it. IAM users are separate named logins you create for people, each given only the access their job needs. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) asks for a second proof after the password, such as a code from a phone app or a tap on a physical security key. Think of the root user as a building's master key: you lock it in a safe, and staff get badges that open only their own floors.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company's only AWS login is the one created at sign-up, and three engineers share its password for daily work. Which risks can you name, and what would you change first?
lessons.teach:
IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the AWS service that decides who can sign in and what each identity may do. The root user is the identity created with the account's sign-up email. It has unrestricted power, and identity policies cannot reduce it. An IAM user is a named identity for one person or program, with its own password or access keys. An access key is a long-lived ID-and-secret pair used for programmatic (API and command-line) calls. MFA (multi-factor authentication) requires something you have, such as a code-generating app or a hardware key, in addition to something you know.

The core practices are these. Turn on MFA for the root user. Never create root access keys, and delete any that already exist. Use root only for the rare tasks that truly need it. Do daily work through separate identities that follow least privilege, meaning only the permissions the task requires. Require MFA for human IAM users. Set an account password policy that enforces length and complexity. Regularly remove or rotate unused access keys and passwords. These practices work because they make one stolen secret less damaging: a leaked password alone fails MFA, and a leaked narrow key cannot touch billing or delete everything.

Worked example. A founder uses root for everything, has no MFA, and keeps root access keys in a laptop script. Step 1: sign in as root and register an MFA device. Step 2: create an administrator identity protected by MFA, then stop using root. Step 3: give the script a new identity scoped only to what it does, then deactivate and delete the root keys. Step 4: set a password policy. Step 5: review the account's credential report for missing MFA or stale keys. If the laptop is later stolen, the attacker gets one narrow key, not the whole account.

A common mistake is assuming console MFA also protects access keys. API calls made with keys never prompt for MFA unless a policy explicitly requires it. Leaked keys are therefore a full bypass, and this is an identity-layer fix, not a network one.

questions.prompt: A 12-person design studio downloads its account credential report and works through each finding. Finding 1: the root user has MFA registered and no access keys. Action: nothing to change, and root stays reserved for rare tasks that truly need it. Finding 2: an IAM user named "maya" signs in to the console with a password but has no MFA. Action: require MFA for maya, because a leaked password alone should not be enough to get in. Finding 3: an IAM user named "render-bot" has an access key (a long-lived ID-and-secret pair used for API and command-line calls) that was last used 240 days ago, and no current job uses it. Action: ??? Which action correctly fills the missing step?
choices: Leave the key in place, since a key nobody has used in months cannot cause any harm.
Keep the key and block it with a network firewall rule, since leaked keys are a network-layer problem.
Turn on console MFA for render-bot, because console MFA will then also be required when its access key makes API calls.
Deactivate the unused access key and then delete it, so there is no stale secret left to leak.
questions.why: Regularly removing unused access keys is an identity-layer practice that eliminates a stale secret, and console MFA would not protect API calls made with that key anyway.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the AWS root user (the identity created with the account's sign-up email) is accurate?
choices: Identity policies cannot reduce its power, so you protect it with MFA, avoid root access keys, and use it only for the rare tasks that need it.
The root user should hold access keys so automated scripts always have enough permission.
The root user only needs MFA if the account has more than a few IAM users.
You can attach a least-privilege policy to the root user so it is safe to use for daily work.
questions.why: Because the root user's unrestricted power cannot be limited by identity policies, the only protection is guarding its sign-in with MFA, having no keys, and rarely using it.

questions.prompt: At a logistics startup, a developer's IAM user has console MFA turned on. The developer accidentally pushes that same user's access key to a public code repository. No policy in the account requires MFA for API calls. What is the most accurate assessment?
choices: The risk is limited, because access keys can only be used from inside the company's office network.
Anyone with the key can make API calls without an MFA prompt, so the key must be deactivated and replaced. This is an identity-layer fix.
The risk is mainly a network issue, so the first fix is to change the firewall settings on the company's servers.
The account is safe, because the developer's console MFA will block any sign-in attempt that uses the key.
questions.why: API calls made with access keys do not prompt for MFA unless a policy explicitly requires it, so a leaked key bypasses console MFA and must be handled in identity.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs a nightly reporting script that only needs to read files from one storage bucket. The script was given an access key belonging to an IAM user with full administrator permissions. The key later leaks. Which earlier change would have most limited the damage?
choices: Registering an MFA device for the root user.
Giving the script its own identity with only read access to that one bucket, following least privilege.
Setting an account password policy that requires 16-character passwords.
Requiring MFA when human users sign in to the console.
questions.why: Least privilege means a leaked narrow key can only read one bucket, while password rules and MFA do nothing to limit what an already-leaked access key can do.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would secure the root user and the human IAM users in a new AWS account, and name one limit of MFA that still leaves a gap.
lessons.modelAnswer: First, I'd lock down root. It's the sign-up identity, it can do anything, and no policy we write can restrict it. So I'd enable MFA on it, make sure it has no access keys, and use it only for the few tasks that require it. For daily work, everyone gets their own IAM identity with only the permissions their job needs, never a shared login. I'd require MFA for those people, set a strong password policy, and use the credential report to find unused keys and passwords to delete or rotate. The limit is that MFA protects interactive sign-in, but access keys used for API calls don't trigger an MFA prompt by default. A leaked key still works unless we scope it tightly, add a policy condition requiring MFA for sensitive actions, or replace long-term keys with short-lived credentials.
rubricPoints: Defines the root user as the unrestricted sign-up identity that identity policies cannot limit.
Enables MFA on root, removes root access keys, and reserves root for rare required tasks.
Uses individual least-privilege identities for daily work instead of root or shared logins.
Requires MFA for human users and enforces a password policy.
Removes or rotates unused credentials, using a review such as the credential report.
Notes that access keys bypass console MFA unless a policy requires it.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present an account with a weak root or user setup and ask for the missing identity control, so reasoning through such scenarios teaches this best.

lessons.plain: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the system that decides who may do what in an AWS account. Think of an office building. Each employee gets a badge (an IAM user). Badges are grouped by department (an IAM group), so access is set once per department, not per person. A visitor gets a temporary pass that stops working at day's end (an IAM role). The rules about which doors a badge opens are written on a list (a policy). Mixing these four pieces lets you grant exactly the access each person or program needs, and change it easily as people come and go.
lessons.guessPrompt: A new engineer joins a team of ten who all need the same access. Would you write her permissions directly onto her own account, or add her to a shared set of permissions the team already uses? What could go wrong with each choice?
lessons.teach:
IAM (AWS Identity and Access Management) is an authorization system: it decides whether each request is allowed. It has four building blocks. An IAM user is a long-lived identity for one person or program, signing in with a password or access keys (long-term credentials that do not expire on their own). An IAM group is a collection of users; it holds permissions but cannot sign in itself. An IAM role is an identity with no permanent credentials; a trusted person or service assumes it and receives temporary credentials that expire, often within an hour. A policy is a JSON document of statements, each naming an Effect (Allow or Deny), Actions (API calls such as s3:PutObject) and Resources (which things). Attached to a user, group or role it is an identity-based policy.

The model is flexible because you write permissions once, attach them to a group or role, and then change membership instead of editing each person. Evaluation follows three rules: everything is denied by default; an Allow in any applicable policy grants access; an explicit Deny anywhere overrides every Allow.

Worked example. Priya is a user in the Developers group. One group policy allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on all buckets. A second group policy explicitly denies s3:PutObject on the bucket prod-invoices. Priya uploads to prod-invoices. Step one: default deny. Step two: the Allow matches. Step three: the explicit Deny also matches, so it wins and the request is refused. Her upload to test-logs succeeds, because only the Allow matches. Her attempt to delete an object fails, because nothing allows deletion, so the default deny stands.

Common mistake: giving an application on a server an IAM user's access keys saved in a config file. If that file leaks, the attacker keeps access until someone notices and revokes the keys. The fix is to attach a role to the server (on EC2, through an instance profile) so the code gets short-lived credentials that rotate automatically. Also attach policies to groups, not individuals, and grant least privilege: only the actions and resources the job requires.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, Marco is an IAM user in the Analysts group. One group policy allows dynamodb:GetItem and dynamodb:Query on all tables. A second group policy explicitly denies dynamodb:Query on the table named payroll. Marco runs a query against payroll. Step one: everything starts denied by default. Step two: the Allow for dynamodb:Query on all tables matches this request. Step three: ______. Which choice correctly completes step three?
choices: The explicit Deny on payroll also matches, and an explicit Deny overrides every Allow, so the query is refused.
Because the two group policies conflict, the more specific one is ignored and the request falls back to default deny.
Because an Allow matched in step two, the request is granted and the evaluation stops there.
Because Marco has no policy attached to him personally, group policies do not apply and the request is refused.
questions.why: An explicit Deny that matches the request always overrides any matching Allow, so the query on payroll is refused.

questions.prompt: A hospital's scheduling service needs AWS access, and the security team wants credentials that expire on their own instead of long-term access keys. Which IAM identity provides that?
choices: An IAM role, because a trusted person or service assumes it and receives temporary credentials that expire.
An identity-based policy, because it is a JSON document that issues credentials when it is attached.
An IAM group, because it holds permissions and can sign in on behalf of all of its members.
An IAM user, because it signs in with a password or access keys that belong to one person or program.
questions.why: A role has no permanent credentials; assuming it yields temporary credentials that expire, often within an hour.

questions.prompt: A media company runs a nightly video-transcoding program on an EC2 server that must write files to a storage bucket. A developer proposes saving an IAM user's access keys in the program's config file. What is the better design, and why?
choices: Keep the access keys but grant the user every S3 action, so the program never fails on a missing permission.
Attach a role to the server through an instance profile, so the program gets short-lived credentials that rotate automatically.
Store the access keys in a second config file as a backup, so the program keeps working if one file is lost.
Create an IAM group for the server and add the server to it, so the group's credentials are used instead.
questions.why: Leaked long-term keys give an attacker access until someone revokes them, whereas a role supplies temporary credentials that expire and rotate on their own.

questions.prompt: A retail chain has 25 data analysts, all in an IAM group called Reporting. They now all need permission to run one additional read action on a sales database. What change best fits a flexible, least-privilege IAM model?
choices: Create one shared IAM user with that permission and give its password to all 25 analysts.
Add an Allow for just that action and resource to a policy attached to the Reporting group, once.
Attach a new policy granting that action directly to each of the 25 analyst users, one at a time.
Give the Reporting group full administrator access so analysts are not blocked by future requests.
questions.why: Writing the permission once on the group gives every member access through membership, and limiting it to the needed action and resource keeps least privilege.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how IAM users, groups, roles and policies fit together, how AWS decides whether a request is allowed, and name one tradeoff or limit, such as why a role is preferred over a user's access keys for an application.
lessons.modelAnswer: Users are long-lived identities for people or programs, groups bundle users so we manage permissions once per team, and roles are identities that anyone or anything trusted can assume to get temporary credentials. Policies are the JSON rules, each saying Allow or Deny, which actions, on which resources, and we attach them to users, groups or roles. When a request arrives, AWS starts from deny, looks for a matching Allow, and if any explicit Deny matches, the Deny wins no matter how many Allows exist. The tradeoff: user access keys are simple but never expire on their own, so a leaked key keeps working until revoked. For an application on a server, a role is better because its credentials are short-lived and rotate automatically, at the cost of setting up the trust. We also keep policies least-privilege, which takes more effort to write but limits damage.
rubricPoints: Defines users as long-lived identities and groups as permission bundles for users that cannot sign in.
Defines roles as assumable identities that hand out temporary, expiring credentials.
Describes a policy as Effect, Action and Resource attached to an identity.
States the evaluation order: default deny, Allow grants, explicit Deny overrides.
Names a tradeoff, such as long-term keys versus roles for applications or effort of least privilege.

suggested.rationale: Tracing real requests through default deny, Allow and explicit Deny in a policy evaluator builds the exact reasoning this objective needs.

lessons.plain: A cross-account role lets someone who signs in to one AWS account temporarily act inside a different AWS account, without getting a separate username or permanent keys there. Think of a hotel key card. You keep your own ID, and the front desk gives you a card that opens only certain doors and stops working at checkout. The account being entered decides who may have a card and which doors it opens. A token service hands out the short-lived card each time it is asked. When the card expires, there is nothing left for anyone to steal or misuse.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company has a Dev account and a Prod account. Developers need to read logs in Prod now and then. Which do you think is safer: creating a user in Prod and sharing its permanent keys with the team, or letting developers borrow a temporary identity in Prod that expires after an hour? Why?
lessons.teach:
A cross-account role is an IAM role that lives in one AWS account and can be taken on by identities from another account. An IAM role is an identity that has permissions but no password and no permanent keys. AWS Security Token Service (STS) is the service that hands out temporary credentials when someone assumes a role. Those credentials are an access key, a secret key and a session token, and they expire after a set time, one hour by default. Role switching is the console version of this: a user picks the role, works under its permissions, then switches back.

Two policies on the role must agree. The trust policy says who may assume the role. The permissions policy says what the role can do once assumed. A third check sits on the calling side: the caller's own identity policy must allow the sts:AssumeRole action on that role. Both accounts have to consent, so neither one can grant access alone.

Here is a worked example. Dana is a user in the Dev account, 111111111111. The Prod account, 222222222222, has a role named ReadLogs.
Step 1: the ReadLogs trust policy names account 111111111111 as an allowed principal, meaning an identity allowed to assume the role.
Step 2: the ReadLogs permissions policy allows reading one log bucket.
Step 3: Dana's policy in Dev allows sts:AssumeRole on ReadLogs.
Step 4: Dana asks STS to assume the role. STS checks the trust policy and Dana's permission, then returns credentials that last one hour.
Step 5: Dana reads the Prod logs but cannot delete them. When the credentials expire, there is nothing left to leak.

Sometimes an outside vendor assumes a role in your account. In that case, add an external ID condition to the trust policy. An external ID is a shared value that only the vendor and you know, and it stops another customer of that vendor from tricking the vendor into using your role. This trick is called the confused deputy problem.

A common mistake is to create a user in Prod and share its permanent access keys. Those keys never expire, get copied into scripts, and if leaked give an attacker standing access until someone notices. The fix belongs in identity: one sign-in per person, plus temporary, scoped access into each account.

questions.prompt: Raj is a user in the Analytics account, 555555555555. He needs to read monthly reports stored in a bucket in the Finance account, 777777777777, through a role there named ReportReader. Steps so far. Step 1: the ReportReader permissions policy allows reading the reports bucket and nothing else. Step 2: Raj's own identity policy in Analytics allows the sts:AssumeRole action on ReportReader. Step 3: missing. Step 4: Raj asks STS to assume ReportReader, and STS returns temporary credentials that expire after one hour. Step 5: Raj reads the reports but cannot change or delete them. Which step 3 is needed for step 4 to succeed?
choices: Raj's identity policy in Analytics also allows reading the Finance reports bucket directly.
The ReportReader trust policy names account 555555555555 as an allowed principal.
The ReportReader trust policy adds an external ID condition that only Raj knows.
Finance creates an IAM user for Raj and sends him its permanent access keys as a backup way in.
questions.why: STS only hands out credentials if the role's trust policy, which says who may assume it, lists Raj's account as an allowed principal, so Finance must consent alongside Raj's sts:AssumeRole permission.

questions.prompt: A cross-account role in a Payments account has two policies attached. A new engineer asks which of them decides which outside accounts or identities are allowed to take on the role in the first place. Which answer is right?
choices: The trust policy, which lists the principals allowed to assume the role.
The caller's identity policy, which on its own is enough to grant the role to anyone it names.
The permissions policy, which lists the principals allowed to assume the role.
STS itself, which lets any authenticated AWS user assume any role for one hour.
questions.why: The trust policy says who may assume the role, while the permissions policy says what the role can do once assumed.

questions.prompt: A retail company lets an outside cost-monitoring vendor assume a role in its AWS account. The vendor serves many other customers. The security team worries that another of the vendor's customers could trick the vendor into using the retail company's role. What should be added, and what is the problem it prevents called?
choices: Permanent access keys for the vendor, which prevents the vendor from being impersonated.
A longer session duration on the role, which prevents credential expiry problems.
An external ID condition in the role's trust policy, which prevents the confused deputy problem.
A permissions policy that allows sts:AssumeRole, which prevents the role-switching problem.
questions.why: An external ID is a shared value only the vendor and the customer know, so placing it as a condition in the trust policy stops other customers of the vendor from steering it into the wrong role, which is the confused deputy problem.

questions.prompt: A startup gives three contractors access to its production account by creating one IAM user there and emailing them its permanent access keys. A reviewer flags this as a security hole. Which answer best names the risk and where the fix belongs?
choices: The risk is unencrypted log files; the fix belongs in the data layer by encrypting the bucket.
The keys expire after one hour and break the contractors' scripts; the fix is to give each contractor their own permanent keys.
The risk is slow network traffic between accounts; the fix belongs in the network layer by adding a firewall rule.
The keys never expire and can be copied into scripts, so a leak gives standing access; the fix belongs in identity, with one sign-in per person and temporary, scoped role access.
questions.why: Shared permanent keys never expire and give an attacker standing access if leaked, so the fix is an identity control: individual sign-ins plus temporary credentials from assuming a role through STS.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a developer in one AWS account gets temporary access to another account through a role and STS, which policies must line up, and one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Prod creates a role and attaches two policies to it. The trust policy says which outside account or identity may assume the role. The permissions policy says what the role can do. In our account, the developer's own policy must allow sts:AssumeRole on that role. When the developer assumes it, STS checks all of this and returns temporary credentials, by default for an hour. The developer works under the role's permissions only, and nothing permanent is handed out, so a leaked credential soon dies. Both accounts must agree, so neither can open the door alone. The tradeoff is that sessions expire, so long jobs must refresh credentials. We also have to keep trust policies tight. If we trust a whole account with no conditions, we are relying on that account to limit who assumes the role. For outside vendors, we add an external ID to avoid the confused deputy problem.
rubricPoints: The role lives in the target account and its trust policy names who may assume it.
The role's permissions policy limits what the assumed session can do.
The caller's own policy must allow sts:AssumeRole, so both sides consent.
STS returns temporary credentials that expire, unlike permanent access keys.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as session expiry, an overly broad trust, or the external ID for third parties.

suggested.rationale: An authorization policy evaluator would let the learner see an assume-role request succeed or fail as trust, permissions and caller policies are changed, which is the core skill here.

lessons.plain: When a company grows, it usually splits its cloud work into many separate AWS accounts: one for production, one for testing, one per team. Each account is like a separate apartment with its own locks. AWS Organizations is the building management office that groups all those apartments, pays one combined bill, and can post building rules that no tenant can override. A service control policy is one of those rules, for example "nobody here may turn off the audit log." AWS Control Tower is a ready-made setup kit that builds the whole building to a sensible standard, rules included, so you do not start from scratch.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer has full administrator rights inside their team's AWS account, but the company has placed a rule above that account saying "no one may delete the audit log." If the developer tries to delete the audit log, what do you think happens, and why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Organizations is a service for centrally managing many AWS accounts. One account is the management account, which creates the organization and pays the consolidated bill (a single combined invoice for all accounts). The others are member accounts. You group member accounts into organizational units (OUs), which are folders such as Production or Sandbox, so a rule attached to an OU applies to every account inside it.

A service control policy (SCP) is a rule attached to the organization root, an OU, or an account. It sets the maximum permissions available there. It never grants anything; it only limits. A request succeeds only if the SCP allows it and an IAM policy (the normal permission document on a user or role) also allows it. An explicit Deny in an SCP wins over any Allow. SCPs bind every identity in a member account, even that account's root user, which is why they work as guardrails that local administrators cannot remove.

Worked example: the Production OU has an SCP denying the action that stops or deletes the CloudTrail audit trail. Step 1: an engineer in a production account, holding an IAM policy allowing everything, calls delete-trail. Step 2: IAM says allow. Step 3: AWS checks the SCPs on the account, its OU, and the root; the OU's SCP explicitly denies it. Step 4: the call is refused. The audit trail survives, even if the engineer's credentials were stolen.

AWS Control Tower is a managed service that builds a landing zone: a pre-configured multi-account environment on top of Organizations, with shared logging and audit accounts, an account factory for creating new accounts to a standard, and controls (guardrails). Preventive controls are usually SCPs that block actions; detective controls use AWS Config rules to flag drift after it happens.

Common mistake: expecting an SCP to give access, or expecting it to restrict the management account. It does neither, so keep workloads out of the management account. Otherwise a compromised identity there escapes every guardrail.

questions.prompt: Northwind Labs attaches a service control policy (SCP) to its Sandbox organizational unit (OU). The SCP explicitly denies launching EC2 virtual servers in any region except eu-west-1. A developer in one sandbox account has an IAM policy that allows every EC2 action in every region. Step 1: the developer asks to launch a server in ap-southeast-2. Step 2: the developer's IAM policy allows the action. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: the launch is refused and no server is created. What is Step 3?
choices: AWS sees the IAM Allow and treats it as final, because an IAM permission outranks any SCP placed above the account
AWS Config lets the server launch, then flags it as drift and removes it a few minutes later
AWS checks the SCPs on the account, its OU and the root, and the Sandbox OU's explicit Deny matches
AWS checks only SCPs attached directly to the account, finds none there, and lets the request continue
questions.why: A request needs both an IAM Allow and an SCP Allow at every level above the account, and the explicit Deny in the OU's SCP overrides the developer's IAM Allow, so the launch is refused before it happens.

questions.prompt: At a retail company, an SCP on the Analytics OU allows all S3 storage actions. An analyst in an account inside that OU has an IAM policy that grants no S3 permissions at all. The analyst tries to read a file from an S3 bucket in the same account. What happens?
choices: The read is refused only if the account's root user has also been blocked
The read succeeds, because the SCP grants S3 access to everyone in the OU
The read is refused, because an SCP only sets a ceiling and no IAM policy allows the action
The read succeeds, because an SCP Allow overrides a missing IAM permission
questions.why: An SCP never grants access, so a request also needs an IAM policy that allows it, and here none does.

questions.prompt: A startup runs its main web application inside its AWS Organizations management account. It has an SCP on the organization root that denies deleting audit logs. An attacker steals an administrator's credentials in the management account and deletes the audit logs. Why did the guardrail fail?
choices: Deny statements in SCPs work only when AWS Control Tower is also enabled
The SCP needed an explicit Allow for the logs as well as the Deny
SCPs attached to the organization root apply only to OUs, not to individual accounts
SCPs do not restrict the management account, so identities there escape them
questions.why: SCPs bind member accounts but never the management account, which is why workloads should be kept out of the management account.

questions.prompt: A bank uses AWS Control Tower. One control checks for storage buckets that have been made public, and it raises an alert after such a bucket appears. It does not stop anyone from making the change. What kind of control is this, and what is it usually built on?
choices: A preventive control, usually built on an SCP that blocks the action in advance
A preventive control, usually built on IAM policies in each member account
A detective control, usually built on an SCP explicit Deny on the OU
A detective control, usually built on AWS Config rules that flag drift after it happens
questions.why: Detective controls find and flag drift after it happens, using AWS Config rules, while preventive controls (usually SCPs) block the action before it can happen.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how AWS Organizations, SCPs, and Control Tower fit together to secure many accounts, including one thing an SCP cannot do.
lessons.modelAnswer: Organizations lets us manage all our AWS accounts as one group: a management account at the top, member accounts sorted into organizational units like Production and Sandbox, and one consolidated bill. Service control policies attach to the root, an OU, or an account and act as a ceiling on permissions. An action only works if both the SCP and the person's IAM policy allow it, and an SCP Deny beats any Allow, even for a member account's root user. So we can say "nobody in Production may disable CloudTrail" and a local admin cannot undo it. Control Tower automates building this: it sets up a landing zone with log and audit accounts, an account factory, and preventive controls (SCPs) plus detective controls (Config rules). The limits: an SCP never grants access by itself, and it does not apply to the management account, so we keep workloads out of that account.
rubricPoints: Organizations groups accounts under a management account, with OUs and consolidated billing.
An SCP sets maximum permissions and never grants access on its own.
Effective access requires both the SCP and IAM to allow, and an explicit Deny wins.
SCPs bind member-account identities including the root user, but not the management account.
Control Tower builds a governed landing zone with preventive (SCP) and detective (Config) controls.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a request through IAM allows and an SCP deny in an authorization policy evaluator makes the intersection rule concrete in a way reading cannot.

lessons.plain: A resource-based policy is a permission rule attached to the thing being protected, such as a storage bucket, a message queue or an encryption key, rather than to the person or program asking for it. It answers the question "who may touch me, and how?" Think of a guest list held by the door of a club: the bouncer checks it no matter which company the guest works for. An identity-based policy is more like a badge your own employer gives you. Resource-based policies matter most when the visitor comes from another account, is an AWS service, or when one owner must control access in one place.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company keeps reports in a storage bucket in Account A. A partner team works in Account B and needs to read those reports. Would you rather write the permission on the bucket itself or on each partner user, and why?
lessons.teach:
An identity-based policy is a set of permissions attached to an IAM identity (a user, group or role) saying what that identity may do. A resource-based policy is attached to a resource, for example an S3 bucket policy, an SQS queue policy, an SNS topic policy, a Lambda function policy or a KMS key policy. Because it sits on the resource, it must name a Principal: the account, role, user or AWS service being allowed or denied.

How they combine: inside one account, an Allow in either policy type is enough, unless something explicitly denies. An explicit Deny always wins. Across accounts, both sides must agree: the resource owner's policy must allow the outside principal, and the caller's own account must also grant that identity the permission.

Resource-based policies beat identity-based ones in four situations. Cross-account access without switching roles, so the caller keeps its own identity and permissions. Letting an AWS service act, such as S3 invoking a Lambda function or SNS writing to a queue, since a service has no identity in your account to attach a policy to. Central control by the owner, such as denying all access unless it comes through a particular private endpoint. And deliberate public access, like a static website bucket.

Worked example: Account A owns bucket reports. Step 1, its bucket policy allows Principal = Account B's role analyst to perform GetObject on reports. Step 2, Account B attaches an identity policy to analyst allowing GetObject on that bucket. Step 3, analyst requests a file; AWS checks both policies, finds Allows and no Deny, and returns the file. Remove either step and the request is denied.

Common mistake: assuming the bucket policy alone grants another account access, or the opposite fix of setting Principal to "*" to make the error go away. In a running system, the first produces Access Denied errors in the partner's job; the second silently makes the data readable by anyone on the internet.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics runs a message queue (Amazon SQS, a managed queue) called inbound-orders in its AWS account 1111. A partner, Northwind Retail, has account 2222 with an IAM role named order-pusher that must send messages to that queue. The role must keep its own identity and must not switch roles. Step 1: ______. Step 2: Northwind's account 2222 attaches an identity-based policy to order-pusher allowing SendMessage on inbound-orders. Step 3: order-pusher sends a message. AWS checks both sides, finds an Allow on each and no explicit Deny, and accepts the message. Which action completes Step 1?
choices: Harbor's account 1111 adds a queue policy with Principal set to "*" allowing SendMessage, so any caller can reach the queue.
Nothing is needed in Step 1, because the identity policy in account 2222 already grants SendMessage.
Harbor's account 1111 attaches an identity-based policy directly to order-pusher allowing SendMessage.
Harbor's account 1111 adds a queue policy allowing Principal = account 2222's role order-pusher to perform SendMessage on inbound-orders.
questions.why: For cross-account access both sides must agree, so the queue owner's resource-based policy must name order-pusher as the allowed Principal, and naming only that role avoids opening the queue to everyone.

questions.prompt: Why must a resource-based policy, such as a policy on a message topic or an encryption key, include a Principal element, while an identity-based policy does not?
choices: Because a Principal is what turns an Allow into an explicit Deny.
Because only policies with a Principal can be used inside a single account.
Because the Principal tells AWS which region the resource is stored in.
Because the policy sits on the resource, it has to state which account, role, user or AWS service is being allowed or denied.
questions.why: An identity-based policy already belongs to a user, group or role, but a resource-based policy is attached to the resource, so it must name who the permission applies to.

questions.prompt: Greenleaf Photos wants a Lambda function (a managed piece of code that runs on demand) to run automatically whenever a new image is uploaded to its S3 bucket uploads-2024. Which control lets S3 trigger the function?
choices: An IAM user created for S3 with an access key that allows invoking the function.
A bucket policy on uploads-2024 with Principal set to "*".
A Lambda function policy, a resource-based policy, that allows the S3 service as Principal to invoke the function.
An identity-based policy attached to the S3 service inside Greenleaf's account.
questions.why: An AWS service has no identity in your account to attach a policy to, so the permission must sit on the function itself and name the service as Principal.

questions.prompt: Inside one AWS account at Copperline Bank, the role cleanup-job has an identity-based policy allowing DeleteObject on the bucket archive-7. The bucket policy on archive-7 contains an explicit Deny of DeleteObject for cleanup-job. What happens when cleanup-job tries to delete an object?
choices: The delete is denied, because an explicit Deny always wins over any Allow.
The delete succeeds, because identity-based policies take priority over resource-based policies.
The delete succeeds, because inside one account an Allow in either policy type is enough.
The delete is denied only if the request comes from a different account.
questions.why: An Allow in either policy is enough inside one account only when nothing explicitly denies, and an explicit Deny always overrides an Allow.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what a resource-based policy is, how it differs from an identity-based policy, and when you would choose one, including at least one limit or risk.
lessons.modelAnswer: An identity-based policy hangs on a user, group or role and says what that identity can do. A resource-based policy hangs on the resource itself, like a bucket, queue, topic, function or key, and names a Principal saying who may use it. I reach for a resource-based policy when access crosses accounts and I don't want the caller to switch roles, when an AWS service like S3 or SNS needs to call my resource, or when I want one owner-controlled place to enforce rules such as a deny unless traffic comes through a private endpoint. The limit: across accounts it isn't enough alone; the caller's own account must also allow the action, and an explicit Deny anywhere still wins. The big risk is a wildcard Principal, which can quietly make a resource public.
rubricPoints: Defines a resource-based policy as attached to the resource and naming a Principal.
Contrasts it with identity-based policies attached to users, groups or roles.
Names when it wins: cross-account without role switching, AWS service access, central owner control, or public access.
States that cross-account access needs an Allow on both sides.
Notes that an explicit Deny overrides any Allow.
Warns about the risk of a wildcard Principal exposing data.

suggested.rationale: Evaluating a request against both a resource policy and an identity policy, across accounts and with explicit denies, is exactly what a policy evaluator lets the learner practise hands-on.

lessons.plain: Federation means letting people sign in to AWS with the company accounts they already have, instead of creating a second username and password for each of them inside AWS. The company directory, the central list of employees and their groups, vouches for who someone is. AWS trusts that vouching and hands the person a temporary role with set permissions. Think of a hotel that accepts a trusted travel agency's booking voucher. The front desk does not re-check your life story. It reads the voucher and gives you a key card that works for your stay only.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has 2,000 employees in its own office directory and wants them to use AWS. If an employee leaves and is disabled in that directory, what would you want to happen to their AWS access, and where would you prefer to make that change?
lessons.teach:
Federating a directory with IAM roles means AWS accepts sign-ins proven by an outside identity system and maps each person to an IAM role rather than to a permanent IAM user. A directory is the store of people and groups, such as Microsoft Active Directory. An identity provider (IdP) is the service that checks a person's password and vouches for them. Examples are AD FS, Okta, or AWS IAM Identity Center. SAML 2.0 is a standard format for that vouching. The IdP sends a signed message called an assertion, which states who the user is and which groups they belong to. An IAM role is a set of permissions with no long-term password. Its trust policy says who may assume it, and here that is the registered IdP. AWS STS (Security Token Service) issues temporary credentials that expire, often after one to twelve hours.

This works because identity lives in one place. AWS never stores the employee's password. It only checks that the assertion is signed by a provider it trusts.

Here is a worked example. Priya is in the AD group AWS-DBA. She opens the company sign-in portal, and AD checks her password. The IdP builds a SAML assertion that maps AWS-DBA to the role DatabaseAdmin and signs it. AWS verifies the signature against the IdP it has registered. Then STS (through its AssumeRoleWithSAML action) returns credentials for DatabaseAdmin that last one hour. Later Priya leaves and is disabled in AD. She can no longer get new assertions, so her access ends when the current session expires.

AWS Directory Service can supply the directory side. AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a hosted directory. AD Connector is a proxy that passes sign-in requests to an on-premises AD without copying its data. IAM Identity Center is the usual modern hub for single sign-on across many accounts.

A common mistake is to create an IAM user for every employee, or to map every group to one broad admin role. Duplicate users drift out of sync with the directory, and former staff keep working access keys. A single broad role erases least privilege. Either way, offboarding and audits fail in the running system.

questions.prompt: Harbor Freight Lines federates its Okta identity provider (the service that checks passwords and vouches for users) with AWS using SAML 2.0. Contractor Mateo belongs to the Okta group AWS-Auditors, which the signed assertion maps to the IAM role AuditReadOnly. Sessions for that role last 8 hours. Step 1: At 10:00 Mateo signs in, and Okta checks his password. Step 2: AWS verifies the assertion's signature, and STS issues temporary AuditReadOnly credentials valid until 18:00. Step 3: At 13:00 his contract ends, and an administrator disables Mateo in Okta. Step 4: ??? Which statement correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Mateo's access ends at 13:00, because AWS checks Okta on every API call.
Mateo keeps access indefinitely until someone deletes his IAM user and its access keys.
Mateo cannot obtain new assertions, so his access ends when the current session expires at 18:00.
Mateo's access ends at 14:00, because STS always cuts sessions to one hour after a directory change.
questions.why: Disabling him in the identity provider blocks new signed assertions, but the temporary credentials already issued keep working until they expire at 18:00.

questions.prompt: In a SAML federation setup, an IAM role named FinanceReports is meant to be used by employees who sign in through the company's identity provider. What does this role's trust policy specify?
choices: Which S3 buckets and reports the role is permitted to read
The list of IAM users who were copied from the directory into AWS
The long-term password each finance employee uses to sign in to AWS
That the registered identity provider is allowed to have users assume the role
questions.why: A trust policy states who may assume the role, and in federation that is the registered identity provider. Permissions such as bucket access belong to the role's permission set, and the role has no long-term password.

questions.prompt: A regional bank runs Microsoft Active Directory in its own data center. It wants AWS sign-ins to be checked against that existing directory, and its security team forbids copying any directory data into AWS. Which AWS Directory Service option fits best?
choices: AWS Managed Microsoft AD, hosting a new copy of the bank's directory in AWS
One shared IAM user whose access keys are handed out to all staff
AD Connector, a proxy that passes sign-in requests to the on-premises directory
A separate IAM user created for each bank employee, kept in sync manually
questions.why: AD Connector forwards sign-in requests to the on-premises directory without copying its data. AWS Managed Microsoft AD is a separate hosted directory, so it does not meet the rule against copying.

questions.prompt: A design-agency startup federates its directory with AWS. To keep setup simple, it maps the Designers, Interns, and Finance groups all to one role, FullAdmin, which has every permission. Sign-in works fine. What problem does this design create in the running system?
choices: Least privilege is lost: an intern can change finance resources, and audits cannot separate what each group is allowed to do
Former staff keep working access keys after they are disabled in the directory
Employees' directory passwords end up stored in AWS, where they could leak
STS can no longer issue temporary credentials, so every session becomes permanent
questions.why: Mapping every group to one broad role removes least privilege, so every user gets every permission and audits fail. Passwords still stay with the identity provider, and credentials are still temporary.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why the company should federate its existing directory with IAM roles instead of creating IAM users for staff. Include one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Federation keeps the company directory as the single source of truth for who someone is. An employee signs in to the identity provider, which checks their password and sends AWS a signed SAML assertion listing their groups. AWS trusts that provider through a role's trust policy. STS then gives the employee temporary credentials for a role mapped to their group, such as DatabaseAdmin. No long-lived AWS passwords or access keys exist for staff. When someone leaves, we disable them in the directory and they can't get new sessions. One tradeoff is dependency: if the IdP or the connection to on-premises AD is down, people can't sign in. That means we still need a protected break-glass path. Another limit is that disabling a user doesn't cut off a session already issued. Access lasts until those credentials expire, so session length should be kept short.
rubricPoints: The directory or IdP authenticates the user, and AWS does not store their password.
A signed SAML assertion carries identity and group information to AWS.
The role's trust policy names the IdP, and group membership maps to specific roles.
STS issues temporary credentials that expire, so there are no long-lived staff keys.
Offboarding happens in one place, the directory.
It names a tradeoff, such as dependence on the IdP or sessions lasting until expiry.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through scenarios like 'employees must use existing corporate credentials', so reasoning through situations that pick between federation, IAM users, Identity Center and AD Connector teaches the most.

lessons.plain: The shared responsibility model is the line between what the cloud provider protects and what you protect. AWS secures the buildings, hardware, network cables and the software that runs its services. You secure what you put on top: your data, who can access it, and how you configure things. Think of renting a flat. The landlord keeps the walls, roof and front-door lock sound. You decide who gets a copy of your key and whether you leave the window open. The line moves depending on how much of the service the provider runs for you, and a good design checks where it sits before anything is built.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you run your own database software on a rented virtual server, and later switch to a database service the provider fully manages, which security chores do you think stop being yours, and which ones stay with you no matter what?
lessons.teach:
The shared responsibility model splits security work between AWS and the customer. AWS owns security OF the cloud: data centres, physical hosts, the hypervisor (the software that splits one physical machine into many virtual ones), and the internals of each managed service. You own security IN the cloud: your data, identity and access settings, network rules, encryption choices, and any software you install yourself.

The line moves with the service type. With an unmanaged service such as Amazon EC2 (rented virtual servers), you get a raw machine, so you patch the guest operating system (the OS running inside your virtual server), install the database, and configure the firewall. With a managed service such as Amazon RDS (a managed relational database), AWS patches the OS and database engine, but you still choose who can connect and whether storage is encrypted. With an abstracted, serverless service such as AWS Lambda (run code without managing servers) or Amazon S3 (object storage), AWS runs almost everything underneath, yet your code, your permissions and your data settings remain yours.

Using it as a design constraint means: for every component, list the duties that land on your side, and make sure each one has an owner and a control. Worked example: a team needs a database and has no one to apply security patches. Step 1, on EC2 the OS and database patches are theirs, an unowned duty. Step 2, on RDS those patches move to AWS. Step 3, what remains is access control and encryption, which they can configure once. So the requirement "no patching staff" points to the managed option.

The common mistake is believing "managed" means "secured for me." AWS will run S3 reliably, but if you set a bucket to allow public reads, AWS will serve your files to anyone. In a running system that misreading becomes a data leak that no provider control would have stopped, because access configuration was always on the customer side.

questions.prompt: A small analytics firm plans to run a function on AWS Lambda (a serverless service: you upload code and AWS runs it without you managing servers). The function reads CSV reports from one Amazon S3 bucket (S3 is object storage) and writes summaries to a second bucket. They list the duties that land on their side of the shared responsibility model. Step 1: the physical hosts, the hypervisor and the operating system running the function belong to AWS, so nothing to do there. Step 2: the function's code and the libraries it bundles are theirs, so someone must review and update them. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the two buckets' data settings, such as blocking public access and turning on encryption, are theirs to configure. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Set the function's permissions so it can read only the reports bucket and write only the summaries bucket.
Harden the hypervisor beneath the function so other customers cannot reach its memory.
Skip access control, because Lambda is a managed service and AWS decides what it may reach.
Patch the operating system on the servers that run the function, since the code depends on it.
questions.why: Identity and access settings stay on the customer side even for serverless services, so the firm must decide exactly what the function is allowed to touch.

questions.prompt: A logistics company moves its order database from a self-run database on Amazon EC2 (rented virtual servers) to Amazon RDS (a managed relational database). Under the shared responsibility model, which duty now belongs to AWS rather than the company?
choices: Applying security patches to the database engine and its operating system.
Choosing whether the database's storage is encrypted.
Deciding which application servers are allowed to connect to the database.
Writing the network rules that limit traffic to the database port.
questions.why: With a managed service like RDS, AWS takes over OS and engine patching, while connection access, network rules and encryption choices stay with the customer.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop runs its storefront on three Amazon EC2 instances (virtual servers it rents and configures itself). A security scan finds the guest operating system (the OS inside each virtual server) is two years out of date and has a known flaw. Who is responsible for fixing it, and why?
choices: AWS, because EC2 is an AWS service and all AWS services are patched by AWS.
The bookshop, because with an unmanaged service like EC2 the guest operating system is the customer's to patch.
AWS, because it owns the hypervisor and therefore every layer running on top of it.
Both share it equally, so either side may apply the patch whenever it is convenient.
questions.why: EC2 hands the customer a raw virtual machine, so everything installed inside it, including the guest OS, is the customer's duty.

questions.prompt: A marketing agency stores client campaign images in an Amazon S3 bucket. A staff member changed the bucket to allow public reads to share one file quickly, and weeks later the full set of client images was found on the internet. Which statement best describes this failure under the shared responsibility model?
choices: It is a customer-side failure: access configuration was the agency's duty, and AWS correctly served files the settings allowed anyone to read.
It is a hypervisor failure: another tenant on the same physical host must have read the agency's data.
It is a patching failure: AWS was late applying an operating system update to the S3 storage servers.
It is an AWS-side failure: S3 is a managed service, so AWS should have refused to serve the files publicly.
questions.why: Managed does not mean secured for you; who may read a bucket is always the customer's setting, so no AWS control would have stopped this leak.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how the shared responsibility model should shape a design choice between running software on your own virtual servers and using a managed service, and name one duty that never moves to AWS.
lessons.modelAnswer: AWS secures the cloud itself: the buildings, hardware, hypervisor and the inside of its managed services. We secure what we put in it: data, who has access, network rules, encryption settings and any software we install. The split depends on the service. On EC2 we own the guest operating system, so patching and hardening are our job. On RDS, AWS patches the OS and engine, so choosing it removes work we might not have staff for. On Lambda or S3 even more moves to AWS. The tradeoff is control: a managed service hands off chores but also limits how much we can tune or customise. What never moves is our side of access and data: if we grant broad permissions or make a bucket public, AWS will faithfully do what we configured, and the leak is ours.
rubricPoints: States that AWS secures the underlying infrastructure and service internals while the customer secures data, access and configuration.
Explains that the dividing line shifts between unmanaged, managed and serverless services.
Gives a concrete duty such as OS patching that moves to AWS with a managed service.
Names a duty that always stays with the customer, such as access permissions or data protection.
Mentions a tradeoff, such as losing control or customisation when handing more to AWS.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reasoning through a requirement to decide which side owns each duty and which service type removes it, which exam-style scenarios practise best.

lessons.plain: A VPC (virtual private cloud) is a private network you own inside AWS. Four parts decide how traffic moves through it. Route tables are signposts that say where traffic for each destination goes next. A NAT gateway is a one-way exit that lets private machines reach the internet without letting the internet reach them. Network ACLs are guards at each neighbourhood gate who check every person both ways. Security groups are bouncers at each building door who remember who left and let them back in. Together they decide whether a path exists and who may use it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A firewall lets your server send a request out to a website. Should that firewall automatically let the website's reply back in? What would you expect to break if it did not?
lessons.teach:
A VPC is a virtual network in AWS. It is split into subnets, which are smaller address ranges that each sit in one Availability Zone (one data-centre location). Four components control traffic.

A route table is a list of rules attached to a subnet that says where packets for each destination go next. If a subnet's table sends 0.0.0.0/0 (every internet address) to an internet gateway, the VPC's door to the internet, that subnet is public.

A NAT gateway (network address translation) sits in a public subnet. It lets instances in private subnets start outbound connections, such as downloading patches, and it refuses connections that begin outside.

A security group is a firewall attached to an instance's network interface. It has allow rules only. It is stateful, meaning replies to an allowed request come back in automatically.

A network ACL (access control list) is a firewall at the subnet boundary. It has numbered allow and deny rules, checked lowest number first. It is stateless, so return traffic must be allowed explicitly.

The layering works because each part does a different job. Routes decide whether a path exists at all. NACLs give a coarse filter for a whole subnet and are the only one of these that can deny a specific address. Security groups give fine control for each instance.

Worked example: a private app server fetches an update over HTTPS. First, its subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway. Second, its security group allows outbound port 443, and the reply returns automatically. Third, its NACL allows outbound 443 and inbound ephemeral ports 1024-65535. Ephemeral ports are the temporary high ports the server picked for the reply. Fourth, the NAT gateway's subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway.

The common mistake is to treat a NACL like a security group and open only port 443 inbound. Replies then arrive on ephemeral ports and are silently dropped. The running system shows timeouts with no clear error. Placing the NAT gateway in a private subnet also fails, because the gateway itself has no route out.

questions.prompt: A small veterinary clinic runs its booking website on one instance in a public subnet. Visitors on the internet connect to it on port 80 (plain HTTP). The clinic's engineer traces what must be true for a visitor's page request to succeed. Step 1: the subnet's route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway, so a path to and from the internet exists. Step 2: the instance's security group allows inbound port 80; because a security group is stateful, the web page sent back to the visitor is allowed out automatically. Step 3: the subnet's network ACL allows inbound port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. Step 4: ??? Which completes Step 4?
choices: The security group gets an extra outbound rule for ports 1024-65535 so that the replies can leave
The route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway so the replies have a way out to the internet
The network ACL allows outbound port 80, so the reply leaves on the same port the request used
The network ACL allows outbound traffic to the temporary high ports 1024-65535 chosen by the visitor's computer
questions.why: A network ACL is stateless, so the reply, which travels to the visitor's ephemeral port rather than to port 80, must be allowed out explicitly by its own rule.

questions.prompt: A delivery-tracking company runs a fleet of instances across one subnet. Its logs show repeated attack traffic from a single internet address, 198.51.100.23, and the team wants to block that one address for the whole subnet while leaving all other traffic as it is. Which component can do this?
choices: The subnet's route table, by removing the route to the internet gateway
The security groups on each instance, by adding a deny rule for that address
The subnet's network ACL, by adding a numbered deny rule for that address
A NAT gateway, because it refuses connections that start outside the VPC
questions.why: Of these components, only a network ACL supports deny rules, so it is the one that can block a specific address at the subnet boundary; security groups have allow rules only, and removing the route would cut off everyone.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop puts its NAT gateway in a private subnet, next to its order-processing instances. Those private subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway, but the instances still cannot download software patches. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The NAT gateway's own subnet has no route to the internet gateway, so the gateway itself has no way out
The NAT gateway is refusing the patch downloads because they count as connections that begin outside
The instances' security groups are stateful, so they block the patch data coming back in
A NAT gateway can only serve instances that sit in a different Availability Zone from it
questions.why: A NAT gateway only works when its subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway, which makes that subnet public; placed in a private subnet, it has no path out to forward traffic on.

questions.prompt: A university research lab's subnet has a network ACL with these inbound rules: rule 50 denies all traffic from 203.0.113.40; rule 100 allows port 22 (remote login) from 0.0.0.0/0. A researcher at 203.0.113.40 tries to log in on port 22. What happens?
choices: The login is denied, because rule 50 matches first and rules are checked lowest number first
The login is denied only if the instance's security group also has a rule denying that address
The login is allowed, because network ACLs ignore deny rules when an allow rule also matches
The login is allowed, because the allow rule for port 22 is more specific than the deny
questions.why: Network ACL rules are checked in order from the lowest number, so rule 50's deny matches the address before rule 100 is ever reached.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how security groups, network ACLs, route tables and a NAT gateway work together to let a private server download updates. Include one limit or tradeoff, for example what a security group cannot do or what statelessness costs you.
lessons.modelAnswer: Route tables decide whether a path exists. Our private subnet sends internet-bound traffic to a NAT gateway. The NAT gateway lives in a public subnet whose route goes to the internet gateway. That lets the server start outbound connections, but nobody outside can start one in. Then two firewalls filter. The security group sits on the instance, allows only what we list, and is stateful, so the reply to our HTTPS request comes back automatically. The network ACL sits on the subnet edge and is stateless. It needs outbound 443 and inbound ephemeral ports 1024-65535, or replies get silently dropped and we see timeouts. The tradeoff: security groups are easy and precise but can only allow, never deny. To block one hostile IP we need a NACL deny rule. NACLs cost more care because we have to manage return traffic ourselves.
rubricPoints: Route tables decide where traffic goes, and a public subnet routes to an internet gateway.
A NAT gateway sits in a public subnet and allows outbound-only internet access for private instances.
Security groups are instance-level, stateful, and allow-only.
Network ACLs are subnet-level, stateless, have ordered allow and deny rules, and need return ephemeral ports opened.
Names a limit, such as security groups being unable to deny, or the silent timeouts caused by missing NACL return rules.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet hop by hop through routes, NACLs, security groups and a NAT gateway is exactly what a virtual network path tracer would let the learner practise.

lessons.plain: A virtual private cloud (VPC) is your own fenced-off network inside AWS. You divide it into smaller sections called subnets. A public subnet has a direct road to the internet, so things placed there can be reached from outside if you allow it. A private subnet has no such road, so nobody on the internet can start a conversation with anything inside it. Picture an office building: the reception desk faces the street, while the records room sits deep inside with no outside door. Only what must face the public goes at reception; everything else stays inside.
lessons.guessPrompt: You are building a website with web servers and a customer database. If you could put each one either in a part of the network that faces the internet or in a part that does not, where would you put the database, and why?
lessons.teach:
Network segmentation means splitting a network into zones so each resource is only as reachable as it needs to be. In AWS the zone is the subnet: a block of IP addresses carved out of a VPC (virtual private cloud, your isolated network in AWS) and placed in one Availability Zone (one data-centre location).

A subnet is public or private because of its route table, not its name. A route table is the list of rules saying where traffic goes next. If it sends traffic for 0.0.0.0/0 (meaning any address) to an internet gateway, the VPC's managed doorway to the internet, the subnet is public. With no such route it is private: the internet cannot open a connection to anything there, even if a firewall rule is wrong, because no path exists.

Private resources often still need to reach out, for example to download patches. A NAT gateway (network address translation), placed in a public subnet, lets them start outbound connections while refusing connections started from outside.

Worked example, a three-tier web app. Step 1: the load balancer, which receives user requests, goes in public subnets because users must reach it. Step 2: application servers go in private subnets; the load balancer forwards requests to them over internal routes. Step 3: the database goes in separate private subnets reachable only from the app tier. Step 4: the app subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway so servers can fetch updates. Trace an attacker: they can reach the load balancer, but there is no route from the internet to the app servers or database.

Common mistake: putting the database in a public subnet and trusting a password or one firewall rule. A single misconfiguration then exposes it to internet scanning, brute-force attempts and data theft. Segmentation adds defence in depth, meaning layers so one failure is not a breach. Its limit is that a subnet controls whether a path exists, not who is allowed to use it, so firewall rules and identity controls are still needed inside each zone.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs a nightly reporting worker. It reads from a cache server and then uploads finished reports to a partner's web service on the internet. Nobody on the internet should ever be able to open a connection to the worker. Step 1: put the worker in a private subnet whose route table has no 0.0.0.0/0 route to an internet gateway. Step 2: put the cache server in a separate private subnet that is reachable only from the worker's subnet. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: trace it. The worker starts an upload and it succeeds. The partner's service, or anyone else, tries to start a connection to the worker and fails, because nothing routes inbound traffic to it. Which choice is Step 3?
choices: Rename the worker subnet to "outbound-only" and add a firewall rule that allows outbound connections to the partner.
Change the worker subnet's route table so 0.0.0.0/0 points to the internet gateway, letting the worker reach the partner directly.
Create a NAT gateway inside the worker's private subnet and add a firewall rule that allows only outbound traffic.
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet and route the worker subnet's 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to that NAT gateway.
questions.why: A NAT gateway placed in a public subnet lets private resources start outbound connections while refusing connections started from outside, so the worker can upload reports but cannot be reached from the internet.

questions.prompt: A team creates a subnet named "private-db". Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 traffic to the VPC's internet gateway. Is this subnet public or private, and why?
choices: Public, because its route table sends traffic for any address to an internet gateway, whatever the subnet is called.
Public only if a NAT gateway is also attached to it; otherwise it stays private.
Private, as long as no firewall rule allows inbound traffic from the internet.
Private, because the name marks it as private and AWS treats it that way.
questions.why: A subnet's route table makes it public or private, not its name: a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an internet gateway makes it public.

questions.prompt: An insurance company keeps its claims-processing servers and its document-scanning servers in the same private subnet, with no route from the internet. An attacker takes over one scanning server through a malicious uploaded file. What does the private subnet do about the attacker then reaching a claims server?
choices: It blocks them, because a NAT gateway refuses connections between servers in the same subnet.
It blocks them only if the subnet is placed in a different Availability Zone from the claims servers.
Nothing; a subnet only controls whether a path exists, so firewall rules and identity controls are needed inside the zone.
It blocks them, because resources in a private subnet cannot reach each other.
questions.why: Segmentation controls whether a path exists, not who may use it, so traffic inside a zone still needs firewall and identity controls.

questions.prompt: A small online bookshop puts its customer database in a public subnet and protects it with a strong password and one firewall rule. During testing, an engineer changes that rule to allow connections from any address. What is the most likely result, and what change would have prevented it?
choices: Nothing bad happens, because the strong password alone keeps the database safe from the internet.
The database is exposed, and the fix is a NAT gateway in front of it so that internet users can reach it safely.
The database is exposed to internet scanning and brute-force attempts. In a private subnet there would have been no route from the internet, so the mistaken rule would not have exposed it.
The database stays hidden, because a database in a public subnet can only be reached by the load balancer.
questions.why: With the database in a public subnet, a single firewall misconfiguration exposes it to the internet, while a private subnet adds defence in depth because no internet path exists.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate wants to put every server in one public subnet because it is simpler. Explain to them, in your own words, what actually makes a subnet public or private, where you would place a web tier, app tier and database, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on subnets for security.
lessons.modelAnswer: A subnet is public only because its route table sends internet-bound traffic to an internet gateway; a private subnet has no such route, so nothing on the internet can start a connection to it. The label means nothing, the route does. I'd put only the internet-facing load balancer in public subnets, the app servers in private subnets behind it, and the database in its own private subnets reachable only from the app tier. If the private servers need patches, a NAT gateway in a public subnet lets them reach out without letting anyone reach in. That way one bad firewall rule doesn't expose the database, because there's no path anyway. The tradeoff is extra pieces to run and pay for, like the NAT gateway, and subnets only control reachability, not permission, so we still need security groups and IAM.
rubricPoints: A subnet is public when its route table points 0.0.0.0/0 at an internet gateway, and private when it does not.
Only internet-facing components such as a load balancer belong in public subnets.
Application servers and databases belong in private subnets, with the database reachable only from the app tier.
A NAT gateway allows outbound-only internet access for private resources.
Segmentation is defence in depth: a single misconfigured rule does not expose a resource that has no route.
Subnets control reachability, not authorization, so firewall and identity controls are still required.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet's path through route tables, internet gateways and NAT gateways is the most direct way to see why a resource in a private subnet cannot be reached from the internet.

lessons.plain: Every networked computer listens on numbered doors called ports, and traffic arrives speaking a protocol, an agreed set of rules such as TCP or UDP. Controlling ports, protocols, and traffic means deciding exactly which doors are open, which language may be spoken through them, and who is allowed to knock. Think of an office building: the lobby is open to the public, the server room only lets in badge holders from IT, and every other door stays locked. In AWS you write these rules as small firewalls attached to your resources, so that only the traffic your application genuinely needs can reach it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web app has a public website and a private database behind it. Which outside visitors should be able to reach the database directly, and why?
lessons.teach:
Controlling traffic means writing allow rules that name a protocol, a port or port range, and a source or destination, and opening nothing else. A port is a number that identifies one service on a machine, for example 443 for HTTPS (encrypted web traffic), 22 for SSH (remote admin login), and 3306 for MySQL. A protocol is the transport rule set, usually TCP (connection-based, reliable) or UDP (connectionless, fast). A CIDR block is an address range written like 10.0.0.0/16; 0.0.0.0/0 means every IPv4 address on the internet.

In AWS the main tool is the security group, a stateful virtual firewall attached to a resource such as an EC2 instance, load balancer, or database. Stateful means that if a request is allowed in, its reply is automatically allowed out. Security groups only allow; anything not listed is denied. A rule's source can be another security group instead of an IP range, which means any resource wearing that group, even as servers come and go.

Worked example, a three-tier app. The load balancer group allows TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. The app group allows TCP 8080 only from the load balancer group. The database group allows TCP 3306 only from the app group. Trace a user: they hit 443 on the load balancer, which matches the first rule. The load balancer forwards to 8080 on an app server, which matches because the sender wears the load balancer group. The app queries 3306 on the database, allowed because the sender wears the app group. An attacker trying 3306 directly from the internet matches no rule and is dropped.

Common mistake: opening SSH port 22, or all ports, to 0.0.0.0/0 for convenience. In a running system that invites constant password-guessing and, if a database port is exposed, direct data theft. Prefer the narrowest port, the narrowest source, and admin access through a managed tool instead of an open SSH port.

questions.prompt: A recipe website runs a load balancer, a fleet of web servers, and an in-memory cache server that listens on TCP port 6379. Web servers are added and removed all day as traffic changes. The team wants the cache reachable only by the web servers. Their security group plan so far: Step 1, the load balancer group allows TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0, so visitors can reach the site over HTTPS. Step 2, the web server group allows TCP 80 only from the load balancer group, so only the load balancer can forward requests to the web servers. Step 3 is missing: what rule should the cache group have? Check your answer: a web server queries the cache on port 6379 and must match the rule, while an attacker on the internet trying port 6379 directly must match nothing and be dropped.
choices: Allow TCP 6379 only from the web server group
Allow TCP 6379 only from the load balancer group, since it is the entry point
Allow all ports from the web server group, so future features also work
Allow TCP 6379 from 0.0.0.0/0, because the cache is only reached by the website anyway
questions.why: Only the web servers talk to the cache, so the narrowest rule is the cache's one port with the web server group as the source, and this keeps working as servers come and go.

questions.prompt: A reporting server's security group has one inbound rule: allow TCP 5432 (the port for a PostgreSQL database) from the analytics group. An analytics server sends a query to port 5432 and the request is allowed in. The group has no rule mentioning the reply. What happens to the database's reply?
choices: It is allowed back out automatically, because security groups are stateful
It is dropped, because every reply needs its own matching outbound rule
It is dropped unless a deny rule for other traffic is also added
It is allowed only if it is sent over UDP instead of TCP
questions.why: Stateful means that once a request is allowed in, its reply is automatically allowed out, with no separate rule needed.
