questions.prompt: A logistics company's operations staff manage 40 EC2 instances (virtual servers). For convenience, the instances' security group allows TCP 22 (SSH, remote admin login) from 0.0.0.0/0. The logs now show thousands of failed login attempts every day from unknown addresses. Which change best fixes the problem?
choices: Replace the SSH rule with one that allows all ports from 0.0.0.0/0
Keep the rule, but move SSH to UDP so the login attempts cannot connect
Remove the open SSH rule and give admins access through a managed tool
Add a second rule allowing TCP 22 from the company's office range
questions.why: Opening port 22 to every internet address invites constant password-guessing, so the fix is to close it and use a managed admin tool, not to add or widen rules.

questions.prompt: An engineer notices that one specific IP address, 198.51.100.25, keeps probing a web server whose security group allows TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0. The engineer wants to add a security group rule that says "deny 198.51.100.25". What is the problem with this plan?
choices: Deny rules only work for UDP, and HTTPS uses TCP on port 443
The deny rule would also block the reply traffic for every other visitor
Deny rules must use a security group as the source, not an IP address
Security groups only contain allow rules, so a deny rule cannot be written
questions.why: Security groups only allow traffic, and anything not listed is denied, so there is no way to write a rule that denies one address.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would lock down traffic for a web tier and a database tier in AWS, and name one tradeoff or limit of relying on security groups alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I treat every resource as closed by default and only open the exact protocol, port, and source it needs. The public load balancer gets TCP 443 from anywhere, because customers must reach it. The app servers accept their app port only from the load balancer's security group, and the database accepts its port only from the app servers' security group. Referencing groups instead of IP addresses keeps the rules correct as instances scale up and down. Because security groups are stateful, replies flow back without extra rules. I never open SSH or database ports to 0.0.0.0/0. The limit is that security groups can only allow, not explicitly deny, so if I need to block a specific bad address range for a whole subnet I need another layer such as a network ACL, and port rules do nothing against attacks hidden inside allowed traffic like injection over HTTPS.
rubricPoints: Defines a rule as protocol plus port plus source or destination, with everything else denied.
Applies least privilege: only needed ports, narrowest sources, no admin or database ports open to the internet.
Uses security-group-to-security-group references to chain tiers.
Notes security groups are stateful so return traffic is automatic.
Names a limit, such as no explicit deny or no protection against attacks inside allowed traffic.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet through rules and seeing exactly which one allows or drops it is the core skill, and the planned virtual network path tracer would make the learner do that.

lessons.plain: Any application open to the internet faces two kinds of outside attack. One is a flood: attackers send so much traffic that real users cannot get through, called a distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack. The other is a trick: a single cleverly written request that makes your application run commands it should not, such as injecting database instructions into a login form. AWS Shield is a managed flood defence, and AWS WAF is a web application firewall that reads each web request and blocks the malicious ones. Think of Shield as crowd control at the stadium gates and WAF as the guard who checks each ticket for forgery.
lessons.guessPrompt: A firewall rule that only allows traffic on port 443 (HTTPS) is in place. Do you think it would stop an attacker who types a database command into your website's search box? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A DDoS attack overwhelms a target with traffic from many machines at once. Floods aimed at the network and transport layers (layers 3 and 4, raw packets and connections) differ from floods at the application layer (layer 7, real-looking web requests such as thousands of page loads). An injection attack hides instructions inside input: SQL injection slips database commands into a form field, and cross-site scripting (XSS) slips browser script into a page.

AWS Shield Standard is free, automatic protection for every AWS customer against common layer 3 and 4 floods. Shield Advanced is a paid tier adding stronger detection, access to an AWS response team during attacks, cost protection against scaling bills caused by an attack, and help with layer 7 floods.

AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests. You build a web ACL (access control list): an ordered set of rules, each of which allows, blocks, or counts matching requests. Managed rule groups are prebuilt rule sets, for example ones detecting SQL injection patterns. A rate-based rule blocks any client IP that exceeds a request limit in a time window. WAF attaches to request-facing services such as a CloudFront content delivery network, an Application Load Balancer, or API Gateway, not directly to a server.

Worked example: a shop behind an Application Load Balancer has its login form attacked with SQL injection, and its product page hammered by one botnet. Step one, attach a web ACL to the load balancer. Step two, add a managed SQL injection rule group, which blocks the poisoned login requests. Step three, add a rate-based rule, which throttles the page hammering. Step four, Shield Standard already absorbs packet floods.

Common mistake: expecting security groups or network ACLs to stop injection. They filter by address and port; an injection request arrives on the allowed port 443 looking legitimate. Without WAF, it reaches the database, and data can be read or deleted. This fix belongs in the network edge layer, before the application.

questions.prompt: A ticket-selling company runs its site through a CloudFront content delivery network (a global network of caching servers that sits in front of the site). For a big concert sale, it plans its defences like this. Step one: rely on Shield Standard, which is already free and automatic, to absorb common layer 3 and 4 floods (raw packet and connection floods). Step two: attach a web ACL (an ordered list of WAF rules) to the CloudFront distribution, with a rate-based rule that blocks any IP sending more than 3,000 requests in five minutes. Step three: missing. The company also wants an AWS response team available during an attack, stronger help against large layer 7 floods (floods of real-looking web requests), and protection against the surprise scaling bill an attack could cause. What is step three?
choices: Subscribe to Shield Advanced, the paid tier of Shield
Tighten the security groups so only port 443 is allowed in from the internet
Add a managed rule group that detects SQL injection patterns to the web ACL
Attach a second web ACL directly to each web server behind CloudFront
questions.why: Only Shield Advanced, the paid tier, adds access to an AWS response team, extra help with layer 7 floods, and cost protection against attack-driven scaling bills.

questions.prompt: A hotel-booking API is served through API Gateway, a managed front door for APIs. Logs show one IP address sending about 8,000 requests a minute to the search endpoint, slowing it for everyone else. The requests are well-formed and contain no hidden commands. Which control fits best?
choices: A managed SQL injection rule group, because a high request volume always means injection
Shield Standard alone, because it is designed to stop floods of real-looking web requests
A network ACL rule that closes port 443 for the whole API
A WAF rate-based rule on a web ACL attached to API Gateway, which blocks any IP that goes over a set request limit in a time window
questions.why: A rate-based rule blocks a single client IP that exceeds a request limit, which matches one IP sending a flood of otherwise normal requests, and WAF can attach to API Gateway.

questions.prompt: A charity's website has a public review form. The team's only protection is a network ACL (a subnet-level filter on addresses and ports) that allows inbound traffic just on port 443. An attacker submits a review containing browser script, a cross-site scripting (XSS) attack. What happens?
choices: The network ACL spots the script in the review text and drops the request
The request arrives on the allowed port 443, looks legitimate, and passes through, so the script can reach the page
The request is blocked because XSS traffic can only arrive on a port other than 443
Shield Standard automatically removes the script, because it inspects every web request
questions.why: Network ACLs and security groups filter only by address and port, so an injection request on an allowed port passes; inspecting request content needs WAF.

questions.prompt: A small team wants AWS WAF to protect a web application that currently runs on a single virtual server (an EC2 instance) that faces the internet directly. Which plan matches how WAF works?
choices: Add a security group rule that blocks SQL injection on port 443
Attach the web ACL directly to the EC2 instance, since WAF can protect any server
Put a request-facing service such as an Application Load Balancer or CloudFront in front of the server, and attach the web ACL to that service
Replace WAF with Shield Standard, which inspects HTTP requests for injection
questions.why: WAF attaches to request-facing services such as CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, or API Gateway, not directly to a server.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use AWS WAF versus AWS Shield Standard versus Shield Advanced, and name one thing each cannot do on its own.
lessons.modelAnswer: Shield and WAF cover different attacks. Shield Standard is free and always on, and soaks up common network and transport floods like packet or connection floods, but it does not read web requests, so it won't catch a SQL injection or a slow flood of realistic HTTP requests. WAF is a web application firewall: we attach a web ACL to CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer, or API Gateway, and its rules inspect each request, using managed rule groups for injection and cross-site scripting and rate-based rules to throttle noisy IPs. It can't attach straight to a server and rules need tuning to avoid blocking real users. Shield Advanced costs money, but adds an attack response team, cost protection, and better layer 7 help. Security groups don't replace any of these, since injection arrives on allowed ports.
rubricPoints: Shield Standard is free, automatic protection against network and transport layer floods.
WAF inspects HTTP requests using web ACL rules to block injection and cross-site scripting.
Rate-based rules in WAF help against application layer floods.
Shield Advanced is paid and adds response team support, cost protection, and stronger layer 7 defence.
WAF attaches to CloudFront, Application Load Balancers, or API Gateway, not directly to servers.
Security groups and network ACLs cannot stop injection because it arrives on allowed ports.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or planned engine exercises web request filtering, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that separate floods from injection teaches the choice best.

lessons.plain: Every application needs settings, such as which database to talk to, and secrets, such as the password for that database. Writing these directly into the code is like taping your house key to the front door: anyone who sees the code gets in. AWS offers two managed stores instead. Systems Manager Parameter Store is a general shelf for settings, and it can also hold encrypted values. Secrets Manager is a safe built specifically for credentials, and it can change them on a schedule automatically. Your application asks the store for the value when it runs, so the secret never lives in the code.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app needs two things: a feature-flag setting that is not sensitive, and a database password that a policy says must change every 30 days without anyone typing it in. Would you keep both in the same kind of store, and what goes wrong if the password is simply written into the source code?
lessons.teach:
A secret is any value that grants access, such as a password, an API key, or a token. Configuration is a non-secret setting, such as a URL or a timeout. Both should live outside the code in a managed store, and the application reads them at runtime. Access to the store is controlled by IAM (AWS's permission system). The role attached to the server or function decides who may read which value. Encryption is handled by KMS (AWS's managed encryption-key service).

Systems Manager Parameter Store is a hierarchical key-value store with paths like /prod/app/db-url. A parameter can be plain text or a SecureString, which means it is encrypted with a KMS key. The standard tier costs nothing for normal use, so it suits configuration and simple secrets. It has no built-in automatic rotation. Rotation means replacing a credential with a new one on a schedule.

Secrets Manager is a store built for credentials. It charges per secret per month plus a fee per API call. In return, it can rotate secrets automatically, either with a small function it runs on a schedule or natively for supported databases such as Amazon RDS. It can also copy secrets to other Regions.

Here is a worked example. An app on EC2 must use a database password that rotates every 30 days.
Step one: store the password in Secrets Manager and turn on 30-day rotation.
Step two: give the EC2 instance's IAM role permission to read only that secret.
Step three: at startup, or when a login fails, the app fetches the current value.
Step four: on day 30, Secrets Manager sets a new password on the database and updates the stored secret. The app's next fetch gets the new value, and nobody touched it.

A common mistake is putting the password in source code, in a server image, or in a plain-text parameter. The secret then leaks through the repository or backups. Rotating it also means redeploying, so a manual password change becomes an outage. Choosing Parameter Store when the requirement says automatic rotation is also wrong, because you would have to build the rotation yourself. The rule of thumb is Secrets Manager when rotation is required, and Parameter Store for configuration and cheap static secrets.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking startup runs an AWS Lambda function (a small piece of code that AWS runs on demand) that calls a payment partner. The function needs two values. The first is a request timeout of 8 seconds, which is configuration (a non-secret setting). The second is the partner's API key, which is a secret, and the security team requires that it be replaced automatically every 45 days. Here is the design, with one step missing. Step 1: Store the timeout as a plain-text parameter at /prod/booking/timeout in Systems Manager Parameter Store (a hierarchical key-value store), using the free standard tier. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Give the function's IAM role (the identity whose permissions decide what the function may read) permission to read only these two values. Step 4: On day 45 a new API key is put in place, and the function's next fetch returns it without anyone redeploying. Which choice completes Step 2?
choices: Write the API key into the function's source code, encrypted, and push a new version of the code every 45 days.
Store the API key as a SecureString parameter (encrypted with a KMS key) at /prod/booking/api-key and rely on Parameter Store to replace it every 45 days.
Store the API key as a plain-text parameter at /prod/booking/api-key, because the IAM role already limits who can read it.
Store the API key in AWS Secrets Manager (a managed store built for credentials) and turn on automatic rotation every 45 days, using a small rotation function on a schedule.
questions.why: Only Secrets Manager rotates a secret automatically on a schedule, which is what makes Step 4 happen with no human action; Parameter Store has no built-in automatic rotation, even for a SecureString.

questions.prompt: A logistics company baked its database password into the server image used to launch 20 EC2 instances (virtual servers). An administrator later changes the password on the database by hand. What is the most likely result for the running system?
choices: The instances fetch the new password from the image on their next login attempt, so nothing breaks.
Systems Manager Parameter Store automatically detects the change and updates the image.
Only new instances fail, because running instances keep a cached database session forever.
The instances keep using the old password, their logins fail, and the application is down until a new image is built and the servers are redeployed.
questions.why: A password stored inside an image cannot change without a redeploy, so a manual password change turns into an outage, and the secret can also leak through image backups.

questions.prompt: A small nonprofit's web app needs about 150 configuration values, such as service URLs and page-size limits, plus three API keys that never need to be rotated. The main requirement is to keep cost as low as possible while keeping the keys encrypted. Which design fits best?
choices: Store the configuration in Secrets Manager and the API keys in source code to avoid per-call fees.
Store the configuration as plain-text parameters and the three API keys as SecureString parameters in the Parameter Store standard tier.
Store everything as plain-text parameters in Parameter Store, since none of the values rotate.
Store everything in AWS Secrets Manager, because it is the only store that can encrypt values.
questions.why: Parameter Store's standard tier costs nothing for normal use, and a SecureString encrypts the keys with KMS, which suits configuration and cheap static secrets that need no rotation.

questions.prompt: In Systems Manager Parameter Store, what does it mean when a parameter at /dev/reports/smtp-password is a SecureString?
choices: Its value is automatically copied to other AWS Regions.
Its value is automatically replaced with a new one on a schedule.
Its value is encrypted using a key from KMS (AWS's managed encryption-key service).
Its value can be read by anyone in the account without an IAM permission.
questions.why: A SecureString is a parameter encrypted with a KMS key; rotation and copying to other Regions are Secrets Manager features, and reading is still controlled by IAM.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when you would put a value in Systems Manager Parameter Store versus Secrets Manager. Name at least one tradeoff between them, and say what failure keeping credentials out of the code prevents.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both services keep settings and secrets out of our code. The app reads them at runtime, and an IAM role controls which values it can read. Values can be encrypted with KMS keys. Parameter Store is a general key-value store with folder-like paths. Its standard tier is free, so I use it for configuration like URLs and flags, and SecureString parameters work for secrets that rarely change. Secrets Manager costs money per secret and per API call, but it can rotate credentials automatically, natively for databases like RDS. It can also replicate secrets to other Regions. So the tradeoff is cost versus built-in rotation: if a requirement says passwords must change automatically, I pick Secrets Manager. Keeping credentials out of code prevents them from leaking through the repository or server images. It also means a password change doesn't force a redeploy or cause an outage.
rubricPoints: Both stores keep secrets and configuration out of code, and the app reads values at runtime.
Read access is controlled by IAM roles, and values can be encrypted with KMS.
Parameter Store suits configuration and static secrets, and its standard tier is free.
Secrets Manager adds built-in automatic rotation, such as for RDS, at a per-secret cost.
An automatic-rotation requirement points to Secrets Manager.
Hardcoded credentials leak through repositories or images, and rotating them forces redeploys.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner wire a credential into a deployment from a managed store without exposing it, which is the core habit this objective builds.

lessons.plain: Amazon Cognito is a managed service that signs in the people who use your app: your customers, not your engineers. You do not build your own login page, password storage, password reset and second-factor checks. Cognito does that work for you. Think of a hotel front desk. It checks your ID once and hands you a key card. After that, each door checks the card instead of asking for your passport again. A second desk can swap that card for a short-lived pass that opens only certain AWS storage, such as your own folder.
lessons.guessPrompt: A mobile app needs millions of customers to sign in and upload photos to cloud storage. Would you give each customer their own permanent cloud account and password key, or something else? What could go wrong with permanent keys stored on a phone?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Cognito is a managed service for authenticating the end users of an application. Authentication means proving who someone is. Authorization means deciding what they may do. Cognito has two parts that people often confuse.

A user pool is a managed user directory. It handles sign-up, sign-in, password resets and MFA (multi-factor authentication, a second proof such as a one-time code). It can also federate, which means it accepts a login from an outside identity provider such as Google or a corporate SAML directory. After a sign-in succeeds, the user pool issues tokens. These are signed JSON Web Tokens (JWTs, small data blobs that show if anyone tampered with them). The ID token describes the user. The access token states what the app may call. The refresh token gets new short-lived tokens when the old ones expire. Amazon API Gateway and an Application Load Balancer can check these tokens themselves, so your backend never handles passwords.

An identity pool exchanges a token for temporary AWS credentials linked to an IAM role (a set of permissions anyone allowed can borrow). The credentials expire, and the role's policy limits what they can reach.

Worked example: customers of a photo app upload to their own folder in an S3 bucket. Step 1: the user signs in to the user pool with a password and an MFA code. Step 2: the user pool returns ID, access and refresh tokens. Step 3: the app sends the ID token to the identity pool. Step 4: the identity pool returns temporary credentials for an authenticated-user role. That role allows writes only under that user's own folder. Step 5: the app uploads straight to S3. The phone stores nothing long-lived.

Common mistake: creating an IAM user for each customer, or putting one access key inside the app. IAM users are meant for staff and workloads, not millions of customers. Anyone can pull a key out of an installed app. In production, that one leaked key gives every attacker the same access, and rotating it breaks every installed copy. The fix belongs in identity: a user pool for sign-in, and an identity pool for scoped, expiring AWS access.

questions.prompt: A gym chain's mobile app lets its 40,000 members book classes through a booking API published on Amazon API Gateway. The team never wants the booking backend to see a password. Step 1: a member signs in with their Google account, which the Cognito user pool accepts through federation. Step 2: the user pool issues an ID token, an access token and a refresh token. Step 3: the app attaches the access token to each booking request it sends to API Gateway. Step 4: ??? Step 5: when the short-lived tokens expire, the app uses the refresh token to get new ones, so the member does not sign in again. Which choice correctly fills Step 4?
choices: API Gateway forwards the member's Google password to the booking backend so the backend can confirm who the member is.
The backend reads a single access key built into the app and uses it to decide which member is calling.
API Gateway checks the signed token itself and rejects tampered or expired ones before any request reaches the backend.
API Gateway sends the token to an identity pool and creates a permanent IAM user for that member.
questions.why: API Gateway can validate Cognito user pool tokens on its own, so only requests with genuine, unexpired tokens reach the backend, and the backend never handles passwords.

questions.prompt: A field-survey app for a forestry company lets its 3,000 contract surveyors upload readings directly to their own prefix in an S3 bucket. The surveyors already sign in through a Cognito user pool. Which Cognito component turns a surveyor's token into temporary, scoped AWS credentials for that upload?
choices: A separate IAM user created for each surveyor at sign-up
The user pool, which stores the surveyors' passwords and MFA settings
An identity pool, which exchanges the token for expiring credentials tied to an IAM role
The refresh token, which holds a permanent AWS access key for the surveyor
questions.why: An identity pool exchanges a token for temporary AWS credentials linked to an IAM role whose policy limits what they can reach. The user pool only handles sign-in and token issuing.

questions.prompt: A language-learning startup ships a desktop app to 25,000 customers. The app contains one AWS access key that it uses to save each customer's progress files. Someone extracts the key from an installed copy and posts it online. Which statement best describes the result and the right fix?
choices: The fix belongs in the network layer: put the bucket behind a load balancer and keep the shared key.
The key is safe because a signed JSON Web Token protects it, so no change is needed.
Only the customer whose copy was examined is affected, so the team should reset that one customer's password.
Every attacker now has the same access, and rotating the key breaks every installed copy. The fix belongs in identity: a user pool for sign-in plus an identity pool for scoped, expiring credentials.
questions.why: Anyone can pull a key out of an installed app. One shared key gives every attacker identical access, and rotating it breaks every install, so the fix is in identity with user pools and identity pools.

questions.prompt: A ticket-resale app keeps its Cognito-issued tokens short-lived, so they expire after a set time. The product team wants buyers to stay signed in during a long session without typing their password again. Which token makes this possible?
choices: The ID token, because it describes the user
The access token, because it states which APIs the app may call
An MFA one-time code saved on the device
The refresh token
questions.why: The refresh token's job is to get new short-lived tokens when the old ones expire. The ID token describes the user, and the access token states what the app may call.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a Cognito user pool and an identity pool, using an app where customers upload files. Name one limit or tradeoff, such as when you would not need an identity pool at all.
lessons.modelAnswer: A user pool answers the question 'who are you?'. It is a managed directory that handles sign-up, sign-in, MFA and password resets, and it can federate logins from Google or a corporate SAML provider. When sign-in succeeds, it issues signed JWTs: an ID token, an access token, and a refresh token for renewal. An identity pool answers the question 'what AWS resources may you touch?'. It swaps a token for temporary AWS credentials tied to an IAM role, and that role is scoped to the user's own folder, for example. A tradeoff is that if customers only call our own API through API Gateway or a load balancer, we can check user pool tokens there and skip the identity pool. We need the identity pool only when the client calls AWS services like S3 directly. Either way, we never ship permanent keys in the app or create IAM users for customers.
rubricPoints: A user pool authenticates app users and issues signed tokens (ID, access, refresh).
An identity pool exchanges those tokens for temporary, role-scoped AWS credentials.
Authentication (who you are) is distinct from authorization (what you may access).
Embedding long-lived keys in an app or creating IAM users per customer is the security hole Cognito avoids.
An identity pool is only needed when clients call AWS services directly; API Gateway or ALB can validate user pool tokens alone.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests whether you can pick the user pool, the identity pool, or both for a given scenario, so working through exam-style situations builds that judgment best, and no current mission covers end-user sign-in.

lessons.plain: Amazon GuardDuty and Amazon Macie are two AWS services that watch for trouble rather than stop it. GuardDuty is a managed threat-detection service: it reads activity records from your account and network and raises an alert when something looks like an attack, such as a server talking to a known criminal address. Macie is a data-discovery service: it scans your Amazon S3 storage buckets, finds sensitive data such as personal details or passwords, and warns you when that data is exposed. Think of GuardDuty as a security guard watching the doors and Macie as an auditor checking which filing cabinets hold confidential papers and whether they are locked.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company stores customer records in cloud storage and runs servers in the same account. If one tool reports 'a server is contacting a known malicious address' and another reports 'a file full of credit card numbers sits in a publicly readable bucket', which of those two problems is about suspicious behaviour and which is about where sensitive data lives?
lessons.teach:
Amazon GuardDuty is a managed threat-detection service. Managed means AWS runs it; you just switch it on, with no agents or appliances to install. It continuously analyses three main log sources: AWS CloudTrail (the record of every API call made in the account), VPC Flow Logs (records of network connections in your virtual network) and DNS query logs (which domain names your resources look up). It compares this activity against threat intelligence, meaning lists of known bad addresses and domains, and against machine-learning models of normal behaviour. When something stands out, it produces a finding: a structured alert with a type, a severity and the affected resource.

Amazon Macie is a data-security service for Amazon S3, AWS's object storage. It uses pattern matching and machine learning to discover sensitive data such as names, national ID numbers, card numbers and secret keys, and it also flags risky bucket settings such as public access or missing encryption.

Both are detective controls: they tell you something is wrong but do not block it. Preventive controls, such as security groups or bucket policies, do the blocking.

Worked example. An attacker steals an access key and launches a server that mines cryptocurrency. Step one: the server looks up a mining-pool domain, which appears in DNS logs. Step two: GuardDuty matches that domain against threat intelligence. Step three: it raises a high-severity finding naming the instance. Step four: the finding is sent to Amazon EventBridge, an event-routing service, which triggers an AWS Lambda function that moves the instance into an isolating security group. Detection plus automation turns an alert into a response.

A common mistake is choosing GuardDuty to stop an attack or Macie to protect a database. GuardDuty only reports; blocking needs another control. Macie only examines S3, not relational databases. In a running system, enabling these services without routing findings anywhere means alerts pile up unread while the breach continues.

questions.prompt: Northwind Freight, a logistics firm, keeps shipping manifests in an Amazon S3 bucket. Here is how they handle one problem, with one step missing. Step 1: Amazon Macie runs a discovery job over the bucket's 4,000 objects. Step 2: Macie reports that 37 files contain payment card numbers, and it also flags that the bucket allows public access. Step 3: the finding is sent through Amazon EventBridge to the security team's alert channel, so it is not left unread. Step 4: ______. Which action completes Step 4 so that outsiders can no longer read the files?
choices: Turn on Amazon GuardDuty for the bucket so that it deletes the files holding card numbers
Point Macie at the company's relational database so that the card numbers there get scanned too
Change the bucket policy to block public access, which is a preventive control that stops the reads
Wait for Macie to remove public access automatically, now that it has raised a finding about it
questions.why: Macie is a detective control that only reports problems, so a preventive control such as a bucket policy has to do the actual blocking.

questions.prompt: A security lead describes Amazon GuardDuty and Amazon Macie as "detective controls." What does that term mean?
choices: They encrypt data automatically wherever they find it stored without protection
They tell you that something is wrong but do not stop it, so blocking needs a separate control
They block bad traffic before it reaches your resources, in the same way a security group does
They are agents you install on every server to watch what happens on that machine
questions.why: A detective control only reports a problem; preventive controls such as security groups and bucket policies are what block it.

questions.prompt: Harbor Analytics wants an alert whenever one of its servers opens network connections to an IP address that is known to be malicious. They do not want to install or maintain any software for this. Which choice fits best?
choices: Amazon GuardDuty, comparing VPC Flow Logs against threat intelligence lists
Amazon Macie, because it uses machine learning to spot unusual activity
A security group, because it detects connections to bad addresses and reports them
Amazon Macie scanning the servers' disks for sensitive data such as secret keys
questions.why: GuardDuty is a managed service that needs no agents, and it checks VPC Flow Logs (records of network connections) against lists of known bad addresses.

questions.prompt: A retailer switched on both GuardDuty and Macie eight months ago. During an incident review, the team discovers that GuardDuty raised high-severity findings about a compromised server for six weeks while the attack carried on. What was most likely missing from their design?
choices: The findings were never routed anywhere, for example through EventBridge to people or an automated response
GuardDuty's severity levels were set too high, so the service declined to block the attack
Macie should have been pointed at the server, because it is the service that stops attacks
GuardDuty was missing an agent, which has to be installed on each server before its findings count
questions.why: Enabling these services without routing their findings to someone or something lets alerts pile up unread while the breach continues.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what GuardDuty and Macie each look at, what kind of problem each one catches, and the main limit they share, using a scenario where you would pick one over the other.
lessons.modelAnswer: GuardDuty is AWS's managed threat detector. It reads CloudTrail API logs, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs, compares the activity with known-bad addresses and normal-behaviour models, and raises findings like 'this instance is talking to a crypto-mining domain' or 'this key is being used from an unusual country'. Macie looks at S3 only: it finds sensitive data such as personal information or credentials inside objects and flags buckets that are public or unencrypted. So if the worry is a compromised server or stolen key, I pick GuardDuty; if the worry is customer data leaking from storage, I pick Macie. The shared limit is that both are detective, not preventive. They don't block anything, so I still need security groups, bucket policies and encryption, and I should route findings through EventBridge to alerting or automated remediation, otherwise nobody acts on them.
rubricPoints: GuardDuty detects threats by analysing CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs.
Macie discovers sensitive data and risky settings in Amazon S3 buckets.
Both are detective controls that alert but do not block.
Findings should be routed, for example through EventBridge, to alerting or automated response.
Choosing between them depends on whether the concern is malicious activity or exposed sensitive data.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests picking the right detective service for a described symptom, so reasoning through scenario situations that contrast GuardDuty, Macie and preventive controls adds the most.

lessons.plain: When a company has its own office or data centre and also runs systems in AWS, the two sides need a way to talk privately. There are two main options. AWS Site-to-Site VPN builds an encrypted tunnel across the ordinary public internet, like sending a locked box through the regular postal service. AWS Direct Connect is a private physical cable from your building's network into AWS, like having your own private road. The VPN is quick and cheap but shares the internet's unpredictable traffic. The private line is steady and fast but takes weeks to set up. On its own, the private line is not scrambled (encrypted).
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has a private, dedicated cable running from its data centre into AWS. Do you think the data on that cable is automatically encrypted, and why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Both services connect an on-premises network (your own office or data centre) to a VPC, which is your private virtual network inside AWS.

AWS Site-to-Site VPN is a managed encrypted connection over the public internet. It uses IPsec, a standard protocol that encrypts and authenticates network packets. On your side sits a customer gateway, which is your router or firewall. On the AWS side sits a virtual private gateway (attached to one VPC) or a transit gateway (a hub that links many VPCs). Each VPN connection has two tunnels landing on different AWS endpoints, so one can fail without cutting you off. It is ready in minutes and costs little, but throughput is capped per tunnel and latency varies with internet conditions.

AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated private circuit from your network to an AWS Direct Connect location, a data centre where your carrier hands traffic to AWS. Because it skips the public internet, bandwidth is high and latency is consistent. It takes weeks to provision, and a single link is a single point of failure.

Worked example: a bank must copy 40 TB to AWS every night, and its auditor requires encryption in transit. Step 1: large, steady volume points to Direct Connect. Step 2: Direct Connect does not encrypt traffic by default, so the requirement is not yet met. Step 3: add encryption, either by running an IPsec VPN over the Direct Connect link or by enabling MACsec (link-level encryption available on certain dedicated connections). Step 4: for resilience, add a second Direct Connect link at another location, or a Site-to-Site VPN as a cheaper backup path.

The common mistake is treating "private" as "encrypted." A private line keeps traffic off the internet but leaves it readable to anyone who can tap the circuit. In a running system, that gap fails a compliance audit even though everything appears to work. The fix sits in the network layer: choose the path for performance, then layer encryption on top.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs 12 separate VPCs in AWS and must connect its warehouse network to all of them within three days. Traffic is light (order updates and reports), and policy requires the data to be encrypted in transit. Step 1: Direct Connect takes weeks to provision, so the three-day deadline points to AWS Site-to-Site VPN. Step 2: Site-to-Site VPN uses IPsec, which encrypts and authenticates packets, so the encryption requirement is met even though traffic crosses the public internet. Step 3: ??? Step 4: configure the warehouse router (the customer gateway) to use both tunnels of the connection, so a failure at one AWS endpoint does not cut the warehouse off. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Terminate the VPN on a virtual private gateway, because it is the standard AWS-side endpoint and reaches every VPC.
Enable MACsec on the connection, because the VPN tunnels alone do not encrypt the order data.
Terminate the VPN on a transit gateway, the hub that links many VPCs, so one connection reaches all 12.
Place a customer gateway inside each of the 12 VPCs so every VPC gets its own encrypted tunnel.
questions.why: A virtual private gateway attaches to only one VPC, so a transit gateway is the AWS-side hub that lets one VPN connection reach all 12 VPCs.

questions.prompt: A manufacturer sends design files from its factory to AWS over a single Direct Connect link. Everything works and transfers are fast, but a security audit fails because the files cross the circuit unencrypted. What is the right fix, and which layer does it belong in?
choices: Replace Direct Connect with a second Direct Connect link at another location. This is a network-layer fix.
Give fewer people permission to read the files in AWS. This is an identity-layer fix.
Nothing is needed. Direct Connect is private, so the traffic already counts as encrypted. No layer applies.
Run an IPsec VPN over the Direct Connect link, or enable MACsec where supported. This is a network-layer fix.
questions.why: Direct Connect keeps traffic off the internet but does not encrypt it by default, so you add IPsec or MACsec on top of the network path.

questions.prompt: A game studio replicates large amounts of live data between its data centre and AWS all day. Its engineers need high bandwidth and latency that stays consistent from hour to hour. They have several months before launch. Which connection fits best?
choices: A transit gateway alone, because it links many VPCs without any on-premises connection.
AWS Direct Connect, because a dedicated private circuit skips the public internet.
AWS Site-to-Site VPN, because two tunnels double the throughput and steady the latency.
AWS Site-to-Site VPN, because it is ready in minutes and costs little.
questions.why: Direct Connect gives high bandwidth and consistent latency by avoiding the internet, and the months of lead time cover its weeks-long provisioning.

questions.prompt: A research lab connects to AWS through one Direct Connect link. The link is fast and encrypted with MACsec, but if it fails the lab loses all access to AWS. What is the cheapest way to remove this single point of failure?
choices: Add an AWS Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path over the internet.
Run an IPsec VPN inside the same Direct Connect link as a second path.
Turn on a second MACsec key on the same link, so the connection has a spare to fall back on.
Move the existing link to a different Direct Connect location.
questions.why: A Site-to-Site VPN uses a separate path over the public internet and is quick and cheap to set up, so it keeps the lab connected if the single Direct Connect link goes down.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose Site-to-Site VPN versus Direct Connect for linking the data centre to AWS, and name one limit or tradeoff of each, including what happens to encryption.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both link our data centre to our VPC. Site-to-Site VPN builds two IPsec-encrypted tunnels across the public internet between our router, the customer gateway, and a virtual private gateway or transit gateway in AWS. It is fast to set up and cheap, and it is encrypted by default. Its tradeoff is that bandwidth per tunnel is limited and latency changes with internet conditions. Direct Connect is a dedicated private circuit into AWS through a Direct Connect location. It gives high, predictable bandwidth and latency, but it takes weeks to provision, one link is a single point of failure, and it is not encrypted by default. If we need encryption on it, we run a VPN over it or use MACsec where supported. A common pattern is Direct Connect as the main path with a VPN as a backup.
rubricPoints: Site-to-Site VPN uses IPsec tunnels over the public internet and is encrypted by default.
VPN is quick and cheap, but bandwidth is capped and latency is variable.
Direct Connect is a dedicated private link with high, consistent bandwidth that takes weeks to set up.
Direct Connect is not encrypted by default; add IPsec VPN over it or MACsec.
A single Direct Connect link is a single point of failure, so add a second link or a backup VPN.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is reading a scenario's bandwidth, timeline, encryption and resilience requirements and picking VPN, Direct Connect, or both, which is best practised by reasoning through situations.

lessons.plain: Every AWS service, such as file storage or a message queue, is reached at a web address called a service endpoint, and by default that address is on the public internet. A server in a private network with no internet path cannot reach it. A VPC endpoint is a private doorway from your own isolated AWS network straight to the service, so traffic never travels over the public internet. Think of an office with a locked internal mail chute to the bank's vault, instead of sending a courier out onto the street. AWS PrivateLink is the technology behind most of these private doorways.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server sits in a private subnet with no route to the internet, and its code tries to save a file to Amazon S3. What do you think happens, and what would you need to add so it works without opening the server to the internet?
lessons.teach:
A service endpoint is the address of an AWS service in a Region, for example the public web address for S3 in us-east-1. A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your isolated virtual network. A VPC endpoint lets resources in that network reach a service privately, with no internet gateway, NAT gateway (a device that lets private servers make outbound internet calls), or public IP. There are two main kinds.

A gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB. It works by adding a route to chosen route tables. The route points traffic bound for the service's address ranges, held in a managed list called a prefix list, at the endpoint. It is free.

An interface endpoint is powered by AWS PrivateLink. It places an elastic network interface, a virtual network card with a private IP address, in your subnet. With private DNS turned on, the service's normal name resolves to that private IP, so application code does not change. It protects traffic with a security group (a stateful firewall on the interface) and costs an hourly fee plus a data charge. PrivateLink also lets you publish your own service, fronted by a Network Load Balancer, to other VPCs or accounts without connecting whole networks.

Both kinds accept an endpoint policy, a resource-style policy that limits which actions or resources can pass through, for example only one company bucket.

Worked example: a private app with no NAT writes to S3 and reads from SQS, a managed queue. Step 1: calls time out because there is no route out. Step 2: add an S3 gateway endpoint and associate it with the private subnet's route table, and S3 writes succeed. Step 3: add an SQS interface endpoint with private DNS. The queue name now resolves to a private IP. Step 4: allow inbound port 443 from the app's security group, and the reads succeed.

Common mistake: creating the endpoint but not associating the right route table, or leaving its security group closed. The running system keeps timing out, or quietly routes through a NAT gateway and pays its data processing charges.

questions.prompt:
A weather research lab runs data-processing servers in private subnets with no internet gateway and no NAT gateway. The servers must send records to Amazon Kinesis, a managed streaming service, and the team does not want to change any application code. Here is how they fix it, with one step missing.

Step 1: Create an interface endpoint for Kinesis, which places an elastic network interface with a private IP address in each of the two private subnets.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: Attach a security group to the endpoint that allows inbound port 443 from the servers' security group.
Step 4: The servers keep calling Kinesis by its usual service name, and the calls now succeed without leaving the private network.

What is Step 2?
choices: Attach an internet gateway to the VPC so the Kinesis public address becomes reachable
Add a NAT gateway so the servers can reach Kinesis while the endpoint warms up
Add a route to the private route tables that points the Kinesis prefix list at the endpoint
Turn on private DNS for the endpoint so the normal Kinesis name resolves to the interface's private IP
questions.why: An interface endpoint is reached through its private IP, and private DNS makes the service's normal name resolve to that IP, which is why the code works unchanged; route-table prefix-list entries belong to gateway endpoints, not interface endpoints.

questions.prompt: A payroll company lets its private servers reach Amazon S3 through a gateway endpoint. The security team worries that someone could copy payroll files to a personal bucket in another account through that same endpoint. Which control directly limits what can pass through the endpoint?
choices: A security group on the gateway endpoint that blocks port 443
A NAT gateway placed in front of the endpoint to inspect the traffic
Turning on private DNS so the bucket names resolve to private IPs
An endpoint policy that only allows access to the company's own payroll bucket
questions.why: An endpoint policy is a resource-style policy on the endpoint that limits which actions or resources can pass through it, such as only one company bucket; gateway endpoints work through route tables, not security groups.

questions.prompt: An online retailer creates a DynamoDB gateway endpoint so its order servers in a private subnet stop using the NAT gateway. A month later, the order servers still work, but the NAT gateway data processing charges have not dropped at all. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The endpoint's security group is closed, so traffic falls back to the NAT gateway
The endpoint was not associated with the route table used by the order servers' subnet
Private DNS was left off, so DynamoDB names still resolve to public addresses
Gateway endpoints for DynamoDB charge the same hourly fee as a NAT gateway
questions.why: A gateway endpoint only takes effect through a route added to the chosen route tables, so if the servers' route table is not associated, their DynamoDB traffic keeps flowing through the NAT gateway and keeps incurring its charges.

questions.prompt: A fraud-scoring company runs its scoring service in its own VPC behind a Network Load Balancer. Several bank customers, each in their own AWS accounts, need private access to just this one service, and the company does not want to connect its whole network to theirs. What should it use?
choices: Publish the service with AWS PrivateLink so each bank reaches it through an interface endpoint in its own VPC
Create an S3 gateway endpoint in each bank's VPC pointing at the scoring service
Give the scoring servers public IPs and add the banks' addresses to an endpoint policy
Add a route in each bank's route table using a prefix list for the scoring service
questions.why: PrivateLink lets you publish your own service fronted by a Network Load Balancer to other VPCs or accounts, which consumers reach through interface endpoints, without connecting whole networks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a private-subnet workload should use VPC endpoints instead of a NAT gateway to reach AWS services, and say when you would choose a gateway endpoint versus an interface endpoint, including one limit or cost tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Normally AWS services live at public endpoints, so a private server needs a NAT gateway to reach them. That sends traffic toward the internet path, and it costs NAT data charges. A VPC endpoint gives a private path from our VPC to the service instead, so we can drop the internet route entirely. For S3 and DynamoDB I'd use a gateway endpoint. It's just a route-table entry pointing at the service's prefix list, and it's free, but it only covers those two services and only works for route tables we associate. For anything else, like SQS or Secrets Manager, I'd use an interface endpoint built on PrivateLink. It puts a network interface with a private IP in our subnet, and private DNS makes the normal service name resolve to it. Interface endpoints cost per hour per Availability Zone plus data, and they need a security group allowing 443. On either kind I'd add an endpoint policy to restrict what can pass through.
rubricPoints: States that service endpoints are public by default and VPC endpoints give a private path without internet or NAT.
Gateway endpoints cover only S3 and DynamoDB, work through route tables, and are free.
Interface endpoints use PrivateLink to place a private-IP network interface in a subnet, with private DNS and a security group.
Names a tradeoff such as interface endpoint hourly and data cost, or gateway endpoint's limited service list.
Mentions endpoint policies as a way to restrict which actions or resources can pass through.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet from a private subnet through route tables, endpoint interfaces, and security groups is the clearest way to see why a call times out and which endpoint fixes it.

lessons.plain: Encrypting data at rest means scrambling stored data so a stolen disk, snapshot or file is unreadable without a key. AWS Key Management Service (KMS) is a managed key vault: it creates and guards master keys that never leave it, and it decides who may use them. Every key has a key policy, a rulebook attached to the key that lists who can manage it and who can use it to encrypt or decrypt. Think of a bank safe-deposit box: the bank holds the master key, and you get in only if your name is on the box's access card.
lessons.guessPrompt: Suppose someone has permission to download a file from a storage bucket, but the file was encrypted with a key they are not allowed to use. Do you think they can read the file? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
AWS KMS is a managed service that creates and stores encryption keys and performs operations with them. A KMS key is a master key that stays inside KMS. A customer managed key is one you create and control. An AWS managed key is created for you by a service, and you cannot edit its policy.

KMS uses envelope encryption, meaning data is encrypted with a short-lived data key, and that data key is in turn encrypted by the KMS key. It works because bulk data never travels to KMS, and the only thing protecting the data key is a key that cannot leave KMS.

Worked example with Amazon S3 (object storage) using server-side encryption with KMS. On upload, S3 asks KMS for a data key. KMS returns two copies: one plaintext and one encrypted under your KMS key. S3 encrypts the object with the plaintext copy, discards it, and stores the encrypted copy beside the object. On download, S3 sends the encrypted data key to KMS to be decrypted. KMS then checks whether the caller is allowed kms:Decrypt on that key. If not, the download fails, even though the caller has s3:GetObject. That gives you two separate locks: storage permission and key permission.

A key policy is a resource-based policy, meaning a policy attached to the key itself. It is the primary control: identity policies in IAM (Identity and Access Management) count only if the key policy lets them. That permission comes from a statement naming the account itself as the principal. A sound policy separates key administrators, who can change or schedule deletion of the key, from key users, who can only encrypt and decrypt.

A common mistake is editing the key policy so that no one can administer the key, or granting kms:* to everyone. The first can leave the key unmanageable until you get help from AWS Support. The second means anyone who can reach the storage can also unlock the data. Disabling a key, or deleting it after the 7 to 30 day waiting period, makes every object encrypted under it permanently unreadable.

questions.prompt: Harbor Logistics keeps nightly database backup files in object storage. The files are encrypted at rest with server-side encryption using a customer managed KMS key, which is an encryption key the company created and controls inside AWS KMS. A role called ReportingAnalyst has the storage read permission on the backup files. The key policy names only the BackupService role as a key user, meaning a principal allowed to encrypt and decrypt with the key. Trace what happens when ReportingAnalyst tries to read last night's 40 GB backup file. Step 1: The analyst requests the file, and the storage service confirms the analyst has read permission on it. Step 2: The storage service finds the encrypted data key stored beside the file. A data key is the short-lived key that actually encrypted the file. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: The read fails with an access-denied error, even though the analyst has storage read permission. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The storage service asks KMS to send the KMS key itself so the storage service can decrypt the data key locally, and KMS refuses because the file is larger than KMS allows.
The storage service sends the whole 40 GB backup file to KMS for decryption, and KMS rejects the request because the analyst lacks storage read permission.
The storage service sends the encrypted data key to KMS to be decrypted, and KMS checks whether ReportingAnalyst is allowed kms:Decrypt on that key. The analyst is not, so KMS refuses.
The storage service reuses the plaintext data key it kept from the original upload, but finds the copy has expired after 24 hours.
questions.why: With envelope encryption, only the small encrypted data key goes to KMS, and KMS refuses to decrypt it unless the caller has kms:Decrypt on the key, whatever storage permission the caller holds.

questions.prompt: Brightwell Clinic's data is encrypted under an AWS managed key, which is a KMS key a service created on the clinic's behalf. The security team now wants only one role, AuditReader, to be able to decrypt that data, and they plan to do this by changing the key's key policy. What should they do?
choices: Leave the key as is and remove the storage read permission from every other role, because storage permission is the only lock that matters.
Create a customer managed key, write its key policy so that only AuditReader is a key user, and encrypt the data under that key, because an AWS managed key's policy cannot be edited.
Edit the AWS managed key's policy to remove every principal except AuditReader, because a key policy is the primary control.
Delete the AWS managed key, because AWS then lets you set a new policy when the key is recreated after the waiting period.
questions.why: You cannot edit the policy of an AWS managed key, so restricting decryption through a key policy requires a customer managed key, which you create and control.

questions.prompt: At Tessaro Games, an engineer attaches an IAM identity policy to the role BuildRunner that allows kms:Decrypt on a customer managed key. IAM (Identity and Access Management) is AWS's service for defining who can do what. The key policy lists two administrator roles and one other key user. It has no statement naming the Tessaro account itself as the principal. BuildRunner's decrypt calls are still denied. Why?
choices: Identity policies never apply to KMS. Only roles listed by name in the key policy can ever use a key.
The key must be disabled and then re-enabled before a new identity policy takes effect.
BuildRunner also needs kms:* in its identity policy, because kms:Decrypt alone is not enough to decrypt.
The key policy is the primary control, and IAM identity policies count only when the key policy has a statement naming the account itself as the principal. This key policy has no such statement.
questions.why: A key policy is a resource-based policy that decides access first, and IAM identity policies only take effect when the key policy names the account as a principal.

questions.prompt: Orchard Freight stores 2 million shipping invoices in object storage, all encrypted under one customer managed KMS key. To tidy up, an administrator schedules that key for deletion with a 14-day waiting period. Nobody intervenes, and the 14 days pass. What is the result for the running system?
choices: Every invoice encrypted under that key becomes permanently unreadable, because no remaining key can decrypt the stored data keys.
Reads keep working for anyone who still has storage read permission, because only uploads need the KMS key.
The invoices stay readable for another 30 days, and then AWS Support can restore the key on request.
The invoices are automatically re-encrypted under an AWS managed key, so reads continue without interruption.
questions.why: Once a KMS key is deleted after its 7 to 30 day waiting period, the encrypted data keys can never be decrypted again, so every object encrypted under that key is permanently unreadable.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how KMS protects an encrypted S3 object even when someone has read access to the bucket. Name one way a badly written key policy can backfire.
lessons.modelAnswer: KMS keeps a master key that never leaves the service. S3 encrypts each object with a data key, and it stores only an encrypted copy of that data key next to the object. To read the object, S3 must ask KMS to decrypt the data key. KMS checks the key policy, the rulebook attached to the key, to see whether this caller may use kms:Decrypt. So bucket access alone is not enough, because you also need permission on the key. The key policy is the main gate, and IAM policies only apply if the key policy allows the account to delegate to them. I would separate admins, who manage the key, from users, who only encrypt and decrypt. The tradeoff is risk in both directions. If the policy is too loose, the second lock is useless. If it is too tight, you can lock out administrators. A disabled or deleted key also makes the data permanently unreadable.
rubricPoints: The KMS key stays inside KMS, and data is encrypted with a data key that is itself encrypted (envelope encryption).
Reading encrypted data needs permission on the key as well as on the storage.
The key policy is a resource-based policy and the primary control, and IAM policies apply only if it allows them.
Key administrators should be kept separate from key users.
An overly broad policy defeats the control, and a lockout or deleted key makes data unrecoverable.

suggested.rationale: Tracing data keys being wrapped and unwrapped, and watching a decrypt fail under a restrictive key policy, builds this understanding better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Data in transit is information moving across a network, such as a customer's password travelling from a browser to your website. Encrypting it in transit means scrambling it while it moves, so anyone listening on the wire sees only noise. TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the standard way to do this, and it relies on a certificate: a digital ID card proving your site really is who it claims to be. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) is a managed service that issues these ID cards, attaches them to AWS front doors such as load balancers, and renews them for you. It works like a passport office that also replaces your passport before it expires.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your website runs behind a load balancer that accepts plain HTTP. Customers type credit card numbers into it. If you add a TLS certificate only at the load balancer, which part of the journey is now protected, and which part might still travel unencrypted?
lessons.teach:
TLS (Transport Layer Security) is a protocol, meaning an agreed set of rules, that encrypts traffic between two parties and lets the client verify the server's identity. Verification uses a certificate: a file binding a domain name (like shop.example.com) to a public key, signed by a certificate authority (CA), an organisation that browsers already trust. HTTPS is simply HTTP carried inside TLS.

AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) is a managed certificate service. It issues public certificates at no charge, proves you own the domain through domain validation (usually by having you add a DNS record), and renews those certificates automatically while the validation record stays in place. ACM certificates attach to integrated services: Elastic Load Balancing (a managed load balancer that spreads traffic across servers), Amazon CloudFront (a content delivery network that caches content near users), and Amazon API Gateway (a managed front door for APIs). You cannot export an ACM public certificate to install yourself on a server; for that you would import your own certificate or use AWS Private CA, a managed private certificate authority for internal names.

Worked example. A shop wants HTTPS. Step one: request a certificate in ACM for shop.example.com. Step two: add the DNS validation record ACM gives you; ACM confirms ownership and issues the certificate. Step three: add an HTTPS listener on port 443 to the Application Load Balancer and select the certificate. Step four: a browser connects, receives the certificate, checks the CA signature, and agrees encryption keys. The load balancer now performs TLS termination, meaning it decrypts traffic there. Step five: if the requirement says encrypted end to end, the load balancer must re-encrypt to the servers using a certificate those servers hold.

Common mistake: requesting the certificate in the wrong Region. ACM certificates are regional and must sit in the same Region as the load balancer, while CloudFront only accepts certificates from us-east-1 (North Virginia). In a running system, the wrong choice means the certificate never appears in the list, and the site stays on unencrypted HTTP.

questions.prompt: A city museum serves its ticket site, tickets.citymuseum.org, through Amazon CloudFront, a content delivery network that caches pages near visitors. It wants HTTPS (web traffic carried inside TLS) using a free AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificate. Step 1: request a public certificate in ACM in us-east-1 (North Virginia) for tickets.citymuseum.org, because CloudFront only accepts certificates from that Region. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: ACM confirms the museum owns the domain and issues the certificate. Step 4: select the certificate on the CloudFront distribution, and a visitor's browser can now check the certificate authority's signature and agree encryption keys. Step 5: a year later, ACM renews the certificate with no manual work. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Ask a certificate authority by email to sign the museum's public key for CloudFront
Add the DNS validation record that ACM supplies for the domain and leave it in place
Request a second copy of the certificate in the Region where the museum's servers run
Export the issued certificate from ACM and copy it onto the museum's own web servers
questions.why: ACM proves domain ownership through a DNS validation record, and keeping that record in place is also what lets ACM renew the certificate automatically in Step 5.

questions.prompt: A travel booking company puts an Application Load Balancer (a managed load balancer that spreads traffic across servers) in front of 6 application servers. The load balancer has an HTTPS listener on port 443 with an ACM certificate, and it forwards traffic to the servers over plain HTTP. A new compliance rule says customer data must be encrypted end to end. What is missing?
choices: A second ACM certificate on the same listener so that browsers encrypt the traffic twice
Moving the certificate to us-east-1 so that the encryption covers every Region
The load balancer re-encrypting traffic to the servers, using certificates the servers hold
Nothing; TLS termination at the load balancer already means the traffic is end-to-end encrypted
questions.why: TLS termination means the load balancer decrypts traffic there, so for end-to-end encryption it must encrypt again on the hop to servers that hold their own certificates.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a logistics firm requests an ACM certificate for track.haulfast.com in us-east-1. The firm's Application Load Balancer runs in eu-central-1 (Frankfurt). When the engineer adds an HTTPS listener on that load balancer, the certificate is not in the list. Why?
choices: ACM certificates are regional, so it must be requested in the load balancer's Region
ACM certificates only work with CloudFront, never with load balancers
The certificate is still waiting for the browser to check the CA signature
Load balancers need an exported certificate file instead of an ACM certificate
questions.why: An ACM certificate must sit in the same Region as the load balancer that uses it; only CloudFront requires us-east-1.

questions.prompt: A small bakery chain issued an ACM public certificate for order.bakeright.com 10 months ago and attached it to its API Gateway (a managed front door for APIs). During a DNS cleanup last month, someone deleted the validation record that ACM had asked them to add. What risk does this create?
choices: ACM can no longer renew the certificate automatically, so it may expire and HTTPS will break
Nothing; ACM certificates renew automatically whether or not the record exists
API Gateway switches to AWS Private CA certificates and keeps serving traffic
The certificate is immediately exported to the public and must be revoked
questions.why: ACM renews certificates automatically only while the domain validation record stays in place, so deleting it puts renewal, and the site's HTTPS, at risk.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how ACM gets our public website onto HTTPS, and name one limit or tradeoff they need to plan around.
lessons.modelAnswer: ACM is AWS's managed certificate service. We request a certificate for our domain, prove we own it by adding a DNS record, and ACM issues it free and renews it automatically as long as that record stays. We then attach it to an integrated front door, like our Application Load Balancer's port 443 listener or a CloudFront distribution, and browsers get a trusted certificate so traffic is encrypted with TLS. The tradeoffs: the load balancer terminates TLS, so traffic from it to our servers is plain unless we re-encrypt with a certificate on the servers, and if a requirement says end-to-end encryption we must do that. ACM public certificates cannot be exported onto an EC2 instance. Certificates are regional too, so they must match the load balancer's Region, and CloudFront needs one in us-east-1.
rubricPoints: TLS encrypts data in transit and the certificate proves the server's identity.
ACM issues free public certificates, validates domain ownership, and auto-renews them.
Certificates attach to integrated services such as load balancers, CloudFront, and API Gateway, not exported to servers.
TLS terminates at the load balancer, so end-to-end encryption needs re-encryption to the backends.
ACM certificates are regional, and CloudFront requires one in us-east-1.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises TLS certificates, and the exam tests this by scenarios about termination points, Regions, and exportability that are best learned by reasoning through situations.

lessons.plain: Encryption keys and certificates both wear out over time, a bit like the locks and ID badges in an office. Rotating a key means swapping in fresh secret material on a schedule, so a key that leaked quietly long ago stops being useful for new data. Renewing a certificate means getting a fresh copy of the digital ID card that proves a website is genuine, before the old one passes its printed expiry date. If a certificate expires, browsers and apps refuse to connect, so the site looks broken even though nothing else changed. The skill is knowing which of these happen automatically and which need a person or an alarm.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company switches to a new encryption key every year, what do you think must happen so that files encrypted with last year's key can still be opened?
lessons.teach:
Key rotation is replacing the secret material inside an encryption key on a schedule. Certificate renewal is replacing a TLS certificate, the signed digital ID that lets clients trust an encrypted connection, before its expiry date.

In AWS Key Management Service (KMS), a managed key-storage service, a customer managed key is one you create and control. For symmetric customer managed keys you can turn on automatic rotation, which defaults to yearly and can be set to a different period. AWS managed keys, created by services on your behalf, rotate automatically. Rotation keeps the same key ID, name and policy, and KMS keeps every older version of the key material. That is why it works: new encryptions use the newest material, while old data still decrypts with the version that encrypted it. Rotation does not re-encrypt existing data.

Keys whose material you imported yourself, and asymmetric keys, cannot rotate automatically. You rotate them manually: create a new key and repoint an alias, a friendly name your application uses, to the new key.

AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), a managed certificate service, renews public certificates it issued automatically, if the certificate is in use and its domain can still be proved. DNS validation, a record you leave in your domain's DNS, lets ACM prove ownership with no human step. Email validation needs someone to respond. Certificates you imported into ACM are never renewed for you; ACM only sends expiry warnings you can route to an alarm.

Worked example: an app encrypts invoices with key K, rotation on. In year one invoice A uses material v1. After rotation, invoice B uses v2. Decrypting A, KMS spots v1 in the ciphertext and uses it. Both open.

Common mistake: deleting the DNS validation record, or assuming an imported certificate renews. The consequence in a running system is a sudden outage when the certificate expires, with every client rejecting the connection.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain stores pet medical records in object storage, encrypted with a symmetric customer managed key in AWS KMS (a managed key-storage service) named clinic-records. Automatic rotation is on, set to every 180 days. Trace it: (1) In March, record R1 is encrypted, so it uses key material version 1. (2) In September, KMS rotates the key. The key ID, name and policy stay the same, and version 1 is kept. (3) In October, record R2 is encrypted, so it uses version 2. (4) In November, a vet opens R1. What happens at this step?
choices: Decryption fails, because rotation deleted version 1 and R1 must first be restored from a backup.
KMS decrypts R1 with version 2, because the newest material is always used for every operation.
KMS reads which version encrypted R1 from the ciphertext and decrypts it with the kept version 1.
Decryption works only if R1 was re-encrypted with version 2 during the September rotation.
questions.why: KMS keeps every older version of the key material and uses the version that encrypted a piece of data to decrypt it, so R1 opens with version 1 and nothing has to be re-encrypted.

questions.prompt: A payments startup uses a KMS key whose material it imported itself (generated outside AWS and loaded in). Its application refers to the key by the alias payments-key, a friendly name that points to a key. Security policy says the key must be rotated. What is the correct way to rotate it?
choices: Do nothing, because AWS rotates imported key material automatically.
Delete the current key, then turn on automatic rotation on a replacement.
Create a new key, then repoint the payments-key alias to the new key.
Turn on automatic rotation for the key and set the period to one year.
questions.why: Keys with imported material cannot rotate automatically, so you rotate them manually by creating a new key and pointing the alias the application uses at it.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company bought a TLS certificate (the signed digital ID that lets browsers trust an encrypted connection) from an outside provider and imported it into AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), a managed certificate service, for its load balancer. It expires in 60 days. What should the team do to avoid an outage?
choices: Nothing, because ACM renews every certificate that is attached to a resource.
Switch to email validation so ACM can renew the imported certificate.
Route ACM's expiry warnings to an alarm and replace the certificate before it expires.
Add a DNS validation record so ACM can renew the imported certificate itself.
questions.why: ACM never renews imported certificates; it only sends expiry warnings, so the team must alarm on those and replace the certificate themselves.

questions.prompt: A travel site uses a public certificate issued by ACM, validated by DNS. During a DNS cleanup, an engineer deletes the validation record because it looks unused. What is the most likely result?
choices: Nothing changes, because ACM only checks the DNS record once when the certificate is first issued.
The certificate is immediately revoked, so connections fail on the same day the record is deleted.
ACM can no longer prove the domain at renewal, the certificate expires, and clients reject connections.
ACM switches the certificate to email validation and renews it automatically without any human step.
questions.why: ACM's automatic renewal depends on still being able to prove domain ownership through the DNS record. Without the record, the certificate does not renew and it expires, which causes a sudden outage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how KMS key rotation and ACM certificate renewal work, and name one case where each one will not happen automatically.
lessons.modelAnswer: Key rotation swaps the secret material inside a KMS key on a schedule, which limits how much data any single piece of key material protects. With automatic rotation on a symmetric customer managed key, the key ID and policy stay the same and KMS keeps old versions, so old data still decrypts while new data uses the new material. It does not re-encrypt old data. Keys with imported material or asymmetric keys will not rotate automatically; we would create a new key and move the alias. For certificates, ACM renews public certificates it issued as long as they are in use and the DNS validation record still exists. Imported certificates are never auto-renewed, so we need an expiry alarm and an owner, or the site will fail when the certificate expires.
rubricPoints: Rotation changes key material but keeps the key ID, policy and older versions so old ciphertext still decrypts.
Rotation does not re-encrypt existing data.
