Imported-material and asymmetric KMS keys need manual rotation, typically by repointing an alias.
ACM auto-renews certificates it issued when they are in use and validation, ideally DNS, still works.
Imported certificates are not auto-renewed and need monitoring of expiry.
An expired certificate causes clients to refuse connections, an outage.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests whether you can spot which keys and certificates renew themselves and which silently need manual action, so reasoning through scenario situations builds that judgment best.

lessons.plain: Data classification means sorting your information by how sensitive it is and how long you must keep it, for example public marketing images, internal reports, and customer records a regulation says must be kept for seven years. Retention is the rule for how long each class lives before it is moved or deleted. On AWS you write those decisions down as rules the system enforces for you. Access rules decide who may read each class, and lifecycle rules decide where data moves and when it is deleted. Think of a records office with colour-coded folders, where each colour has a lock and a shredding date.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company must keep invoices for seven years and nobody, not even an administrator, may delete them early. Is a rule that says 'delete after seven years' enough? What else might be needed?
lessons.teach:
Data classification is labelling data by sensitivity and legal obligation. Common classes are public, internal, confidential, and regulated. On AWS a label is usually a tag, which is a key-value pair attached to a bucket or object, such as class=confidential. The class then drives two kinds of policy.

Access policies decide who can touch the data. A bucket policy is a resource-based policy, meaning the rule lives on the storage itself. It can deny reads of objects tagged confidential unless the caller is in an approved role, or deny any request that is not encrypted.

Lifecycle policies decide where data lives over time. An S3 Lifecycle rule is a managed schedule. It can move objects to cheaper storage classes, such as S3 Standard-IA for infrequent access or S3 Glacier for archives, and it can expire objects, which means deleting them, after a set age.

Retention is enforced differently. S3 Object Lock is a write-once-read-many (WORM) control, so a locked object cannot be overwritten or deleted until its retention date. Governance mode lets specially permitted users bypass the lock. Compliance mode lets nobody bypass it, including the root user. A legal hold blocks deletion with no end date until someone removes the hold.

Worked example: invoices must be kept seven years and are rarely read after 90 days. Step 1: tag the objects class=regulated. Step 2: turn on versioning and Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention. Step 3: add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to Standard-IA at 30 days and Glacier at 90 days, then expires them after seven years. Step 4: add a bucket policy limiting reads to the finance role.

Common mistake: treating a lifecycle expiration as a retention guarantee. An expiration rule only deletes data late. It does not stop an attacker or admin from deleting it early, and only Object Lock does that. A related mistake is forgetting that in a versioned bucket, deletes leave old versions behind, so they need their own noncurrent-version expiration. In a running system, the first mistake loses audit records, and the second quietly grows storage costs.

questions.prompt: A university research lab stores raw sensor logs in an S3 bucket. The logs are classed internal, have no legal retention requirement, are read often for about 45 days, and should be gone after one year. The bucket keeps versioning on so that accidental overwrites can be undone. The design so far: Step 1, tag the objects class=internal. Step 2, keep versioning enabled. Step 3, add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to S3 Standard-IA at 45 days. Step 4, add a lifecycle rule that expires current objects at 365 days. Step 5 is missing. Without it, the storage bill keeps rising after the first year, even though every current object expires on schedule. What should Step 5 be?
choices: Turn on S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a one-year retention period
Place a legal hold on every object older than 365 days
Add a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent (old) object versions after a set age
Add a bucket policy that denies any request that is not encrypted
questions.why: In a versioned bucket, expiring or deleting an object leaves the older versions behind, so a separate noncurrent-version expiration rule is needed to remove them and stop the storage cost from growing.

questions.prompt: A pharmaceutical company keeps clinical trial results in S3. Its regulator requires that no one, not even the AWS account's root user, can delete or overwrite these files for five years. Which control meets this requirement?
choices: S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a five-year retention period
A bucket policy that limits reads to an approved research role
A lifecycle rule that expires the files after five years
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a five-year retention period
questions.why: Compliance mode is a write-once-read-many lock that nobody can bypass, including the root user, while governance mode lets specially permitted users bypass it.

questions.prompt: A retailer must keep payment audit logs for three years. Its only control is an S3 lifecycle rule that expires the logs at three years. Six months in, an administrator deletes a batch of logs by mistake, and the deletion succeeds. What was wrong with the design?
choices: The lifecycle rule should have moved the logs to S3 Glacier first, because archived objects cannot be deleted
The bucket needed versioning, because versioning alone blocks every delete
A lifecycle expiration only deletes data late; it does not stop an early delete, so S3 Object Lock was needed
The logs needed a tag of class=regulated, because tagged objects cannot be deleted
questions.why: Expiration is a schedule for deleting data after a set age, not a retention guarantee, and only Object Lock blocks early deletion or overwriting.

questions.prompt: An HR team stores staff records in a shared S3 bucket and tags them class=confidential. Only callers using the HR role should be able to read those tagged objects. Where should this rule live, and what kind of policy is it?
choices: In a bucket policy, a resource-based policy attached to the storage itself, that denies reads of confidential-tagged objects unless the caller is in the HR role
In the object tag itself, because a class=confidential tag blocks reads on its own
In an S3 Lifecycle rule, because lifecycle rules decide who can read objects in each storage class
In an S3 Object Lock legal hold, which blocks reads until someone removes the hold
questions.why: Access policies decide who can touch the data, and a bucket policy is a resource-based policy that can deny reads of tagged objects unless the caller holds an approved role; a tag is only a label and does not enforce anything alone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn 'customer records are confidential and must be kept exactly seven years' into AWS policies, and name one tradeoff or limit of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd tag the records with a class, say class=confidential, so policies can key off it. For access, a bucket policy, which is a rule attached to the storage itself, would allow reads only from the approved role and deny unencrypted requests. For the 'at least seven years' part, I'd enable versioning and S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a seven-year retention, so nobody, not even root, can delete early. For the 'no longer than seven years' part and for cost, a lifecycle rule moves objects to Standard-IA, then Glacier, and expires them at seven years, including old noncurrent versions. The tradeoff is that compliance mode is irreversible. If we set the period wrong or need to purge data early, we can't, and we pay to store it until the lock ends. Governance mode is more flexible but weaker.
rubricPoints: Classification is recorded as a label such as a tag that drives policy.
Access is restricted with a policy such as a bucket policy tied to roles.
Lifecycle rules handle transitions to cheaper storage and expiration.
Object Lock, not lifecycle expiration, prevents early deletion.
Compliance mode cannot be bypassed even by root, while governance mode can be bypassed by permitted users.
Names a tradeoff such as irreversibility, cost of locked data, or noncurrent versions needing their own rule.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests choosing between lifecycle expiration, Object Lock modes, and access policies from a stated requirement, so reasoning through scenario-style situations builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: A backup is a saved copy of your data that you can return to later. Most people think of backups as protection against broken hardware or a region going offline. They also protect against people: an attacker with stolen keys, ransomware that scrambles files, or an insider who deletes things on purpose. For that job, the copy has to be out of the attacker's reach and impossible to change for a set time. Think of a fireproof safe at a friend's house that only opens on a timer. A burglar in your home cannot burn it, and neither can you by mistake.
lessons.guessPrompt: An attacker steals an administrator's credentials and deletes your production database. You have a live replica in another region and nightly snapshots stored in the same account. Which of these copies do you think survives, and why?
lessons.teach:
Backup, replication, and recovery become a security control when they are designed to survive someone who is trying to destroy your data. A backup is a point-in-time copy you can restore from. Replication continuously copies changes to another location. Recovery is the act of restoring, measured by the recovery point objective (RPO, how much recent data you can afford to lose) and the recovery time objective (RTO, how long you can afford to be down).

Three properties turn a copy into a security control. Isolation: the copy lives in a separate account, so stolen credentials from production cannot reach it. Immutability: the copy cannot be changed or deleted until a retention period ends. On AWS, S3 Object Lock does this for stored files, and AWS Backup Vault Lock does it for a central backup store, called a vault. History: versioning keeps older versions of each object, so an overwrite or delete can be undone.

Worked example. An attacker gets an administrator's keys. Step one, they delete the database. Step two, the cross-region replica dutifully copies the deletion and is now empty too. Step three, they delete every snapshot in the account, because their keys allow it. Step four, they find a backup vault in a separate security account, locked with a 30-day retention. Their keys have no access there, and even an administrator there could not delete it early. You restore from last night's copy and lose under a day of data.

The common mistake is treating replication as a backup. Replication faithfully copies deletion, corruption, and ransomware-encrypted data, usually within seconds. It protects availability, not integrity.

The consequence in a running system is stark. Without an isolated, immutable copy, one leaked credential can turn into permanent data loss, and paying a ransom becomes the only recovery path. In identity, network, or data terms, this fix belongs in data, backed by identity separation between accounts.

questions.prompt:
A logistics firm keeps 40,000 invoice files in an Amazon S3 bucket (S3 is AWS's object storage service, which stores files called objects). The bucket is in its production account and has versioning turned on. It also uses cross-region replication, which continuously copies changes to a second bucket in another region but in the same account. An attacker steals an administrator's access keys. The attack is traced below with one step missing.

Step 1: The attacker overwrites every invoice with a ransomware-encrypted copy.
Step 2: [missing]
Step 3: Because the stolen keys have full permissions in that account, the attacker deletes all older object versions in both buckets.
Step 4: The firm finds a copy in a separate audit account, protected by S3 Object Lock with a 14-day retention period. The attacker's keys cannot reach it, and no one can delete it early. The firm restores from it.

Which statement correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Within seconds, the second bucket receives the encrypted overwrites, so it now holds the same unusable files.
Replication copies only newly created objects, so the overwrites never reach the second bucket.
The second bucket is safe because it sits in another region, which the attacker's keys cannot reach.
Replication notices the unusual burst of changes and pauses, so the second bucket keeps the original invoices.
questions.why: Replication faithfully copies overwrites, including ransomware-encrypted data, usually within seconds, and a different region in the same account gives no isolation from stolen credentials.

questions.prompt: A backup must be impossible to change or delete until a set retention period ends, even for an administrator. Which of the three security properties of a backup does this describe?
choices: Isolation
Immutability
History (versioning)
Replication
questions.why: Immutability means a copy cannot be changed or deleted until its retention period ends. On AWS, S3 Object Lock and AWS Backup Vault Lock provide it.

questions.prompt: A healthcare startup has this requirement: "If an attacker gains full administrator access to our production account, our patient-record backups must still be recoverable." Which design meets it?
choices: Store backups in an S3 bucket in the production account with versioning turned on.
Send backups to an AWS Backup vault (a central backup store) in a separate account, locked with Vault Lock and a retention period.
Take nightly database snapshots in the production account and copy them to a second region in that same account.
Run a continuously replicated standby database in a different region.
questions.why: Only this design gives both isolation, because the stolen production credentials cannot reach the other account, and immutability, because Vault Lock blocks early deletion. Every other option leaves the copies reachable by the attacker's administrator keys.

questions.prompt: An online retailer says: "We're protected against ransomware. Our database replicates to a standby in another region within two seconds, so our RPO is tiny." (RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much recent data you can afford to lose.) What is the flaw in this reasoning?
choices: A small RPO only matters for hardware failures, so it says nothing about how long recovery takes.
The standby is fine. The real risk is that the RTO, the recovery time objective, is too long.
Replication copies the ransomware-encrypted data to the standby within seconds too. It protects availability, not integrity.
Cross-region replication is too slow to keep up during an attack, so the standby falls behind.
questions.why: Replication faithfully copies corruption, deletion, and encrypted data. Without an isolated, immutable copy, the standby is ruined along with the primary.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why your cross-region database replica does not count as ransomware protection, what you would add so the data survives a stolen admin credential, and one tradeoff that addition brings.
lessons.modelAnswer: A replica copies every change almost instantly, and that includes the bad ones. If an attacker deletes or encrypts the primary, the replica follows within seconds. So it helps if a region fails, but it does not protect our data from an attacker. For that we need a copy the attacker cannot reach or change. I would send backups into a vault in a separate account that production credentials cannot touch. I would also lock it with AWS Backup Vault Lock, or S3 Object Lock for files, so nothing can be deleted before the retention period ends. Versioning on buckets helps undo overwrites. The tradeoffs: locked backups cost storage for the full retention period, and we cannot delete them early even when we want to, including mistakes or data we are asked to remove. Restoring from a nightly backup also means accepting a worse recovery point than a live replica gives us.
rubricPoints: Replication copies deletions, corruption, and encryption, so it protects availability but not integrity.
A security-grade backup is isolated in a separate account that compromised production credentials cannot reach.
Immutability through Object Lock or Backup Vault Lock stops deletion before retention ends, even by administrators.
Versioning keeps prior object versions so overwrites and deletes can be undone.
Names a tradeoff such as locked storage cost, inability to delete early, or a worse recovery point than a live replica.

suggested.rationale: The skill is spotting, in an exam-style scenario, that a replica or same-account snapshot fails against a compromised credential, and choosing isolation plus immutability instead.

lessons.plain: A compliance requirement is a rule your system must follow because a law, a contract, or an auditor says so, for example "customer data must stay in the EU" or "every change must be logged and kept for a year." Aligning technology to it means reading the rule, working out what kind of control it really asks for, and picking the cloud feature that enforces it and proves it. Think of a building inspector: they don't care which brand of smoke alarm you bought, only that one is fitted in every room and that you can show the inspection record.
lessons.guessPrompt: A rule says "you must be able to show an auditor who deleted a database last March." Before any teaching, guess: does that rule ask you to prevent something, record something, or encrypt something?
lessons.teach:
Aligning AWS technologies to a compliance requirement means translating a rule into one or more control types, then choosing the service that enforces or evidences each one. Most rules fall into four buckets. Residency means data must stay in a place; you meet it by choosing an AWS Region (a geographic group of data centres) and blocking others. Protection means data must be unreadable to outsiders; AWS KMS (a managed encryption-key service) handles encryption at rest. Audit means you must show who did what; AWS CloudTrail is a log of every API call (every request made to AWS) with the caller and time. Configuration evidence means you must show resources stayed in an approved state; AWS Config records each resource's settings over time and flags rules that are broken. AWS Security Hub gathers findings from these and scores them against named standards, and AWS Artifact is a portal where you download AWS's own audit reports about AWS's half of the work.

Why this works: auditors want enforcement plus proof, so each requirement usually needs a preventing service and a recording service.

Worked example. Requirement: "Payment records must stay in the EU, be encrypted, and all access must be traceable for one year." Step 1, residency: deploy in an EU Region and deny other Regions. Step 2, protection: encrypt the storage with a KMS key. Step 3, traceability: turn on CloudTrail for all Regions and send logs to a storage bucket kept for at least a year. Step 4, proof: add a Config rule that flags any unencrypted storage, so drift is caught.

Common mistake: believing that because AWS holds a certification, your workload is compliant. AWS's reports cover the infrastructure; your settings, access, and data handling are yours. Another mix-up is confusing CloudTrail (who acted) with Config (what state the resource is in).

In a running system, a missing recording control means a breach you cannot reconstruct and an audit you fail even if nothing went wrong.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic chain in Canada has this rule: "X-ray images must stay in Canada, be unreadable to outsiders, and each quarter we must show auditors that no image storage bucket was ever switched to public access." The architect works through it. Step 1, residency: deploy in a Canadian AWS Region and deny all other Regions. Step 2, protection: encrypt the image storage with a key from AWS KMS (the managed encryption-key service). Step 3, configuration evidence: ??? Step 4: feed the findings into AWS Security Hub so they are scored against a named standard for the quarterly review. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Add an AWS Config rule that records each bucket's settings over time and flags any bucket that becomes public
Encrypt the bucket a second time with another KMS key, because encrypted data counts as proof that it was never public
Turn on AWS CloudTrail in all Regions, because a log of every API call proves that each bucket stayed private
Download AWS's audit reports from AWS Artifact, because they certify that the clinic's buckets are configured correctly
questions.why: The rule asks for proof that resources stayed in an approved state, and AWS Config records resource settings over time and flags broken rules, whereas CloudTrail shows who acted, Artifact covers only AWS's half, and encryption protects data without proving anything about configuration.

questions.prompt: An auditor at a logistics company asks: "Which user deleted the shipping-manifest database at 03:10 last Tuesday?" Which AWS service records the information needed to answer this?
choices: AWS CloudTrail, because it logs every API call with the caller and the time
AWS Config, because it tracks each resource's settings over time
AWS KMS, because it controls who can read the stored data
AWS Artifact, because it holds audit reports about AWS activity
questions.why: The question is about who did what and when, which is an audit need, and CloudTrail logs every API call with the caller and the time; Config records resource state, not who acted.

questions.prompt: A small analytics startup tells its customers: "We run on AWS, and AWS holds several security certifications, so our application is fully compliant." What is wrong with this claim?
choices: Nothing is wrong, because AWS's certifications automatically extend to every workload hosted on AWS
The claim fails only because the startup has not yet downloaded the reports from AWS Artifact
The claim would only be true if the startup also turned on AWS Security Hub
AWS's reports cover AWS's infrastructure, while the startup's own settings, access, and data handling remain its responsibility
questions.why: AWS's certifications cover only AWS's half of the work, so the customer must still configure and evidence its own settings, access, and data handling.

questions.prompt: An Australian insurance firm has a rule: "Policyholder data must never be stored outside Australia." Which control type does this rule describe, and how is it met on AWS?
choices: Protection: encrypt the policyholder data with an AWS KMS key so outsiders cannot read it
Audit: turn on AWS CloudTrail so every access to the data is logged with the caller
Configuration evidence: download AWS Artifact reports showing where AWS's data centres are
Residency: run workloads in an Australian AWS Region and block the use of other Regions
questions.why: A rule about where data must stay is a residency requirement, met by choosing a Region (a geographic group of data centres) and blocking the others; encryption, logging, and AWS's reports do not keep data in a location.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would turn a written compliance requirement into a set of AWS services, and name one limit: what does using AWS's certified services not do for you?
lessons.modelAnswer: I read the requirement and sort it into control types: residency, protection, audit, and configuration evidence. Residency I meet by picking an approved Region and blocking the others. Protection usually means encryption with KMS keys. Audit means CloudTrail, which records every API call with who made it and when, stored for as long as the rule demands. Configuration evidence means AWS Config, which tracks resource settings over time and flags breaks against rules; Security Hub can roll those findings up against a named standard. For each requirement I want one service that enforces and one that proves. The limit is shared responsibility: AWS Artifact gives me AWS's audit reports for the infrastructure, but that does not make my workload compliant. My configurations, access rights, and data handling still have to be shown separately.
rubricPoints: Sorts the requirement into a control type such as residency, protection, audit, or configuration evidence.
Matches each type to a service: Region choice, KMS, CloudTrail, Config or Security Hub.
Notes that compliance needs both enforcement and recorded proof.
Distinguishes CloudTrail (who did what) from Config (what state a resource is in).
States that AWS's certifications via Artifact cover only AWS's side, not the customer's workload.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reading an exam-style requirement and reasoning out which control and service it maps to, which scenario practice builds better than any single existing mission.

lessons.plain: A multi-tier architecture splits one application into separate layers, called tiers, that each do one job. The usual three are a front door that talks to users, a middle layer that applies the business rules, and a back room that stores the data. Think of a restaurant. The host greets guests, the kitchen cooks, and the pantry holds ingredients. Guests never walk into the pantry. If the dining room gets busy, you add servers without rebuilding the pantry. Splitting the work this way lets each layer grow, fail and be protected on its own.
lessons.guessPrompt: In an online shop with a web front end, an order-processing layer and a customer database, which of those three layers do you think should be reachable directly from the internet, and why?
lessons.teach:
A multi-tier architecture divides an application into layers, called tiers, and gives each one its own job, scaling and security rules. The classic three are the presentation (web) tier, which receives user requests and serves pages; the application (logic) tier, which runs business rules such as pricing an order; and the data tier, which stores records durably, often in a managed relational database such as Amazon RDS.

This works because each tier can scale, fail and be secured independently. A load balancer is a service that spreads requests across several servers and skips unhealthy ones. One sits in front of the web tier, and often an internal one sits in front of the app tier. Each compute tier runs in an Auto Scaling group, which is a managed set of virtual machines that adds or removes copies as load changes. Tiers live in subnets, which are slices of a virtual network. Only the internet-facing load balancer goes in a public subnet, meaning one reachable from the internet. App servers and the database go in private subnets. Security groups are instance-level firewalls, and they let each tier accept traffic only from the tier directly above it.

Worked example: a shopper clicks Buy. First, the request reaches the public load balancer. Second, the load balancer forwards it to a healthy web server in a private subnet. Third, the web server calls the app tier, which checks stock and totals the order. Fourth, the app tier writes the order to the database, whose security group admits only the app tier. Finally, the response travels back up. Every tier spans at least two Availability Zones, which are separate data centres within a Region, so losing one zone does not break the flow.

A common mistake is keeping state, such as login sessions or uploaded files, on a web or app server's local disk. When that server is replaced or scaled away, the data vanishes and users are logged out. Keep state in the data tier or a shared store so that compute servers stay disposable.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing company is setting up security groups (instance-level firewalls) for its three-tier app. The design is mostly done. (1) The internet-facing load balancer's security group accepts HTTPS from anyone on the internet. (2) The web tier's security group accepts traffic only from the load balancer's security group. (3) The app tier's security group accepts traffic only from the web tier's security group. (4) The rule for the ticket database's security group is missing. Which rule completes the design?
choices: Accept traffic from anywhere, because the database already sits in a private subnet
Accept traffic only from the web tier's security group, since web servers start each purchase
Accept traffic only from the app tier's security group
Accept traffic only from the load balancer's security group, since every request passes through it first
questions.why: Each tier should accept traffic only from the tier directly above it, and the app tier is the only tier that talks to the database.

questions.prompt: A streaming service is building a sign-up site with an internet-facing load balancer, web servers, app servers and a managed relational database. Which of these should be placed in a public subnet, meaning one reachable from the internet?
choices: The load balancer and the web servers, because the web servers serve pages to users
All four, so that every tier can be reached for troubleshooting
The web servers and the app servers, so that they can scale freely
Only the internet-facing load balancer
questions.why: Only the internet-facing load balancer belongs in a public subnet; the app servers and the database go in private subnets, and in this design the web servers do too, behind the load balancer.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing app saves each uploaded image to the local disk of whichever web server received it. One night the Auto Scaling group shrinks from 6 web servers to 3. What happens, and what is the right fix?
choices: Nothing is lost, because the load balancer copies the files to the remaining servers before removing any
Some images are lost, and the fix is to turn off Auto Scaling so that servers are never removed
Images on the removed servers are lost, and the fix is to store uploads in the data tier or a shared store so the web servers stay disposable
Nothing is lost, because Auto Scaling keeps the disks of removed servers until the next scale-out
questions.why: State kept on a server's local disk disappears when that server is scaled away, so it belongs in a shared store, which lets compute servers be replaced freely.

questions.prompt: A city council's permit system runs its web tier and app tier in Auto Scaling groups that span two Availability Zones (separate data centres within a Region). Its database runs in only one of those zones. What is the main resilience weakness?
choices: The database is a single point of failure: if its zone goes down, the whole permit flow breaks, even though the web and app servers survive
There is no weakness, because the load balancer will route around the failed zone
The web tier needs a third Availability Zone before the system counts as resilient
The app tier should be moved into a public subnet so that it can fail over faster
questions.why: Every tier, including the data tier, should span at least two Availability Zones so that losing one zone does not break the flow.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what belongs in each tier of a three-tier web application and why you separate them, and name one tradeoff or limit of splitting an application this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: We split the app into three tiers. The web tier sits behind a public load balancer and handles user requests. The app tier runs the business logic. The data tier holds the database in private subnets. Security groups chain them, so the database only accepts connections from the app tier and the internet can only reach the load balancer. Each compute tier runs in an Auto Scaling group across at least two Availability Zones, so we can add capacity where the load is and survive losing a zone. The web and app servers keep no state, which makes any one of them replaceable. The tradeoff is extra network hops and more pieces to configure and monitor, which adds a little latency and operational work. The data tier also remains the hardest part to scale and protect, so it needs its own redundancy plan.
rubricPoints: Names the presentation, application and data tiers and what each one does.
Explains that only the front load balancer is public and that the app and data tiers sit in private subnets.
Describes security groups allowing each tier to receive traffic only from the tier above.
Notes that each tier scales and spans Availability Zones independently.
Says the compute tiers should be stateless, with state kept in the data tier.
States a tradeoff such as added latency, complexity, or the data tier remaining the hard part.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present a scenario and ask where a component or rule belongs, so reasoning through tier placement, subnet exposure and security-group chaining in realistic situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A stateless service keeps no memory of earlier requests on the machine that handles them. Every request carries, or looks up, everything needed, so any copy of the service can answer it. A stateful service keeps something it needs later, such as a login session, a shopping cart or open connections, inside one particular machine. Think of a bank with many tellers. If your account details live in a shared system, any teller can serve you. If one teller keeps your file in a desk drawer, you must queue for that teller, and if they go home, your file goes with them.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop runs three identical web servers behind a load balancer, which spreads requests across them. A customer's cart is kept in the memory of whichever server handled their first click. What do you think happens when their next click lands on a different server, or when the first server crashes?
lessons.teach:
State is any data a service must remember between requests, such as who is logged in, what is in a cart, or how far a job has progressed. A stateless workload keeps none of it on the compute instance, meaning the virtual server or container running the code. It writes state to an external store that every instance can reach, for example Amazon DynamoDB (a managed key-value database) or Amazon ElastiCache (a managed in-memory cache). A stateful workload keeps state locally, in memory or on the instance's own disk.

Statelessness matters because it makes instances interchangeable. A load balancer is a component that spreads incoming requests across instances, and it can send any request to any healthy instance. An Auto Scaling group is a managed set of instances that grows and shrinks with demand, and it can add or remove instances freely. If one instance fails, nothing is lost except the requests it was handling at that moment.

Here is a worked example. Step 1: a user logs in and the request reaches instance A, which stores the session in its memory. Step 2: the next request goes to instance B, which has no session, so the user appears logged out. Step 3: the fix is to have A write the session to ElastiCache under a session ID that is sent back to the browser in a cookie. Step 4: B reads that ID, fetches the session from ElastiCache, and serves the user. Step 5: A now crashes, and no user notices.

A common mistake is to rely on sticky sessions, a load balancer setting that pins each user to one instance. The setting hides the problem, but load becomes uneven, and the users pinned to an instance lose their sessions when it fails or when scaling removes it.

Some components must stay stateful, such as databases. Give them their own replication and backups, and keep the many application instances stateless so they can scale and fail safely.

questions.prompt: A print shop runs an image-resizing service on 8 worker containers in an Auto Scaling group. Each job is a batch of 400 photos. Today, a worker tracks how many photos it has finished only in its own memory. Here is the stateless redesign, traced step by step. Step 1: worker W2 picks up job 77 and starts resizing photos. Step 2: (missing step). Step 3: after photo 250, Auto Scaling removes W2 during a quiet period. Step 4: worker W6 picks up job 77, looks up its progress in DynamoDB (a managed key-value database), and sees that 250 photos are done. Step 5: W6 resumes at photo 251, and no finished work is repeated or lost. Which choice completes Step 2?
choices: The load balancer turns on sticky sessions, so every request for job 77 is pinned to W2.
W2 saves its photo count to a file on its own disk, so the count survives if that container restarts.
The Auto Scaling group's minimum size is raised, so that W2 is never removed while it is busy.
After each photo, W2 writes job 77's count of finished photos to DynamoDB, keyed by the job ID.
questions.why: W6 can only resume at photo 251 if the progress was written, as the work happened, to an external store that every worker can reach. Local disk, sticky sessions and a larger minimum all leave the state tied to W2 or merely hide the problem.

questions.prompt: A team says its new order API is "stateless." Which statement best matches that claim?
choices: Each container saves users' data to its own attached disk, so the data survives a restart of that container.
The API stores no data anywhere at all, so it cannot use a database or a cache.
Each container keeps no data it needs between requests. Anything it must remember goes to an external store that every container can reach.
Each container keeps users' data in memory, and the load balancer always sends a given user back to the same container.
questions.why: A stateless workload keeps no state on the compute instance; it writes state to a shared external store rather than doing without state entirely.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking site runs 5 instances behind a load balancer and keeps each user's half-finished itinerary in instance memory. To stop users losing their itineraries, the site enables sticky sessions. One evening, the Auto Scaling group scales in from 5 instances to 3. What happens?
choices: Every user on the site loses their itinerary, because sticky sessions must be reset after any scaling event.
Users pinned to the 2 removed instances lose their itineraries. Load across the instances may also have been uneven.
Nothing is lost, because the load balancer stores the itineraries for the pinned users.
Nothing is lost, because sticky sessions copy each itinerary to the remaining instances before an instance is removed.
questions.why: Sticky sessions only pin users to an instance; the state still lives on that instance, so it disappears when scaling removes the instance.

questions.prompt: A library is designing a lending system made up of 12 application instances in an Auto Scaling group and one relational database that holds book loans. Which design follows the stateless-versus-stateful guidance?
choices: Keep each application instance's loan records on its local disk, so that the database can be removed.
Make the database stateless by storing loans in application instance memory, and let Auto Scaling replace it.
Keep the application instances stateless, and give the database its own replication and backups.
Run a single large application instance, so that there is only one place where state can live.
questions.why: Some components, such as databases, must stay stateful, so they should be protected with replication and backups. The many application instances stay stateless so they can scale and fail safely.

lessons.explainPrompt: In your own words, explain to a teammate why we should move user sessions out of the web servers' memory, and name one cost or tradeoff of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: Right now each web server keeps sessions in its own memory, so a user only works properly if every request returns to the same server. That makes servers non-interchangeable. If one crashes, or Auto Scaling removes it during a quiet period, every user on it is logged out, and the load balancer can't spread traffic evenly. If we write sessions to a shared store such as ElastiCache or DynamoDB, any server can answer any request. We can then add or terminate instances freely, and losing one costs us almost nothing. The tradeoff is that every request now makes an extra network call to fetch its session, which adds a little latency. We also take on a new component to pay for, and it has to be highly available itself, or it simply becomes our new single point of failure. Sticky sessions would be cheaper but only hide the problem.
rubricPoints: Defines state and explains that a stateless instance keeps none of it locally.
Explains that statelessness makes instances interchangeable for load balancing, scaling and failure.
Names an external shared store such as ElastiCache or DynamoDB as where state goes.
Identifies sticky sessions as a workaround that loses sessions when an instance fails or is scaled in.
Names a tradeoff such as extra latency, extra cost, or the store needing its own high availability.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present a scenario such as lost sessions after scaling and ask for the fix, so reasoning through situations like that is the most useful practice for this objective.

lessons.plain: Event-driven architecture means parts of a system tell each other "something happened" instead of calling each other directly. The thing that happened is an event, such as "order placed". Amazon EventBridge is AWS's managed event router: services drop events onto it, and it delivers each event to whoever has said they care about that kind of event. Think of a building's mailroom. Senders hand letters to the mailroom without knowing who works where, and staff tell the mailroom which letters they want. Senders and receivers never deal with each other, so either side can change, grow, or break without dragging the other down.
lessons.guessPrompt: An order service must trigger three things when an order is placed: send a receipt, update stock, and start fraud checks. If it calls all three directly and the fraud service is down, what happens to the order? How could you design it so the order service does not need to know those three services exist?
lessons.teach:
An event is a small record saying something happened, for example {source: orders, type: OrderPlaced, total: 250}. A producer is any service that emits events. Amazon EventBridge is a managed event bus, meaning a router in the middle that receives events and forwards them. A rule is a filter attached to the bus. It contains an event pattern, which describes which events it matches by their fields, and one or more targets, the destinations that receive matched events, such as a Lambda function, a queue, or a workflow. Rules can also fire on a schedule instead of on an event.

This works because producers only know the bus, not the consumers. That loose coupling removes a failure chain: one slow or broken consumer no longer blocks the producer, and a new consumer is added by writing a rule, with no change to the producer.

Worked example. The order service puts OrderPlaced with total 250 on the bus. Rule A matches every OrderPlaced and targets the receipt function. Rule B matches OrderPlaced and targets the stock queue. Rule C matches OrderPlaced where total is over 200 and targets the fraud workflow. EventBridge checks all three patterns, finds all match, and delivers three copies. An order of 50 would match only A and B. If the fraud target is down, EventBridge retries for a period, and you can attach a dead-letter queue, a holding queue for events that could not be delivered, so nothing is silently lost. An archive can store past events so you can replay them later.

Common mistake: assuming each event arrives exactly once and in order. Delivery is at least once, and order is not guaranteed. In a running system that means a consumer that charges a card can charge twice unless it is idempotent, meaning it recognises a repeated event by its ID and does the work only once.

questions.prompt:
A city library puts events on an Amazon EventBridge event bus (a managed router that receives events and forwards them). Three rules are attached. Rule X matches every BookReturned event and targets a catalog-update function. Rule Y matches BookReturned events where daysLate is over 7 and targets a fines queue. Rule Z matches BookBorrowed events and targets a reminder workflow. The checkout desk now emits {source: library, type: BookReturned, daysLate: 3}.

Step 1: EventBridge compares the event against the event pattern of every rule on the bus, not just the first one.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: If a matched target cannot be reached, EventBridge retries it for a period, and any event still undelivered goes to a dead-letter queue if one is attached.

Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Only Rule X matches, because daysLate 3 is not over 7 and the type is not BookBorrowed, so one copy goes to the catalog function.
Rule X matches first, so EventBridge stops checking and delivers to the catalog function without looking at Y or Z.
All three rules match, because every rule on the bus receives every event, so three copies are delivered.
Rules X and Y match, because both look for BookReturned, so the catalog function and the fines queue each get a copy.
questions.why: An event goes to every rule whose pattern matches all its conditions, and only Rule X matches here because daysLate 3 fails Y's over-7 condition and the type fails Z's BookBorrowed condition.

questions.prompt: A weather company's sensor service emits SensorReading events to an EventBridge bus, where existing rules send them to an alerting function. A new analytics team now wants a copy of every SensorReading delivered to their own queue. What is the right change?
choices: Update the sensor service so it sends each reading to the bus and also directly to the analytics queue.
Have the alerting function forward each reading to the analytics queue after it finishes its own work.
Add a new rule on the bus whose pattern matches SensorReading and whose target is the analytics queue, leaving the sensor service unchanged.
Replace the alerting rule's target with the analytics queue, because a pattern can only have one consumer.
questions.why: Producers only know the bus, so a new consumer is added by writing a new rule with its own target, with no change to the producer and no chain through another consumer.

questions.prompt: A hotel booking platform uses EventBridge to send RoomBooked events to a housekeeping-scheduling function. During a two-hour outage of that function, the team must make sure no RoomBooked events are silently lost. Which addition meets this need?
choices: Make the booking service wait for the housekeeping function to confirm each event before accepting the next booking.
Add a second rule with the same pattern so the event is sent twice and one copy will probably get through.
Rely on EventBridge to hold every undelivered event on the bus indefinitely until the function returns.
Attach a dead-letter queue to the target so events that still cannot be delivered after retries are kept for later processing.
questions.why: EventBridge retries only for a limited period, so a dead-letter queue, a holding queue for events that could not be delivered, is what keeps failed events from being lost.

questions.prompt: A fitness app's LoyaltyPoints function receives WorkoutCompleted events from EventBridge and adds 10 points per event. Some customers occasionally get 20 points for one workout. What is the most likely cause, and the right fix?
choices: Two rules on the bus match the same event; fix it by deleting every rule except one so each event is delivered exactly once.
The producer emitted the event twice; fix it by having the app call the LoyaltyPoints function directly instead of using the bus.
EventBridge delivers at least once, so a repeat can arrive; make the function idempotent by recording each event ID and skipping IDs it has already processed.
EventBridge delivered the events out of order; fix it by sorting events by timestamp before adding points.
questions.why: Delivery is at least once, so the same event can arrive more than once, and an idempotent consumer that recognises a repeated event by its ID does the work only once.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how EventBridge routes an event from a producer to consumers, why that makes the system more resilient, and name one limit you must design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: A producer, say the order service, puts an event like OrderPlaced onto an EventBridge event bus. The bus holds rules, and each rule has an event pattern that filters on the event's fields and targets to deliver matches to, such as a function or a queue. One event can match several rules, so several consumers each get a copy. The producer never knows who the consumers are, so a broken fraud service cannot block orders, and adding a new consumer is just a new rule. Failed deliveries are retried, and a dead-letter queue catches what still fails, while an archive lets you replay events. The limit is that delivery is at least once with no ordering guarantee, so consumers must be idempotent, using the event ID to skip duplicates, and must not rely on events arriving in sequence.
rubricPoints: Defines producer, event bus, rule with event pattern, and target.
Explains that one event can fan out to every rule it matches.
States that producers do not know consumers, so a failing consumer does not block the producer.
Mentions retries and a dead-letter queue so undeliverable events are kept.
Names at-least-once delivery and no ordering guarantee as a limit.
Concludes consumers must be idempotent.

suggested.rationale: Writing event patterns and watching which targets receive an event, including retries and duplicates, teaches routing far better than reading about it.

lessons.plain: Decoupling means letting parts of a system pass work to each other without both having to be online and equally fast at the same moment. A queue is like a ticket rail in a restaurant kitchen: waiters clip orders on the rail and cooks take them off when they are ready, so a rush of orders waits instead of being lost. Publish/subscribe (pub/sub) is like a radio broadcast: one announcement reaches everyone tuned in. On AWS, Amazon SQS provides the managed queue and Amazon SNS provides the managed broadcast channel. Used together, they keep one slow or crashed component from dragging down the rest.
lessons.guessPrompt: An order website must tell both a billing system and a shipping system about every new order, and the shipping system sometimes goes offline for an hour. How would you make sure shipping still gets every order without making the website wait for it?
lessons.teach:
Decoupling lets components exchange work without depending on each other's speed or uptime. Amazon SQS (Simple Queue Service) is a managed message queue, a durable holding area. A producer (the sender) drops messages into it, and a consumer (the worker) pulls them out later. Each message is meant to be handled by one consumer. Amazon SNS (Simple Notification Service) is a managed publish/subscribe service. A publisher sends one message to a topic, which is a named channel, and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber, such as an SQS queue, a Lambda function or an HTTP endpoint.

Why this works: a queue absorbs bursts, so the producer never waits on a slow consumer, and you can add more consumers to drain it faster. A topic lets you add new listeners without changing the publisher.

Worked example. An order service publishes "order placed" once to an SNS topic. Two SQS queues, billing and shipping, are subscribed, so SNS copies the message into both. This pattern is called fan-out. The billing worker reads its copy. SQS then hides that message for the visibility timeout, which is the period when other consumers cannot see a message that is being worked on. The worker finishes and deletes the message. Meanwhile, shipping is down for an hour, so its copies simply wait in its queue (up to 14 days) and drain when it returns.

A standard queue delivers at least once with best-effort ordering, so duplicates can occur. A FIFO (first-in-first-out) queue keeps order and removes duplicates, at lower throughput. A dead-letter queue is a side queue that collects messages which failed processing too many times, so they stop blocking everything else.

Common mistake: relying on SNS alone for work that must survive a subscriber outage. SNS retries delivery but does not store messages for long the way a queue does, so put SQS behind it. Another mistake is setting a visibility timeout shorter than the processing time. The message then reappears and is processed twice, which in a running system can mean duplicate charges.

questions.prompt: ClipCast, a video-sharing site, uses an Amazon SQS queue (a managed message queue) to hand transcoding jobs to a pool of worker servers. Each transcoding job takes about 8 minutes. The flow is mostly worked out. Step 1: the upload service (the producer) sends the message "transcode video 42" to the queue. Step 2: one transcoding worker (a consumer) pulls that message and starts working. Step 3: missing. Step 4: the worker finishes after about 8 minutes and deletes the message, so no other worker ever processes video 42. Which choice correctly fills Step 3 so that video 42 is transcoded only once?
choices: Set the queue's visibility timeout to about 10 minutes, longer than the 8-minute job, so the message stays hidden while it is worked on.
Publish the message to an SNS topic as well, so that every transcoding worker receives its own copy of the job.
Move the message into a dead-letter queue while the worker is processing it, then move it back when the work is done.
Set the queue's visibility timeout to 2 minutes so another worker can take over the job quickly if this one is slow.
questions.why: The visibility timeout hides a message from other consumers while it is being processed, so it must be longer than the 8-minute job or the message reappears and is transcoded twice.

questions.prompt: Pulse Fitness publishes a "workout completed" event to an Amazon SNS topic (a managed publish/subscribe channel). The rewards service is subscribed directly as an HTTP endpoint. Next week the rewards service will be offline for 3 hours of maintenance, and no events may be lost during that time. What is the best change?
choices: Subscribe an SQS queue to the topic and have the rewards service read its events from that queue.
Replace the SNS topic with a single FIFO queue that all services read from.
Do nothing, because SNS keeps every message stored until each subscriber comes back online.
Add a second HTTP endpoint subscription that points at the same rewards service.
questions.why: SNS retries delivery but does not hold messages for long, while an SQS queue subscribed to the topic stores the copies (up to 14 days) until the rewards service returns and drains them.

questions.prompt: A small credit union is building a ledger service. Account transactions arrive as messages, they must be applied in the exact order they were sent, and a deposit must never be applied twice. Message volume is modest. Which option fits best?
choices: An SQS standard queue with a very long visibility timeout
An SQS FIFO queue
An SQS standard queue
An SNS topic with the ledger service subscribed as an HTTP endpoint
questions.why: A FIFO (first-in-first-out) queue keeps message order and removes duplicates, accepting lower throughput, which suits a modest-volume ledger, whereas a standard queue gives only best-effort ordering and can deliver duplicates.

questions.prompt: An invoicing team runs workers that read from an SQS queue and generate PDF invoices. One malformed message fails every time it is processed. After each failure it reappears in the queue, workers keep retrying it, and other invoices are delayed. What should the team add?
choices: A shorter visibility timeout, so the failing message comes back sooner and is retried faster
A dead-letter queue, so the message is set aside after too many failed attempts
More consumers, so the same malformed message is attempted by several workers in parallel
An SNS topic in front of the queue, so the failing message is pushed to more subscribers
questions.why: A dead-letter queue is a side queue that collects messages that have failed processing too many times, so a bad message stops blocking the rest of the work.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when you would use SQS, when you would use SNS, and why you might combine them. Include one limit or tradeoff, such as duplicates, ordering, or what happens when a subscriber is offline.
lessons.modelAnswer: SQS is a queue: producers drop messages in and a consumer pulls each one out when it has capacity. That way bursts wait instead of overwhelming the worker, and a crashed worker does not lose work. SNS is pub/sub: you publish one message to a topic and every subscriber gets a copy. I use SQS when one kind of worker must process each job reliably. I use SNS when several systems need to hear about the same event. Combining them is fan-out: SNS sends a copy into a separate SQS queue per consumer, so each one gets the event and can be offline without losing it. The tradeoff is that standard queues deliver at least once and may reorder messages, so handlers must tolerate duplicates. FIFO fixes ordering and duplicates but has lower throughput. The visibility timeout must also exceed the processing time, or messages get processed twice.
rubricPoints: SQS is a queue where each message is pulled and handled by one consumer, buffering bursts and outages.
SNS is pub/sub, pushing a copy of each published message to every subscriber of a topic.
Fan-out with SNS plus one SQS queue per consumer lets independent systems receive the same event durably.
Standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort order; FIFO trades throughput for ordering and deduplication.
Visibility timeout and dead-letter queues control reprocessing and stop failing messages from blocking work.

suggested.rationale: A messaging engine would let the learner build queues, topics and fan-out, then watch buffering, visibility timeouts and dead-letter queues behave, which no current mission covers end to end.

lessons.plain: AWS Step Functions is a managed workflow service: you describe a multi-step business process as a diagram of steps, and the service runs it, remembering where each run is, what it has done, and what to do if a step fails. Think of a restaurant ticket rail. The ticket says starter, then main, then dessert. If the kitchen drops a plate, the ticket shows exactly which course to redo, and nobody has to remember the order in their head. Step Functions is that ticket rail for your code. Small functions do the cooking, and the workflow keeps the order, the retries and the record of progress.
lessons.guessPrompt: An order process has three steps: charge the card, reserve stock, send a confirmation email. If the email step fails halfway through a run, what would you want the system to remember, and what would you want it to do next?
lessons.teach:
AWS Step Functions is a managed orchestration service. Orchestration means one central coordinator decides which step runs next, instead of each component calling the next one directly. You define a state machine, which is a workflow made of named states (steps) and the transitions between them, written in a JSON-based language. Each run of the state machine is called an execution. Common state types are Task (do work, such as invoking an AWS Lambda function, which runs your code without servers), Choice (branch on data), Parallel (run branches at once), Map (repeat a step for each item in a list), and Wait (pause for a time).

This helps resilience because the service, not your code, stores the execution's progress and input/output between steps. Each step can declare Retry rules, such as retrying up to 3 times with exponential backoff, meaning the gap between attempts grows each time. Each step can also declare Catch rules, which send the execution to a fallback state when retries run out. Your functions stay small and stateless.

Worked example: an order workflow. Step 1, ChargeCard, succeeds. Step 2, ReserveStock, times out. Its Retry rule waits 2 seconds and tries again, then waits 4 seconds and tries again, and the second retry succeeds. Step 3, SendEmail, fails three times, so its Catch rule routes the execution to a RefundAndAlert state, which reverses the charge. The execution history shows every step, its input and its error.

Standard workflows can run for up to a year, run each step once unless your retries say otherwise, and are billed per state transition. They suit long or human-approval processes. Express workflows last up to five minutes, can run their steps more than once, and are billed by duration. They suit high-volume, short event processing.

A common mistake is chaining Lambda functions so each calls the next and handles its own retries. Then the order of steps and the error handling are scattered across code, a failure midway leaves no record of progress, and you pay for functions sitting idle while they wait. In a running system, a failed step then means half-finished orders that nobody can see or resume.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain uses AWS Step Functions (a managed service that coordinates the steps of a workflow) to book surgeries. Its state machine has these steps. Step 1, a Task state called CheckVetSchedule, invokes a Lambda function and succeeds. Step 2, a Choice state, reads the animal's weight from the input and branches to the large-animal path. Step 3, a Task state called BookOperatingRoom, declares a Retry rule of up to 2 retries with exponential backoff, plus a Catch rule pointing to a state called NotifyFrontDesk. BookOperatingRoom fails, waits 1 second and fails again, then waits a longer gap and fails a third time. Step 4 is missing: what happens next?
choices: The Retry rule starts the whole execution again from CheckVetSchedule, because a failed step always resets the workflow.
The retries are used up, so the Catch rule sends the execution to NotifyFrontDesk, and the execution history records the error.
The BookOperatingRoom Lambda function must call NotifyFrontDesk itself, because Step Functions only moves forward when a step succeeds.
The execution pauses with no time limit until an engineer resumes it, because Retry and Catch cannot both be set on one step.
questions.why: When a step's retries run out, its Catch rule routes the execution to the declared fallback state, and the service keeps a record of every step and its error.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's claim workflow needs a human adjuster to approve each claim, and approval can take up to three weeks. Each step should run exactly once unless a retry is declared. Which Step Functions workflow type fits, and why?
choices: Express, because it is billed by duration, which is always cheaper for workflows that wait a long time.
Express, because it suits human-approval processes and can run for several months.
Standard, because it is the only type that can invoke Lambda functions and use Choice states.
Standard, because it can run for up to a year and runs each step once unless your retries say otherwise.
questions.why: Standard workflows can last up to a year and run steps once unless retries say otherwise, which suits long human-approval processes. Express workflows stop at five minutes.

questions.prompt: In AWS Step Functions, what is an execution?
choices: The JSON-based definition of the states and the transitions between them.
One run of a state machine, with its progress and step inputs and outputs stored by the service.
A rule that sends the workflow to a fallback state after retries run out.
A Lambda function that calls the next function directly in a chain.
questions.why: An execution is a single run of a state machine. The state machine is the definition, and a Catch rule is the fallback mechanism.

questions.prompt: A logistics startup links its shipment steps by having each Lambda function call the next one directly, and each function handles its own retries. The third function in the chain crashes partway through. What is the most likely result in the running system?
choices: Shipments are left half-finished with no central record of progress, so nobody can easily see or resume them.
Step Functions automatically resumes the chain from the failed function, using the stored execution history.
Nothing is lost, because the error handling sits in one central place that can restart the chain.
The earlier functions roll back their work on their own, because Lambda functions keep the state between calls.
questions.why: With chained functions there is no central coordinator storing progress, and the error handling is scattered across the code. A midway failure therefore leaves invisible, half-finished work.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you would put a multi-step order process in Step Functions instead of having each Lambda function call the next one, and name one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Step Functions is a managed coordinator. We describe the order process as a state machine, which is a set of named steps and the rules for moving between them, and the service runs each execution for us. It records which steps finished and passes data between them, so our functions stay small and stateless. Retries with backoff and Catch fallbacks, such as refunding the card if the email step keeps failing, are declared in the workflow instead of copied into every function. We also get a visual history of every run, which makes failures easy to find. If functions called each other directly, the error handling would be scattered, a crash midway would lose track of progress, and we would pay for functions waiting on other functions. Tradeoffs: we pay per state transition on Standard workflows, there is a limit on how much data can pass between steps, and Express workflows can repeat a step, so those steps must be safe to run twice.
rubricPoints: Defines Step Functions as a managed orchestrator that runs a state machine of steps.
Explains that the service keeps execution state and passes data between steps, so the workers stay stateless.
Mentions declarative Retry with backoff and Catch fallback handling per step.
Contrasts this with Lambda functions chaining each other directly and the problems that causes.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as per-transition cost, the payload size limit, or Express workflows running a step more than once.
Distinguishes Standard workflows (long-running) from Express workflows (short, high-volume).

suggested.rationale: Building a state machine and watching retries and catch paths route a failing execution is the core skill, and the planned workflow engine would let the learner do exactly that.

lessons.plain: Amazon API Gateway is a managed front door for your application's APIs. An API (application programming interface) is the set of web addresses and rules that other programs use to ask your system for data or actions. Instead of exposing your servers or functions directly, callers knock on API Gateway, which checks who they are, limits how fast they can call, can remember recent answers, and then passes each request to the right backend. Think of a hotel reception desk: guests never wander the corridors; reception checks them in, answers simple questions, and routes requests to housekeeping or the kitchen.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a single partner suddenly sends ten times their normal number of requests to your API, what would you want the front door to do so your other customers still get answers?
lessons.teach:
Amazon API Gateway is a managed service that publishes, secures, throttles and routes API calls to backends you choose. A backend, called an integration, can be an AWS Lambda function (code that runs on demand), an HTTP endpoint such as a load balancer, or another AWS service called directly. API Gateway offers REST APIs (most features, such as response caching and API keys), HTTP APIs (simpler and cheaper, lower latency) and WebSocket APIs (long-lived two-way connections for chat or live updates). A stage is a named deployment, such as dev or prod, so versions can live side by side.

Why it helps resilience: the gateway is run across multiple Availability Zones by AWS, so it is not a single point of failure you manage, and it shields backends. Throttling caps request rates using a token bucket: a bucket holds burst tokens and refills at a steady rate; each request spends one token, and an empty bucket means the caller gets HTTP 429 Too Many Requests. A usage plan attaches rate and quota limits to an API key, so each customer gets their own bucket. Caching (REST APIs) stores responses for a set time so repeated reads skip the backend. Authorizers check identity first, for example via Amazon Cognito or a custom Lambda.

Worked example: a usage plan sets rate 100 requests per second and burst 200. A partner fires 250 requests at once. The bucket holds 200 tokens, so 200 pass and 50 receive 429. One second later the bucket has refilled 100 tokens, so the partner's retries succeed gradually, while other customers, on their own plans, are untouched.

Common mistake: assuming the gateway makes the backend limitless. If the gateway allows more requests than the Lambda concurrency or database can handle, the backend still fails; set gateway limits below backend capacity, or put a queue behind it. In a running system, a missing limit lets one noisy client exhaust shared capacity and cause an outage for everyone.

questions.prompt:
A weather-data company publishes its forecast API through Amazon API Gateway, a managed service that receives API calls and routes them to backends. A hobby customer's usage plan (rate and quota limits attached to that customer's API key) sets a steady rate of 20 requests per second and a burst of 30. Throttling works like a token bucket: the bucket holds up to the burst number of tokens and refills at the rate. The customer's script fires 45 requests at the same instant.

Step 1: The bucket starts full, holding 30 tokens.
Step 2: ______
Step 3: One second later the bucket has refilled 20 tokens, so up to 20 of the customer's retries can now pass, while other customers on their own plans are unaffected.

Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Each request spends one token, so 30 requests pass and the other 15 receive HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
Only 20 requests pass, matching the rate, and the remaining 25 receive HTTP 429
All 45 receive HTTP 429, because the batch is larger than the burst of 30
All 45 pass, because the gateway holds the extra 15 until new tokens arrive
questions.why: The full bucket holds 30 tokens and each request spends one, so 30 succeed and the 15 that find the bucket empty get HTTP 429.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing startup wants seat availability pushed instantly to every open browser. Each browser should keep one long-lived connection open that can both send and receive messages. Which Amazon API Gateway API type fits this requirement?
choices: A WebSocket API, because it keeps long-lived two-way connections open
Any API type with a stage named prod, because stages control connection type
A REST API, because it has the most features, including response caching
An HTTP API, because it is the cheapest option and has the lowest latency
questions.why: WebSocket APIs are built for long-lived, two-way connections such as live updates, while REST and HTTP APIs handle individual request-response calls, and stages only name deployments.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm puts Amazon API Gateway in front of an order service. The gateway's throttling allows 3,000 requests per second, but the order database behind the service can handle only about 600 per second. During a sales spike, traffic reaches 2,500 requests per second. What is the most likely outcome, and what should the architect change?
choices: Caching fixes it automatically, because API Gateway caches every write so the database never sees it
The database is overwhelmed. Set gateway limits below what the backend can handle, or put a queue behind the gateway
The gateway returns HTTP 429 for everything above 600, because it detects the database's limit on its own
Nothing fails, because API Gateway runs across multiple Availability Zones and absorbs the extra load
questions.why: API Gateway does not make the backend limitless, so letting through more requests than the database can serve still breaks it. Limits must sit below backend capacity, or a queue must buffer the excess.

questions.prompt: A mapping SaaS company sells API access to many business customers through Amazon API Gateway. Last week one customer's buggy script flooded the API and slowed it down for everyone. The company wants each customer to have its own separate request-rate and quota limit. Which feature does this?
choices: A usage plan attached to each customer's API key, giving every customer its own token bucket
An authorizer, such as Amazon Cognito, that checks each caller's identity before the request is routed
Response caching, which stores answers for a set time so repeated reads skip the backend
A separate stage, such as dev and prod, so each version of the API runs side by side
questions.why: A usage plan ties rate and quota limits to an API key, so one noisy customer empties only its own bucket and cannot exhaust capacity shared with the others.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Amazon API Gateway does for a backend and how its throttling protects the system, and name one limit or tradeoff they should not overlook.
lessons.modelAnswer: API Gateway is a managed front door: callers hit it instead of our functions or servers, and it authenticates them, applies rate limits, optionally caches responses, and routes each request to an integration such as a Lambda function or an HTTP backend behind a load balancer. AWS runs it across Availability Zones, so we do not operate that layer ourselves. Throttling works like a token bucket: there is a burst size and a steady refill rate, each request uses a token, and when tokens run out the caller gets a 429 and should retry later. With usage plans and API keys, each customer gets their own limits, so one noisy client cannot starve the rest. The tradeoff is that the gateway only shields the backend if its limits sit below what the backend can actually handle; otherwise Lambda concurrency or the database still falls over. Also, features differ: caching and API keys come with REST APIs, while HTTP APIs are cheaper but simpler.
rubricPoints: Defines API Gateway as a managed front door that routes requests to integrations such as Lambda or HTTP backends.
Explains throttling as a burst plus steady rate, with excess requests rejected with 429.
Mentions usage plans and API keys giving per-client limits.
Notes the gateway is managed across Availability Zones, so it is not a self-run single point of failure.
States that gateway limits must sit below backend capacity or the backend can still fail.
Distinguishes REST, HTTP and WebSocket API types or their feature and cost tradeoff.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present a scenario (noisy client, need for caching, cheapest option, backend overload) and ask which gateway feature or API type fits, so reasoning through situations teaches this best.

lessons.plain: Scaling means giving a system more capacity when demand grows. There are two basic ways to do it. Vertical scaling means making one machine bigger: more processor power, more memory. Horizontal scaling means adding more machines of the same size and sharing the work between them. Think of a busy bakery. You can swap your one oven for a giant oven, which is vertical. Or you can install several ordinary ovens side by side, which is horizontal. The giant oven has a size limit, and if it breaks, baking stops. Several ovens can keep growing, and one breaking only slows you down.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app runs on one server that is struggling at lunchtime. Which do you think keeps the app online if a server suddenly fails: replacing it with one much bigger server, or running four servers of the current size? Why?
lessons.teach:
Vertical scaling, also called scaling up, means moving a workload onto a larger server. In AWS terms that usually means changing an EC2 instance (a rented virtual machine) to a bigger instance type with more CPU and memory. Horizontal scaling, also called scaling out, means adding more servers that each run a copy of the workload. A load balancer, which is a service that spreads incoming requests across several servers, sends traffic to all of them. An Auto Scaling group, which is a managed set of identical instances, can add or remove servers automatically based on a metric such as CPU use.

Why does the choice matter for resilience? A single server, however large, is a single point of failure: one component whose failure takes the whole system down. Vertical scaling also has a ceiling, because the biggest available instance type is finite, and resizing usually needs a stop and restart, which means downtime. Horizontal scaling removes the single point of failure, has almost no ceiling, and lets you place servers in different Availability Zones, which are separate data centre groups within a Region.

Worked example. An app on one large instance hits 90 percent CPU each morning. Step one: put it behind a load balancer. Step two: replace the single instance with an Auto Scaling group of two smaller instances in two Availability Zones. Step three: set a rule to add an instance when average CPU passes 60 percent. Step four: at the morning peak the group grows to four instances; at night it shrinks to two, so you pay less. If one zone fails, the other keeps serving.

The common mistake is scaling out an app that is stateful, meaning it keeps user data such as login sessions in a server's own memory. Users then get logged out when the load balancer sends them to a different server. Horizontal scaling works best when servers are stateless and keep shared data in a database or cache.

Vertical scaling still has a place: some databases and legacy apps cannot be split, so making one machine bigger is the practical option.

questions.prompt: A regional concert-ticket website runs on one EC2 instance (a rented virtual machine). It stores each customer's login session in that server's own memory. During ticket releases, memory use hits 95 percent and the site slows. The team plans to switch to horizontal scaling (adding more servers that each run a copy of the app). Step one: [missing]. Step two: place an Application Load Balancer (a service that spreads incoming requests across several servers) in front of the app. Step three: create an Auto Scaling group (a managed set of identical instances that grows or shrinks automatically) with three small instances across three Availability Zones (separate data centre groups within a Region).
