Step four: add a rule that launches another instance when average memory use passes 70 percent. Which action belongs in step one?
choices: Resize the single instance to the largest available instance type so it can absorb the release-day peak
Move login sessions out of each server's memory into a shared cache or database so that any server can handle any user
Turn off the load balancer during ticket releases so that each customer stays connected to the server they started on
Put all three instances in a single Availability Zone so that every server can share the same memory
questions.why: The app is stateful because it keeps sessions in local memory, so it must become stateless by storing sessions in a shared store before scaling out, or users will be logged out when the load balancer routes them to a different server.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's tracking API is slow at peak times. An engineer proposes keeping the same instance type and running six copies of the API behind a load balancer instead of one. What is this approach called?
choices: Horizontal scaling, also called scaling out
Stateful scaling, because each server keeps its own copy
Vertical scaling, also called scaling up
Vertical scaling, because the total amount of CPU goes up
questions.why: Adding more servers that each run a copy of the workload, with a load balancer spreading requests across them, is horizontal scaling (scaling out). Vertical scaling would mean moving to one bigger server.

questions.prompt: A hospital runs an old patient-records database on one EC2 instance. The vendor's software cannot be split across several machines, and it now needs twice the memory. What is the practical scaling option?
choices: Add an Auto Scaling group of four small instances, each running a copy of the database
Put a load balancer in front of the current instance to spread its memory load
Copy the database onto servers in two Availability Zones and send requests to both
Change the instance to a larger instance type with more memory, accepting a stop and restart
questions.why: When an app or database cannot be split across machines, vertical scaling is the practical choice: you move it to a bigger instance type, which usually means a short downtime for the resize.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop moved its web app to the largest instance type AWS offers, so it never runs out of CPU. One afternoon that instance's hardware fails and the whole shop goes offline. What design weakness caused the outage?
choices: The instance was too small, so the next larger instance type would have prevented the outage
The Auto Scaling group added too many instances and overloaded the load balancer
The app was stateless, so the server could not keep running when its hardware failed
The single instance was a single point of failure, so its failure took down the whole system
questions.why: However large it is, one server is a single point of failure. Running several servers across Availability Zones (scaling out) would keep the shop serving when one of them fails.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between horizontal and vertical scaling, why horizontal scaling usually gives better resilience, and name one limit or tradeoff of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Vertical scaling means making one server bigger, for example moving to an instance type with more CPU and memory. Horizontal scaling means adding more servers of the same kind behind a load balancer, often managed by an Auto Scaling group that adds and removes them based on load. Horizontal scaling is usually more resilient because there is no single server whose failure stops everything, and you can spread servers across Availability Zones. It also grows almost without limit and can shrink at quiet times to save money. Its tradeoff is that the application should be stateless; if sessions live in one server's memory, users break when traffic moves between servers. Vertical scaling is simple and suits apps that cannot be split, like some databases, but it hits a size ceiling, usually needs a restart, and leaves a single point of failure.
rubricPoints: Vertical scaling makes one server bigger; horizontal scaling adds more servers.
Horizontal scaling uses a load balancer and often an Auto Scaling group to share and adjust work.
A single scaled-up server remains a single point of failure and has a size ceiling.
Horizontal scaling across Availability Zones improves availability and can scale in to cut cost.
Horizontal scaling needs stateless servers or externally stored state.
Vertical scaling still fits workloads that cannot be split, such as some databases or legacy apps.

suggested.rationale: Working a capacity-exhaustion incident makes the learner decide between adding servers and enlarging one, which is exactly the tradeoff this objective tests.

lessons.plain: A container is a sealed lunchbox for software: the program plus everything it needs to run, packed so it behaves the same on any machine. Containers start fast and many fit on one server. Once you have dozens or hundreds, you need a manager that decides where each one runs, restarts any that crash, and keeps the right number alive. That manager is called an orchestrator. On AWS, Amazon ECS is Amazon's own simpler orchestrator. Amazon EKS runs Kubernetes, the popular open-source orchestrator, for teams that already use it or want to move their setup between providers.
lessons.guessPrompt: You run three identical copies of a web app in containers, and one server suddenly dies, taking one copy with it. What would you want an automatic manager to do next, and why does it matter that the three copies were on different servers?
lessons.teach:
A container is an application packaged with its libraries and runtime, built from a read-only template called an image, and run as an isolated process that shares the host's operating system kernel. Because it carries no full operating system, it starts in seconds and many fit on one server. Use containers when the same artifact must run identically on a laptop and in production. They also suit an app split into small services that deploy independently, and workloads you want to pack densely onto servers. They fit poorly for a short event-triggered function or an app tied to one full operating-system install.

Running one container is easy. Running hundreds is not. An orchestrator is software that places each container on a server, restarts failures, keeps a requested count running, and spreads copies across Availability Zones (isolated data-centre groups inside a Region). The servers it manages form a cluster.

Amazon ECS (Elastic Container Service) is AWS's native orchestrator. A task definition describes your containers. A running copy is a task. A service keeps a chosen number of tasks alive, usually behind a load balancer. Amazon EKS (Elastic Kubernetes Service) runs Kubernetes, the open-source orchestrator. AWS operates its control plane, the brain that stores desired state and schedules work. Its smallest unit is a pod, one or more containers scheduled together.

Worked example: a team wants three copies of an API across two zones. First, they build an image. Second, they create an ECS service with a desired count of 3 spread across both zones. Third, one zone fails and a task dies. Fourth, the service sees only 2 healthy tasks and launches a replacement in the surviving zone, with no human involved.

Choosing: pick ECS for the simplest AWS-native path. Pick EKS when the team already runs Kubernetes, needs its tooling, or wants portability to other clouds or on-premises.

Common mistake: choosing EKS just because Kubernetes is popular. You inherit more concepts and version upgrades, while exam answers usually favour the least operational overhead that meets the requirement. Remember also that a single task in one zone is still a single point of failure.

questions.prompt:
A freight-tracking company is deciding how to run its new system. Here is its reasoning, with one step missing.

Step 1: The system is split into six small services that each team deploys on its own schedule, and the same image must behave identically on developer laptops and in production. So containers are a good fit.

Step 2: Nobody on the team has used Kubernetes. There is no plan to run the system outside AWS, and the requirement asks for the least operational overhead.

Step 3: ???

Step 4: For each service, they ask the orchestrator to keep 2 running copies spread across two Availability Zones (isolated data-centre groups), so that losing one zone does not take the service down.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Skip an orchestrator and run each container by hand on one server, because six services is a small number.
Choose Amazon ECS, because it is the simplest AWS-native orchestrator and nothing here needs Kubernetes tooling or portability.
Choose Amazon EKS, because AWS operates its control plane, so it carries no extra concepts or upgrades for the team.
Choose Amazon EKS, because Kubernetes is the most popular orchestrator and the team should learn it now.
questions.why: With no Kubernetes experience, no portability need and a least-overhead requirement, the simplest AWS-native orchestrator, ECS, meets the need without the extra concepts and version upgrades EKS brings.

questions.prompt: An engineer moving to a company that runs Amazon EKS sees the word "pod" everywhere. In Kubernetes, what is a pod?
choices: The full set of servers the orchestrator manages
The read-only template a container is built from
The smallest schedulable unit: one or more containers scheduled together
The control plane that stores desired state and schedules work
questions.why: A pod is Kubernetes' smallest unit, one or more containers that are scheduled together; the servers form the cluster, the template is the image, and the brain is the control plane.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing site needs a piece of code that runs for about two seconds each time a user uploads a picture, to create a thumbnail, and sits idle otherwise. Based on when containers fit well and poorly, how should you judge using an orchestrated container service for this?
choices: A strong fit, because any workload becomes resilient once it runs in a container
A strong fit, because containers start in seconds and pack densely onto servers
A poor fit, because a short, event-triggered function is a case where containers suit poorly
A good fit only if the team picks Amazon EKS instead of Amazon ECS
questions.why: A brief piece of code triggered by an event is exactly the kind of workload that fits containers poorly, so a container service is not the natural choice here.

questions.prompt: A booking company runs its checkout API as an Amazon ECS service with a desired count of 1, and that one task sits in a single Availability Zone. An architect says the design still has a single point of failure. Which change removes it?
choices: Migrate the service to Amazon EKS, since Kubernetes handles failures better
Rebuild the image so the container carries a full operating system
Raise the desired count to at least 2 and spread the tasks across two or more Availability Zones
Move the single task onto a larger, more powerful server in the same zone
questions.why: One task in one zone fails along with that zone; keeping several copies across zones lets the service keep running and replace lost tasks in a surviving zone.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we should put our services in containers at all, and whether to use ECS or EKS. Explain it in your own words, including one limit of containers and the tradeoff between the two orchestrators.
lessons.modelAnswer: A container bundles our app with its dependencies, so the image we test is exactly what runs in production. Containers start quickly and pack many per server. They aren't ideal for tiny event-triggered jobs, though, and they don't make an app resilient by themselves. Resilience comes from an orchestrator, which keeps a set number of copies running, replaces failed ones, and spreads them across Availability Zones. With one copy, we still have a single point of failure. ECS is AWS's own orchestrator: fewer concepts and less to operate, but it ties us to AWS. EKS runs Kubernetes with AWS managing the control plane. It gives us the standard tooling and portability, but costs more learning and more upgrade work. Since we're AWS-only and don't know Kubernetes, I'd pick ECS. If we already ran Kubernetes elsewhere, EKS would make sense.
rubricPoints: Defines a container as an app packaged with its dependencies from an image, sharing the host kernel.
States when containers fit well and names at least one case where they fit poorly.
Explains that an orchestrator places, restarts, and maintains a desired count of containers across Availability Zones.
Distinguishes ECS as the simpler AWS-native option from EKS as managed Kubernetes for existing Kubernetes users or portability.
Names the tradeoff that EKS brings more operational complexity in exchange for portability and ecosystem.
Notes that resilience requires multiple copies across zones, not just using containers.

suggested.rationale: No existing mission or planned engine runs container orchestration, and the exam skill is reasoning through a scenario to pick ECS or EKS with the least operational overhead, so a worked exam-style situation adds the most.

lessons.plain: Serverless means you run your code without owning, patching or sizing any servers; the cloud provider handles the machines and charges you for the work done. AWS Lambda is a function service: you hand it a small piece of code, and it runs that code each time an event arrives, then stops. AWS Fargate runs containers, which are packaged applications, without you managing the virtual machines underneath. Think of Lambda as a taxi you hail for each short trip, and Fargate as a rental car you keep while you need it, with no garage to look after.
lessons.guessPrompt: A job converts uploaded videos and usually takes about 40 minutes per file. Would you run it as a short-lived function that starts on each upload, or as a container that keeps running until the work is done? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Lambda is event-driven function compute. An event (a file landing in storage, an API request, a message on a queue) triggers your function. Lambda starts an execution environment, runs your code, and bills you per request and per millisecond of run time. With no traffic it scales to zero and costs nothing. Its limits matter: a single invocation can run at most 15 minutes, a cold start (the delay while a new environment is created) adds latency, and concurrency, meaning how many copies run at once, is capped by an account quota, so a surge can be throttled.

AWS Fargate is serverless compute for containers. You describe a task, which is one or more containers plus the CPU and memory they need, and Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS (the container orchestrators) run it on Fargate. You never pick or patch the host machines. You pay per second for the CPU and memory the task reserves while it runs, whether busy or idle. There is no 15-minute ceiling, so it suits long-running services, long batch jobs, and existing applications already packaged as containers.

Worked example: a fleet company has two needs. First, generate a thumbnail when a driver uploads a photo. Trace it: an event per upload, a task of a few seconds, bursty traffic with quiet nights. Short, event-triggered, idle often, so Lambda fits and costs nothing overnight. Second, a route-optimisation job that runs for 90 minutes each night. Trace it: 90 minutes exceeds Lambda's 15-minute limit, so Lambda is ruled out; Fargate runs the container to completion with no servers to manage.

Common mistake: treating serverless as limitless. Picking Lambda for work that can exceed 15 minutes means invocations are killed partway, leaving half-finished work and retries in a running system. The reverse mistake is running a steady, always-busy workload on Lambda when a constantly running Fargate service would be simpler and often cheaper. Both remove server management; the deciding factors are run duration, traffic shape, and how the code is packaged.

questions.prompt: A podcast company wants to run a job that cleans up audio after each episode is uploaded. Most runs take about 8 minutes, but long episodes push the job to 25 minutes. The team is choosing between AWS Lambda (event-driven function compute that bills per request and per millisecond) and AWS Fargate (serverless compute that runs containers). Step 1: Each upload is an event, so the job is event-triggered. Step 2: Uploads are occasional, so the compute sits idle much of the time. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The team packages the job as a container task and runs it on Fargate, which has no 15-minute ceiling, so even the 25-minute runs finish with no servers to manage. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Lambda's cold start delay would add about 25 minutes to each long run, so Lambda is too slow for this job and must be ruled out.
The longest runs reach 25 minutes, which is past Lambda's 15-minute limit per invocation, so those runs would be killed partway and Lambda is ruled out.
The typical run of 8 minutes is under Lambda's 15-minute limit, so Lambda fits, and the rare long runs will simply be retried until they succeed.
Because the compute is idle often, Lambda's ability to scale to zero makes it the cheapest option, so the job should stay on Lambda.
questions.why: You have to design for the longest run, not the typical one, and a 25-minute run goes past Lambda's 15-minute per-invocation limit, so Lambda is ruled out.

questions.prompt: In AWS Lambda, what is a cold start?
choices: The account quota that limits how many copies of a function can run at the same time.
The extra delay while Lambda creates a new execution environment before your code runs.
The period overnight when a function receives no traffic and costs nothing.
The 15-minute cap on how long one invocation can run before it is stopped.
questions.why: A cold start is the added latency that comes from creating a new execution environment. The 15-minute cap, the concurrency quota and scaling to zero are separate ideas.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs an inventory-sync service that processes requests steadily all day and is almost never idle. The code is already packaged as a container image. The team wants to stop managing servers. Which option fits best?
choices: Run it as a constantly running service on AWS Fargate, because the workload is steady, always busy and already in a container.
Run it on AWS Lambda, because scaling to zero will remove the cost during its busy hours.
Run it on AWS Fargate only at night, because Fargate cannot run long-running services.
Run it on AWS Lambda, because any serverless choice is limitless and Lambda always costs less.
questions.why: A steady, always-busy workload that is already packaged as a container is simpler and often cheaper as a constantly running Fargate service, and scaling to zero gives no saving when there is never any idle time.

questions.prompt: A startup runs a Fargate task that reserves 2 vCPU and 4 GB of memory around the clock. Its only job is to handle occasional webhook calls that each take about 2 seconds, and it sits idle most of the day. What is the main problem with this design, and what fits better?
choices: Fargate requires the team to patch the host machines. Lambda would remove that patching work.
Fargate kills tasks after 15 minutes, so the service keeps restarting. Lambda would avoid that.
Fargate tasks cannot be triggered by events, so the webhooks are lost. A queue in front of Fargate would fix it.
Fargate bills for the reserved CPU and memory even while idle. Lambda would cost nothing between calls.
questions.why: Fargate charges per second for the resources a task reserves, whether it is busy or idle. Short, occasional, event-triggered work suits Lambda, which scales to zero and costs nothing when there is no traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you decide between AWS Lambda and AWS Fargate for a new workload, and name at least one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both are serverless, so neither makes us manage or patch servers; the choice is about the shape of the work. Lambda runs a function per event and bills per request and millisecond, scaling to zero when idle, so it is ideal for short, bursty, event-triggered tasks like reacting to an upload or a queue message. Its tradeoffs are a hard 15-minute limit per invocation, cold-start latency, and a concurrency quota that can throttle us during surges. Fargate runs containers for ECS or EKS and bills per second for reserved CPU and memory while the task runs, so it suits long-running services, jobs over 15 minutes, and apps already in containers. Its tradeoff is that we pay while tasks run even if idle, and it does not scale to zero the way Lambda does. Steady, constant load often favours Fargate on cost.
rubricPoints: States that both remove server management from the user.
Says Lambda suits short, event-driven, bursty work and scales to zero.
Names Lambda's 15-minute limit, cold starts, or concurrency quota as a limit.
Says Fargate runs containers with no time ceiling, suiting long-running or containerised workloads.
Notes Fargate bills for reserved resources while tasks run, so idle time still costs.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reading a requirement's duration, traffic shape and packaging and choosing the right compute, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios.

lessons.plain: Migrating an application into containers means taking a program that already runs on a server and repackaging it so it runs inside a container. A container is a sealed box that holds the program plus everything it needs: libraries, runtime and settings. It runs the same way on a laptop, a test server or the cloud. Think of moving house with shipping containers: you pack once, and any truck or ship can carry the box without unpacking it. The hard part is not the packing. It is finding what the application quietly kept on its old server, such as files and logged-in users, and moving that somewhere safer.
lessons.guessPrompt: An old web application saves uploaded photos to the server's own hard disk. You package it into a container, and the platform later replaces that container with a fresh copy. What do you think happens to the photos, and where would you put them instead?
lessons.teach:
Migrating into containers means building a container image of an existing application and running it on a container platform. A container image is a read-only package holding the code, its runtime and its libraries. A running container is started from that image. A recipe file, often called a Dockerfile, lists the steps to build the image. Built images are stored in a registry, which is a catalogue of images. On AWS this is Amazon ECR (Elastic Container Registry), a managed private registry. Orchestrators such as Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS then start and replace containers. AWS App2Container is a tool that inspects a running Java or .NET application and generates a starting image and deployment files for it.

This works because containers are disposable and identical. Any copy can be killed and replaced, and you can run many copies behind a load balancer. That only holds if nothing important lives inside the container. So a migration moves state out. User sessions go to a shared store such as Amazon ElastiCache or DynamoDB. Uploaded files go to object storage (Amazon S3) or a shared file system (Amazon EFS). Settings and passwords are passed in from outside, for example through Secrets Manager or Parameter Store. Logs are written to standard output so the platform can collect them.

Here is a worked example. A shop app runs on one virtual machine. It keeps sessions in memory, writes invoices to its local disk and reads a database password from a file. Step 1: write a Dockerfile that builds the app image. Step 2: push the image to ECR. Step 3: move sessions to ElastiCache. Step 4: write invoices to S3. Step 5: inject the password from Secrets Manager. Step 6: run three copies across Availability Zones behind a load balancer. If one copy dies, a replacement starts and no user notices.

A common mistake is packing the app as it is, with local files and in-memory sessions. When the platform replaces a container, those files vanish and users are logged out. The service looks containerized but is still a single point of failure for its own data.

questions.prompt: A city library runs its room-booking app, written in .NET, on one virtual machine. The app keeps login sessions in memory, saves members' uploaded ID-card scans to a folder on the local disk, reads an API key from a config file and writes logs to a local log file. The team is moving it into containers so that any copy can be killed and replaced without losing anything. So far they have: (a) written a Dockerfile and built the app image; (b) pushed the image to Amazon ECR, a managed private registry; (c) moved sessions to DynamoDB, a shared store; (d) passed the API key in from Parameter Store at runtime; (e) changed logging to write to standard output; (f) the missing step; (g) run four copies across two Availability Zones behind a load balancer. What should step (f) be?
choices: Keep saving the ID-card scans to the local folder inside each container, because every copy has its own disk anyway.
Write the ID-card scans to object storage such as Amazon S3, or a shared file system such as Amazon EFS.
Store the ID-card scans in Secrets Manager, because they are sensitive and secrets belong there.
Copy the existing ID-card scans into the image during the Dockerfile build so every container starts with them.
questions.why: Uploaded files are state, so they must leave the disposable container and go to shared storage like S3 or EFS, where every copy can reach them and they survive when a container is replaced.

questions.prompt: In a container migration, what is a container registry such as Amazon ECR?
choices: An orchestrator that starts, stops and replaces running containers.
A shared store that holds user sessions so any container can serve any user.
The recipe file that lists the steps used to build a container image.
A catalogue that stores built container images so a platform can pull them and start containers.
questions.why: A registry is a catalogue of images; the Dockerfile is the recipe, ECS or EKS are orchestrators, and a session store is a separate piece.

questions.prompt: A travel agency packed its booking app into a container exactly as it was and runs it on Amazon ECS. After the platform replaces a failed container, customers are logged out and some generated PDF itineraries are missing. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Too many copies were running behind the load balancer at the same time.
Sessions were kept in memory and PDFs were written to the container's local disk, so both vanished with the container.
The image was stored in Amazon ECR instead of being kept on the virtual machine.
Logs were written to standard output, so the platform deleted the files.
questions.why: State left inside a container is lost when the container is replaced, so in-memory sessions and local files disappear and the service is still a single point of failure for its own data.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm has a running Java application on a server and wants a tool that inspects it and generates a starting container image and deployment files, rather than writing everything by hand. Which AWS tool fits?
choices: AWS App2Container
Amazon ECR
AWS Secrets Manager
Amazon ElastiCache
questions.why: App2Container inspects a running Java or .NET application and generates a starting image and deployment files; the others store images, sessions or secrets.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, "Containerizing our app is just putting it in a Docker image." Explain in your own words what else a migration has to do, and name one limit or tradeoff of moving an existing application into containers.
lessons.modelAnswer: Building the image is the easy part. An image packages the app with its runtime and libraries. We store it in a registry like Amazon ECR, and an orchestrator like ECS or EKS runs copies of it. The real work is making those copies disposable. Anything the app kept on its own server has to move out. Sessions go to a shared cache or database. Files go to S3 or EFS. Secrets and config get injected from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and logs go to standard output. Once that is done, we can run several copies across Availability Zones, and one can die without losing data. The tradeoff is effort and risk. Refactoring state out takes changes and testing. If we skip it and just lift and shift, we get containers that still lose files and sessions whenever they restart, so we gain packaging but not resilience.
rubricPoints: Defines a container image and the registry where images are stored, such as Amazon ECR.
States that containers must be disposable, so state has to move outside them.
Names where state goes: sessions to a shared store, files to S3 or EFS, secrets injected from outside.
Explains that disposable copies allow several replicas across Availability Zones for resilience.
Names a tradeoff, such as refactoring effort, or a lift and shift that loses data on restart.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present a legacy app with hidden local state and ask which changes make it safe to containerize, so reasoning through such scenarios adds the most.

lessons.plain: A cache is a short-term copy of data kept somewhere faster or closer than the original, so repeat requests skip the slow trip. Think of a busy coffee shop that brews a big pot of the house blend ahead of the morning rush instead of grinding beans for every order. Most customers get served instantly. Occasionally the pot runs out or goes stale and must be remade. Edge caching does the same thing geographically. Copies of web content sit on servers in many cities, so a visitor is served from nearby instead of from your one central server far away.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website stores one popular photo on a single server in Virginia, and thousands of people in Tokyo view it every minute. If a copy were kept on a server in Tokyo, what two things would improve, and what new problem might appear when the photo is updated?
lessons.teach:
A cache is a fast store that keeps copies of data so later requests skip slower work. A cache hit means the copy was found. A cache miss means the request goes to the origin, the real source such as a database or web server. Caching works because many requests ask for the same thing, and memory or a nearby server answers far faster than recomputing the result or crossing the world.

Two layers matter here. An in-memory cache sits beside your application and holds results from the database. Amazon ElastiCache is an example: it is a managed service running Redis or Memcached, two popular in-memory data stores. Edge caching uses a content delivery network (CDN). A CDN is a fleet of servers spread across many cities, called edge locations. Amazon CloudFront is the AWS CDN. Each user is routed to a nearby edge, which serves the cached copy or forwards a miss to your origin.

There are two common ways to fill a cache. Lazy loading, also called cache-aside, stores an item only after a miss. The cache then holds only data people actually ask for, but the first read of each item is slow. Write-through updates the cache every time the database is written. Reads stay fresh, but you may store data nobody reads. A TTL (time to live) is how long a copy is kept before it expires and is fetched again. It sets the upper limit on how stale data can get.

Worked example: a product image is cached in CloudFront with a 24-hour TTL. A user in Paris requests it. The Paris edge misses, fetches the image from the origin (an S3 storage bucket), stores it and returns it. The next 10,000 Paris users all get hits, so the origin serves one request instead of 10,001. If the image changes, users may see the old one for up to a day, unless you send an invalidation, which is a request telling the CDN to drop its copy.

One common mistake is setting long TTLs on data that must always be current, such as account balances. Another is letting many items expire at the same moment. Every request then misses together and floods the database, a failure called a cache stampede. Done well, caching also makes the system more resilient, because the origin carries less load and can survive traffic spikes.

questions.prompt: A recipe website puts an in-memory cache (Amazon ElastiCache) beside its application and fills it by lazy loading (cache-aside). Each cached item has a 10-minute TTL. Trace one request for recipe #42 when the cache is empty. Step 1: the request arrives and the application checks the cache for recipe #42. Step 2: the item is not there, so this is a cache miss. Step 3: the application queries the database (the origin) and gets the recipe. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the application returns the recipe to the user. Step 6: another user asks for recipe #42 eight minutes later and gets a cache hit. What is Step 4?
choices: Send an invalidation so the cache drops any old copy of recipe #42
Wait for the next database write to the recipe, which will copy it into the cache
Store the recipe in the cache with a 10-minute TTL
Write the recipe back into the database so the next read is faster
questions.why: Lazy loading stores an item in the cache right after a miss, and that stored copy is what turns the request eight minutes later into a hit.

questions.prompt: A game studio runs its servers in one AWS Region in the United States. Players in Asia and Europe complain that large map files download slowly, mostly because the files travel a long distance. Which caching approach best addresses this?
choices: Serve the files through a CDN such as Amazon CloudFront, so nearby edge locations hold cached copies
Add an in-memory cache such as ElastiCache beside the application servers in the US Region
Switch the database to write-through caching so map files stay fresh
Set a very short TTL on the map files so they are fetched more often
questions.why: The slowness comes from distance, and a CDN answers from an edge location near each player, while an in-memory cache beside the app is still far away from them.

questions.prompt: A weather site caches its forecast page in a CDN with a 15-minute TTL. The forecast at the origin is updated, and nobody sends an invalidation. What is the longest time a user could see the old forecast?
choices: Up to 15 minutes
Exactly 15 minutes for every user, every time
None, because the CDN always checks the origin before answering
Until the origin server is restarted
questions.why: The TTL sets the upper limit on staleness, so a cached copy can be served for at most 15 minutes before it expires and is fetched again.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing app loads 50,000 event listings into its cache at 9:00, all with the same 60-minute TTL. At exactly 10:00, database load jumps sharply and pages slow down. What is this failure called?
choices: Write-through
Cache hit
Cache stampede
Invalidation
questions.why: All the items expired at the same moment, so every request missed together and flooded the database, which is a cache stampede.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use caching to make a global web app faster and more resilient, covering both an in-memory cache and a CDN, and name the main tradeoff you have to manage.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd cache at two layers. For static content like images, scripts and pages that rarely change, I'd put a CDN such as CloudFront in front of the origin. Users are then served from a nearby edge location, which cuts latency, and most requests never reach our servers. For repeated database reads, I'd add an in-memory cache like ElastiCache. Using lazy loading, the app checks the cache first and only queries the database on a miss, then stores the result. Write-through is the alternative if reads must stay fresh. Both layers lower origin load, so the system rides out spikes better. The tradeoff is freshness against speed. A long TTL gives more hits but staler data, so must-be-current data gets short TTLs or no caching. I'd also stagger expiries and know how to invalidate CDN copies, so we avoid stampedes and stale content after an update.
rubricPoints: Defines a cache as a fast copy and distinguishes a hit from a miss that goes to the origin.
Describes a CDN serving content from edge locations near users.
Describes an in-memory cache such as ElastiCache sitting in front of a database.
Contrasts lazy loading with write-through.
Names the staleness-versus-speed tradeoff controlled by TTL and invalidation.
Mentions reduced origin load as a resilience benefit, or the risk of a cache stampede.

suggested.rationale: The cache stampede incident has the learner work through cache misses, expiry and origin overload in a live scenario, which reinforces why TTL and fill strategy matter.

lessons.plain: A read replica is an automatically updated copy of a database that only answers questions (reads) and never accepts changes (writes). The main database, called the primary, still handles every write, then sends those changes on to the copies. Picture a busy library with one head librarian. Instead of everyone queuing for her, you open extra help desks holding copies of the catalogue that can answer lookups. Only she can change the master catalogue. The desks get her updates a moment later, so for a short time a copy can be slightly behind.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your database is overloaded, and almost all of the traffic is people looking things up rather than saving anything new. Without buying a bigger server, how could you spread that load out, and what new problem might your fix create?
lessons.teach:
A read replica is a read-only copy of a database that the primary keeps updated through replication, which means copying each change from one database to another. In AWS, Amazon RDS and Amazon Aurora (managed relational database services) let you add replicas, and each replica has its own connection address, called an endpoint. The specific problem replicas solve is a read-heavy workload, where most queries only fetch data. That read traffic can overload the primary even though writes are light.

Replicas work because reads do not change anything, so any up-to-date copy can answer them. Replication is usually asynchronous, meaning the primary confirms a write to the application without waiting for the replicas to receive it. That keeps writes fast. The cost is replica lag, the delay before a change shows up on a replica. Data on a replica is therefore eventually consistent: it will match the primary soon, but not instantly.

Worked example: a shop's primary database runs at 90% CPU, and 80% of its queries come from product browsing and reports. You add two replicas and send browsing and reports to the replica endpoints. Checkout writes still go to the primary, and its CPU falls to about 30%. Now trace a single order. A customer places it, and the primary saves it at time 0. It reaches the replicas at 0.5 seconds. If the customer's "my orders" page reads from a replica at 0.2 seconds, the order is missing. Pages that must show a user's own write should read from the primary.

A common mistake is treating replicas as a fix for write load or for high availability. Every write still lands on the one primary, so replicas add no write capacity. For availability, RDS Multi-AZ keeps a standby copy in another Availability Zone (a separate data centre). Its replication is synchronous, meaning each write is confirmed only after the standby has it, and failover to it is automatic. A replica can be promoted to become a primary, but recent writes may be lost to lag. In a running system, ignoring lag shows users stale or missing data.

questions.prompt: A university runs its course-registration app on Amazon RDS. The primary database sits at 85% CPU. Writes are light, and about 70% of queries are students browsing the course catalogue and staff running enrolment reports. Step 1: Recognise this as a read-heavy workload, where most queries only fetch data, so read replicas fit. Step 2: Add three read replicas and point catalogue browsing and enrolment reports at the replica endpoints. Registration writes keep going to the primary, and its CPU drops to about 35%. Step 3: After a student registers for a course, a page shows "Your timetable", which must include the course they just added. Replication to the replicas takes about 0.4 seconds, and the timetable page loads about 0.1 seconds after the registration is saved. What should Step 3 be?
choices: Read the timetable page from a replica endpoint, because replicas receive each change before the primary confirms the write
Read the timetable page from the primary endpoint, because the replicas may not have the new registration yet
Read the timetable page from any replica endpoint, because a 0.4-second lag is too short for students to notice
Spread the registration writes across the three replicas so the timetable data is already on whichever replica the page reads
questions.why: The page loads at 0.1 seconds, but the change reaches the replicas at 0.4 seconds, so a replica would show a timetable missing the new course. A page that must show the user's own write should read from the primary.

questions.prompt: A team says their read replicas use asynchronous replication. What does that mean for an application writing to the primary?
choices: The primary confirms the write without waiting for replicas, so a change can take a short time to appear on them
The primary sends changes to replicas only when a replica is promoted to become the primary
The primary confirms each write only after every replica has stored it, so replicas are always identical to the primary
The replicas accept writes on their own and send them back to the primary on a schedule
questions.why: Asynchronous replication means the primary confirms writes without waiting for the replicas. That keeps writes fast, but it causes replica lag, so replica data is only eventually consistent.

questions.prompt: A fleet-tracking company's RDS primary is overloaded. 85% of its queries are GPS updates inserting new location rows, and only 15% are reads. An engineer proposes adding four read replicas. What is the most accurate assessment?
choices: It will relieve the primary, because each replica takes a share of the location inserts
It will relieve the primary, because replicas also give automatic failover to another Availability Zone
It will not relieve the primary, because replicas only help if the application stops writing during busy periods
It will not relieve the primary much, because every write still lands on the primary and replicas add no write capacity
questions.why: Replicas only take read traffic. This workload is write-heavy, and every write still goes to the single primary, so adding replicas does not remove the load.

questions.prompt: A payments service on Amazon RDS needs automatic failover if its Availability Zone (a separate data centre) fails. It must not lose any write that was already confirmed to the application. Which design meets this requirement?
choices: Add a read replica in another Availability Zone and promote it when the primary fails
Send all reads to replica endpoints so the primary has spare capacity to survive a failure
Add two read replicas in the same Availability Zone so one is always ready to answer reads
Enable RDS Multi-AZ, which keeps a synchronously updated standby in another Availability Zone and fails over automatically
questions.why: With Multi-AZ, a write is confirmed only after the standby has it, and failover is automatic. Promoting a replica is a manual step, and recent writes can be lost to replica lag.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what problem a read replica solves and when you would add one. Name at least one limit or tradeoff, such as lag or what replicas do not fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: A read replica is a read-only copy of our database that the primary keeps updated in the background. We add replicas when the database is struggling because of reads, like browsing, searches or reports, and not because of writes. We point that read traffic at the replica endpoints, so the primary has spare capacity for writes. The tradeoff is that replication is usually asynchronous, so replicas lag a little behind. Anything that must show a user what they just saved should read from the primary, or the user might see old data. Replicas also do nothing for write load, because every write still goes to the single primary. They are not our main high-availability plan either. A Multi-AZ standby is kept in sync on every write and fails over automatically. Promoting a replica takes deliberate action and can lose the last few writes.
rubricPoints: A read replica is a read-only copy kept updated from the primary.
It solves read-heavy load by moving reads off the primary.
Replication is usually asynchronous, so replicas lag and can return stale data.
Writes, and reads that must see the latest data, still go to the primary.
Replicas do not add write capacity.
Replicas are not a substitute for a synchronous Multi-AZ standby with automatic failover.

suggested.rationale: In this mission the learner investigates stale data caused by replica lag, which is the core tradeoff of using read replicas.

lessons.plain: Cloud storage comes in three basic shapes. Block storage is like a blank hard drive plugged into one computer: that computer formats it and quickly reads or changes tiny pieces anywhere on it. File storage is like a shared office network drive: many computers see the same folders and files at the same time. Object storage is like a coat check: you hand over a whole item, get a ticket (a key), and later fetch the whole item back with that ticket. You don't alter part of it in place. Choosing well means asking who needs the data, how many machines need it at once, and whether they change small parts or whole items.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website stores millions of user-uploaded photos that are written once and then viewed many times by browsers. Should those photos live on a disk attached to one server, a shared network drive, or a store where each photo is saved whole under a unique name? Why?
lessons.teach:
Block storage gives one server a raw virtual disk. The operating system puts its own file system on it and can read or rewrite any small chunk, called a block, with very low delay. On AWS this is Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store). It is a network-attached virtual disk that lives in one Availability Zone, meaning one isolated group of data centers inside a Region, and it normally attaches to one instance at a time. Instance store is a faster disk built into the host machine, but it loses its data when the instance stops. Use block storage for boot volumes and for databases you run yourself.

File storage is a shared file system reached over a network protocol such as NFS (common on Linux) or SMB (common on Windows). It has folders, permissions and file locking, and many servers can mount it at once. Amazon EFS (Elastic File System) serves Linux clients and spans multiple Availability Zones. Amazon FSx provides managed file systems for other needs, such as Windows file shares or Lustre for high-performance computing.

Object storage keeps each item whole, with a unique key and descriptive metadata, behind a web (HTTP) interface. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) holds an effectively unlimited amount of data, copies it across Availability Zones, and is the cheapest per gigabyte. To change an object, you replace the whole thing rather than editing bytes in place.

Why this works: each shape trades sharing and scale against fine-grained speed. Block storage is fastest for one server. File storage adds sharing. Object storage adds massive scale and low cost.

Worked example, a photo-sharing site. First, the self-managed database needs fast, small random writes from one host, so it goes on EBS. Second, ten web servers must all read and write the same shared content folder, so that goes on EFS. Third, millions of photos are written once and read often, so they go in S3.

A common mistake is putting data that many instances must share on EBS. The volume is tied to one Availability Zone and usually one instance. If that instance or zone fails, the other servers lose the data, and you have created a single point of failure.

questions.prompt: A language-learning company runs a video course platform on AWS. Its architect is choosing storage step by step. Step 1: each of the five Linux transcoding servers needs a boot volume, a raw disk the operating system formats and starts from, so each server gets its own Amazon EBS volume (block storage). Step 2: about 60,000 finished lesson videos are written once, never edited, and then streamed to students over the web (HTTP) many times. They must be kept cheaply and must survive the loss of an Availability Zone. Step 2 is missing. Step 3: all five transcoding servers must read and write the same folder of half-finished files at the same time over NFS, so that folder goes on Amazon EFS (shared file storage). Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Put the videos on instance store, because the disk built into the host is the fastest option available
Put the videos on one large EBS volume, because block storage gives the lowest delay for reading files
Put the videos on Amazon EFS, because many students need to reach the same files at once
Put the videos in Amazon S3, because write-once items served over HTTP at large scale fit object storage at the lowest cost per gigabyte
questions.why: The videos are whole items that are never edited and are served over HTTP, and they must be cheap and survive an Availability Zone failure, which matches object storage (S3): it scales almost without limit, copies data across Availability Zones, and costs the least per gigabyte.

questions.prompt: Which description fits object storage, such as Amazon S3?
choices: A raw virtual disk that one server formats with its own file system and edits in small chunks
A very fast disk built into the host machine that loses its data when the instance stops
A shared folder tree with permissions and file locking that many servers mount over NFS or SMB
Each item is stored whole with a unique key and metadata, is reached over HTTP, and is changed by replacing the entire item
questions.why: Object storage keeps each item whole under a unique key with metadata behind an HTTP interface, and you update an object by replacing all of it rather than editing bytes in place.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm moves to AWS. Its 25 Windows desktops must all open the same set of spreadsheets through an ordinary Windows network share using the SMB protocol, with folder permissions and file locking so two people cannot overwrite the same file at once. Which storage fits best?
choices: Amazon S3, with each spreadsheet stored as an object
Amazon FSx, providing a managed Windows file share
Instance store on a Windows server
Amazon EBS, attached to a single Windows server
questions.why: The need is shared file storage over SMB with folders, permissions and locking, and Amazon FSx is the managed file system service that covers Windows file shares.

questions.prompt: A small retailer runs three web servers in different Availability Zones. Customer-uploaded receipts are saved to a single Amazon EBS volume attached to the first web server, and the other two servers reach the receipts through that first server. What is the main resilience problem with this design?
choices: EBS cannot hold files that customers upload, because it only stores whole objects addressed by key
EBS loses all its data whenever the instance stops, so the receipts disappear after any reboot
The EBS volume lives in one Availability Zone and is attached to one instance, so if that instance or zone fails the other servers lose access to the receipts, creating a single point of failure
EBS is the most expensive storage per gigabyte, so the design is costly but otherwise fully resilient
questions.why: An EBS volume is tied to one Availability Zone and usually one instance, so putting shared data on it makes that one instance and zone a single point of failure; shared file storage like EFS or object storage like S3 would remove it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between object, file and block storage for a new workload, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: I ask three questions: how many servers need the data at once, do they change small pieces or whole items, and how much data is there. If one server needs fast, low-latency random reads and writes, like a boot disk or a database I run myself, I pick block storage such as EBS. The limit is that it lives in one Availability Zone and usually attaches to one instance, so it isn't shared. If many servers need the same folders at the same time, I pick file storage: EFS for Linux, or FSx for Windows or high-performance computing. The tradeoff is higher cost per gigabyte than object storage. If I have huge amounts of data written once and read often, like photos, backups or logs, I pick object storage such as S3. It is cheap, durable and scales almost without limit, but I can't edit part of an object in place.
rubricPoints: Block storage is a raw disk for one server with fast small reads and writes, such as EBS.
EBS lives in one Availability Zone and usually attaches to one instance, so it is not shared.
File storage is a shared file system that many servers mount at once, such as EFS or FSx.
Object storage keeps whole items under keys behind an HTTP interface, such as S3, and is cheap and massively scalable.
Objects are replaced whole, not edited in place, so object storage is wrong for databases.
The choice depends on how many servers share the data, the access pattern, and the scale.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises storage choice, so reasoning through exam-style workload scenarios builds the matching skill best.

lessons.plain: Using purpose-built services means giving each kind of job to a tool designed for that job, instead of making one tool handle everything. Think of a kitchen. You could boil pasta, bake bread and chill drinks all in one big pot, but it would be slow, messy and fragile. A cloud application has similar jobs: storing files, remembering user sessions, holding records, passing messages between parts. Each has a managed service built for it. Splitting the work this way means one overloaded piece no longer drags everything else down, and each piece can grow on its own.
lessons.guessPrompt: An app keeps uploaded photos, user login sessions and a list of background jobs all inside one relational database. During a busy hour the database slows to a crawl. Which of those three jobs do you think is most likely hurting the others, and why?
lessons.teach:
A purpose-built service is a managed service designed around one access pattern, such as files, fast lookups or messages. The idea is to match each job to the service built for it, not to bend one service, usually a relational database (tables queried with SQL), into doing everything.

It works because every service is tuned for its own pattern. Amazon S3 is object storage: it holds files almost without limit and charges little per gigabyte. Amazon ElastiCache is an in-memory cache (data held in RAM for very fast reads), which suits short-lived data like login sessions. Amazon SQS is a managed queue: it holds messages until a worker takes them. Amazon DynamoDB is a key-value database that answers simple lookups quickly at almost any scale. Amazon RDS is a managed relational database, best for related records that need joins and transactions (changes that succeed or fail as a group).

Worked example. One RDS database holds photos, sessions, orders and a jobs table. Step 1: photos are large, so every backup and replica copies gigabytes of pictures. Move them to S3 and keep only the file's address in the database. Step 2: sessions are read on every page view. Move them to ElastiCache, which removes most of the read load. Step 3: workers keep querying the jobs table to see if anything is new. Replace that table with SQS, so workers simply receive messages. Step 4: RDS now holds only orders, which is the work it was built for. When it is busy, uploads and logins keep working.

A common mistake is splitting too far: adding a service nobody needs creates more parts to secure, watch and pay for. Split only where an access pattern really differs.

The effect on a running system is resilience. When one service does everything, it is a single point of failure, so any overload or outage takes down every feature. Separate services fail separately and can be scaled separately.

questions.prompt: A city library's lending app runs everything on one Amazon RDS database. It stores scanned book covers (about 3 MB each, 200,000 of them), a 'currently signed-in' record that is read on every screen tap, a table of overdue-notice requests that five email workers check every 15 seconds for new rows, and loan records that join members, books and branches. The architect works through it. Step 1: covers are large files and bloat every backup, so move them to Amazon S3 and keep only each cover's address in the database. Step 2: sign-in records are short-lived and read constantly, so move them to Amazon ElastiCache. Step 3: ??? Step 4: RDS now holds only the loan records, which need joins and transactions. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Move the overdue-notice requests into ElastiCache, because the workers read them often and RAM gives faster reads.
Replace the overdue-notice table with Amazon SQS, a managed queue, so each email worker receives a message instead of querying the table.
Keep the overdue-notice table in RDS but have the workers check it every 2 seconds, so notices go out sooner.
Store the overdue-notice requests as files in Amazon S3, because S3 holds data almost without limit at low cost.
questions.why: The workers keep polling a table to find new work, and that is the access pattern a managed queue like SQS is built for: it holds each message until a worker takes it.

questions.prompt: A smart-thermostat company has 50 million devices. Each device asks for its own settings using only its device ID, many thousands of times per second, and no request ever needs to combine data from different records. Which purpose-built service fits this access pattern best?
choices: Amazon RDS, because a relational database can store the settings in a table
Amazon SQS, because each settings request can be treated as a message
Amazon S3, because it holds data almost without limit at low cost
Amazon DynamoDB, a key-value database that answers simple lookups quickly at almost any scale
questions.why: Simple lookups by a single key at very large scale are the access pattern DynamoDB is designed for.

questions.prompt: A five-person team runs a small internal holiday-booking tool on one Amazon RDS database. Bookings link staff, managers and dates, and they need joins and transactions. One engineer proposes adding Amazon ElastiCache, Amazon SQS and Amazon DynamoDB so that the design uses purpose-built services. The database is lightly loaded, and its tables are read a few times a day. What is the best response?
choices: Add all three, because using more purpose-built services always makes a design more resilient.
Keep RDS on its own, because no workload here has a different access pattern and extra services add more to secure, watch and pay for.
Move the bookings to DynamoDB, because key-value databases scale better than relational ones.
Add ElastiCache only, because every database benefits from an in-memory cache in front of it.
questions.why: The guidance is to split only where an access pattern really differs, and adding services nobody needs only increases the parts to secure, monitor and pay for.

questions.prompt: A ticket-selling website keeps venue seating images, shopper logins, a queue-like table of email confirmations and ticket purchases all in one relational database. During a big concert sale, the purchase traffic overloads that database. What is the most likely effect, and what would separating the workloads into purpose-built services change?
choices: All features fail, and splitting services would not help, because every AWS service shares the same capacity.
Only purchases slow down, because a relational database automatically isolates each table's load from the others.
Images, logins, confirmations and purchases all suffer because the one database is a single point of failure, and separate services would fail and scale separately.
Nothing changes for logins, because login data is small, and splitting services would only reduce storage cost.
questions.why: When one service does everything, its overload takes down every feature, whereas separate purpose-built services can fail and be scaled independently.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why our design should use separate purpose-built services instead of keeping everything in one database, and name one tradeoff or limit of doing that.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each kind of data and work has its own access pattern, and AWS has managed services tuned for each one. Big files belong in S3 object storage. Hot, short-lived data like sessions belongs in an in-memory cache such as ElastiCache. Work that needs to be handed off belongs in a queue such as SQS. Related records that need transactions stay in a relational database like RDS. If one database does all of that, it is a single point of failure: a flood of uploads or session reads can slow down orders too, and the only way to grow is to make that one database bigger. Splitting the jobs lets each piece scale and fail on its own. The tradeoff is that there are more services to secure, monitor, pay for and understand, so we should split only where an access pattern really differs, not just for the sake of it.
rubricPoints: Defines a purpose-built service as one designed for a specific access pattern.
Gives at least one concrete match, such as files to S3, sessions to a cache or jobs to a queue.
Explains that one overloaded do-everything service is a single point of failure.
Notes that separate services can scale and fail independently.
Names the tradeoff of extra operational complexity and cost from too many services.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present a described workload and ask which managed service fits each part, so reasoning through realistic scenarios builds this matching skill best.

lessons.plain: A managed AI service is a ready-made skill, such as understanding text or speaking aloud, that a cloud provider trains, hosts and keeps running for you. You send it data over the network and get an answer back. Amazon Comprehend reads text and reports things like its mood or the names it mentions. Amazon Polly turns written text into natural-sounding speech. It is like hiring a professional translator by the page instead of training your own staff for years. You get the result quickly and reliably, but you accept the translator's style and pay for every page.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team needs to tag thousands of customer reviews each day as positive or negative. If you trained and hosted your own model for this, what ongoing jobs would your team take on that would disappear if you called a provider's ready-made service instead?
lessons.teach:
Offloading to a managed AI service means calling a provider-run machine learning feature through an API (a defined request-and-response interface) instead of training, hosting and scaling a model yourself. Amazon Comprehend does natural language processing (NLP, software that extracts meaning from text). It can detect sentiment, meaning whether text is positive, negative, neutral or mixed. It can also find entities, meaning named people, places or products. Amazon Polly does text-to-speech: you send text and get back an audio file or stream.

Other services follow the same pattern. Amazon Transcribe turns speech into text. Amazon Translate converts text between languages. Amazon Rekognition analyses images and video. Amazon Textract pulls text and form fields out of scanned documents. Amazon Lex builds chatbots. Amazon SageMaker is different: it is a platform for building and hosting your own models, so you keep more of the work.

Offloading helps resilience because the provider runs the service across several data centres, scales it, and patches it. Your design no longer has a self-built model server that could become a single point of failure.

Worked example: a support app must flag angry tickets. A ticket arrives and is saved. The app sends the ticket text to Comprehend's sentiment feature. Comprehend returns NEGATIVE with a confidence score of 0.94. The app sees that the score is above its 0.8 threshold and routes the ticket to the urgent queue. Nobody on your team ran a model server.

A common mistake is reaching for SageMaker or self-managed GPU servers when the requirement says "least operational overhead" and a ready-made service already does the task. That choice adds the most work for the same result.

The tradeoffs are real. You get less customisation, you pay per request, and every call counts against service quotas, which are rate limits on how many requests you may send. During a traffic surge, direct calls can be throttled, meaning rejected for exceeding the rate limit. Placing a queue in front of the calls and retrying with backoff (waiting longer between each attempt) keeps the system working.

questions.prompt: A city museum wants an audio guide in Spanish for every exhibit, with the least operational overhead. Here is the flow, with one step missing. Step 1: a curator writes a new exhibit description in English and saves it. Step 2: the app sends the English text to Amazon Translate and gets back the Spanish text. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the app stores the returned audio file and links it to the exhibit page, so visitors can press play. Nobody on the team trains or hosts a model. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The app sends the Spanish text to Amazon Comprehend, which returns a sentiment label that the player reads aloud.
The app sends the Spanish text to Amazon Polly, which returns an audio file of the text being spoken.
The app sends the Spanish text to a speech model the team trained and hosts in Amazon SageMaker.
The app sends the Spanish text to Amazon Transcribe, which returns the spoken audio file.
questions.why: Polly is the managed text-to-speech service: you send it text and get audio back, so no team-run model is needed.

questions.prompt: An insurance company receives thousands of scanned claim forms each day. It must pull out the printed text and the filled-in form fields, such as policy number and claim amount, with the least operational overhead. Which approach fits best?
choices: Send the scanned forms to Amazon Textract, a managed service that extracts text and form fields from scanned documents.
Send the scans to Amazon Comprehend to detect the entities in each image.
Build and host a custom document-reading model in Amazon SageMaker.
Run a self-managed GPU server cluster with an open-source text-reading model.
questions.why: Textract already extracts text and form fields from scanned documents, so offloading to it avoids building, hosting and scaling your own model.

questions.prompt: A news site calls Amazon Polly directly each time an article is published, to create a spoken version. During a breaking-news surge, many Polly calls are rejected because the site is sending more requests than its service quota (the rate limit on requests) allows. What change keeps the system working?
choices: Retry each rejected call immediately in a tight loop until it succeeds.
Replace Polly with a self-built text-to-speech model on a single server.
Put the conversion requests into a queue and retry failed calls with backoff, waiting longer between each attempt.
Switch the calls to Amazon Transcribe, which has its own separate quota.
questions.why: A queue absorbs the surge and retrying with backoff spreads calls out, so throttled requests eventually succeed without exceeding the rate limit.

questions.prompt: A retailer currently scores product reviews for sentiment using a model it built itself, hosted on one virtual server that the team patches by hand. The team replaces this with calls to Amazon Comprehend. From a resilience point of view, what is the main gain?
choices: Comprehend lets the team customise the model far more than their own server did.
Service quotas no longer apply, so the app can never be throttled.
Each request now costs nothing, because managed services are not billed per call.
The self-built model server, a single point of failure, is gone because the provider runs, scales and patches the service across several data centres.
questions.why: Offloading removes the team's own model server as a single point of failure, since the provider operates the service across multiple data centres; the other choices misstate the trade-offs of less customisation, per-request cost and quotas.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you would call a managed AI service like Comprehend or Polly instead of building your own model. Name at least one limit or tradeoff you accept by doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: A managed AI service is a capability the provider has already trained and runs for us, and we reach it through an API. Comprehend reads text and gives us sentiment or entities. Polly turns text into speech. If we use them, we don't collect training data, host model servers, patch them or scale them. The provider runs them across multiple data centres, so our design loses a component that could fail. That fits requirements like "least operational overhead" or "fastest to deliver." The tradeoffs are that we get only the features and accuracy the service offers, we pay per request, and we are bound by quotas. A burst of traffic can get our calls throttled, so we should buffer the requests in a queue and retry with backoff. If we need a truly custom model, a build-your-own platform like SageMaker fits better, but it brings back much of that operational work.
rubricPoints: Defines a managed AI service as a provider-trained, provider-run capability called through an API.
Correctly describes what Comprehend (text analysis such as sentiment and entities) and Polly (text-to-speech) do.
Explains the benefit: no model training, hosting, scaling or patching, and no self-run single point of failure.
Names a tradeoff such as limited customisation, per-request cost, or quotas and throttling.
Mentions a mitigation for throttling, such as a queue with retries and backoff, or knows when a custom-model platform fits better.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is reading a requirement such as "least operational overhead", matching it to the right ready-made AI service, and weighing that against custom builds, which exam-style scenarios practise best.

lessons.plain: AWS builds its cloud in layers of physical separation. A Region is a geographic area, such as a part of Europe, holding several Availability Zones. An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more data centres with their own power, cooling and networking, placed far enough from the others that one fire or flood should not take out two. Amazon Route 53 is AWS's managed DNS service, the internet's phone book that turns a name into an address. Think of a shop chain: AZs are separate branches in one city, Regions are different cities, and Route 53 is the sign telling customers which open branch to visit.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your whole application runs in one data centre and that building loses power, what happens to users? Where would you put a second copy so that the same power cut cannot reach both?
lessons.teach:
A Region is a separate geographic area of AWS infrastructure. An Availability Zone (AZ) is an isolated location inside a Region, with independent power and networking, joined to the other AZs by fast, low-latency private links. Because AZs in one Region are close and well connected, you can spread one application across them and keep data in sync almost instantly. That is a multi-AZ design, and it protects against the loss of one data centre. Regions are far apart and largely independent, so a multi-Region design protects against a whole Region failing, at the cost of higher latency between copies, more complex data replication and roughly doubled spend.

Amazon Route 53 is a managed DNS (Domain Name System) service: it answers the question "what address does this name point to?" It supports routing policies, which are rules for choosing an answer. Failover routing returns a primary target while it is healthy and a secondary target otherwise. Latency routing sends users to the Region that responds fastest for them. Weighted routing splits traffic by percentages. A health check is a probe Route 53 sends regularly to a target to decide whether it is healthy.

Worked example. A shop runs web servers in two AZs in Region A behind a load balancer, with a standby copy in Region B. First, AZ 1 loses power. The load balancer stops sending traffic there, and AZ 2 carries on. Route 53 is not involved, because the Region's entry point is still healthy. Later, all of Region A fails. Route 53's health check on Region A's endpoint fails, so the failover record now answers with Region B's address, and new users land in Region B.

A common mistake is believing multi-AZ protects you from a Regional outage. It does not; only a second Region does. A second mistake is expecting DNS failover to be instant. Clients cache DNS answers for the record's TTL (time to live, a cache lifetime in seconds), so a long TTL keeps some users pointed at the dead Region for minutes after failover.

questions.prompt:
A ticket-booking company runs its application servers in three Availability Zones (isolated locations inside one Region, each with its own power and networking) in Region X, behind a load balancer. It keeps a standby copy in Region Y. Amazon Route 53 (a managed DNS service that answers which address a name points to) holds a failover record for the site's name, with a health check (a regular probe that decides whether a target is healthy) on Region X's entry point. The record's TTL (time to live, how long clients may cache an answer) is 300 seconds.

Step 1: One AZ in Region X loses networking. The load balancer stops sending requests there, and the other two AZs carry the load. Route 53 changes nothing, because Region X's entry point is still healthy.
Step 2: Later, all of Region X fails.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Users whose devices still hold the old cached answer keep trying Region X for up to about 5 minutes. New lookups get Region Y.

Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Region X's load balancer detects the outage and forwards incoming requests across to Region Y.
Every client switches to Region Y at once, because DNS failover takes effect instantly for all users.
Route 53's health check on Region X's endpoint fails, so the failover record now answers with Region Y's address.
Route 53 switches to latency routing and sends each user to whichever Region responds fastest.
questions.why: Failover routing returns the primary only while its health check passes, so once Region X's check fails the record answers with the secondary, Region Y.

questions.prompt: A payroll company says its service must keep running even if an entire AWS Region (a separate geographic area of AWS infrastructure) goes down. It currently runs in two Availability Zones in one Region. Which change actually meets the requirement?
choices: Lower the DNS TTL on the record that points at the current Region.
Add a third Availability Zone in the same Region so there are more copies.
Run a copy in a second Region and use Route 53 failover routing with a health check.
Move everything into one Availability Zone with larger servers for headroom.
questions.why: Multi-AZ only protects against losing one data centre; surviving a whole Region outage needs a second Region, with Route 53 failover moving users there when the first Region's health check fails.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming firm runs identical copies of its app in Regions in Europe, North America and Asia. It wants each viewer sent to whichever Region will respond fastest for that viewer. Which Route 53 routing policy (a rule for choosing which answer to return) fits?
choices: A health check on its own
Weighted routing
Failover routing
Latency routing
questions.why: Latency routing sends users to the Region that responds fastest for them, whereas failover picks a primary/secondary and weighted splits traffic by fixed percentages.

questions.prompt: A news site's Route 53 failover record has a TTL (time to live, the number of seconds clients may cache a DNS answer) of 3,600 seconds. After its primary Region failed and Route 53 switched to the secondary Region, some readers kept hitting the dead Region for close to an hour. Which change most directly shortens that window next time?
choices: Add more Availability Zones in the primary Region.
Raise the TTL so the DNS answers stay stable for longer.
Replace failover routing with a 50/50 weighted split between the Regions.
Lower the record's TTL so clients drop the cached answer much sooner.
questions.why: Clients reuse a cached DNS answer for the record's TTL, so a shorter TTL makes them look up the name again, and receive the secondary Region's address, sooner.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when a multi-AZ design is enough and when you need multiple Regions with Route 53 in front. Name one tradeoff or limit of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: An Availability Zone is an isolated data-centre location inside a Region, with its own power and network. Spreading servers and a synchronised database across two or three AZs, with a load balancer in front, survives the loss of one building. That is enough for most applications, and it is fairly cheap and simple because the AZs are close together. Its limit is that it does nothing if the whole Region goes down. For that you need a copy in a second Region. Route 53, AWS's managed DNS, uses health checks and failover or latency routing to send users to a Region that is healthy. The tradeoffs are cost, harder cross-Region data replication with possible data lag, and slower failover, because clients cache DNS answers until the TTL expires. Multi-Region is worth it only when the requirement demands surviving a Regional outage.
rubricPoints: Defines a Region as a geographic area and an AZ as an isolated location within it.
States that multi-AZ survives a data-centre failure but not a Regional one.
Describes Route 53 as managed DNS that uses health checks and routing policies to steer users.
Names a multi-Region cost: more spend, replication complexity, or latency between copies.
Notes that DNS caching and TTL delay failover.
