questions.prompt: A ticketing company traces requests with AWS X-Ray. Its engineers want to pull up only the traces for customers on the premium tier, so they can check whether those customers see slower responses. How should they record the customer tier on each trace?
choices: As a separate trace ID for each tier, so premium requests get their own trace
As a CloudWatch alarm, because alarms let you search traces by a label
As an annotation, because annotations are indexed key-value labels you can filter traces by
As metadata, because metadata holds extra detail that is stored with the trace
questions.why: Annotations are indexed and searchable, so you can filter traces by them; metadata is stored but cannot be searched.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm uses AWS X-Ray with default settings. A customer reports that one particular shipment lookup was very slow, but engineers cannot find any trace for that request. X-Ray is otherwise working and showing other traces. What is the most likely reason?
choices: CloudTrail took over the trace because the request called an AWS service
Sampling is on by default, so X-Ray records only a portion of requests and this one was not recorded
The trace was recorded but stored as metadata, so it cannot be seen in X-Ray
The request crossed more than one service, and X-Ray can only trace requests that stay on a single machine
questions.why: By default X-Ray samples requests to limit cost and overhead, so not every request gets a trace.

questions.prompt: At a healthcare startup, a message queue was deleted overnight and an application broke. The team lead wants to find out which user or role deleted it. Which AWS service should they look in?
choices: AWS X-Ray, because its service map shows every component in the application
AWS CloudTrail, because it logs API activity in the account, such as who deleted a resource
Amazon CloudWatch, because its metrics show when the queue stopped receiving messages
AWS X-Ray, because annotations record which user made each change
questions.why: Auditing who changed a resource is the job of CloudTrail, which logs account API activity; X-Ray follows requests through an application.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what AWS X-Ray gives you that CloudWatch metrics and logs alone do not, and name one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: X-Ray follows one request end to end. A trace ID is passed along in a header, each service records a segment with its timing and errors, and finer steps like a database call become subsegments. X-Ray stitches these into a trace and a service map, so I can see that a slow checkout spent most of its time in, say, a throttled DynamoDB call. CloudWatch metrics give me averages per service and logs give me per-service lines, but neither connects one request across services by itself. The tradeoff is sampling: by default only some requests are traced, which keeps cost and overhead down but means a rare failure might not have a trace. It also needs instrumentation in each service, and it is not an audit tool; CloudTrail answers who changed what.
rubricPoints: States that X-Ray traces a single request across multiple services.
Explains trace ID propagation and segments or subsegments carrying timing and errors.
Contrasts it with CloudWatch metrics or logs, which lack the per-request cross-service view.
Names a limit such as sampling, instrumentation effort, or cost.
Distinguishes X-Ray from CloudTrail auditing.

suggested.rationale: The exam mostly tests picking X-Ray over CloudWatch or CloudTrail for a described symptom, so reasoning through scenario situations builds that judgment best since no current mission or planned engine performs tracing.

lessons.plain: Sometimes you inherit an old application that keeps falling over, and you are told you may not touch its code: no rewrite, no new libraries, maybe not even a config change. You can still make it more dependable by changing everything around it instead. Think of an old car you cannot open the bonnet of: you cannot fix the engine, but you can keep a spare car ready, park it in a different garage, and have someone check every minute whether it still starts. Reliability comes from the surroundings: spare copies, automatic replacement, a managed database, and checks that steer users away from a broken copy.
lessons.guessPrompt: An old web application runs on one server and crashes about once a week; you are forbidden from editing its code. Without changing the program at all, what could you put around it so that users barely notice when it crashes?
lessons.teach:
Raising reliability without changing code means wrapping the application in infrastructure that detects failure and replaces or bypasses the broken part. The code stays identical; the environment absorbs the failures.

Key terms. A single point of failure is any one component whose loss stops the whole service. An Availability Zone (AZ) is a separate data centre group within an AWS Region, with its own power and networking. A load balancer is a managed service that spreads incoming requests across several servers. A health check is a regular probe, such as requesting a page, that marks a server unhealthy if it stops answering correctly. An Auto Scaling group keeps a set number of servers running and launches a replacement when one fails a health check. Amazon RDS Multi-AZ is a managed database option that keeps a synchronous standby copy in another AZ and switches to it automatically, using the same connection address, so the app does not notice a new endpoint.

Why it works: failures still happen, but detection and replacement become automatic and redundancy hides them from users.

Worked example. A legacy app runs on one EC2 server with a database on the same machine. Step one: move the database to RDS Multi-AZ; the app only needs its connection address pointed at RDS, not a code change. Step two: build a server image of the app and run two copies in an Auto Scaling group across two AZs. Step three: put an Application Load Balancer in front with a health check. Now, if one server hangs, the load balancer stops sending it traffic, Auto Scaling replaces it, and if an AZ fails the database fails over. Three single points of failure are gone.

Common mistake: running several copies of an app that stores user sessions in its own memory. Users get bounced between servers and lose their login. If the code cannot change, enable sticky sessions on the load balancer, which pins each user to one server, or run one copy with Auto Scaling set to minimum and maximum of one, which self-heals without scaling. Also reject exam answers that require rewriting into microservices or Lambda when the requirement forbids code changes.

questions.prompt: A small clinic runs a legacy appointment-booking web app that the vendor no longer supports, so its code cannot be changed. The team is removing single points of failure. Step 1: they build a server image of the app and run three copies in an Auto Scaling group spread across three Availability Zones. Step 2: they place an Application Load Balancer in front, with a health check that requests the login page. Step 3: testing shows a problem. Staff are logged out at random because the app keeps each user's login session in its own memory, and the load balancer sends each request to whichever copy it chooses. Step 4: [missing]. Result: each staff member stays on the same server for their visit, logins survive, and failed servers are still bypassed and replaced. What is Step 4?
choices: Change the app so it saves sessions in the database, letting any copy read any user's login
Enable sticky sessions on the load balancer so each user is pinned to one server
Remove the health check so the load balancer stops moving users between the servers
Move the booking app into Lambda functions so no server ever holds session data in memory
questions.why: Sticky sessions pin each user to one server, which fixes the lost logins without touching code, while the health check and Auto Scaling keep handling failures.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs its legacy ticketing app on two EC2 servers in two Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer with health checks. Both servers connect to one database installed on a single server in one Availability Zone. Which component is still a single point of failure, meaning its loss alone would stop the whole service?
choices: The single database server in one Availability Zone
The health check, because it probes only one page
The Application Load Balancer, because all requests pass through it
Each EC2 app server, because either one could hang
questions.why: Only one database exists, so losing it stops the service, while the two app servers already cover for each other behind the load balancer.

questions.prompt: A museum runs a legacy ticket app that breaks if two copies run at once, and its code cannot be changed. Today it runs on one server, and when that server crashes someone must restart it by hand. Which design gives automatic recovery while respecting both limits?
choices: Move the app to a larger server so it is less likely to crash under load
Run two copies behind a load balancer with sticky sessions turned on for every user
Put the server in an Auto Scaling group with minimum and maximum both set to one, using a health check
Rewrite the app into microservices so each part can be restarted on its own
questions.why: An Auto Scaling group fixed at one server replaces it automatically when it fails a health check, giving self-healing without ever running a second copy or changing code.

questions.prompt: A charity moves its legacy donations app's database to Amazon RDS Multi-AZ. Why can the app keep working through a database failover without any code change?
choices: The load balancer health-checks the database and reroutes its queries
The standby in another zone takes over behind the same connection address
Auto Scaling launches a fresh database server and copies the data across
The app is given a list of database addresses and tries each one in turn
questions.why: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone and switches to it automatically using the same connection address, so the app never sees a new endpoint.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a legacy application more reliable when nobody is allowed to change its code, and name one limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: If we cannot touch the code, we change what surrounds it. First I find the single points of failure: usually one server and a database on that same box. I move the database to a managed Multi-AZ database so a standby in another Availability Zone takes over automatically behind the same address. I capture the app as a server image and run it in an Auto Scaling group across two zones behind a load balancer whose health checks stop sending traffic to a broken copy, while Auto Scaling replaces it. The limit is that wrapping cannot fix bugs inside the app. If it keeps sessions in memory, running several copies breaks logins, so I would need sticky sessions or a single self-healing instance, and that gives recovery rather than true redundancy. Memory leaks or bad logic still happen; we just recover faster.
rubricPoints: Reliability is improved by changing the surrounding infrastructure, not the application code.
Identifies single points of failure such as one server or a co-located database.
Uses health checks with a load balancer and Auto Scaling to detect and replace failed copies.
Moves the database to a managed Multi-AZ option so failover needs no code change.
Names a limit, such as in-memory session state needing sticky sessions or a single self-healing instance.
Notes that wrapping does not fix bugs inside the application itself.

suggested.rationale: The core exam skill is reading a scenario with a 'no code changes' constraint and choosing the infrastructure-only fix, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style situations.

lessons.plain: When an application on cloud servers needs to keep data, AWS gives four main styles of storage, and picking the wrong one makes things slow or broken. Amazon S3 is like a huge warehouse: you hand over whole boxes and fetch them back by label. Amazon EBS is like a private hard drive plugged into one computer. Amazon EFS is like a shared network drive that many Linux computers open at once. Amazon FSx is a set of specialist shared drives: one for Windows offices, one built for very fast scientific number-crunching, and others for teams already using particular storage systems. You choose by asking who needs the data, how they reach it, and how fast.
lessons.guessPrompt: A rendering farm of hundreds of Linux servers must read the same 50 TB of input files at very high speed for a few hours, and the master copy of those files lives in Amazon S3. Would you guess the best fit is a separate disk attached to each server, a general-purpose shared file system, or a specialised high-speed parallel file system that can link to S3?
lessons.teach:
Amazon S3 is object storage: you store whole files, called objects, in containers called buckets, and read or write them through web (HTTP) requests. It scales almost without limit and handles very high parallel throughput, but you cannot mount it like a disk or change part of an object in place, and each request has more latency than a local disk.

Amazon EBS is block storage: a virtual disk attached to one EC2 instance (a virtual server) inside one Availability Zone (an isolated group of data centres). It gives the lowest latency for a single server, so it suits databases and boot disks, but normally only that one instance uses it.

Amazon EFS is a managed shared file system that speaks NFS (Network File System, the usual Linux file-sharing protocol). Many instances across Availability Zones mount it at the same time, and it grows and shrinks automatically.

Amazon FSx is a family of managed file systems for specific needs. FSx for Windows File Server speaks SMB (the Windows file-sharing protocol). FSx for Lustre is a parallel file system for high-performance computing and machine learning, and can link to an S3 bucket. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS serve teams already using those systems.

Why this works: decide by access pattern first (how many servers, which protocol, how much latency is acceptable), then by throughput.

Worked example: forty Linux web servers in three Availability Zones must read and write one shared uploads folder. Step 1: many servers share it, so EBS is out. Step 2: the app expects a mounted folder path, not web requests, so S3 would need a rewrite. Step 3: Linux and NFS, with no Windows or supercomputing need, so EFS fits. Afterwards you would watch the file system's throughput and how close it runs to its I/O limit.

Common mistake: picking EBS for shared data because it is fastest. It is fastest for one server, but other servers cannot see it; in a running system each instance holds a different copy and users see files go missing. Likewise, Windows applications need SMB, so they belong on FSx for Windows File Server, not EFS.

questions.prompt: A research lab runs a machine learning training job on 120 Linux GPU instances. Its 80 TB training dataset already sits in an S3 bucket. The training code expects a mounted folder path, and the job needs very high parallel read throughput. Step 1: all 120 instances must read the same data, so EBS, a disk attached to one instance, is out. Step 2: the code expects a mounted path rather than web requests, so reading S3 directly would mean rewriting the code. Step 3: ??? Afterwards, the team would watch the file system's throughput while the job runs. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Choose FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket, because it is a parallel file system built for machine learning and high-performance computing.
Choose FSx for Windows File Server, because it is a managed shared file system that many instances can mount at the same time.
Give each instance its own large EBS volume holding a full copy of the dataset, because EBS has the lowest latency.
Choose EFS, because the instances run Linux and EFS is the standard shared NFS file system that many instances can mount at once.
questions.why: The job is a machine learning workload that needs very high parallel throughput on data already in S3, and FSx for Lustre is the parallel file system for exactly that need and can link to the bucket.

questions.prompt: An inventory company runs a single relational database on one EC2 instance in one Availability Zone. The database needs the lowest possible storage latency, and no other server reads its data files. Which storage service fits best?
choices: Amazon EBS, a block-storage virtual disk attached to that one instance
Amazon S3, object storage that is read and written through web requests
Amazon EFS, a shared NFS file system mounted across Availability Zones
Amazon FSx for Lustre, a parallel file system for high-performance computing
questions.why: One server that needs the lowest latency is the case block storage is designed for, which is why EBS suits databases.

questions.prompt: A travel booking site runs six EC2 instances behind a load balancer. To make file access fast, each instance saves customer-uploaded documents to its own EBS volume. Users now report that a document they just uploaded is sometimes missing when they reload the page. What is the most likely cause?
choices: EBS deletes objects automatically unless the bucket has versioning
EBS volumes have too little throughput, so writes fail under load
Each instance writes to its own disk, which the other instances cannot see
The load balancer is corrupting files as they pass through it
questions.why: An EBS volume is normally used by only one instance, so a reload served by a different instance looks at a different copy that lacks the file.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm moves a Windows-based document management application to eight EC2 instances in two Availability Zones. All eight need the same shared drive, and the application uses the Windows file-sharing protocol, SMB. Which storage service should the architect choose?
choices: Amazon EBS, because it gives the lowest latency for the application's servers
Amazon S3, because it scales almost without limit and handles high parallel throughput
Amazon EFS, because it lets many instances across Availability Zones mount one shared file system
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, because it is a managed shared file system that speaks SMB
questions.why: EFS speaks NFS, not SMB, so a Windows application that needs a shared drive belongs on FSx for Windows File Server.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between S3, EBS, EFS and FSx for a new workload, and name one tradeoff or limit of the option that looks fastest.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the access pattern, not raw speed. If one server needs a low-latency disk, say for a database, I use EBS, a virtual disk attached to one instance in one Availability Zone. The tradeoff is that it is normally tied to that single server, so it cannot serve as shared storage. If many Linux servers need the same mounted folder, I use EFS, a shared NFS file system that spans zones and grows by itself. If the clients are Windows and need SMB, I use FSx for Windows File Server; for heavy parallel compute like simulations, FSx for Lustre, which can link to S3. If the app stores and fetches whole files over web requests at huge scale, S3 is cheapest and most scalable, but it is not a mountable disk and has higher per-request latency. Then I watch throughput and I/O limits to confirm.
rubricPoints: Decides by access pattern: number of servers, protocol and latency need.
EBS is a low-latency block disk normally attached to one instance in one Availability Zone.
EFS is a shared NFS file system for many Linux instances across zones.
FSx covers specialised needs such as Windows SMB shares and Lustre for high-performance computing.
S3 is massively scalable object storage reached by web requests, not a mounted disk.
Names a limit, such as EBS not being shareable or S3 having higher per-request latency.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises storage selection, and the skill is reading a requirement to spot the access pattern, which exam-style scenarios to reason through practise best.

lessons.plain: Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store) is a network-attached virtual hard drive for a virtual server. You choose a volume type, which is a performance and price class. IOPS (input/output operations per second) counts how many small reads and writes a disk can handle each second. Throughput counts how many megabytes per second it can move. Some types are solid-state drives built for many small, fast operations. Others are spinning-disk types built for long, steady streams of data. Provisioned IOPS means you reserve a specific IOPS figure and pay for it, much like booking a dedicated lane on a motorway instead of sharing traffic.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database writes thousands of tiny records every second, and a log-archiving job reads huge files from start to finish once a night. Which of these two jobs would you put on a solid-state disk, and which could use a cheaper spinning disk? Why?
lessons.teach:
An EBS volume type sets how a block storage volume behaves. Block storage is a raw disk that an operating system formats and mounts. The SSD (solid-state) types are gp3, gp2, io1 and io2. The HDD (spinning-disk) types are st1 and sc1.

gp3 is general purpose SSD. Every gp3 volume gets a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, whatever its size. You can pay to raise these to about 16,000 IOPS and 1,000 MiB/s without growing the disk. gp2 is the older general purpose type. Its IOPS scale with size, at 3 IOPS per GiB. Small gp2 volumes rely on burst credits, a saved-up allowance that runs out under sustained load. io1 and io2 are Provisioned IOPS SSD. You state the exact IOPS you need, and the volume delivers it consistently at low latency. That is why they suit busy relational databases. io2 adds higher durability, and io2 Block Express reaches far beyond 16,000 IOPS. Only the io types support Multi-Attach, which connects one volume to several instances. st1 (throughput optimized HDD) is cheap and fast for large sequential reads, such as log processing. sc1 (cold HDD) is cheapest, for rarely touched data. Neither HDD type can be a boot volume.

Worked example. A database needs 10,000 steady IOPS on 200 GiB. Step 1: gp2 gives 200 × 3 = 600 baseline IOPS, which is far too low. Step 2: gp3 gives 3,000 by default, and you can provision 10,000 because that is under its ceiling. Pick gp3. Step 3: if the need were 40,000 IOPS, gp3's ceiling is exceeded, so choose io2.

Common mistake: buying a huge gp2 volume just to get IOPS, or ignoring the instance's own EBS bandwidth limit. A fast volume on a small instance is capped by that instance. In a running system, an undersized volume shows a rising VolumeQueueLength metric (requests waiting for the disk), a draining BurstBalance on gp2, and slow queries.

questions.prompt: A payroll service at a regional bank needs 8,000 steady IOPS (input/output operations per second) on a 1,000 GiB EBS volume. EBS is block storage, a raw disk the operating system formats and mounts. Step 1: a gp2 volume gives 1,000 × 3 = 3,000 baseline IOPS, which is too low for a steady 8,000. Step 2: ??? Step 3: Choose gp3, provision 8,000 IOPS, and watch the VolumeQueueLength metric to confirm requests are not piling up. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: gp2 would reach 8,000 IOPS at about 2,667 GiB, so the volume should be grown to that size instead.
st1 handles heavy load cheaply, so it should be compared against gp3 before deciding.
gp3 starts at 3,000 IOPS, and 8,000 is under its ceiling of about 16,000, so it can be raised without growing the disk.
8,000 is above gp3's 3,000 baseline, so only a Provisioned IOPS type such as io2 can deliver it.
questions.why: gp3 lets you pay to raise IOPS up to about 16,000 regardless of size, and 8,000 sits below that ceiling, which is why Step 3 picks gp3.

questions.prompt: An engineering firm runs a clustered application on three EC2 instances (virtual servers). All three must attach the same EBS block storage volume at the same time using Multi-Attach. Which volume type can do this?
choices: io2
gp3
gp2
st1
questions.why: Only the Provisioned IOPS SSD types (io1 and io2) support Multi-Attach, which connects one volume to several instances.

questions.prompt: A logistics company attaches an io2 volume provisioned for 30,000 IOPS to a small EC2 instance. Database queries are still slow, and the VolumeQueueLength metric (requests waiting for the disk) keeps rising. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The io2 volume has used up its burst credits under sustained load.
io2 cannot deliver consistent latency, so it should be swapped for gp2.
The volume needs a higher provisioned IOPS figure than 30,000.
The small instance's own EBS bandwidth limit caps what the volume can deliver.
questions.why: A fast volume attached to a small instance is capped by that instance's EBS bandwidth limit, so the instance, not the volume, is the bottleneck.

questions.prompt: A media startup runs a reporting job on a 100 GiB gp2 volume. Performance is fine for the first stretch, then drops sharply during a long, sustained run. Which metric would most directly show the cause?
choices: The volume's size in GiB shrinking
The instance count in the cluster
The volume's boot flag changing
BurstBalance falling toward zero
questions.why: Small gp2 volumes rely on burst credits, a saved-up allowance that drains under sustained load, and a draining BurstBalance metric shows that happening.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between gp3, io2 and st1 for a new workload, and name one limit or tradeoff that could make your choice fail in production.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I look at the access pattern. Many small random reads and writes need IOPS, so that points to SSD. Large sequential scans need throughput, so that points to HDD. For most SSD workloads I start with gp3. It gives 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size, and I can raise IOPS and throughput separately up to about 16,000 IOPS without paying for extra space. If a database needs more than that, or needs very consistent latency, or Multi-Attach, I use io2 Provisioned IOPS and pay for the exact IOPS I reserve. For big sequential jobs like log processing I use st1, which is cheap per GiB but bad at random I/O and cannot be a boot disk. One tradeoff is that the instance has its own EBS bandwidth cap, so a fast volume can still be throttled. I would watch VolumeQueueLength and the IOPS metrics to confirm the choice worked.
rubricPoints: Matches small random I/O to SSD types and large sequential I/O to HDD types such as st1.
States that gp3 has a 3,000 IOPS baseline at any size and lets IOPS and throughput be raised independently.
Uses io1 or io2 Provisioned IOPS when IOPS exceed gp3's ceiling or latency must be consistent.
Notes that gp2 IOPS scale with size and depend on burst credits.
Names a limit such as instance EBS bandwidth caps or HDD types not being bootable.
Names a metric to verify, such as VolumeQueueLength or BurstBalance.

suggested.rationale: Picking a volume type is mainly about reasoning from a stated IOPS, throughput or cost requirement to the right class, which exam-style scenarios practise best, and no current mission or planned engine simulates block storage.

lessons.plain: Hybrid storage means your data lives partly in your own building and partly in the cloud, but your applications see it as one place. The trick that makes it fast is a local cache: a small, quick store on site that keeps copies of the data people use most. The full, durable copy sits in the cloud. Think of a home bookshelf plus a big public library. The books you read this week stay on your shelf, and older ones go back to the library. You only wait when you need something that is not on the shelf.
lessons.guessPrompt: An office keeps 40 TB of project files in the cloud, but staff only open about 2 TB of recent files each week. If you could put a fast local disk in the office, roughly how big would it need to be for most file opens to feel instant, and why?
lessons.teach:
Hybrid storage connects on-premises applications (software running in your own data center) to cloud storage while keeping access fast. On AWS the main tool is AWS Storage Gateway, a virtual or hardware appliance you run on site. It speaks familiar protocols, such as file shares (NFS or SMB), block disks (iSCSI) or virtual tape, and stores data in AWS behind the scenes. Its performance comes from a local cache, meaning fast local disk that holds recently used data so reads do not cross the internet.

The common modes are these. S3 File Gateway presents a file share whose files become objects in Amazon S3, which is object storage. FSx File Gateway gives low-latency local access to a managed Windows file system in Amazon FSx. Volume Gateway presents block disks in one of two ways. In cached mode, the full volume lives in AWS and only hot data stays local. In stored mode, the full volume stays local and is backed up asynchronously to AWS, so every read is local. Tape Gateway replaces physical backup tapes.

Here is a worked example. A studio has a 30 TB block volume, and editors touch about 3 TB a week. In step one, the requirement is low latency on active data, but not on all of it, so you pick cached mode. In step two, you size the cache above the working set, about 4 TB. In step three, you watch the cache hit percentage, which is the share of reads served locally. It should stay high, ideally above 90 percent. You also watch the cache percent dirty, which is data written locally but not yet uploaded, to make sure uploads keep pace.

A common mistake is undersizing the cache or picking cached mode when every byte must be read at local speed. Reads then miss the cache and fetch data over the WAN link, which is the network connection between the site and AWS, so users see slow, unpredictable latency. When the whole dataset needs local speed, stored mode is the right choice.

questions.prompt: A food-processing plant runs a quality-control database on site. Its block volume is 8 TB, and the plant's rule is that every read, including rare reads of old records, must come back at local-disk speed. Leadership still wants a copy of the data in AWS for safety. Step one: the requirement is local-speed reads on the whole dataset, not only on recently used data. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the team confirms that reads never have to cross the WAN link (the network connection between the plant and AWS), because the full volume sits on local disk while copies go to AWS in the background. What is the missing step two?
choices: Choose S3 File Gateway, so the database files become objects in Amazon S3, which is object storage
Choose Tape Gateway, so the database is written to virtual tapes in AWS instead of physical tapes
Choose Volume Gateway in cached mode and size the local cache at about 1 TB, so the most recently used records stay local
Choose Volume Gateway in stored mode, so the full 8 TB volume stays local and is backed up asynchronously to AWS
questions.why: Stored mode keeps the whole volume on local disk and backs it up to AWS asynchronously, so every read is served locally, which is exactly what the plant requires.

questions.prompt: An engineer monitoring an AWS Storage Gateway (an on-site appliance that connects local applications to cloud storage) sees a cache hit percentage of 95 percent. What does this number tell them?
choices: 95 percent of reads were served from the fast local cache instead of being fetched from AWS over the WAN link
95 percent of data written locally has already been uploaded to AWS
95 percent of the full volume is stored on local disk rather than in AWS
95 percent of the local cache disk is full and needs to be expanded soon
questions.why: Cache hit percentage is the share of reads served locally from the cache, so 95 percent means almost all reads avoided the slower trip to AWS.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm's office staff use Windows file shares every day. The firm wants the files to live in a managed Windows file system in AWS, but staff in the office must still get low-latency access. Which Storage Gateway mode fits best?
choices: Tape Gateway, which replaces physical backup tapes with virtual tapes
FSx File Gateway, which gives low-latency local access to a managed Windows file system in Amazon FSx
S3 File Gateway, which turns each file into an object in Amazon S3
Volume Gateway in stored mode, which presents block disks kept fully on local disk
questions.why: FSx File Gateway is the mode built to give on-site users fast local access to a managed Windows file system in Amazon FSx.

questions.prompt: A logistics company uses Volume Gateway in cached mode for a 40 TB volume. Its staff actively use about 6 TB of that data, but the local cache was sized at 1.5 TB. The cache hit percentage has dropped to about 55 percent and users complain of slow, unpredictable response times. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The volume is too large for cached mode, so the fix is to split it into smaller S3 objects
The cache is smaller than the working set, so many reads miss it and go over the WAN link; the fix is to grow the cache above about 6 TB
Uploads to AWS are too slow, so the fix is to switch to Tape Gateway to reduce upload traffic
The cache hit percentage is fine at 55 percent, so the fix is to upgrade the users' desktop computers
questions.why: An undersized cache cannot hold the actively used data, so reads miss and fetch over the WAN link; sizing the cache above the working set restores a high hit percentage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a hybrid storage gateway keeps on-premises access fast while the data lives in the cloud, when you would choose cached versus stored volume mode, and which metric tells you the design is working. Name one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: A storage gateway sits in our data center and looks like a normal file share or disk to our servers, but it keeps the durable copy in AWS. It stays fast because it holds recently used data in a local cache, so most reads never leave the building. In cached volume mode the full dataset lives in AWS and only the hot working set is local. That saves local hardware, but anything outside the cache is fetched over the WAN and is slower. In stored mode the whole volume stays local and is backed up to AWS asynchronously. Every read is fast, but we need local disk for all of it. To check that it works, I would watch the cache hit percentage, which should stay high, and the dirty-cache percentage to make sure uploads keep up. The tradeoff is that the cache must be larger than the working set, or latency spikes.
rubricPoints: Defines hybrid storage as on-premises apps using cloud-backed storage through a local gateway.
Explains that the local cache is what delivers low latency for frequently used data.
Distinguishes cached mode, with hot data local, from stored mode, with all data local and asynchronous backup to the cloud.
Names cache hit percentage as the key metric, and optionally dirty cache or upload backlog.
States the tradeoff: an undersized cache sends reads over the WAN, while stored mode needs full local capacity.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates a storage gateway, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that match a requirement to a gateway mode, a cache size and a metric builds this skill best.

lessons.plain: Storage that can scale is storage that keeps working as your data and traffic grow, without you rebuilding it. Some storage is like a rented storage unit of a fixed size: when it fills up, you must book a bigger one and move in. Other storage is like a parcel service that accepts any number of boxes and charges per box: you never run out of room, and it handles more deliveries as you send more. Designing for future demand means asking two questions: how much data will we hold later, and how many reads and writes per second will we need later? Then you pick storage that grows to meet both.
lessons.guessPrompt: An app saves user photos to a single fixed-size disk attached to one server, and uploads are growing every month. What do you think happens on the day the disk fills, and what kind of storage would avoid that day ever coming?
lessons.teach:
Scalable storage grows in two directions: capacity (how many bytes it holds) and throughput (how many requests or megabytes per second it serves). Elastic storage grows both automatically; provisioned storage gives you a fixed amount you must enlarge yourself.

Amazon S3 is object storage: you store whole files, called objects, by key in a container called a bucket. Capacity has no practical limit and you pay only for what you store. Request rate scales per prefix, the leading part of a key such as "2024/05/". Each prefix supports roughly 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second, so spreading keys across more prefixes multiplies throughput. Amazon EFS is a managed shared file system that many servers mount at once; it grows and shrinks automatically as files are added or deleted, and its elastic throughput mode raises speed with demand. Amazon EBS is block storage, a virtual disk attached to one server. It has a fixed size you choose; you can enlarge it later, but it never grows by itself. Amazon FSx offers managed file systems whose capacity you increase on request.

Worked example: a photo service expects 20,000 reads per second next year. Step one: one S3 prefix handles about 5,500 reads per second. Step two: 20,000 divided by 5,500 is about 3.6. Step three: round up, so keys need at least four prefixes, for example by starting each key with a user-group or date segment. Capacity needs no planning at all.

A common mistake is assuming an EBS volume expands like S3. It does not; and after you enlarge the volume, the operating system's file system must also be extended before the space is usable. In a running system, a full disk means failed writes, crashed services, and an outage at the busiest moment. Watch metrics that show headroom: free disk space on EBS, request rates and errors on S3, and the I/O-limit percentage on EFS.

questions.prompt: A logistics company plans to upload delivery-scan records to Amazon S3 (object storage that holds files, called objects, under keys in a bucket). It expects 12,000 writes per second at peak. A prefix is the leading part of a key, such as "depot-07/". Step one: one S3 prefix handles about 3,500 writes per second. Step two: 12,000 divided by 3,500 is about 3.4. Step three: ______. Step four: start each key with a depot or hour segment so writes spread evenly across those prefixes. Which choice correctly completes step three?
choices: Round down to 3 prefixes, because 3.4 is closer to 3 than to 4
Round up, so the keys need at least 4 prefixes
Use a single prefix, because S3 capacity has no practical limit
Use 3 prefixes, because each prefix supports about 5,500 requests per second
questions.why: Three prefixes would handle only about 10,500 writes per second, so you must round 3.4 up to 4 prefixes to cover 12,000 writes per second.

questions.prompt: A media agency runs 30 web servers that must all read and write the same set of design files at the same time. Nobody can predict how many files will be added each month, and the team does not want to resize storage by hand. Which storage option fits best?
choices: Amazon FSx, a managed file system, with capacity raised on request whenever it fills
Separate Amazon EBS volumes on each server, copied between servers every night
Amazon EBS, a virtual disk attached to one server, sized generously in advance
Amazon EFS, a managed shared file system that many servers mount at once and that grows and shrinks automatically
questions.why: EFS is shared by many servers at once and is elastic, meaning its capacity grows automatically without manual resizing.

questions.prompt: An engineer enlarges an Amazon EBS volume (block storage, a virtual disk attached to one server) from 200 GiB to 500 GiB. Inside the server, the operating system still reports only 200 GiB of usable space. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The server must be moved to Amazon EFS before extra space appears
The operating system's file system has not yet been extended to use the new space
EBS volumes can only grow automatically, so manual enlargement is ignored
The enlargement only applies after the volume is converted to S3 storage
questions.why: Enlarging an EBS volume makes the disk bigger, but the file system inside the operating system must also be extended before the extra space is usable.

questions.prompt: A research lab stores shared datasets on Amazon EFS, a managed shared file system. The team wants an early warning that the file system is nearing its throughput limits before jobs slow down. Which metric should they watch?
choices: The I/O-limit percentage on the EFS file system
Free disk space on an EBS volume
The total bytes stored, since EFS capacity must be enlarged by hand
The number of prefixes in an S3 bucket
questions.why: The I/O-limit percentage shows how close EFS is to its throughput ceiling, giving headroom warning; EFS capacity itself grows automatically.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose storage for data that will grow a lot over the next two years, covering both capacity and throughput, and name one limit or trade-off of the option you would pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would first separate two kinds of growth: how much data we will store, and how many requests per second we will serve. For files that many users upload and read, I would pick S3, because capacity is effectively unlimited and billed per byte, so we never schedule a resize. Throughput scales per key prefix, about 3,500 writes and 5,500 reads per second each, so I would design keys with several prefixes if we expect heavy traffic. If several servers need a shared file system, EFS grows automatically. The trade-off is that S3 is object storage, not a disk: you replace whole objects rather than editing bytes in place, so software expecting a normal file system needs changes. EBS would be simpler for one server but has a fixed size we must enlarge ourselves, then extend the file system, and watch free space so it never fills.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes capacity growth from throughput growth.
Contrasts elastic storage (S3, EFS) with fixed-size provisioned storage (EBS, FSx).
Explains that S3 request throughput scales by spreading keys across prefixes.
Notes that enlarging an EBS volume is manual and the file system must also be extended.
Names a trade-off, such as S3 not behaving like a disk.
Names a metric to watch, such as free space or request rate.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reasoning through a growth requirement to pick elastic versus provisioned storage, which exam-style scenarios practise best, with the disk-full mission showing the cost of getting it wrong.

lessons.plain: Choosing compute means deciding what kind of machine, or machine-like service, runs your code. On AWS you can rent whole virtual servers (Amazon EC2), run packaged applications in containers, or hand small pieces of code to a service that runs them only when called (AWS Lambda). If you pick EC2, you also pick an instance type, which is a fixed recipe of processor power, memory, storage and network speed. It is like hiring a vehicle. A sports car, a moving van and a minibus are all vehicles, but you choose by what you need to carry. Paying for the wrong shape wastes money or leaves the job undone.
lessons.guessPrompt: An application keeps a 150 GB dataset entirely in memory but does only light calculation. Would you rather rent a server with lots of processor cores and little memory, or one with lots of memory and modest processors? Why?
lessons.teach:
An EC2 instance is a virtual server you rent by the second or hour. Its instance type sets the ratio of vCPUs (virtual processor cores) to memory, plus local storage and network bandwidth. Type names read as family, generation and size: in m5.large, m is the family, 5 the generation, and large the size. Each step up in size roughly doubles resources and price.

The families matter most. General purpose (M, and the burstable T) balances CPU and memory for web servers and small apps. Compute optimized (C) gives more CPU per gigabyte, which suits encoding, scientific modelling and busy application servers. Memory optimized (R, X) gives more memory per vCPU, which suits in-memory caches and large databases. Storage optimized (I, D) adds fast local disks for heavy disk reads and writes. Accelerated computing (P, G, Inf) adds GPUs (graphics processors) or machine-learning chips.

This works because you buy capacity in fixed ratios. You match the ratio to the resource your workload runs out of first, so you avoid paying for the rest.

Worked example: a team runs a cache holding 200 GiB in memory with low CPU use. First, the scarce resource is memory. Second, that points to a memory-optimized family, so R. Third, pick the size with enough memory plus headroom. Fourth, watch memory utilization. EC2 does not report memory by default, so you install the CloudWatch agent, which is a small monitoring program, to publish it.

Also weigh the compute model. Choose containers when you want packaged apps that are dense and portable. On Fargate, AWS runs the servers for you. Choose Lambda for short, event-driven code with no servers to manage.

A common mistake is putting a steady, CPU-heavy job on a burstable T instance. T instances earn CPU credits while idle and spend them to run above a baseline. Under constant load the credits run out. In standard mode the instance is then held to its low baseline and slows down. In unlimited mode it keeps running fast but you pay extra. Watch the CPUCreditBalance metric to catch this.

questions.prompt:
A small animation studio renders short video clips overnight on EC2. Each render keeps every vCPU near 100% for hours but uses only about 6 GiB of memory. The architect works through the choice:

Step 1: The resource the job runs out of first is CPU, not memory or disk.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: Pick a size with enough vCPUs to finish the nightly batch on time, with some headroom.
Step 4: Watch CPU use during the renders to confirm the instance is not over- or under-sized.

Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Choose a burstable general-purpose family (T), because it is cheap and can run above its baseline when busy.
Choose a storage-optimized family (I), because video files need fast local disks.
Choose a compute-optimized family (C), because it gives more CPU per gigabyte of memory.
Choose a memory-optimized family (R), because rendering jobs are large and need the most memory per vCPU.
questions.why: CPU is the scarce resource, so a compute-optimized family matches the ratio to the need and avoids paying for memory the job does not use.

questions.prompt: A colleague points at an instance type named c5.2xlarge and asks what the "5" tells you. What is the correct answer?
choices: It is the size, meaning five times a large instance.
It is the number of vCPUs the instance has.
It is the generation of the instance family.
It is the amount of memory in gigabytes.
questions.why: Type names read as family, generation and size, so in c5.2xlarge the c is the family, 5 the generation, and 2xlarge the size.

questions.prompt: A payroll company runs a reporting service on a burstable T instance in standard mode. The service works well for the first few hours of month-end processing, when CPU is busy nonstop, and then becomes very slow. The CPUCreditBalance metric has fallen to zero. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Constant load used up its CPU credits, so it is now held to its low baseline.
The instance ran out of memory, so it started swapping to disk.
Unlimited mode began charging extra and throttled the instance to save money.
The CloudWatch agent was not installed, so the instance could not report its load.
questions.why: T instances spend earned credits to run above baseline, and in standard mode they drop to the baseline once constant load drains the credit balance.

questions.prompt: A retailer wants a small piece of code to run for a few seconds each time a customer uploads a receipt image, to record the upload. Uploads arrive at random times, and the team does not want to manage any servers. Which compute model fits best?
choices: A memory-optimized EC2 instance running all the time
Containers on EC2 instances the team patches and scales itself
A fleet of storage-optimized EC2 instances with fast local disks
Lambda, which runs short event-driven code with no servers to manage
questions.why: The work is short and triggered by events, and the team wants no servers, which is exactly the case Lambda suits.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick an EC2 instance family for a new workload, and name one tradeoff or limit they should watch for after launch.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I find which resource the workload exhausts first: CPU, memory, disk I/O or a GPU. Each EC2 family sells resources in a fixed ratio. C gives lots of CPU per gigabyte, R and X give lots of memory, I and D give fast local disks, P and G give GPUs, and M and T are balanced. I pick the family whose ratio fits, then the smallest size that covers peak load with some headroom. After launch I confirm the choice with a metric. I watch CPUUtilization for compute, and memory utilization through the CloudWatch agent, because EC2 does not report memory by default. The tradeoff to watch is burstable T instances. They are cheap for spiky, light load, but under sustained CPU use their credits drain. They then get throttled to a baseline, or in unlimited mode they cost extra. I also ask whether containers or Lambda would remove server management entirely.
rubricPoints: Identifies the bottleneck resource before choosing a family.
Maps families to strengths: C for compute, R/X for memory, I/D for storage, P/G for accelerators, M/T for balanced.
Names a metric to confirm the choice, noting that memory needs the CloudWatch agent.
Explains the burstable T credit limit under sustained load.
Considers containers or Lambda as alternatives to managing EC2.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this as matching a described workload and its metric to a compute model and instance family, so reasoning through scenario situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A serverless function is a piece of code that a cloud provider runs for you only when an event arrives, so you never manage a server. With AWS Lambda, the main dial you set is memory, and that one dial also controls how much processing power the function gets. Sizing means picking a memory setting that makes the function fast enough without paying for power it never uses. It is like renting a delivery van by the hour: a bigger van costs more per hour, but if it finishes the route in half the time, the total bill can actually be lower.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function takes 4 seconds at its current setting. If you double its memory and it now takes 1.8 seconds, do you think the bill per run goes up or down, given that you pay for memory multiplied by time?
lessons.teach:
Lambda is AWS's managed function service: it runs your code in response to events and bills you for what each run uses. You set memory from 128 MB up to 10,240 MB. The key fact is that CPU (processing power) is allocated in proportion to memory; around 1,769 MB gives roughly one full virtual CPU, and higher settings give more. So memory is really a combined memory-and-compute knob.

Cost is measured in GB-seconds: memory in gigabytes multiplied by run time (duration) in seconds, plus a small per-request charge. Because more CPU often shortens duration, raising memory can make a function both faster and cheaper.

Worked example. A CPU-heavy function runs 4 seconds at 512 MB: 0.5 GB × 4 s = 2 GB-seconds. At 1,024 MB it runs 1.8 seconds: 1 × 1.8 = 1.8 GB-seconds, so it is faster and cheaper. At 2,048 MB it runs 1.6 seconds: 2 × 1.6 = 3.2 GB-seconds, only slightly faster but much more expensive. The sweet spot is 1,024 MB. Testing a range of settings and comparing results this way is called power tuning.

The metrics to watch are Duration (how long each run takes) and Max Memory Used (reported for every run in the function's log). If Max Memory Used sits close to the setting, the function risks running out of memory and failing. If Duration barely drops when you add memory, the function is waiting on something else, such as a slow database or network call, and more memory is wasted money. Also check the timeout setting (maximum 15 minutes) so that a slow run is not cut off partway through.

Common mistake: choosing the smallest memory that fits the data, for example 128 MB because Max Memory Used shows 90 MB. That starves the function of CPU, so CPU-heavy work runs slowly, users wait longer, and the slow runs may cost more in total. Size by measured duration and cost, not by memory footprint alone.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing startup power-tunes its thumbnail-resizing Lambda function, which is CPU-heavy. Cost is measured in GB-seconds: memory in GB multiplied by duration in seconds. Step 1: at 256 MB it runs 6 seconds, so 0.25 GB × 6 s = 1.5 GB-seconds. Step 2: at 1,536 MB it runs 0.9 seconds, so 1.5 GB × 0.9 s = 1.35 GB-seconds. Step 3: at 3,072 MB it runs 0.8 seconds. Step 4 is missing: work out the cost of the 3,072 MB run and decide which setting is the sweet spot. Which choice correctly completes step 4?
choices: 3,072 × 0.8 = 2,457.6 GB-seconds, which is far too costly, so the team should go back down to 256 MB, the cheapest-looking setting
Cost depends only on duration, so the 0.8-second run at 3,072 MB is the cheapest and should be chosen
3 × 0.8 = 2.4 GB-seconds, but 3,072 MB is the sweet spot because it finished fastest of all three settings
3 × 0.8 = 2.4 GB-seconds, so 1,536 MB stays the sweet spot
questions.why: 3,072 MB is 3 GB, and 3 × 0.8 = 2.4 GB-seconds costs much more than 1.35 GB-seconds for only 0.1 seconds less run time, so 1,536 MB remains the best balance.

questions.prompt: An engineer raises a Lambda function's memory setting from 512 MB to 2,048 MB without changing anything else. Besides more memory, what else does the function get?
choices: Nothing else, because memory and CPU are set separately
A longer maximum timeout than the usual 15-minute limit
A lower per-request charge for each run
More CPU, because Lambda allocates processing power in proportion to memory
questions.why: In Lambda, CPU is allocated in proportion to memory, so memory acts as a combined memory-and-compute setting.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's Lambda function looks up shipment records from a slow external database. Power tuning shows: 1,024 MB runs 3.1 seconds, and 2,048 MB runs 3.0 seconds. What does this tell you, and what should you do?
choices: The function is close to running out of memory, so 2,048 MB is needed to stop it from failing
The function is starved of CPU, so it should be raised again to 4,096 MB to bring the duration down
The function mostly waits on the slow database call, so extra memory is wasted money; keep the lower setting
The timeout is too short, so raising memory is the only way to stop runs from being cut off
questions.why: When Duration barely drops as memory rises, the function is waiting on something else such as a database, so doubling memory roughly doubles cost for almost no speed gain.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site sets its Lambda function to 1,024 MB. The log shows Max Memory Used of 1,010 MB on most runs, and occasional runs fail. Which change best addresses the risk?
choices: Leave memory unchanged and raise the timeout to the 15-minute maximum
Lower memory to 128 MB, the smallest setting, to force the function to use less memory
Raise the memory setting, because Max Memory Used close to the setting means the function risks running out of memory
Lower memory to 512 MB to cut cost, since Duration is the only metric that matters
questions.why: Max Memory Used sitting near the configured memory means runs can run out of memory and fail, so the setting needs headroom; a longer timeout does not add memory.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose the memory setting for a Lambda function, and name one situation where adding memory would not help.
lessons.modelAnswer: In Lambda, memory is the one sizing dial, and CPU scales with it, so more memory also means more processing power. We pay in GB-seconds, which is memory multiplied by duration. That means a bigger setting can be cheaper overall if it cuts run time enough. I'd test the function at several settings, record Duration and Max Memory Used for each, and calculate GB-seconds to find the point where speed stops improving much. I'd also keep Max Memory Used comfortably below the setting so the function doesn't fail by running out of memory. The limit is that this only helps CPU-bound or memory-bound work. If the function spends most of its time waiting on a slow database or an external API, extra memory doesn't shorten the wait. We'd pay more per second and get no speedup.
rubricPoints: States that Lambda CPU is allocated in proportion to the memory setting.
Explains cost as memory multiplied by duration (GB-seconds).
Notes that more memory can lower total cost if duration drops enough.
Names Duration and Max Memory Used as the metrics to measure.
Identifies a limit, such as I/O-bound work that gains nothing from more memory, or diminishing returns at high settings.

suggested.rationale: Sizing a Lambda function comes down to reasoning through a requirement with numbers (duration, memory used, GB-seconds), which an exam-style scenario practises well, and no existing mission focuses on the memory dial.

lessons.plain: Auto scaling means letting the cloud add or remove servers for you as demand changes, instead of guessing a fixed number in advance. You tell it a rule, such as keep average processor use near half, and set a smallest and largest allowed fleet. When a measurement crosses the line, it launches more copies of your server or retires spare ones. Think of a supermarket that opens more checkout lanes when queues grow and closes them when the store is quiet. The skill is choosing which measurement truly signals that customers are waiting.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web servers run at 80% average CPU and you want them near 50%. If you have 4 servers now, roughly how many would you need, and what single number would you watch to know the change worked?
lessons.teach:
Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling manages an Auto Scaling group: a set of identical virtual servers (instances) built from a launch template, which is a saved recipe of image, instance type and network settings. The group has a minimum, a maximum, and a desired capacity, which is how many instances it tries to keep running. A scaling policy changes desired capacity when a metric moves. Metrics are published to Amazon CloudWatch, the monitoring service, and an alarm is a rule that fires when a metric stays past a threshold.

Policy types: target tracking keeps one metric near a set value, like a thermostat. Step scaling adds or removes different amounts depending on how far an alarm is breached. Simple scaling makes one fixed change and then pauses. Scheduled scaling changes capacity at known times. Predictive scaling forecasts daily patterns from history and launches capacity early. Separately, health checks replace instances that fail EC2 status checks or, if enabled, load balancer health checks. That is replacement, not scaling.

Common metrics: average CPU utilization, ALBRequestCountPerTarget (requests each instance receives behind an Application Load Balancer), network in and out, and custom metrics such as queue messages waiting per instance. AWS Auto Scaling is a separate umbrella feature that applies scaling plans across several services at once, such as EC2 groups, DynamoDB table capacity, Aurora read replicas and ECS tasks.

Worked example: target tracking at 50% CPU, 4 instances averaging 80%. Required capacity is about 4 × 80 / 50 = 6.4, rounded up to 7, so three launch. After a warmup period, new instances count toward the average, CPU settles near 50%, and the policy stops adding.

Common mistake: scaling a queue worker fleet on CPU, or expecting a memory metric by default. Memory needs the CloudWatch agent, and a backlog is better measured as messages per instance. In a running system the wrong metric means the fleet stays small while users wait, or it oscillates and wastes money. Set the maximum high enough for real peaks.

questions.prompt:
A photo-printing company runs order-processing workers in an Auto Scaling group (a set of identical virtual servers kept at a chosen count). It uses target tracking, a policy that keeps one metric near a set value, on a custom metric: messages waiting in the order queue per instance. The target is 20 messages per instance. The minimum is 2 and the maximum is 12. Right now 6 instances are running and 300 messages are waiting.

Step 1: Current backlog per instance = 300 / 6 = 50 messages.
Step 2: [missing]
Step 3: The maximum is 12, so desired capacity is capped at 12 and 6 new instances launch. Watch messages per instance to see whether the backlog falls toward 20.

Which line correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Required capacity = 50 / 20 = 2.5, so add 3 instances, giving 9.
Required capacity = 300 / 6 = 50 instances, one per waiting message group.
Required capacity = 6 × 20 / 50 = 2.4, rounded up to 3 instances.
Required capacity = 6 × 50 / 20 = 15 instances.
questions.why: Target tracking scales current capacity by the ratio of the metric's current value to its target: 6 × 50 / 20 = 15. The group's maximum of 12 then caps that figure in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site's Auto Scaling group has a desired capacity of 5. One instance starts failing the Application Load Balancer's health checks, and load balancer health checks are enabled on the group. The group terminates that instance and launches a new one, so it still has 5 instances. What is this event?
choices: Health check replacement: an unhealthy instance is swapped out, and desired capacity does not change.
Target tracking: the policy is holding a metric near its target value.
Simple scaling: one fixed change is made, and then the group pauses.
Step scaling: an alarm was breached, so capacity changed by a step.
questions.why: Replacing a failed instance keeps the same count. It is replacement, not scaling, and no scaling policy changed desired capacity.

questions.prompt: A media company runs a fleet of video-encoding workers that pull jobs from a queue. During a busy evening, average CPU stays around 35%, yet thousands of jobs pile up and customers wait hours. The fleet scales on average CPU and never grows. Which metric should drive scaling instead?
choices: ALBRequestCountPerTarget, the number of requests each instance receives behind an Application Load Balancer.
A custom metric of queue messages waiting per instance.
Memory utilization, which CloudWatch publishes for every instance by default.
Network in, because jobs arrive over the network.
questions.why: The backlog is the real measure of unmet demand for queue workers, so messages waiting per instance makes the fleet grow when jobs pile up, even while CPU stays low.

questions.prompt: An online learning platform uses target tracking at 60% average CPU. During an exam-week peak, CloudWatch (the monitoring service) shows average CPU stuck near 95%. Users report slow pages. The group shows 8 running instances, and its maximum is set to 8. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The policy needs a CloudWatch alarm on memory before it can act.
The group has reached its maximum, so the policy cannot raise desired capacity any further.
Target tracking only removes instances and never adds them.
Health checks are terminating instances faster than the group can scale.
questions.why: Desired capacity can never exceed the group's maximum. With the group capped at 8, the policy cannot add instances, so the maximum must be set high enough for real peaks.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an Auto Scaling group decides to add or remove instances, which policy and metric you would pick for a web tier versus a queue worker tier, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: An Auto Scaling group keeps a desired number of identical instances between a minimum and maximum. A scaling policy watches a CloudWatch metric and changes the desired count. For a web tier behind a load balancer, I would use target tracking on ALBRequestCountPerTarget or average CPU, say 50%, and the service works out how many instances bring the metric back to target. For queue workers, CPU is misleading, so I would track a custom backlog-per-instance metric. Scheduled scaling covers known events, and predictive scaling covers repeating daily patterns. Health checks replace broken instances, but that is separate from scaling. Tradeoffs: new instances need time to boot and warm up, so sudden spikes can outrun reactive policies. The maximum caps cost but also caps capacity. A badly chosen metric or target can leave users waiting or make the fleet flap up and down.
rubricPoints: Desired capacity moves between min and max based on a policy driven by a CloudWatch metric.
Names target tracking, and distinguishes step, scheduled or predictive scaling.
Matches the metric to the workload, such as requests per target for web and backlog per instance for queues.
Notes that health-check replacement is not the same as scaling.
States a tradeoff such as launch and warmup lag, the max cap, or flapping from a poor metric.

suggested.rationale: Setting policies and watching a simulated fleet react to metric changes builds the trigger intuition far better than reading alone.

lessons.plain: Decoupling means putting a buffer between two parts of a system so they no longer have to work at the same speed or even be running at the same moment. Picture a restaurant: waiters pin order tickets on a rail and cooks take them when ready. A dinner rush does not make waiters wait at the kitchen door, and a slow cook does not stop new orders. Each side can add staff on its own. In cloud systems the ticket rail is usually a managed message queue or event service, which lets the front end and the back end grow or shrink independently.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website accepts photo uploads and then resizes each photo, which takes several seconds. If a sudden rush of uploads arrives, what do you think happens when the upload page waits for the resize to finish, compared with when it drops a note in a to-do list and returns immediately?
lessons.teach:
Decoupling is designing components so one does not call another directly and wait for the answer. Instead, the producer (the component that creates work) sends a message to an intermediary, and the consumer (the component that does the work) reads it later. Tight coupling is the opposite: a direct, synchronous call where a slow or failed consumer makes the producer slow or fail too.

On AWS the common intermediaries are Amazon SQS, a managed message queue where each message is processed by one consumer, and Amazon SNS, a managed publish/subscribe service that copies one message to many subscribers (called fan-out). Amazon EventBridge, a managed event bus, routes events by rules. They work because the queue absorbs bursts: producers write quickly, the backlog grows, and consumers drain it at their own pace.

Worked example. A web tier receives 500 upload requests per minute during a spike. Step 1: each web server writes a small message (photo location) to an SQS queue and replies to the user in milliseconds. Step 2: worker instances in their own Auto Scaling group poll the queue, resize photos, then delete each message. Step 3: the backlog rises to 3,000 messages. Step 4: a scaling policy based on backlog per worker (queue depth divided by worker count) adds workers until the backlog falls. The web tier never scaled for the resize work; each tier scaled on its own signal.

Common mistake: setting the visibility timeout (how long a received message stays hidden from other consumers) shorter than processing time. The message reappears before the first worker finishes, so a second worker processes it again, causing duplicates and wasted capacity. Also expect occasional duplicates anyway, so consumers should be idempotent (safe to repeat).

The metrics to watch are queue depth (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible) and the age of the oldest message; a steadily rising age means consumers cannot keep up.

questions.prompt:
A city library's website lets members request scanned copies of old newspapers. Each scan takes about 2 minutes to convert into a searchable PDF. During a school project week, requests jump to 300 per minute. The team decouples the work with a managed message queue (Amazon SQS).

Step 1: When a member submits a request, the web server writes a small message (the newspaper ID and the member's email) to the SQS queue and tells the member right away that the request was received.
Step 2: Converter instances run in their own Auto Scaling group. They poll the queue, build the PDF, and delete each message only after the PDF is saved. The team sets the visibility timeout to 5 minutes, longer than the 2-minute conversion time.
Step 3: The backlog climbs to 6,000 messages while only 6 converters are running, so each converter has about 1,000 messages waiting.
Step 4: ???
Result: The converter tier grows until the backlog shrinks, and the web tier never had to scale for the conversion work.

Which action belongs in Step 4?
choices: Add more web servers, because they are the first tier to see the extra requests
Shorten the visibility timeout to 1 minute so that waiting messages reach converters sooner
Add converter instances using a scaling policy based on backlog per worker (queue depth divided by converter count)
Have the web servers call the converters directly so each request is handled the moment it arrives
questions.why: In a decoupled design the consumer tier scales on its own signal, and backlog per worker (queue depth divided by the number of workers) directly measures how much waiting work each converter has.

questions.prompt: An online pet-supply store creates one 'order placed' message for each new order. Three separate systems need their own copy of every message: billing, warehouse picking, and the customer-email service. Which intermediary fits this need best?
choices: A direct synchronous call from the order service to each of the three systems, one after another
Amazon SNS, a managed publish/subscribe service that copies each message to many subscribers (fan-out)
A larger web tier, so the order service can wait longer for the three systems to answer
A single Amazon SQS queue that all three systems poll, because each message is then processed once
questions.why: SNS fans out one message to many subscribers, while a single SQS queue delivers each message to only one consumer, and direct calls would tightly couple the order service to all three systems.

questions.prompt: A travel company's workers read booking messages from an SQS queue. Each booking takes about 90 seconds to process, but the visibility timeout is set to 30 seconds. The team sees many bookings processed twice and workers busier than expected. What is the most direct fix?
choices: Lower the visibility timeout to 10 seconds so messages move through the queue faster
Raise the visibility timeout above the 90-second processing time, and keep consumers idempotent
Add more producer instances so messages arrive in the queue more evenly
Delete each message as soon as it is received, before the worker starts processing it
questions.why: If the visibility timeout is shorter than processing time, the message becomes visible again and a second worker processes it; making the timeout longer than processing time stops that, and idempotent consumers handle the occasional duplicates that still happen.

questions.prompt: A weather-data service pushes sensor readings into an SQS queue, and a group of consumer instances processes them. Over the last hour the queue depth has gone up and down, but the age of the oldest message has risen steadily from 20 seconds to 25 minutes. What does this most likely tell you?
choices: The visibility timeout is too long, so this metric is not useful and can be ignored
The consumers cannot keep up with incoming work, so the consumer tier needs more capacity
The producers are failing, because a growing message age means fewer messages are being sent
The system is healthy, because only queue depth matters and it is not rising steadily
questions.why: A steadily rising age of the oldest message means work is waiting longer and longer, which shows the consumers are not draining the queue fast enough.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why putting a queue between the web tier and the worker tier lets each scale independently, and name one tradeoff or limit this introduces.
lessons.modelAnswer: Without a queue, the web servers call the workers directly and wait, so a slow worker makes every user wait, and we must scale both tiers together. With a queue such as SQS in between, the web tier just writes a message and answers the user immediately. The queue holds the backlog during spikes, and the workers, in their own Auto Scaling group, scale on backlog per instance rather than on web traffic. If workers crash, messages wait instead of being lost. The tradeoff is that work becomes asynchronous: the user does not get the result instantly, so we need a way to report completion later. Messages can also be delivered more than once, so workers must be idempotent and the visibility timeout must exceed processing time. I would watch queue depth and age of the oldest message to confirm consumers keep up.
rubricPoints: Defines decoupling as replacing a direct synchronous call with an intermediary such as a queue.
Explains that the queue absorbs bursts so producers stay fast while consumers drain at their own pace.
States that each tier scales on its own signal, such as backlog per worker for consumers.
Names a tradeoff such as delayed results, duplicate delivery, or need for idempotent consumers.
Names a metric to watch, such as queue depth or age of oldest message.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a job queue that grows while nothing drains it makes the learner see directly how producers and consumers are decoupled and which queue metrics reveal a consumer tier that is not keeping up.

lessons.plain: Some work does not need to answer a user right away; it just needs to get done, often in huge amounts. Batch computing means collecting many independent tasks and running them on borrowed machines until they finish. Big-data computing means splitting one enormous dataset across many machines that work on pieces at the same time. AWS Batch is a managed job scheduler: you hand it tasks and it finds machines to run them. Amazon EMR is a managed cluster for big-data tools like Spark. Think of Batch as a print shop running thousands of separate print jobs, and EMR as a team of people each counting one stack of a giant pile of ballots.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 10,000 photos to resize overnight, and each photo can be processed on its own. Would you rather have one huge machine work through them in order, or many smaller machines each taking some photos at the same time? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Batch runs containerized jobs for you. A job is one unit of work, such as a script in a container. A job queue holds jobs waiting to run, with a priority. A compute environment is the pool of machines Batch launches to run them: EC2 instances, Spot Instances (spare capacity at a deep discount that AWS can reclaim with short notice), or Fargate (serverless containers). Batch scales that pool up when the queue fills and down to zero when it empties, so you pay only while work runs.

Amazon EMR runs big-data frameworks as a managed cluster. Hadoop and Spark are open-source frameworks that split a large dataset into pieces and process them in parallel across many machines. An EMR cluster has a primary node that coordinates, core nodes that run work and store data in HDFS (the Hadoop distributed file system), and task nodes that only compute. EMR Serverless removes cluster management entirely.

Worked example. A nightly job must render 10,000 independent images, and a separate job must aggregate 5 TB of clickstream logs. Step one: images do not depend on each other, so submit 10,000 jobs to a Batch queue backed by a Spot compute environment. Step two: watch the count of jobs waiting in the RUNNABLE state; if it keeps rising, the environment's maximum size is too low. Step three: the log aggregation is one dataset that must be joined and grouped, which is Spark's strength, so run it on EMR reading from S3. Step four: watch YARN memory available and pending containers (YARN is the resource manager handing out cluster memory); low memory with many pending containers means add task nodes.

A common mistake is putting core nodes on Spot. If Spot reclaims them, HDFS data and the job can be lost. Put task nodes on Spot instead, since they hold no data. Another mistake is choosing Lambda for work longer than its 15-minute limit; long-running or heavy jobs belong on Batch or EMR.

questions.prompt: A university research lab must run 3,000 independent protein simulations every night. Each simulation is packaged in a container and takes about 40 minutes. Step one: each simulation runs longer than Lambda's 15-minute limit, so Lambda (a serverless function service) is ruled out. Step two: the simulations do not depend on each other, so the lab submits 3,000 jobs to an AWS Batch job queue (a holding line for waiting work) backed by a compute environment (the pool of machines Batch launches) that uses Spot Instances (spare capacity at a discount that can be reclaimed). Step three: ______. Step four: when the queue empties, Batch shrinks the compute environment to zero, so the lab stops paying until the next night. Which choice correctly fills in step three?
choices: Move the simulations onto EMR core nodes running on Spot so the data is stored in HDFS for safety
Watch the count of jobs in the RUNNABLE state, and raise the compute environment's maximum size if it keeps rising
Watch how long each Lambda function runs, and split any simulation that goes past 15 minutes
Watch YARN memory available and pending containers, and add task nodes to the cluster if memory runs low
questions.why: In Batch, a steadily rising number of jobs waiting in RUNNABLE shows the compute environment cannot grow large enough, so you raise its maximum size.

questions.prompt: A retailer has 8 TB of sales records stored in S3. Every week the records must be joined with a product table and grouped by region into one summary report. Which service is the best fit for this work?
