choices: AWS Batch, with one separate job submitted for every sales record
Amazon EMR running Spark, reading the data from S3
AWS Lambda, with one function invocation processing the whole 8 TB
A single EC2 instance running a script on a Fargate compute environment
questions.why: Joining and grouping one large dataset in parallel across many machines is what Spark on EMR (a managed big-data cluster) is built for, while Batch suits many independent jobs.

questions.prompt: A media company runs a Spark job on an Amazon EMR cluster. During the job, the team sees that YARN (the resource manager that hands out cluster memory) reports very little memory available, and many containers are pending. What is the most appropriate change?
choices: Add task nodes to the cluster so there is more memory to run work
Raise the maximum size of the AWS Batch compute environment
Replace the primary node with a larger instance and remove the core nodes
Move the job to AWS Lambda so it scales automatically
questions.why: Low YARN memory with many pending containers means the cluster lacks compute capacity, and task nodes add compute without needing to store any HDFS data.

questions.prompt: To cut costs, an insurance company runs every node of its EMR cluster, including the core nodes, on Spot Instances. What is the main risk of this design?
choices: If Spot reclaims the core nodes, data stored in HDFS and the running job can be lost
The cluster will be forced to scale down to zero whenever the job queue is empty
YARN will refuse to hand out memory to any node that runs on Spot capacity
The primary node will stop accepting Spark jobs because Spot nodes cannot run Spark
questions.why: Core nodes store HDFS data, so losing them to a Spot reclaim can lose data and break the job, which is why only task nodes, which hold no data, should go on Spot.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick AWS Batch and when you would pick Amazon EMR for a large overnight workload, naming one risk of using Spot Instances and the metric you would watch.
lessons.modelAnswer: I ask whether the work is many independent tasks or one big dataset processed together. Thousands of separate jobs, like rendering images or running simulations, fit AWS Batch: I package each as a container, submit to a job queue, and let a compute environment scale machines up and back to zero. One large dataset that needs joins and aggregations fits Amazon EMR, which runs Spark or Hadoop across a cluster. Spot Instances cut cost a lot, but AWS can reclaim them, so jobs must be retryable, and on EMR I only put task nodes on Spot because core nodes hold HDFS data. For Batch I watch how many jobs sit in RUNNABLE; for EMR I watch YARN available memory and pending containers. The tradeoff is cost and control versus reliability and setup effort.
rubricPoints: AWS Batch fits many independent containerized jobs scheduled through job queues and compute environments.
Amazon EMR fits processing one large dataset in parallel with Spark or Hadoop.
Spot Instances save money but can be reclaimed, so work must tolerate interruption.
On EMR, Spot belongs on task nodes, not core nodes that store HDFS data.
Names a metric: Batch jobs waiting in RUNNABLE, or EMR YARN memory and pending containers.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine runs batch or cluster jobs, and the exam tests this as reasoning through scenarios that distinguish independent jobs from distributed data processing.

lessons.plain: Distributed computing across the global infrastructure means running parts of your application in several physical places instead of one, so each user is served from somewhere close. Distance costs time: a request that must cross an ocean and come back is slow no matter how powerful the server is. Picture a pizza chain. It can have one huge kitchen downtown, or it can open small shops around the city so every delivery is short. Cloud providers offer locations at different sizes: large regional data-center groups, smaller sites inside major cities, and many tiny edge sites that can cache content or forward traffic. You choose where each piece of work runs.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app runs on servers in Virginia, USA, and your fastest-growing customers are in Sydney, Australia. Pages feel slow to them even though the servers sit at 20% CPU. Would doubling the number of Virginia servers help? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
The AWS global infrastructure comes in layers. A Region is a separate geographic area, such as Sydney or Frankfurt, holding its own copy of most services. An Availability Zone (AZ) is one or more isolated data centers inside a Region, with independent power and networking, linked to the other AZs in that Region by fast, low-latency connections. Edge locations are many small sites in cities worldwide. They do not run your full application. They cache content and accept user traffic close by, then pass it onto the provider's private backbone network. Local Zones are small extensions of a Region placed in a large city, used to run compute near users there. Wavelength Zones put compute inside mobile carriers' 5G networks.

This works because latency, the delay before a response arrives, is mostly set by distance and the number of network hops, not by how fast the server is. Light in fiber needs roughly 1 millisecond for every 100 km in each direction.

Worked example: a Sydney user calls an API hosted in Virginia, roughly 15,000 km away. Step 1: one round trip takes about 200 ms or more. Step 2: loading one page needs several round trips for connection setup, encryption setup, and the request, which adds up to close to a second. Step 3: you deploy a copy of the API in the Sydney Region, or cache static files at Sydney edge locations. Step 4: each round trip drops to a few milliseconds. The metric to watch is latency per user location, especially the slow tail (p95 or p99), and time to first byte.

A common mistake is reaching for multi-AZ to fix slowness for distant users. AZs all sit inside one Region. They protect against a data-center failure but do not move the app closer to anyone. Adding servers in the same place does not help either. In a running system, the distant users stay slow while the dashboards show healthy, idle servers. Choosing a placement also has costs: more Regions means data has to be replicated between them, you pay to transfer it, and you run more copies to operate.

questions.prompt: A game studio hosts its leaderboard API in the Frankfurt Region. Many players are in Toronto, about 6,500 km away, and they complain that the leaderboard feels sluggish. The architect works through it like this. Step 1: light in fiber needs about 1 ms per 100 km in each direction, so a one-way trip of 6,500 km takes about 65 ms. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: opening the leaderboard needs about 4 round trips (connection setup, encryption setup, and the request), so the wait is over half a second before any server work happens. Step 4: placing a copy of the API in a Region in Canada cuts each round trip to a few milliseconds. Which statement correctly fills Step 2?
choices: One round trip, there and back, is about 130 ms, because the delay applies in each direction
One round trip is about 650 ms, because each network hop adds ten times the travel time
One round trip is about 65 ms, because the reply travels on the same fiber as the request
One round trip is about 6.5 ms, because 1 ms covers every 1,000 km of fiber in total
questions.why: The 1 ms per 100 km figure applies in each direction, so 65 ms out plus 65 ms back gives a round trip of about 130 ms, and 4 round trips gives roughly 520 ms.

questions.prompt: A media company wants to explain edge locations to a new team member. Which description is accurate?
choices: They are many small sites in cities worldwide that run a complete copy of your application for local users.
They are small sites in cities worldwide that cache content and accept user traffic nearby, then pass it onto the provider's private backbone.
They are compute placed inside mobile carriers' 5G networks so that apps run very close to phones.
They are one or more isolated data centers inside a Region, each with independent power and networking.
questions.why: Edge locations do not run your full application; they cache content and take in user traffic close to the user, then carry it over the private backbone. The other options describe full deployments, Availability Zones, and Wavelength Zones.

questions.prompt: An online retailer runs its store in a single US Region. Shoppers in Singapore report slow page loads. The team adds a second Availability Zone in the same Region and doubles the number of servers. Shoppers in Singapore are still slow, and the dashboards show healthy, mostly idle servers. What is the best explanation?
choices: The servers are too slow, so the team should choose larger server sizes in both Availability Zones.
Two Availability Zones are not enough to help distant users, so the team should add a third one in the same Region.
The new Availability Zone needs more time to warm up, and latency will drop once its caches fill with data.
Availability Zones all sit inside the same Region, so the app is no closer to Singapore and the delay set by distance and hops is unchanged.
questions.why: Latency is mostly set by distance and network hops, and AZs protect against data-center failure without moving the app closer to users. That is why the servers look idle while distant users stay slow.

questions.prompt: A travel booking firm adds a copy of its API in an Asia Pacific Region in Mumbai so that customers in India get faster responses. Which measurement best shows whether the change worked?
choices: Average CPU use across all of the firm's API servers, which should fall now that the load is shared
The number of healthy Availability Zones in the Mumbai Region reported by the provider
The total number of requests handled across every Region the firm runs in
Slow-tail latency (p95 or p99) and time to first byte for users located in India
questions.why: The goal is lower delay for users in a specific place, so you watch latency per user location, especially the slow tail, along with time to first byte. Server load and request counts do not show what those users actually experience.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations each affect performance for users around the world, and name one tradeoff of running in more locations.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Region is a geographic area with its own copy of most services. Availability Zones are isolated data centers inside one Region, and they exist mainly so we survive a single facility failing. Edge locations are small sites in many cities that cache content and take user traffic close by, then carry it over the provider's own network. For users far away, the delay comes from distance, because every round trip across an ocean costs a couple hundred milliseconds. Adding servers or AZs in our current Region won't fix that. Running in a Region near those users, or serving cacheable content from the edge, will. I'd confirm it worked by watching p99 latency and time to first byte broken down by user location. The tradeoff is that more Regions means replicating data, which costs money for transfer, introduces delay or consistency issues between copies, and gives us more deployments to operate.
rubricPoints: Defines Region, Availability Zone, and edge location correctly.
States that latency is driven mainly by distance and round trips, not server power.
Notes that multi-AZ improves resilience but does not reduce latency for distant users.
Names a metric such as p99 latency or time to first byte per user location.
Names a tradeoff such as replication cost, data consistency between copies, or extra operational effort.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine places workloads across geography, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about where users are and which latency metric to watch builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A database is where an application keeps data it needs to find again quickly. Different kinds are built for different jobs, like storage in a kitchen. A labeled shelf system where every jar has a fixed spot and recipes link to each other is like a relational database. Big bins you grab by name are like a non-relational database. The counter beside the stove is like an in-memory database: fastest to reach but small. A pantry that grows and shrinks by itself, billed only for what you use, is like serverless. Choosing well means matching the shape of your data and how it gets read to the right kind.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop must record an order and subtract the item from stock so that either both changes happen or neither does. It also shows each shopper's cart, looked up only by shopper ID, to millions of people at once. Would you keep both in the same kind of database, or use two kinds? Why?
lessons.teach:
A relational database stores data in tables with fixed columns. It is queried with SQL, a language that can join related tables and run transactions. A transaction is a group of changes that either all succeed or all fail. On AWS this means Amazon RDS or Amazon Aurora, which are managed relational engines. Relational databases suit structured data, reports that ask new questions, and money or stock that must stay consistent.

A non-relational (NoSQL) database stores items as key-value pairs or documents with a flexible layout. You read an item by a known key, a unique lookup value such as a user ID. Amazon DynamoDB is AWS's managed key-value and document database. It spreads data across many machines, so it handles enormous request rates at steady millisecond latency. Latency is the time one request takes. The trade-off is that it has no joins, so you must design tables around the questions you will ask.

An in-memory database keeps data in RAM, the computer's fast working memory, and answers in under a millisecond. Amazon ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) is mostly used as a cache, a fast copy in front of a slower store. Amazon MemoryDB is an in-memory store that also keeps its data durably, so it survives a restart.

Serverless describes how capacity is managed, not a data model. You do not pick a server size; capacity scales with demand and you pay for use. Examples are Aurora Serverless v2 and DynamoDB on-demand mode.

Worked example: the shop from the question. Orders need all-or-nothing changes across tables, so they go in Aurora. Carts are read by shopper ID at huge scale, so they go in DynamoDB. Product pages need sub-millisecond reads, so put ElastiCache in front. Traffic is spiky and unpredictable, so serverless capacity fits.

A common mistake is putting everything in DynamoDB "for scale" and then needing ad hoc queries. Those force full-table scans, which are slow and costly. To confirm a choice worked, watch read and write latency, throttled requests on DynamoDB, CPU on RDS, and cache hit rate on ElastiCache.

questions.prompt: A fitness app is choosing its databases. Step 1: each member's workout history is always read by member ID, and millions of members open the app, so it goes in DynamoDB (a managed key-value database). Step 2: subscription billing changes several tables and must be all-or-nothing, so it goes in Aurora (a managed relational database). Step 3: traffic is quiet all day except a sharp 6 a.m. peak, so DynamoDB on-demand mode (serverless capacity that scales with demand) is chosen. Step 4: to confirm that the DynamoDB choice keeps up during the 6 a.m. peak, the team watches which metric?
choices: CPU utilisation on the database server
The number of joins run per minute
Throttled requests, alongside read and write latency
Cache hit rate
questions.why: Throttled requests show DynamoDB turning requests away because it cannot keep up, and with latency they reveal whether the table handles the peak; CPU is the RDS signal, cache hit rate is the ElastiCache signal, and DynamoDB has no joins.

questions.prompt: A colleague says, "We should switch to a serverless database because we need a document data model." What is wrong with this reasoning?
choices: Nothing is wrong; serverless and document database mean the same thing
Serverless describes how capacity is managed, scaling with demand and paid for by use, not what data model the database has
Serverless databases can only store relational tables, so they cannot hold documents
Serverless means the data is kept only in RAM, so it is lost on restart
questions.why: Serverless is about not choosing a server size, because capacity scales and you pay for use; both relational (Aurora Serverless v2) and key-value (DynamoDB on-demand) options exist.

questions.prompt: An online game stores player session state that must be read in under a millisecond. If the store restarts, losing the sessions would log every player out, which is unacceptable. Which choice fits best?
choices: Amazon DynamoDB, because it gives steady millisecond latency
Amazon ElastiCache used purely as a cache in front of the sessions
Amazon RDS, because SQL transactions guarantee speed
Amazon MemoryDB, an in-memory store that also keeps its data durably
questions.why: MemoryDB answers from RAM in under a millisecond and keeps data durably so it survives a restart, while DynamoDB is millisecond rather than sub-millisecond and a cache is a copy of data, not a durable home for it.

questions.prompt: A retailer put all its sales records in DynamoDB "for scale." Now analysts keep asking new questions, such as total sales by region and by month, that the tables were not designed around. What is the most likely result?
choices: The queries force full-table scans, which are slow and costly, so a relational database would have suited this reporting better
Cache hit rate drops, so adding ElastiCache fixes the problem
The queries run faster because DynamoDB spreads data across many machines
DynamoDB automatically builds joins for the new questions
questions.why: DynamoDB has no joins and reads efficiently only by a known key, so unplanned questions require scanning the whole table, whereas relational databases with SQL suit reports that ask new questions.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a relational, non-relational, in-memory, or serverless database for a new feature. Name at least one limit or trade-off of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the shape of the data and how we will read it. If the records relate to each other, we need joins or new reporting questions, or changes must be all-or-nothing like payments, I pick relational: RDS or Aurora. The trade-off is that it scales mainly by bigger machines and read copies. If we always fetch by a known key at huge volume, DynamoDB gives steady millisecond latency. But it has no joins, so we must design around access patterns up front. If we need sub-millisecond reads of hot data, an in-memory store like ElastiCache sits in front. It is small and a cache can lose data, so it is not the system of record unless we use MemoryDB. Serverless is a capacity choice, good for spiky or idle workloads, though steady heavy load can cost more. I would then watch latency, throttling and cache hit rate.
rubricPoints: Relational fits structured, related data that needs joins, ad hoc queries or all-or-nothing transactions.
Non-relational fits known-key lookups at very high scale, but has no joins and needs access patterns designed up front.
In-memory gives sub-millisecond reads, and a cache is not a durable primary store.
Serverless is a capacity and billing model that suits unpredictable or idle load, separate from the data model.
Names a metric to confirm the choice, such as latency, throttled requests or cache hit rate.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a database type is a matter of reading requirement wording like transactions, key lookups, sub-millisecond reads or spiky load, and exam-style scenarios practise exactly that judgement.

lessons.plain: A database engine is the specific software that stores your data and answers your queries, such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle or Microsoft SQL Server. Choosing one is like choosing which language your office speaks: your application, your staff and your licences all depend on it. Moving a database is called a migration. A homogeneous migration keeps the same engine (MySQL to MySQL), like moving house with the same furniture. A heterogeneous migration changes engines (Oracle to PostgreSQL), like moving abroad: the data still travels, but the table designs and built-in logic must first be translated.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants to move its on-premises Oracle database to a cheaper open-source engine in the cloud. Besides copying the rows of data, what else do you think has to change, and why would that be harder than copying data from Oracle to Oracle?
lessons.teach:
A database engine is the software product behind a database. On AWS, Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service: AWS handles patching, backups and failover while you pick the engine (MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle or SQL Server). Amazon Aurora is AWS's own engine, compatible with MySQL or PostgreSQL, built for higher throughput and faster failover. Pick the engine by asking what the application already speaks, what licences you hold, and whether you want to stop paying for a commercial licence.

A migration is homogeneous when source and target use the same engine, and heterogeneous when they differ. The difference matters because of the schema, meaning the table definitions, data types, indexes and stored procedures (code saved inside the database). Same engine, same schema: it copies over as is. Different engines describe these things differently, so the schema must be converted first.

AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is a managed tool that copies data from source to target and can keep copying ongoing changes, called change data capture (CDC), so the old database stays live until cutover. The AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) translates a schema from one engine to another and flags code it cannot convert automatically.

Worked example: Oracle on premises to Aurora PostgreSQL. Step one, run SCT to convert tables and stored procedures, then fix the flagged items by hand. Step two, create the converted schema on Aurora. Step three, run DMS for a full load, then CDC to stream new changes. Step four, test, then switch the application over during a short window. For MySQL to RDS MySQL you skip SCT; DMS or the engine's native dump and replication tools are enough.

Common mistake: assuming DMS converts schemas. It moves data; SCT converts structure. In a running system, skipping conversion means stored procedures break at cutover and the application fails on its first call. Heterogeneous migrations cost more effort but can remove licence fees; homogeneous ones are faster and lower risk.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic chain runs its appointment system on Microsoft SQL Server in its own server room. The database is 300 GB and holds 45 stored procedures (code saved inside the database). To stop paying for the SQL Server licence, the team will move it to Amazon Aurora MySQL-Compatible Edition, a managed MySQL-compatible engine. Step 1: Identify the engines. The source engine is SQL Server; the target engine is MySQL-compatible. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: Because of step 2, run the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT) to translate the tables, data types and stored procedures, then fix the items it flags by hand. Step 4: Use AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) for a full load followed by change data capture, test, and cut over. Which statement correctly fills step 2?
choices: Classify it as heterogeneous, because the engines differ, so the schema must be converted first.
Classify it as homogeneous, because Aurora is managed by AWS and handles schema differences itself.
Classify it as heterogeneous, because the data moves from an on-premises server into the AWS cloud.
Classify it as homogeneous, because both engines are relational and DMS can carry the schema across.
questions.why: A migration is heterogeneous when the source and target engines differ, and different engines describe tables and stored procedures differently, so the schema must be converted before the data is loaded.

questions.prompt: Which of these moves is a homogeneous database migration?
choices: A PostgreSQL database on a self-managed virtual server moved to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL.
A SQL Server database on Amazon RDS moved to Amazon RDS for MySQL.
An Oracle database in a company data centre moved to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL.
A MariaDB database moved to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL to cut licence costs.
questions.why: Homogeneous means source and target use the same engine, and only the PostgreSQL-to-PostgreSQL move keeps the engine unchanged; where the database runs does not matter.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm moved its Oracle claims database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. The team created empty tables by hand and used only AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) to copy the rows. On cutover night, the first call the application makes to a stored procedure fails. What was the most likely cause?
choices: RDS for PostgreSQL does not support stored procedures at all.
DMS was run without change data capture, so the newest rows were lost.
DMS moves data but does not convert schema, so the Oracle stored procedures were never translated.
The team should have picked Aurora, because RDS cannot receive Oracle data.
questions.why: DMS only copies data; converting tables and stored procedures between different engines is the job of the Schema Conversion Tool, and skipping it makes stored procedures break at cutover.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop is moving a 2 TB MySQL database to Amazon RDS for MySQL. The business requires the old database to keep taking orders during the multi-day copy, with only a few minutes of downtime at the switch. Which approach meets this?
choices: Stop the shop, take a single full copy with DMS, and restart on the new database.
Move to Aurora PostgreSQL instead, because Aurora fails over faster during migration.
Run the Schema Conversion Tool first, since every move to AWS needs a converted schema.
Use DMS with a full load followed by change data capture, then cut over in a short window.
questions.why: Change data capture keeps streaming new changes after the full load, so the source stays live until a brief cutover, and SCT is unnecessary because the engine stays MySQL.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a homogeneous and a heterogeneous database migration on AWS, which tools each one needs, and the tradeoff a company accepts when it chooses to change engines.
lessons.modelAnswer: A homogeneous migration keeps the same database engine, for example MySQL on premises to Amazon RDS for MySQL. The schema, meaning tables, data types and stored procedures, works unchanged, so we just move the data with DMS or the engine's native tools. A heterogeneous migration changes engine, for example Oracle to Aurora PostgreSQL. Because the engines describe schemas and procedural code differently, we first run the Schema Conversion Tool to translate the schema and fix whatever it flags by hand, then use DMS for the full load plus change data capture so the source stays live until cutover. DMS moves data; it does not convert structure. The tradeoff: changing engines can remove commercial licence costs and let us use Aurora's performance, but it takes more effort, more testing and more risk of broken code at cutover than a like-for-like move.
rubricPoints: Defines homogeneous as same engine and heterogeneous as different engines.
Explains that schema and stored code must be converted only in heterogeneous moves.
Names SCT for schema conversion and DMS for data movement.
Mentions change data capture keeping the source live until cutover.
States the tradeoff: licence savings or features versus extra effort and risk.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through scenarios where you must spot whether engines differ and pick the right tool combination, so reasoning through situations adds the most.

lessons.plain: Database capacity planning means deciding ahead of time how much work a database must handle each second and buying the right amount of that work. Think of a restaurant kitchen: you size the number of cooks, the size of the stove and how fast orders can reach the cooks before the dinner rush, not during it. On AWS that comes in three forms. Some databases sell you a fixed rate of reads and writes. Others ask you to pick a server size with a set amount of processor power and memory. Their disks can also be given a guaranteed number of input and output operations per second.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table must serve 100 reads per second, and each item is 6 KB. If one unit of read capacity covers one read per second of up to 4 KB, how many units do you think you need, and why might it not simply be 150?
lessons.teach:
Capacity planning is matching what a database can do per second to the load you expect. It has three levers.

Capacity units: in Amazon DynamoDB, a managed key-value database, provisioned mode means you reserve throughput in advance. A read capacity unit (RCU) is one strongly consistent read per second of an item up to 4 KB. Strongly consistent means the read always returns the latest write. The same RCU instead covers two eventually consistent reads, which may briefly return slightly old data. A write capacity unit (WCU) is one write per second of up to 1 KB. Item size is rounded up per item, so the cost depends on each item's size. On-demand mode skips this planning and charges per request instead.

Worked example: 100 strongly consistent reads per second of 6 KB items. Round 6 KB up to 8 KB, which is 2 RCU per read, so you need 100 × 2 = 200 RCU. If the reads can be eventually consistent, you need 100 RCU. Next, 50 writes per second of 2.5 KB items: round up to 3 KB, which is 3 WCU each, so you need 150 WCU.

Instance types: in Amazon RDS, a managed relational database, you choose an instance class, which is a server size. Memory-optimized classes (the r family) suit large working sets that should stay in RAM. General-purpose classes balance processor and memory.

Provisioned IOPS: IOPS means input/output operations per second against the disk. Provisioned IOPS storage (io1/io2) guarantees a steady rate instead of a rate that rises and falls.

Common mistake: dividing total bytes by 4 KB (600 KB ÷ 4 = 150 RCU) instead of rounding up each item. That undersizes the table.

Consequence: an undersized DynamoDB table throttles requests, which means it rejects them and the client must retry. An undersized RDS instance shows high CPU, low free memory or rising disk queue depth, so latency climbs.

Metrics to watch: in DynamoDB, ConsumedReadCapacityUnits, ConsumedWriteCapacityUnits and ThrottledRequests. In RDS, CPUUtilization, FreeableMemory, ReadIOPS, WriteIOPS, DiskQueueDepth and ReadLatency.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company stores booking records in a DynamoDB table using provisioned mode. Each booking record is 1.5 KB, and the app writes 30 bookings per second. The capacity plan so far: Step 1, recall that one write capacity unit (WCU) covers one write per second of an item up to 1 KB. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3, multiply by the write rate: 30 writes per second × 2 WCU = 60 WCU. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Round each 1.5 KB item up to 4 KB, the read unit size, so each write costs 4 WCU.
Round each 1.5 KB item up to 2 KB, so each write costs 2 WCU.
Divide the total bytes by 1 KB: 30 × 1.5 KB = 45 KB, so 45 WCU in total.
Charge each write exactly 1.5 WCU, because 1.5 KB is 1.5 times the 1 KB unit.
questions.why: Item size is rounded up per item to the next whole 1 KB for writes, so a 1.5 KB item costs 2 WCU, giving the 60 WCU in Step 3.

questions.prompt: A news site reads article summaries from a DynamoDB table in provisioned mode. Each summary is 7 KB, the site makes 120 reads per second, and slightly old data is acceptable, so the reads can be eventually consistent. How many read capacity units (RCU) does the table need?
choices: 210 RCU
60 RCU
120 RCU
240 RCU
questions.why: 7 KB rounds up to 8 KB, which is 2 RCU for a strongly consistent read; eventually consistent reads cost half that, so 1 RCU per read × 120 reads = 120 RCU.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm runs its order database on Amazon RDS. During busy hours, ReadLatency climbs and DiskQueueDepth keeps rising, while CPUUtilization stays low and FreeableMemory is plentiful. The disk's operation rate rises and falls instead of staying steady. Which change most directly targets the bottleneck?
choices: Move to a memory-optimized (r family) instance class.
Switch the application to eventually consistent reads.
Move the storage to Provisioned IOPS (io1/io2) so the disk delivers a steady, guaranteed rate.
Add more read capacity units to the database.
questions.why: Rising disk queue depth with low CPU and plenty of memory points to the disk, and Provisioned IOPS storage guarantees a steady input/output rate instead of one that rises and falls.

questions.prompt: An analytics team's Amazon RDS database has a large working set (the data it uses most often) that no longer fits in RAM. FreeableMemory is consistently low and queries keep falling back to disk, so latency is rising. Which instance class choice best fits this need?
choices: A general-purpose class, because it balances processor and memory equally.
Keep the current class and lower the number of write capacity units.
A memory-optimized class from the r family, so more of the working set stays in RAM.
Keep the current class and switch DynamoDB to on-demand mode.
questions.why: Memory-optimized r-family classes are designed for large working sets that should stay in RAM, which addresses the low FreeableMemory directly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would size a database for a known load, using DynamoDB capacity units and an RDS instance with Provisioned IOPS, and name one tradeoff or limit of planning capacity up front.
lessons.modelAnswer: For DynamoDB in provisioned mode, I work out reads and writes per second and round each item's size up. Reads use 4 KB steps per RCU, halved if eventually consistent reads are acceptable. Writes use 1 KB steps per WCU. So 100 strong reads of 6 KB items need 200 RCU, not 150. For RDS, I pick an instance class whose memory holds the hot data, often a memory-optimized class. If the workload needs steady disk performance, I add Provisioned IOPS storage at the IOPS rate I measured. Then I watch the metrics: consumed capacity and throttled requests in DynamoDB, and CPU, freeable memory, IOPS, disk queue depth and latency in RDS. The tradeoff is that fixed capacity is cheaper and predictable for steady load. Size it too low and requests throttle or slow down. Size it too high and you pay for idle capacity. Spiky or unknown traffic may fit on-demand mode better.
rubricPoints: Defines an RCU as 4 KB strongly consistent (or two eventually consistent) reads per second and a WCU as 1 KB writes per second.
Rounds item size up per item when calculating units.
Links RDS instance class choice to CPU and memory needs, such as memory-optimized for large working sets.
Explains Provisioned IOPS as guaranteed, steady disk operations per second.
Names metrics to confirm sizing, such as throttled requests, CPU, freeable memory or disk queue depth.
States a tradeoff, such as under-provisioning causing throttling versus over-provisioning wasting money, or on-demand mode suiting unpredictable traffic.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this with requirement-driven calculations and metric choices, so working through scenario problems that ask you to compute units and pick a size adds the most.

lessons.plain: A read replica is a read-only copy of a database that stays in step with the main copy, called the primary. All changes still go to the primary, but you can send questions that only read data to the copies instead. Think of a busy library with one master catalogue that only the head librarian edits, plus photocopies at side desks so visitors can look things up without queuing at one desk. The copies take load off the original, but each copy is refreshed a moment after the master changes, so a visitor might briefly see a slightly older version.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database is slow because hundreds of dashboards keep reading from it, while only a few users ever save changes. If you add extra read-only copies of the database, which kind of work gets faster, and what new problem might a dashboard user notice?
lessons.teach:
A read replica is a read-only copy of a database that receives every change made on the primary, the single copy that accepts writes. In Amazon RDS (a managed relational database service) and Amazon Aurora (AWS's cloud-built relational engine), you create replicas and point read-only traffic at them. Each replica has its own endpoint, meaning its own connection address; Aurora also offers a reader endpoint, one address that spreads connections across all its replicas.

Why it works: most applications read far more than they write. Moving reads elsewhere frees the primary's CPU and disk for writes. Replication is asynchronous: the primary confirms a write first and ships it to replicas afterwards. The delay is called replica lag, reported as the ReplicaLag metric in RDS and AuroraReplicaLag in Aurora. Replicas can also live in another Region (a separate geographic area of AWS), which puts reads near distant users. A replica can be promoted into a standalone writable database, a useful but manual recovery step.

Worked example: a reporting app's primary runs at 90% CPU and 85% of queries are reads. You add two replicas and send report queries to the reader endpoint. At time 0 a user saves an order on the primary. At 0.2 seconds a report reads from a replica that has not yet applied the change, so the order is missing. At 0.5 seconds the replica applies it and later reports show it. Afterwards, primary CPU drops, and you watch replica lag to confirm copies keep up.

Common mistake: treating a read replica as high availability. In RDS, automatic failover comes from a Multi-AZ standby, a synchronous copy in another Availability Zone (a separate data centre group) that serves no reads; replicas need manual promotion. A second mistake is sending read-after-write traffic, such as showing a user the record they just saved, to a replica. In a running system that produces stale data: users see old values, and under heavy write load lag can grow to seconds or minutes. Reads that must be current belong on the primary.

questions.prompt:
A ticket-booking company runs its event catalogue on Amazon RDS for MySQL (not Aurora). The primary sits at 80% CPU, and about 75% of queries are people browsing event listings. Here is the plan, with one step missing.

Step 1: Confirm from query statistics that reads clearly outnumber writes, so offloading reads will help.
Step 2: Create one read replica of the primary in RDS.
Step 3: Point the event-browsing queries at the replica's own endpoint. Keep the 'your booking is confirmed' page on the primary, because it must show the booking the user just made.
Step 4: (missing) Decide what to watch afterwards to confirm the replica is keeping up with changes on the primary.

Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Watch whether the Multi-AZ standby is serving the browsing reads without falling behind.
Nothing extra is needed, because replication confirms each write on the replica first.
Watch the AuroraReplicaLag metric, because it reports the delay before a replica applies changes.
Watch the ReplicaLag metric on the replica, and check that primary CPU has dropped.
questions.why: For an RDS (non-Aurora) replica, the delay is reported as ReplicaLag, and a drop in primary CPU shows that offloading the reads worked.

questions.prompt: A fitness app sends all read queries to an Amazon RDS read replica. A user changes their weekly goal from 3 to 5 workouts, taps Save, and the app immediately reloads the goal screen. Sometimes the screen still shows 3. What is the best fix?
choices: Send the reload of the record the user just saved to the primary, and keep other reads on the replica.
Promote the read replica to a standalone database so that it can accept the writes.
Move the read replica into another Region so it sits closer to the app's users.
Add a second read replica so that each replica handles less of the read traffic.
questions.why: Replication is asynchronous, so a replica can briefly lag behind, and read-after-write traffic that must be current belongs on the primary.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's claims database runs on Amazon RDS. A new requirement says that if the primary's Availability Zone fails, the database must fail over automatically with no manual action. The team already has one read replica. What meets the requirement?
choices: Point the application at a reader endpoint so connections move to a healthy copy on failure.
Enable a Multi-AZ standby, a synchronous copy in another Availability Zone used for failover.
Create a cross-Region read replica, because a copy in another Region gives automatic failover.
Keep the existing read replica, because RDS promotes it automatically when the primary fails.
questions.why: In RDS, automatic failover comes from a Multi-AZ standby, while read replicas only become writable through a manual promotion.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm uses Amazon Aurora with two replicas behind the reader endpoint for its shipment-tracking dashboard. Each night a large batch job writes millions of rows to the primary. During the batch, the dashboard shows shipment statuses that are several minutes old. Which explanation and metric fit best?
choices: The reader endpoint is caching old results, so the fix is to watch primary CPU instead.
Asynchronous replication is falling behind under heavy writes, which shows up in AuroraReplicaLag.
The replicas have been promoted to standalone databases, which shows up in ReplicaLag.
The Multi-AZ standby is answering the dashboard reads, and it falls behind under write load.
questions.why: Replicas apply changes after the primary confirms them, so under heavy write load the delay can grow to minutes, and Aurora reports this delay as AuroraReplicaLag.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when adding read replicas is the right fix for a slow database, how you would know it worked, and one limit or trade-off they must design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: Read replicas fit when the database is struggling because of reads, not writes, for example dashboards or reports hammering a primary while writes are modest. We create one or more read-only copies and point read traffic at them, using Aurora's reader endpoint if we want connections spread automatically. Success shows as lower CPU and fewer waiting queries on the primary, while ReplicaLag on each replica stays small. The trade-off is that replication is asynchronous, so replicas can be behind by milliseconds or, under heavy writes, much longer. Anything that must show the latest data, like a user viewing what they just saved, should read from the primary. Replicas also do not add write capacity, and they are not an automatic failover target in RDS; that is the Multi-AZ standby's job, while a replica has to be promoted.
rubricPoints: States a read replica is a read-only copy that takes read traffic off the primary.
Says replicas help read-heavy workloads and add no write capacity.
Explains replication is asynchronous, so replicas can serve stale data.
Names replica lag (ReplicaLag or AuroraReplicaLag) as the metric to watch, alongside primary load.
Routes read-after-write or must-be-current queries to the primary.
Distinguishes replicas from a Multi-AZ standby used for automatic failover.

suggested.rationale: That incident has the learner diagnose stale reads caused by replica lag, the central trade-off of using read replicas.

lessons.plain: A cache is a small, very fast memory that keeps copies of answers you have already looked up, so you do not have to fetch them again from the slower original source. Amazon ElastiCache is AWS's managed in-memory cache service: AWS runs the servers and you simply store and read keys and values. Think of a librarian who keeps the ten most-requested books on the front desk instead of walking to the back stacks every time. When most visitors want the same few books, the desk saves enormous walking, and the stacks stay quiet.
lessons.guessPrompt: A product page is viewed 1,000 times a minute but its price changes only once a day. If you kept a fast copy of that page's data in memory, roughly how many times per minute would the database still need to be asked, and what could go wrong when the price does change?
lessons.teach:
Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory data store. AWS handles the servers, patching and failover, and you choose an engine: a Redis-compatible one (Redis OSS or Valkey) or Memcached. Memory is far faster than disk, so a lookup returns in under a millisecond instead of the several milliseconds a database query takes. A cache holds copies; the source of truth, the authoritative data, stays in the database.

The usual pattern is cache-aside, also called lazy loading. The application checks the cache first. On a cache hit (the key is present) it uses that value. On a cache miss (the key is absent) it reads the database, then writes the result into the cache for next time. A TTL (time to live) is an expiry timer on each key, so stale copies eventually disappear. The alternative, write-through, updates the cache whenever the database is written: fresher data, but extra write work and memory spent on items nobody may read.

Worked example: a product page is read 1,000 times a minute and rarely changes. Request 1 misses, the app queries the database (about 8 ms) and stores the result with a 60-second TTL. Requests 2 to 1,000 in that minute hit, about 1 ms each, and the database is untouched. When the TTL expires, the next request misses and refreshes the key. Database reads fall from 1,000 to about 1 per minute.

It works because read-intensive workloads ask for the same keys repeatedly. The metric to watch is cache hit ratio, which is hits divided by hits plus misses. ElastiCache reports CacheHits and CacheMisses. You should also see database CPU and read latency drop.

A common mistake is caching data that changes constantly or is rarely repeated, or setting no TTL, so users see stale values. A related failure: a hot key expires while many requests arrive, and they all miss and hit the database at once. This is a cache stampede, and it can overload the database. Pick a Redis-compatible engine when you need replication, failover, persistence or rich data types. Pick Memcached for simple, multi-threaded key caching.

questions.prompt:
A city library's catalog app serves book-detail lookups that are read heavily and rarely change. The team adds an ElastiCache cache (a managed in-memory data store) using cache-aside, also called lazy loading: the app checks the cache first and, on a miss, reads the database and then stores the result with a 120-second TTL, an expiry timer on the key. After a week they check whether it worked.

Step 1: Pull the ElastiCache metrics for one hour. CacheHits = 4,750 and CacheMisses = 250.
Step 2: Recall that cache hit ratio is hits divided by (hits plus misses).
Step 3: [missing]
Step 4: Confirm the result by checking that database CPU and read latency have dropped since the cache went in.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Hit ratio = 250 / 5,000 = 5%, so the cache answers 5% of lookups
Hit ratio = 4,750 / (4,750 + 250) = 4,750 / 5,000 = 95%, so the cache answers 95% of lookups
Hit ratio = 250 / 4,750 ≈ 5.3%, so about 5% of lookups reach the database
Hit ratio = 4,750 / 250 = 19, so the cache is 19 times faster than the database
questions.why: Hit ratio puts hits over all lookups (hits plus misses), so 4,750 divided by 5,000 gives 95%. The other choices instead calculate the miss ratio, a hits-to-misses comparison, or misses divided by hits.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing site caches the details of its most popular show under a single key with a TTL (time to live, an expiry timer). The moment that key expires, thousands of requests arrive within the same second. None of them finds the key, so all of them query the database at once, and database CPU jumps to 100%. What is this failure called?
choices: Lazy loading working as designed
A cache stampede
A cache hit
Write-through caching
questions.why: A cache stampede happens when a hot key expires and many simultaneous misses hit the database together, which can overload it.

questions.prompt: A gaming company wants to put an ElastiCache cache (a managed in-memory data store) in front of its player database. The cache must copy its data to a replica, fail over automatically if a node is lost, and support rich data types beyond simple key-value pairs. Which engine choice fits these requirements?
choices: Memcached combined with write-through so that data survives a node failure
No cache at all, because only the database can provide failover
Memcached, because it is multi-threaded and suited to simple key caching
A Redis-compatible engine such as Redis OSS or Valkey
questions.why: Redis-compatible engines are the right pick when you need replication, failover, persistence or rich data types, while Memcached is meant for simple, multi-threaded key caching.

questions.prompt: An analytics startup adds cache-aside caching (check the cache first, and on a miss read the database and store the result) for its search results. Almost every user types a unique, one-off query. A week later, the cache hit ratio (hits divided by hits plus misses) is only 3%, and database load has barely changed. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The workload rarely repeats the same keys, so nearly every request is a cache miss
Memory is slower than disk for search queries
The cache is serving stale values, which counts as misses
The TTL is too long, so the keys never expire
questions.why: Caching pays off only when the same keys are requested again and again, so data that is rarely repeated produces mostly misses and leaves the database load almost unchanged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how adding ElastiCache with cache-aside speeds up a read-heavy application, which metric proves it is working, and one tradeoff or limit you accept by caching.
lessons.modelAnswer: ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache that sits in front of our database. With cache-aside, the app asks the cache first. On a hit it returns the stored value in under a millisecond. On a miss it reads the database, then saves the result in the cache with a TTL so the copy expires later. Because read-heavy traffic keeps asking for the same keys, one database read can serve hundreds of requests. That cuts latency and takes load off the database. I'd watch the cache hit ratio, CacheHits divided by hits plus misses, and expect database CPU and read latency to fall. The tradeoff is freshness: until the TTL expires or we update the cache on writes, users can see stale data. There's also stampede risk. If a hot key expires under heavy load, many misses can hit the database together. Caching also adds little for data that changes constantly or is rarely reread.
rubricPoints: Describes ElastiCache as a managed in-memory store holding copies of data whose source of truth is the database.
Explains the cache-aside flow: check cache, on miss read the database and populate the cache.
Names cache hit ratio (CacheHits versus CacheMisses) and falling database load as the success metric.
Mentions TTL as the control for staleness.
Names a tradeoff such as stale data, cache stampede, or poor fit for rarely repeated or fast-changing data.

suggested.rationale: The cache stampede incident makes the learner see cache hits, misses and expiry under real read load, which is the core of using a cache for read-heavy traffic.

lessons.plain: Every time an application wants to talk to a relational database, it first opens a connection: a dedicated, logged-in line between the two. Opening one takes time, and the database can only hold a limited number at once, because each costs it memory. Under heavy load, especially when hundreds of short-lived functions start together, the app can try to open more lines than the database allows, and requests start failing. A database proxy is a middleman that keeps a small set of lines open and lets many callers share them. Think of a hotel switchboard: a hundred guests can make calls through ten outside lines because no single call lasts long.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database accepts at most 400 open connections. A traffic spike makes 1,000 copies of a serverless function run at once, and each copy opens its own connection. What do you expect happens to the extra 600 requests, and what could you put in between to fix it?
lessons.teach:
A database connection is an authenticated session between a client and a database. It is expensive: setting it up takes network round trips and a login, and the database reserves memory for each one. Every engine sets a ceiling called max_connections, which on Amazon RDS depends largely on instance memory. A connection pool keeps connections open and reuses them instead of opening a new one per request.

Servers that run for hours can pool connections themselves. AWS Lambda, the serverless function service, cannot pool well: each concurrent execution is a separate environment, so a surge creates a connection storm. Amazon RDS Proxy is a managed connection pooler that sits between clients and an RDS or Aurora database. Clients connect to the proxy endpoint, and the proxy multiplexes, meaning it hands a small number of real database connections to whichever client is mid-query. It also holds client connections during a database failover, so apps reconnect faster, and it can fetch database credentials from AWS Secrets Manager and accept IAM authentication.

Worked example: max_connections is 400. A spike runs 1,000 Lambda executions. Without a proxy, the first 400 connect and the other 600 get "too many connections" errors. With RDS Proxy, all 1,000 connect to the proxy. Each query takes about 5 milliseconds, so most executions are idle at any instant, and the proxy serves them over roughly 100 database connections, safely under the limit.

A common mistake is treating connection exhaustion as a capacity problem and buying a bigger instance or adding read replicas. That raises the ceiling slightly but a larger surge breaks it again. Another mistake is opening the connection inside the function handler on every call instead of once per execution environment. A proxy also cannot fix slow queries or a CPU-bound database; it only shares connections.

In a running system, watch the CloudWatch metric DatabaseConnections against max_connections, plus the proxy's client and database connection counts. If database connections stay flat while client connections climb, the proxy is doing its job.

questions.prompt:
A concert-ticket startup runs its checkout code on AWS Lambda (serverless functions) against an Amazon Aurora database whose max_connections ceiling is 250. When a big show goes on sale, 800 Lambda executions run at the same moment. Here is the analysis, with one step missing.

Step 1: Each concurrent Lambda execution is its own separate environment, so each one opens its own database connection. They cannot share one pool.

Step 2: [missing]

Step 3: The team adds Amazon RDS Proxy, a managed connection pooler. All 800 executions connect to the proxy endpoint instead. Each checkout query takes about 3 milliseconds, so most executions are idle at any instant. The proxy multiplexes them over roughly 60 real database connections.

Step 4: In CloudWatch, the team checks that DatabaseConnections stays flat near 60 while the proxy's client connection count climbs toward 800.

Which statement correctly fills Step 2, describing what happens without the proxy?
choices: Lambda holds the extra 550 executions in a queue until earlier connections close, so users only notice a short delay and no errors.
RDS notices the surge and raises max_connections to 800 for the duration of the spike, then lowers it again afterward.
The first 250 executions get connections and the remaining 550 receive "too many connections" errors.
All 800 executions connect, but every query slows down in proportion to the extra load, so checkout gets sluggish without failing.
questions.why: max_connections is a hard ceiling, so once 250 sessions are open, every further connection attempt is refused with a "too many connections" error.

questions.prompt: An analytics firm puts Amazon RDS Proxy in front of its PostgreSQL database. The documentation says the proxy "multiplexes" connections. In plain terms, what does multiplexing mean here?
choices: The proxy opens one dedicated database connection for every client and keeps it open permanently so logins are never repeated.
The proxy hands a small number of real database connections to whichever client is in the middle of a query, so many clients share them.
The proxy copies each client's query to several read replicas at once and returns whichever answer arrives first.
The proxy compresses many queries into one larger batch so the database processes them in a single pass.
questions.why: Multiplexing means many client connections take turns sharing a few real database connections, each one used only while a client is actively querying.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's RDS MySQL database is slow. CloudWatch shows CPU at 97% because a few reports run expensive queries. DatabaseConnections sits at about 90, far below the max_connections limit of 600. An engineer proposes adding Amazon RDS Proxy to fix the slowness. What is the best assessment?
choices: It will fix the problem, because the proxy spreads the expensive queries evenly across more database connections.
It will not fix the problem, because a proxy only shares connections and cannot speed up slow queries or a CPU-bound database.
It will fix the problem, because the proxy caches query results and takes the load off the database CPU.
It will help only if the team also adds read replicas, because the proxy needs replicas before it can multiplex.
questions.why: Connections are nowhere near the limit and the bottleneck is CPU spent on heavy queries, which a connection pooler does nothing to reduce.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery app moves its Lambda functions behind Amazon RDS Proxy. During the next lunch rush, which CloudWatch pattern best shows that the proxy is doing its job?
choices: The database's DatabaseConnections stays roughly flat while the proxy's client connection count climbs with the rush.
Both the proxy's client connections and the database's connections stay flat, because the proxy blocks new clients during the rush.
The database's DatabaseConnections climbs while the proxy's client connection count falls, showing clients bypassing the proxy.
The database's DatabaseConnections climbs in step with the proxy's client connection count until both reach max_connections.
questions.why: A working pooler absorbs growing client demand while keeping real database connections steady and below max_connections.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why our Lambda-based API fails with connection errors during traffic spikes even though database CPU is low, how RDS Proxy fixes it, and one thing a proxy will not fix.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each Lambda execution runs in its own environment and opens its own database connection, so a spike to 1,000 concurrent executions tries to open 1,000 connections. The database has a hard max_connections limit tied to its memory, so once that is hit, new connections are refused even though CPU is idle; we are out of connection slots, not compute. RDS Proxy is a managed connection pooler: functions connect to the proxy, and it multiplexes them onto a small, steady set of real database connections, because each query is short and most functions are idle at any instant. It also speeds recovery during failover and can use Secrets Manager or IAM for credentials. The limit is that it only shares connections: if queries are slow or the database is CPU-bound, a proxy will not help, and we would need tuning, caching, or more capacity. I would watch DatabaseConnections to confirm it stays flat during spikes.
rubricPoints: Defines a connection as a costly session and names the max_connections ceiling.
Explains that each concurrent Lambda execution opens its own connection, causing storms.
Describes RDS Proxy as a managed pooler that multiplexes many clients onto few database connections.
Notes that a bigger instance or read replicas is the wrong fix for connection exhaustion.
States a limit: a proxy does not fix slow queries or CPU-bound load.
Names DatabaseConnections (or proxy connection metrics) as the metric to watch.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by describing symptoms like connection errors with low CPU under Lambda surges, so reasoning through such scenarios and naming the metric builds the right instinct better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: Network topology is the floor plan of your private network in the cloud: how big it is, how it is divided into rooms, and which doors lead where. In AWS the building is a VPC (a private virtual network), the rooms are subnets (smaller slices of its address range), and the doors are routes. Public rooms face the street, and private rooms sit deeper inside. A good plan keeps databases away from the internet, leaves enough addresses to grow, and avoids clashing with other networks you may need to connect to later.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a database server should never be reachable from the internet but a web server must be, how would you arrange them in a network, and what would actually stop internet traffic from reaching the database?
lessons.teach:
Network topology is the layout of your cloud network. In AWS that network is a VPC (Virtual Private Cloud), an isolated virtual network with an address range written in CIDR notation (Classless Inter-Domain Routing). In 10.0.0.0/16, the first 16 bits are fixed, which leaves 65,536 addresses. You divide the VPC into subnets, which are smaller ranges. Each subnet lives in one Availability Zone, a separate group of data centers within a Region. AWS reserves 5 addresses in every subnet, so a /24 subnet (256 addresses) gives you 251 usable ones.

Every subnet follows a route table, a list of rules that says where traffic for each destination goes. The most specific match wins. A subnet is public when its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 (every internet address) to an internet gateway, the VPC's door to the internet. A private subnet has no such route. It reaches out through a NAT gateway (network address translation), which lets private hosts start outbound connections while refusing unsolicited inbound ones. The NAT gateway itself sits in a public subnet.

The usual tiers are: public subnets for load balancers, private subnets for app servers, and isolated subnets for databases, with no internet route at all. Routing, not the server, decides what is reachable.

Worked example: a VPC uses 10.0.0.0/16 across two zones. Public subnets are 10.0.1.0/24 and 10.0.2.0/24, app subnets are 10.0.11.0/24 and 10.0.12.0/24, and data subnets are 10.0.21.0/24 and 10.0.22.0/24. App server 10.0.11.20 fetches a patch. First, its route table matches 0.0.0.0/0 to the NAT gateway in 10.0.1.0/24. Next, the NAT replaces the source address. Then the public route table sends the traffic to the internet gateway. Replies return the same way. Traffic to the database at 10.0.21.5 instead matches the local route (the VPC's own range) and never leaves the VPC.

A common mistake is picking a range that is too small, or one that overlaps your office network or another VPC. Overlapping ranges cannot be peered (directly connected VPC to VPC) or cleanly routed over a VPN. A full subnet stops Auto Scaling from launching instances during a spike, so watch available IP addresses per subnet.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain has a VPC with the range 10.50.0.0/16. It needs one subnet for an Auto Scaling group that can grow to 300 instances during its busiest hour, plus 10 more addresses for other resources. The architect works through the sizing. Step 1: the subnet must hold at least 310 usable addresses. Step 2: a /24 subnet has 256 addresses, and AWS reserves 5 in every subnet, leaving 251 usable, which is too few. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the architect creates the subnet as 10.50.4.0/23 and adds an alarm on available IP addresses in that subnet. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: A /25 has more room than a /24 because a bigger prefix number means a bigger range, so a /25 gives 507 usable addresses.
A /23 fixes one fewer bit than a /24, which doubles the range to 512 addresses; minus the 5 reserved, that leaves 507 usable, enough for 310.
A /23 has 512 addresses and no reserved ones, because AWS reserves 5 addresses only in /24 subnets, so all 512 are usable.
A /24 is fine after all, because the 5 reserved addresses only apply to public subnets and this is a private app subnet.
questions.why: Each bit removed from the prefix doubles the range, so a /23 holds 512 addresses, and after AWS reserves 5 in every subnet, 507 usable addresses cover the 310 needed.

questions.prompt: A logistics startup has three subnets in its VPC and asks which one is a public subnet. What makes a subnet public in AWS?
choices: It contains a NAT gateway, which gives the whole subnet internet access in both directions.
It is placed in the first Availability Zone of the Region.
Its address range starts with 10.0., which AWS treats as internet-facing.
Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0, meaning every internet address, to an internet gateway.
questions.why: A subnet is public only because of routing: its route table sends all internet-bound traffic (0.0.0.0/0) to the internet gateway, not because of where it sits or what it contains.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's VPC uses 10.30.0.0/16. A private app subnet's route table has two rules: 10.30.0.0/16 goes to local, and 0.0.0.0/0 goes to a NAT gateway. An app server sends a request to a cache server at 10.30.8.4 in another subnet of the same VPC. Where does that traffic go?
choices: Nowhere; it is dropped because private subnets cannot talk to other subnets.
Along the local route, because 10.30.0.0/16 is the more specific match, so it stays inside the VPC.
To the NAT gateway, because 0.0.0.0/0 matches every address and so it always wins.
To the internet gateway, because the cache is in a different subnet from the app server.
questions.why: The most specific matching route wins, and 10.30.0.0/16 is more specific than 0.0.0.0/0, so traffic to 10.30.8.4 stays inside the VPC on the local route.

questions.prompt: A streaming service runs its app servers in an Auto Scaling group inside one /24 private subnet. During a big live event, traffic spikes, but the group fails to launch new instances even though the app servers are overloaded. Which cause is most likely, and which metric should the team watch to catch it in future?
choices: The subnet has run out of IP addresses; watch available IP addresses per subnet.
The NAT gateway is in a private subnet; watch the NAT gateway's number of route tables.
The subnet is in the wrong Availability Zone; watch how many zones the Region has.
The internet gateway has reached its instance limit; watch the number of internet gateways per VPC.
questions.why: A full subnet leaves no free addresses for new instances, which stops Auto Scaling from launching during a spike, so available IP addresses per subnet is the metric to watch.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would lay out subnets, routes and IP ranges for a three-tier web app, and name one limit or tradeoff of your design.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd give the VPC a roomy range like 10.0.0.0/16 that doesn't overlap our office network or other VPCs, so we can connect them later. In each of two Availability Zones I'd create three subnets. The public one holds the load balancer and NAT gateway, and its route table sends all internet traffic to the internet gateway. The app subnet is private and its default route points to the NAT gateway, so servers can download updates but can't be reached from outside. The database subnet has only the local route, so it talks only inside the VPC. Each subnet loses 5 addresses to AWS, so I'd size them with growth in mind and watch free IPs per subnet. The tradeoff is NAT: one shared NAT gateway is cheaper, but it is a single point of failure and adds cross-zone data charges. One per zone costs more but is resilient.
rubricPoints: Defines VPC, subnet and CIDR and sizes the range with room to grow.
States that a public subnet routes 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway and a private one does not.
Explains that private app servers reach out through a NAT gateway placed in a public subnet.
Places databases in isolated subnets that have only the local route.
Warns against overlapping or undersized ranges and the 5 reserved addresses per subnet.
Names a tradeoff such as one NAT gateway versus one per Availability Zone.

suggested.rationale: Tracing packets through route tables, NAT and gateways in a virtual network path tracer builds exactly the routing intuition this objective needs.

lessons.plain: Both services make an application feel faster for users who are far from where it runs, but they work differently. Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network: it keeps copies of your files on servers spread around the world, so users get them from somewhere nearby. AWS Global Accelerator keeps nothing. It gives users a fixed address that leads to a nearby entry point, then carries their traffic over Amazon's private network instead of the crowded public internet. Think of CloudFront as a chain of local warehouses stocking popular items. Global Accelerator is a private express highway to the one factory that makes everything fresh.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online game sends constantly changing player positions over UDP from servers in Virginia to players in Asia, who complain of lag. Would storing copies of content near the players help? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Amazon CloudFront is a content delivery network (CDN). It is a set of servers at edge locations, which are AWS sites in many cities close to users, and they keep copies of your content. Your origin is where the real content lives, such as an S3 bucket or a load balancer. When a user asks for a file, the nearest edge checks its cache, a temporary stored copy. Each copy has a time to live (TTL), which is how long it counts as fresh. If the copy is there and its TTL has not expired, that is a cache hit and the origin is never touched. CloudFront carries web traffic (HTTP and HTTPS), so it suits websites, images, video and APIs.

AWS Global Accelerator caches nothing. It gives you two static anycast IP addresses. Anycast means the same addresses are announced from many edge locations, so each user reaches the nearest one. From that edge, traffic travels over the AWS backbone, Amazon's private global network, instead of the congested public internet. It arrives at your endpoints, the targets that receive it, such as load balancers, EC2 instances or Elastic IPs, in one or more Regions. It works for any TCP or UDP traffic. Its health checks are regular tests of whether each endpoint is working. They move traffic to a healthy Region within seconds, with no wait for DNS records cached around the internet to expire.

Worked example. A game studio in us-east-1 has players in Asia reporting lag. Step 1: what is the traffic? Real-time UDP game state that is different for every player. Step 2: can it be cached? No. Every packet is new, so a cache adds nothing, and CloudFront does not carry UDP anyway. Step 3: choose Global Accelerator. Asian players enter at a nearby edge and cross the backbone. Step 4: watch round-trip latency and endpoint health. If the complaint were slow product images instead, CloudFront would win, and the metric to watch would be the cache hit ratio, the share of requests answered from the edge.

Common mistake: choosing Global Accelerator for static content because it sounds like it accelerates everything. With no caching, every request still reaches the origin, so origin load and cost stay high. A CloudFront TTL set too short causes a similar problem: a low hit ratio, and the origin keeps getting hammered.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company runs a custom TCP service (not web traffic) that its warehouse barcode scanners call. Endpoints sit behind load balancers in eu-central-1 and ap-southeast-2. The scanners can only be set up with fixed IP addresses. The requirement is that if one Region fails, the scanners keep working within seconds. Here is the reasoning, with one step missing.

Step 1: The traffic is TCP and is different for every scanner. It cannot be cached, and CloudFront only carries HTTP and HTTPS, so CloudFront does not fit.

Step 2: The scanners need fixed addresses. AWS Global Accelerator, a service that routes traffic over Amazon's private network, provides two static anycast IP addresses. Anycast means the same addresses are announced from many edge locations. Global Accelerator also accepts load balancers in more than one Region as endpoints, the targets that receive the traffic.

Step 3: ???

Step 4: Watch endpoint health and round-trip latency.

Which statement correctly fills Step 3, explaining how the failover requirement is met?
choices: Global Accelerator health checks spot that the failed Region's endpoints are down and move traffic to the healthy Region within seconds, with no wait for cached DNS records to expire.
Lower the CloudFront TTL to a few seconds so that each edge quickly fetches fresh copies from whichever Region is still healthy.
Global Accelerator keeps copies of recent responses at the edge, so scanners keep getting answers while the failed Region is down.
Change the DNS records to point at the healthy Region, and the scanners follow once the DNS answers cached around the internet expire.
questions.why: Global Accelerator's health checks regularly test each endpoint and shift traffic to a healthy Region within seconds behind the same static IPs, so nothing waits on cached DNS records to expire.

questions.prompt: In Amazon CloudFront, a content delivery network (CDN), what is a cache hit?
choices: A request that the nearest edge answers from its own stored copy while that copy's TTL is still valid, so the origin is never contacted.
A health check that confirms the origin is working and can receive traffic.
A request that the edge forwards to the origin because the stored copy's TTL has expired.
A request that travels from the nearest edge to the origin over the AWS backbone instead of the public internet.
questions.why: A cache hit means the edge already holds a copy that is still fresh under its time to live (TTL), so it answers the request itself and never touches the origin.

questions.prompt: A recipe website keeps its food photos in an S3 bucket in us-west-2. Visitors in Europe and Africa say the photos load slowly, and every visitor sees the same images. The team also wants to cut the load on the bucket. Which service fits best, and which metric would show it worked?
choices: AWS Global Accelerator, watching endpoint health
AWS Global Accelerator, watching the cache hit ratio
Amazon CloudFront, watching endpoint health across Regions
Amazon CloudFront, watching the cache hit ratio
questions.why: The photos are identical web content that can be cached, so CloudFront edges can serve them close to visitors and spare the origin. The cache hit ratio, the share of requests answered from the edge, shows whether that is happening. Global Accelerator caches nothing, so it has no hit ratio to watch.

questions.prompt: A company puts Amazon CloudFront in front of its website. Its logo and icon images change about once a year, but an engineer set their TTL to 5 seconds. A week later, the origin load balancer is still busy with image requests. What is the most likely cause?
choices: CloudFront cannot cache images that come from a load balancer origin, only images from an S3 bucket.
The edge locations are too far from users, so requests skip the cache and go straight to the origin.
CloudFront is sending the image requests as UDP, which the load balancer handles slowly.
Copies go stale after 5 seconds, so most requests miss the cache. The hit ratio stays low and the origin keeps getting hit.
questions.why: A TTL set far shorter than the content actually changes means copies expire almost at once, so most requests miss the cache and go to the origin. That gives a low cache hit ratio and a heavily loaded origin.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would put CloudFront in front of an application and when you would use Global Accelerator instead. Name one limit of each and the metric you would watch to confirm it helped.
lessons.modelAnswer: CloudFront is a CDN. It caches copies of content at edge locations near users, so repeat requests never travel back to the origin. That makes it the right pick for HTTP or HTTPS content that many users share, like images, video, static sites and cacheable API responses. Its limit is that it only helps when content can be cached and it only handles web traffic. Unique, fast-changing data still goes back to the origin. I'd watch the cache hit ratio. Global Accelerator caches nothing. It gives two static anycast IPs that pull users onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge and route them to healthy endpoints, failing over between Regions in seconds. It suits TCP or UDP workloads like gaming, VoIP or non-HTTP protocols, and cases that need fixed IPs. Its limit is that the origin still serves every request. I'd watch latency and endpoint health.
rubricPoints: CloudFront caches content at edge locations, so cache hits skip the origin.
Global Accelerator does not cache; it routes traffic over the AWS backbone using static anycast IPs.
CloudFront fits cacheable HTTP/HTTPS content; Global Accelerator fits TCP/UDP, non-HTTP, static-IP or fast multi-Region failover needs.
A limit of each is named, such as CloudFront needing cacheable web content or Global Accelerator leaving full load on the origin.
A metric is named: cache hit ratio for CloudFront, latency and endpoint health for Global Accelerator.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises edge services directly, and the exam tests this by asking learners to read a scenario's traffic type and cacheability and pick the right service, which is best practised through reasoning about situations.

lessons.plain: When your company's own building or data center needs to talk to its systems in the cloud, the traffic has to travel somehow. AWS offers three main options. A VPN is like sending sealed, locked envelopes through the public postal system: cheap and quick to set up, but delivery time varies.
