Direct Connect is like leasing your own private road straight to the cloud provider: steady and fast, but it takes weeks to build. PrivateLink is different. It is like a private service window between two buildings on the same campus, so one network can use a specific service in another network without opening up the public street.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company needs a working link from its office to the cloud by tomorrow, and a steady, high-bandwidth link for heavy daily data transfers within the next two months. Would you use the same connection type for both needs, or two different ones? Why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Site-to-Site VPN is a managed virtual private network. It builds encrypted tunnels over the public internet between your on-premises router and AWS. IPsec is the standard used to encrypt those tunnels. Because it rides the internet, setup takes minutes to hours and costs little. The tradeoff is that latency (delay) and throughput (data per second) vary with internet conditions, and each tunnel tops out at roughly 1.25 Gbps.

AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated physical network link. It runs from your network to an AWS Direct Connect location, which is a data center where AWS connects to outside networks. Traffic never crosses the public internet, so latency is consistent and bandwidth can be 1, 10 or 100 Gbps. The tradeoffs are cost and lead time: provisioning often takes weeks. Traffic over it is not encrypted by default. If you need encryption, you can run a VPN over it or use link-layer encryption where it is supported.

AWS PrivateLink lets a client in one virtual network (a VPC) reach a specific service privately. That service can live in another VPC or be an AWS service. The client creates an interface endpoint, which is a private network address in its own subnet that forwards to the service. Traffic stays on the AWS network. Only that one service is exposed, not the whole network, and overlapping IP ranges between the two networks do not matter.

Worked example: a bank must move 5 TB nightly with predictable timing. Step one, the requirement is consistent performance at high volume, which points to Direct Connect. Step two, it must be encrypted, so add a VPN over the Direct Connect link. Step three, Direct Connect takes weeks to arrive, so run a Site-to-Site VPN in the meantime and keep it afterward as a backup path.

Common mistake: choosing PrivateLink to connect an office to AWS. PrivateLink exposes a service to consumers. It is not a general site-to-site link.

To know whether the link is working, watch tunnel state and connection state, along with throughput and latency. A tunnel that drops silently sends traffic down a slower backup path.

questions.prompt: A payroll software company runs its payroll API in its own VPC (a virtual network in AWS). Forty client companies each have their own VPC and need to call that one API privately. Several clients use the same IP address range as the provider, and the provider does not want to expose anything else on its network. Step one: the need is private access to one specific service rather than a link between whole networks, and overlapping IP ranges must not matter, so the provider offers the API through AWS PrivateLink. Step two: ??? Step three: traffic from each client to the API stays on the AWS network, and only the payroll API is reachable. What is step two?
choices: Each client builds Site-to-Site VPN tunnels from its VPC to the provider's VPC so the API can be reached over encrypted IPsec links.
The provider orders an AWS Direct Connect link for each client so the traffic has consistent latency.
The clients first renumber their VPCs so that no IP ranges overlap with the provider's network.
Each client creates an interface endpoint, a private network address in one of its own subnets that forwards requests to the payroll API.
questions.why: With PrivateLink, each consumer reaches the service through an interface endpoint in its own subnet, which exposes only that service and works even when IP ranges overlap.

questions.prompt: A small design studio wants its office network connected to its AWS VPC by tomorrow. It has a tight budget and moves only a few hundred megabits per second. Some variation in speed is acceptable. Which option fits best?
choices: AWS PrivateLink with an interface endpoint in the office
AWS Direct Connect at 1 Gbps with a VPN running over it
AWS Direct Connect at 10 Gbps
AWS Site-to-Site VPN
questions.why: Site-to-Site VPN runs encrypted tunnels over the internet, can be set up in minutes to hours at low cost, and handles modest traffic well. Direct Connect takes weeks to provision, and PrivateLink is not a site-to-site link.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm uses AWS Direct Connect as its main link to AWS and keeps a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path. This week its nightly data transfers have run much slower than usual, and latency keeps jumping around. Nobody received an error. What should the team check first?
choices: The Direct Connect connection state, because the link may have dropped silently and sent traffic down the slower internet-based VPN backup
Whether PrivateLink interface endpoints were created in the wrong subnet
Whether the VPN tunnels are encrypted with IPsec
Whether the Direct Connect link is encrypted by default
questions.why: Variable latency and lower throughput are typical of the internet-based VPN. If the Direct Connect connection is down, traffic quietly falls back to that slower path, so connection state is the metric to check.

questions.prompt: A clinic's network team says: "We moved to AWS Direct Connect, so our patient data is now encrypted in transit automatically." Which statement is accurate?
choices: The statement is correct, because Direct Connect uses IPsec on every link.
Direct Connect traffic is not encrypted by default. To encrypt it, run a VPN over the link or use link-layer encryption where that is supported.
Direct Connect cannot carry encrypted traffic, so the clinic must switch to PrivateLink.
The statement is correct, because Direct Connect traffic never crosses the public internet.
questions.why: Direct Connect is a private dedicated link, but it does not encrypt by default. Encryption comes from adding a VPN over it or using link-layer encryption where supported.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, and PrivateLink for a given requirement, including at least one limitation of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: First, I ask what is being connected. If it is our data center or office to a VPC, the choice is VPN or Direct Connect. If one VPC just needs private access to a specific service, that is PrivateLink. A Site-to-Site VPN is encrypted, cheap and ready in hours. Because it uses the internet, though, latency and throughput vary, and each tunnel caps around 1.25 Gbps. Direct Connect is a dedicated private link with consistent latency and high bandwidth. It costs more, takes weeks to provision, and is not encrypted by default, so for sensitive data I would layer a VPN on top. A common pattern is VPN first, then Direct Connect, keeping the VPN as backup. PrivateLink exposes only one service through an interface endpoint, so it is not a general network link. I would watch tunnel and connection state, plus throughput and latency, to confirm the choice works.
rubricPoints: Site-to-Site VPN is encrypted over the internet, fast and cheap to set up, but performance varies.
Direct Connect is a dedicated private link with consistent latency and high bandwidth, but it takes weeks and costs more.
Direct Connect is not encrypted by default; a VPN can be layered on top.
PrivateLink gives private access to one specific service through an interface endpoint and is not a site-to-site link.
VPN can serve as a quick interim or backup path for Direct Connect.
Names a metric to watch, such as tunnel or connection state, throughput or latency.

suggested.rationale: This objective is about reading a requirement (speed to set up, consistency, encryption, scope of access) and picking the matching link, which is best practised through exam-style scenarios to reason through.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a traffic director that sits in front of a group of servers and spreads incoming requests across them, so no single server gets overwhelmed while others sit idle. Think of a host at a busy restaurant seating guests at whichever tables are free rather than piling everyone into one section. Choosing a load balancing strategy means picking two things. The first is what kind of director you need: one that reads each request's content, or one that just forwards raw connections very fast. The second is how it decides which server gets the next request. The right choice keeps response times low as traffic grows.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app has two kinds of requests. Short page loads take 20 milliseconds, and report exports take 10 seconds. If a load balancer simply hands each new request to the next server in turn, what might go wrong for users?
lessons.teach:
A load balancer accepts client traffic on a listener, which is a port and protocol it watches, and forwards it to a target group, the set of servers or containers that do the work. It sends traffic only to targets that pass a health check, a regular test request that confirms a target is responding.

On AWS, Elastic Load Balancing offers three current types. An Application Load Balancer (ALB) works at layer 7, the application layer. It reads HTTP details such as the path and host name, so it can route /api to one target group and /images to another. A Network Load Balancer (NLB) works at layer 4, the transport layer. It forwards TCP or UDP connections without reading their contents, which gives very low latency, handles extreme connection volumes, and provides static IP addresses. A Gateway Load Balancer passes traffic through security appliances such as firewalls. It exists for inspection, not for speeding up applications.

The routing algorithm also matters. Round robin gives each new request to the next target in rotation. Least outstanding requests gives it to the target with the fewest unfinished requests. Cross-zone load balancing spreads traffic evenly across all targets in every Availability Zone, so a zone with fewer servers is not overloaded.

Here is a worked example. An HTTP service mixes 20 ms page loads with 10-second exports, and p99 latency spikes. Step 1: the traffic is HTTP and needs path awareness, so choose an ALB. Step 2: round robin keeps sending new requests to a server already stuck on exports. Step 3: switch to least outstanding requests, so busy servers receive fewer new requests. Step 4: watch the ALB's TargetResponseTime metric and confirm p99 drops.

A common mistake is choosing an NLB "because it is faster" when the requirement depends on routing by path or header. An NLB cannot see those details. The opposite mistake is choosing an ALB when clients need fixed IP addresses or a non-HTTP protocol. In a running system, the wrong choice shows up as uneven target load, growing latency, or features that cannot be built at all.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing company runs a driver-location service that receives a constant stream of small UDP packets from phones. Partner fleet operators allow outbound traffic only to specific IP addresses listed in their firewalls, so the service's address must never change. The servers sit in two Availability Zones: 3 in zone A and 9 in zone B. Step 1: The traffic is UDP, not HTTP, and nothing needs to be routed by path or header. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: Zone A has far fewer servers than zone B, so turn on cross-zone load balancing, which spreads traffic evenly across all 12 targets instead of splitting it half and half between the zones. Step 4: Configure a health check so that traffic goes only to servers that are responding. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Choose a Network Load Balancer, because it forwards UDP without reading the contents and provides static IP addresses
Choose an Application Load Balancer with least outstanding requests, so that busy servers receive fewer new packets
Choose an Application Load Balancer, because reading the contents of each packet lets it route location updates more precisely
Choose a Gateway Load Balancer, because it passes traffic through firewalls and so matches what the partners require
questions.why: A Network Load Balancer works at layer 4, forwards UDP connections with very low latency, and gives the fixed IP addresses the partners need, while an Application Load Balancer handles only HTTP traffic.

questions.prompt: In a load balancer, what is a listener?
choices: The set of servers or containers that receive the forwarded traffic and do the work
The port and protocol the load balancer watches for incoming client traffic
The rule that picks which target in a group gets the next request
The regular test request that confirms a target is still responding
questions.why: A listener is the port and protocol on which the load balancer accepts client traffic; the target group, health check and routing algorithm are separate parts.

questions.prompt: A publishing company serves two websites over HTTPS from one entry point. Requests whose host name is shop.example.com must go to one group of containers, and requests for news.example.com must go to another. Which load balancer meets this requirement?
choices: A Network Load Balancer, because its very low latency suits two busy sites
A Gateway Load Balancer, because it can inspect each request and pick a site
A Network Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing turned on
An Application Load Balancer, because it reads the host name and can route each site to its own target group
questions.why: Routing by host name requires reading HTTP details at layer 7, and only the Application Load Balancer does that; a Network Load Balancer forwards connections without seeing the host name.

questions.prompt: An online learning platform runs 2 servers in zone A and 6 servers in zone B behind a load balancer. Cross-zone load balancing is turned off, so each zone receives half of the traffic. Users report slow responses, and the zone A servers are much busier than the others. What change best fixes this?
choices: Switch the routing algorithm to round robin so that each zone takes turns receiving requests
Remove the health check so that zone A servers stop being marked as busy
Turn on cross-zone load balancing so that traffic is spread evenly across all 8 servers
Switch to a Gateway Load Balancer so that traffic is inspected before it reaches the servers
questions.why: With cross-zone load balancing off, the 2 servers in zone A each carry far more traffic than the 6 in zone B; turning it on spreads the traffic evenly across every target in every zone.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between an Application Load Balancer and a Network Load Balancer for a new service, which routing algorithm you would pick, and one tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I look at the protocol and what the routing needs to know. If it is HTTP or HTTPS and we want to route by path or host name, I pick an Application Load Balancer, because it reads each request at layer 7. If it is raw TCP or UDP, needs the lowest possible latency, has huge connection counts, or clients require static IP addresses, I pick a Network Load Balancer, which forwards connections at layer 4 without inspecting them. For an ALB whose requests vary a lot in duration, I would use least outstanding requests instead of round robin, so slow requests do not pile up on one target. The tradeoff is that an ALB adds a little processing per request, while an NLB gives up content-based routing. To confirm the choice worked, I would watch target response time and healthy host count.
rubricPoints: The ALB routes at layer 7 using HTTP details like the path or host.
The NLB forwards at layer 4 with very low latency, high connection volume, and static IPs.
Least outstanding requests suits uneven request durations better than round robin.
It names a tradeoff: the ALB's per-request processing versus the NLB's lack of content routing.
It names a metric to watch, such as target response time or healthy host count.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this by asking you to read a requirement and pick the balancer type and algorithm, so practicing with scenarios plus the explanation builds that judgment best, and no listed mission or engine covers load balancers directly.

lessons.plain: Streaming ingestion means taking in a never-ending flow of small records, such as clicks, sensor readings or vehicle positions, as they happen, instead of collecting them into a big file and loading it later. Amazon Kinesis is AWS's family of managed streaming services. Think of it as a multi-lane conveyor belt at a sorting depot. Producers drop parcels onto the belt, each lane moves a fixed amount per second, and workers downstream pick parcels off in order. If you need more throughput, you add lanes. The belt also keeps parcels for a while, so a slow or late worker can still catch up.
lessons.guessPrompt: If one lane of a conveyor belt can carry 1,000 parcels per second, and 5,000 parcels arrive every second, how many lanes do you need, and what happens to parcels if you only build two?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is a managed, durable log of records that many applications can read. Its unit of capacity is the shard, one lane of the stream. In provisioned mode each shard accepts about 1 MB per second or 1,000 records per second of writes, whichever limit you hit first, and serves about 2 MB per second of reads. A producer is any program writing records; a consumer is any program reading them. Each record carries a partition key, a label that is hashed to pick its shard. Records with the same key land on the same shard and stay in order there. Records are retained for 24 hours by default, extendable up to 365 days, so consumers can replay. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB per second per shard instead of sharing. On-demand mode lets AWS add shards automatically for spiky or unknown traffic, at a higher unit price.

Amazon Data Firehose (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose) is different: a fully managed delivery pipe with no shards to size. It buffers records by size or time and writes them to destinations such as Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift or OpenSearch, optionally transforming them. It is near-real-time, typically a minute or so of buffering, and offers no replay or custom consumers.

Worked example: 5,000 vehicles each send a 500-byte position every second. Bytes: 5,000 times 0.5 KB is about 2.5 MB/s, needing 3 shards. Records: 5,000/s divided by 1,000 needs 5 shards. Take the larger: 5 shards. Using vehicle ID as the partition key keeps each vehicle's positions ordered and spreads load evenly.

A common mistake is a low-variety partition key, such as region with three values. All traffic piles onto a few hot shards that throttle while others sit idle. In a running system, watch WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded for throttled writes and GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds for how far consumers lag behind; a rising iterator age means readers are falling behind and data nears expiry.

questions.prompt: A payments company has 2,000 card terminals. Each terminal sends 4 events per second, and each event is 200 bytes. The company is sizing a Kinesis Data Streams stream in provisioned mode. Each shard accepts about 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s of writes, whichever limit is hit first. Step 1 (records): 2,000 terminals x 4 events = 8,000 records/s. At 1,000 records/s per shard, that needs 8 shards. Step 2 (bytes): 8,000 records x 0.2 KB = about 1.6 MB/s. At 1 MB/s per shard, that needs 2 shards. Step 3: ??? Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Average the two figures to balance cost and capacity: 5 shards
Size for the byte figure, because data volume is what costs money: 2 shards
Add the two figures together to cover both limits: 10 shards
Take the larger of the two figures, because both limits must be met: 8 shards
questions.why: A shard is throttled by whichever write limit it reaches first, so the stream needs enough shards to satisfy the stricter limit, which here is 8 shards for the record count.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm wants its application logs to land in Amazon S3 for later analysis. It wants nothing to size or manage, a delay of a minute or two is acceptable, and no team needs to replay the data or run its own reader programs. Which service fits best?
choices: Amazon Data Firehose, a managed delivery pipe that buffers records and writes them to S3
Kinesis Data Streams with retention extended to 365 days so the logs stay available
Kinesis Data Streams in on-demand mode, with enhanced fan-out for each consumer
Kinesis Data Streams in provisioned mode, with shards sized for peak log volume
questions.why: Firehose needs no shard sizing and delivers buffered records straight to destinations such as S3 in near-real-time, and the firm needs neither replay nor custom consumers.

questions.prompt: A retailer streams order events into a Kinesis data stream with 12 shards. The partition key is the sales channel, which has only two values: online and in-store. Total traffic is far below what 12 shards can handle, yet WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded keeps rising. What is the most effective fix?
choices: Double the shard count to 24 so there is more total write capacity
Extend record retention from 24 hours to 7 days
Use a partition key with many distinct values, such as order ID, so load spreads across all shards
Switch the stream to on-demand mode so AWS adds shards automatically
questions.why: With only two key values, all writes hash to at most two hot shards that throttle while the others sit idle, and only a high-variety key spreads the load evenly.

questions.prompt: A media company's Kinesis data stream shows WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded at zero. However, GetRecords.IteratorAgeMilliseconds has climbed steadily for several hours. What does this most likely mean?
choices: The partition key has too little variety, so writes are piling onto a few shards
Consumers are falling behind the stream, and unread records are getting closer to expiring
Producers are being throttled because the shards have reached their write limit
The stream is healthy, because a higher iterator age means records are kept longer
questions.why: Iterator age measures how far consumers lag behind the newest data, so a rising value means readers cannot keep up and unread records are moving toward the end of the retention period.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Kinesis Data Streams and Data Firehose for a new ingest feed, how you would size it, and name one tradeoff or limit of your choice plus the metric you would watch.
lessons.modelAnswer: Kinesis Data Streams is a retained log split into shards; each shard takes roughly 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s of writes and 2 MB/s of reads. I'd pick it when we need sub-second processing, several independent consumers, per-key ordering, or replay. To size it, I compute shards needed for bytes and for records and take the larger, then pick a high-variety partition key like device ID so load spreads evenly. The tradeoff is that in provisioned mode we own capacity: too few shards throttle, too many waste money; on-demand removes sizing but costs more per unit. If we just need to land data in S3 or Redshift, Firehose is simpler with no shards, but it buffers for about a minute and cannot replay. I'd watch WriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded for throttling and IteratorAgeMilliseconds for consumer lag.
rubricPoints: Defines a shard and its approximate write and read limits.
Sizes by taking the larger of the byte-based and record-based shard counts.
Explains that the partition key sets ordering and must spread load to avoid hot shards.
Contrasts Data Streams (replay, multiple consumers, real time) with Firehose (managed delivery, buffering, no replay).
Names a tradeoff such as provisioned versus on-demand cost or Firehose latency.
Names a metric like iterator age or write throughput exceeded to confirm it works.

suggested.rationale: The vehicle-position ingest design exercise makes the learner size and shape a high-volume streaming ingest path, which is exactly the shard, partition key and consumer reasoning taught here.

lessons.plain: Companies often keep files on servers in their own building and need to get them into the cloud. AWS offers two tools for this, and they solve different problems. AWS DataSync is a moving truck. It copies large amounts of data from one place to another quickly, checks that everything arrived intact, and then its job is done. AWS Storage Gateway is a permanent shop counter in your building. Your local applications keep talking to it as if it were ordinary local storage, while it quietly keeps the real copy in the cloud. The skill is knowing which of the two a situation needs.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants to copy 200 TB of old project files from its office file server into the cloud once, then retire the server. Another company wants its office staff to keep saving files to a shared drive every day while those files are stored in the cloud. Which situation sounds like a one-time move, and which sounds like an ongoing bridge?
lessons.teach:
AWS DataSync is a managed data transfer service. It moves files between on-premises storage (servers in your own data center) and AWS storage such as Amazon S3 (object storage), Amazon EFS (a shared network file system) or Amazon FSx (managed Windows or high-performance file systems). You install an agent, a small virtual machine that reads your local storage, and define a task: a source, a destination and options. DataSync runs many transfers in parallel, compresses the data, encrypts it in transit, verifies integrity at the end, and on later runs copies only changed files. It suits migrations, scheduled copies and replication.

AWS Storage Gateway is a hybrid storage service. It is an appliance in your data center that presents standard storage protocols to local applications and stores the data in AWS. It comes in three types. File Gateway offers NFS or SMB file shares (the protocols Linux and Windows use for network drives) backed by S3 or FSx. Volume Gateway offers iSCSI block disks, the protocol servers use to attach remote hard drives. Tape Gateway acts as a virtual tape library for existing backup software. Each type keeps a local cache, a store of recently used data, so frequent reads stay fast.

Worked example: a hospital must migrate 50 TB of imaging archives in two weeks and then let a lab keep writing new scans locally that end up in S3. Step 1: the one-time 50 TB move is a transfer job, so run DataSync and watch how many bytes it moves per second to confirm the deadline is realistic. Step 2: the ongoing local writes need a protocol the lab already uses, so deploy a File Gateway. Step 3: watch its cache hit percentage. A low value means reads are going to the cloud, so enlarge the cache.

A common mistake is pushing a huge migration through Storage Gateway. It is built for steady access, not bulk copying. In a running system, the result is a full cache, slow uploads and users who notice lag.

questions.prompt: A video production studio has two needs. First, it must copy 12 TB of finished footage from its office storage server to Amazon S3 once, within ten days. Second, its existing backup software writes nightly backups to physical tapes, and the studio wants to stop buying and shipping tapes without changing that backup software. Step 1: The 12 TB one-time copy is a bulk transfer job, so install a DataSync agent, create a task with the office server as source and S3 as destination, and watch the bytes moved per second to confirm ten days is enough. Step 2: (missing) Step 3: Watch the gateway's cache hit percentage, and enlarge the local cache if it stays low. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Deploy a Tape Gateway so the existing backup software sees a virtual tape library that stores data in AWS.
Schedule the DataSync task to run every night so the backups are copied to S3 instead of tape.
Deploy a File Gateway so the backup software can write its tapes to an SMB file share backed by S3.
Deploy a Volume Gateway so the backup software can write tapes to iSCSI block disks stored in AWS.
questions.why: Tape Gateway acts as a virtual tape library, so backup software that already writes to tapes can keep working unchanged while the data lands in AWS.

questions.prompt: An accounting firm has database servers that need to attach extra disks over the network, using the same protocol servers normally use to connect remote hard drives, with the data stored in AWS. Which Storage Gateway type fits, and what does it present to the servers?
choices: Volume Gateway, presenting iSCSI block disks to the servers
DataSync, presenting an agent that the servers mount as a disk
File Gateway, presenting NFS or SMB file shares to the servers
Tape Gateway, presenting a virtual tape library to the servers
questions.why: Volume Gateway offers iSCSI block disks, the protocol servers use to attach remote hard drives, with the data stored in AWS.

questions.prompt: A research lab sets up a DataSync task to copy a 30 TB on-premises share to Amazon EFS (a shared network file system) every night. The first run takes many hours, but the second night's run finishes in a fraction of the time even though nothing about the network changed. What best explains this?
choices: The local cache on the DataSync agent now holds the whole share, so reads skip the network.
DataSync skips the integrity check on later runs to save time on large tasks.
On later runs DataSync copies only the files that changed since the previous run.
DataSync stops encrypting data after the first run because it trusts the connection.
questions.why: After the first full copy, DataSync transfers only changed files, so repeat runs move far less data.

questions.prompt: A retailer tries to migrate 80 TB of old sales records to Amazon S3 by copying everything into a File Gateway share in one week. Office users who rely on that share start complaining about lag. What is the most likely cause, and the better approach?
choices: The gateway's cache is too large and wastes bandwidth; shrink the cache so more data goes straight to S3.
The gateway's cache filled and uploads slowed because it is built for steady access, not bulk copying; use DataSync for the 80 TB move.
The SMB protocol cannot handle files larger than a few gigabytes; switch the share to NFS and retry the copy.
File Gateway does not support S3 as a destination; deploy a Volume Gateway to complete the migration.
questions.why: Storage Gateway is meant for steady, ongoing access, so a huge bulk copy fills its cache and slows uploads, while DataSync is the service built for large one-time transfers.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, when you would pick DataSync and when you would pick Storage Gateway. Include one limit or tradeoff of each, and the metric you would watch to know the choice worked.
lessons.modelAnswer: DataSync is for moving data. You run an agent near your storage, define a task, and it copies files to S3, EFS or FSx in parallel, encrypts them in transit, checks their integrity, and on later runs sends only what changed. It is ideal for migrations or scheduled replication, but it is not a place applications read and write live data. I would watch how many bytes per second it moves to confirm we will meet the deadline. Storage Gateway is for ongoing hybrid access. Local apps keep using NFS, SMB, iSCSI or virtual tape while the data lives in AWS, with a local cache for speed. Its limit is that performance depends on cache size and on the link to AWS, so it is a poor tool for bulk migration. I would watch the cache hit percentage. Often you use both: DataSync for the initial bulk move, then a gateway for daily use.
rubricPoints: DataSync is a managed transfer service for one-time or scheduled bulk copies, with incremental copying and integrity verification.
Storage Gateway is an ongoing hybrid bridge that presents local file, block or tape protocols while storing the data in AWS.
Names the gateway types: File (NFS/SMB), Volume (iSCSI) and Tape (virtual tape library).
Identifies a tradeoff, such as a gateway being slow for bulk migration or DataSync not serving live application access.
Names a metric to watch, such as DataSync bytes transferred per second or the gateway's cache hit percentage.
Recognizes that the two are often combined: a bulk move first, then ongoing access.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine simulates hybrid data transfer, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios that separate a one-time move from ongoing access is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: AWS Glue is a managed service that takes data sitting in one shape and rewrites it into a more useful shape, without you running any servers. Think of a mailroom that receives thousands of handwritten letters and retypes them into a neat filing cabinet sorted by topic, so anyone looking for one subject opens one drawer instead of reading every letter. A common job is turning CSV files (plain text, one row per line) into Parquet files (a compact format stored column by column), which makes later analysis faster and cheaper.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a year of sales records in plain text files, and most questions people ask only need two of the forty columns, such as date and total. Would you rather store the data row by row or column by column, and why?
lessons.teach:
AWS Glue is a serverless ETL service. ETL means extract, transform, load: read data from a source, change it, and write it to a destination. Serverless means AWS runs the compute; you pay only while a job runs. Glue has three parts worth knowing. A crawler scans files and guesses their schema, meaning the column names and types. The Data Catalog is a shared metadata store that records those schemas as tables so query tools can find the data. A job is the script, usually Apache Spark (a distributed processing engine), that does the transform.

Why convert CSV to Parquet? CSV is row-oriented text: to read one column, a tool must read every whole row. Parquet is columnar, meaning values of each column are stored together and compressed, so a query touching two columns reads only those two. Partitioning adds folder-style splits such as year=2024/month=05, so queries filtering on a date skip whole folders.

Worked example: 500 GB of daily CSV order logs land in an S3 bucket. Step one, a crawler catalogs them as a table. Step two, a Glue job reads that table, casts the total column to a number, drops bad rows, and writes Parquet partitioned by order date to a second bucket. Step three, a crawler catalogs the output. Step four, an analyst asks for last month's revenue; the engine reads only the date and total columns for one month's partitions, perhaps a few gigabytes instead of 500.

A common mistake is writing thousands of tiny Parquet files, or skipping partitioning. Every file adds open-and-read overhead, so queries stay slow even after conversion. In a running system, the metric to watch is data scanned per query and query run time; per-scan pricing in query services means a successful conversion shows up as both dropping sharply. Glue is the right pick when the requirement says managed, serverless transformation; heavy custom cluster tuning points elsewhere.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency stores 300 GB of fare-tap records as CSV in S3. Each row has 20 columns. An analyst asks for total fares by station for one week, which needs only 2 columns (station and fare). Step 1: With CSV, which is row-oriented text, the query engine must read every whole row, so it scans all 300 GB. Step 2: A Glue job (the serverless transform script) rewrites the data as Parquet, a columnar format, partitioned by tap date into folders such as date=2024-03-04. Step 3: ______. Step 4: The team confirms the change worked by watching data scanned per query and query run time, and both drop sharply. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The engine reads only the station and fare columns, and only inside the folders for the requested week.
The engine still reads all 300 GB, but faster, because Parquet files are kept in memory.
The engine reads only the station and fare columns, but across every date folder in the dataset.
The engine reads all 20 columns, but only inside the folders for the requested week.
questions.why: Columnar storage lets the engine skip the 18 unneeded columns, and date partitioning lets it skip every folder outside the requested week, so both savings apply together.

questions.prompt: A retail company runs a Glue crawler over its supplier price files. Afterwards, an analyst's query tool can find the data as a table with named, typed columns. Which part of AWS Glue holds that table definition so query tools can look it up?
choices: The Data Catalog, the shared metadata store that records schemas as tables
The crawler, which keeps the schema stored inside itself after scanning
The Glue job, the Spark script that performs the transformation
A partition, the folder-style split such as year=2024/month=05
questions.why: The crawler only scans files and guesses the schema; the Data Catalog is where that schema is stored as a table for query tools to find.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm converted 80 GB of shipment CSV files to Parquet with a Glue job. Queries are still almost as slow as before. Looking at the output bucket, the team finds about 50,000 Parquet files of roughly 2 MB each, all in one folder with no partitions. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The crawler should have been run before the job instead of after it
Parquet is row-oriented, so it cannot speed up queries that touch only a few columns
Many tiny files add open-and-read overhead, and without partitioning every query must look at all of them
Glue is serverless, so the job did not have enough compute to finish the conversion properly
questions.why: Every file adds overhead and missing partitions mean no folders can be skipped, so the conversion's benefit is lost even though the format is now columnar.

questions.prompt: A media company uses a Glue job to turn its daily viewing-event CSV files into partitioned Parquet. The team is queried by a service that charges per amount of data scanned. Which pair of measurements best shows that the conversion actually worked?
choices: The total size of the raw CSV bucket and the number of rows dropped as bad
The Glue job's run time and the number of Spark workers it used
The number of crawlers run per day and the size of the Data Catalog
Data scanned per query and query run time, which should both drop sharply
questions.why: The goal of the conversion is cheaper, faster queries, so less data scanned per query and shorter query run time are the direct signs of success.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we would run an AWS Glue job to convert our CSV logs into partitioned Parquet, what it improves, and one limit or tradeoff of doing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Glue is AWS's serverless ETL service: a crawler figures out the schema and records it in the Data Catalog, and a Spark job reads the CSV, cleans it, and writes it out as Parquet. Parquet stores each column together and compressed, so a query that needs only date and total reads just those columns, and partitioning by date lets it skip months it does not need. The payoff is far less data scanned, faster queries and lower per-scan cost, which we would confirm by watching bytes scanned and query duration before and after. The tradeoffs: the job itself costs money and time to run, the converted data is a copy that lags the raw files, and if we write many tiny files or partition on the wrong column we lose most of the benefit.
rubricPoints: Defines Glue as a managed, serverless ETL service with crawlers, a Data Catalog and jobs.
Explains that Parquet is columnar and compressed, so queries read only needed columns.
Mentions partitioning so queries skip irrelevant data.
Names a metric to confirm success, such as data scanned or query time.
States a tradeoff, such as job cost, data freshness lag, or the small-files problem.

suggested.rationale: No mission runs Glue, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about when a managed CSV-to-Parquet transform meets a performance or cost requirement builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: A data lake is one big, cheap storage place where an organisation keeps all its data, raw and cleaned, in its original files, so many teams can analyse it later without first forcing it into one database design. Think of a public library's stacks: every book is kept in one building, a catalogue tells you what exists and where, and a librarian decides which rooms each visitor may enter. On AWS the shelves are usually Amazon S3 (object storage), and AWS Lake Formation acts as the catalogue keeper and librarian, controlling who may see which tables, columns and rows.
lessons.guessPrompt: If ten teams share one storage bucket full of customer data, and the marketing team should see purchase totals but never email addresses, would you rather control access per file or per column of a table? Why?
lessons.teach:
A data lake is a central store, normally Amazon S3 object storage, that holds data in open file formats so many analytics tools can read it. Building one has three parts: storage, a catalog, and access control. The catalog, the AWS Glue Data Catalog, is a metadata store: it records each table's name, columns and the S3 location of its files, so query engines know what the files mean. AWS Lake Formation is a managed service that sits over the catalog and storage. It sets up the lake, can load data with templates called blueprints, and, most importantly for the exam, centralises permissions.

Why this works: plain IAM (Identity and Access Management) policies and bucket policies only control whole objects or prefixes. Lake Formation lets an administrator grant SELECT on a database, a table, specific columns, or rows matching a data filter. When you register an S3 location with Lake Formation, query services ask Lake Formation for access, and it hands back temporary credentials limited to what that user is granted. LF-tags are labels such as sensitivity=pii attached to resources; you grant on tags, so new tables tagged the same way are covered automatically. Grants can also be shared with other AWS accounts.

Worked example: an analyst runs a query on the orders table. Step one, the query engine looks up orders in the catalog. Step two, it asks Lake Formation what the analyst may read. Step three, Lake Formation sees a grant on order_id and total only, with a row filter region='EU'. Step four, the analyst receives EU rows with two columns; the email column never appears.

Common mistake: leaving broad IAM or bucket permissions in place, or keeping the default setting where catalog resources are still governed by IAM alone. Users can then read the raw S3 files directly and bypass every column rule. The running consequence is a quiet data leak that audits only find later. Lock raw S3 access down to Lake Formation and grant through it.

questions.prompt: A logistics company stores shipment data in Amazon S3 and wants its planning team to query every table about routes, including tables created in the future, without an admin writing a new grant each time. The steps are: Step 1, the admin registers the S3 location with Lake Formation so query services must ask Lake Formation for access. Step 2, the admin attaches the LF-tag domain=routing to the existing route tables in the catalog. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, a new table called depot_delays is created and tagged domain=routing, and the planning team can query it straight away with no further action. What is Step 3?
choices: Add a bucket policy giving the planning team read access to the whole routing prefix in S3
Grant the planning team SELECT on resources matching the LF-tag domain=routing
Grant the planning team SELECT on each existing route table by name
Create a Lake Formation blueprint that copies the route tables into a separate bucket for the planning team
questions.why: A grant made on an LF-tag covers any resource carrying that tag, so the new depot_delays table is included automatically, while grants on table names would not cover new tables.

questions.prompt: In a data lake, what does the AWS Glue Data Catalog hold?
choices: The data files themselves, converted into a proprietary format for faster queries
The list of IAM users allowed to sign in to the AWS account
Metadata such as each table's name, its columns and the S3 location of its files
Temporary credentials that query engines use to read S3 objects
questions.why: The catalog is a metadata store that tells query engines what the files mean and where they are; the data stays in S3 and permissions come from Lake Formation.

questions.prompt: A university keeps a staff table in its S3-based data lake. Interns in the HR office must be able to query staff names and departments but must never see the salary column, which is stored in the same files. Which approach meets this requirement?
choices: Write an S3 bucket policy that denies interns access to the salary column
Give interns an IAM policy allowing read access to the staff table's S3 prefix
Move the staff table into a separate AWS account and share the whole table
Register the S3 location with Lake Formation and grant interns SELECT on only the name and department columns
questions.why: IAM and bucket policies only control whole objects or prefixes, so column-level restriction needs a Lake Formation grant on specific columns.

questions.prompt: An insurer set up Lake Formation column grants so claims analysts cannot see the policyholder_phone column. A later audit finds analysts downloaded full raw files containing phone numbers. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Glue Data Catalog listed the wrong S3 location for the claims table
Lake Formation row filters always override column grants
Broad IAM or bucket permissions were left in place, so analysts read the S3 files directly and bypassed Lake Formation
The analysts' LF-tag grants were made on tags instead of on table names
questions.why: If raw S3 access is not locked down to Lake Formation, users can read the files directly and every column rule is bypassed, causing a quiet leak.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we would put Lake Formation in front of our S3 data lake instead of just writing bucket policies, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing so.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our data lake is files in S3 plus a catalog that describes them as tables. Bucket policies and IAM can only say yes or no to whole files or folders, so they cannot hide one sensitive column or show only one region's rows. Lake Formation centralises permissions at the database, table, column and row level, and query services get temporary credentials scoped to exactly those grants. LF-tags let us grant by label, so newly tagged tables are protected without new policies, and we can share with other accounts from one place. The tradeoff is that it only protects us if it is actually the gatekeeper: we must register the S3 locations, switch off the default IAM-only access, and remove direct bucket access. It also adds another permission layer to learn and debug, so when access fails we check both IAM and Lake Formation grants.
rubricPoints: Defines a data lake as central S3 storage plus a catalog describing the files as tables.
States that Lake Formation centralises fine-grained permissions at table, column and row level.
Contrasts this with IAM or bucket policies that only control whole objects or prefixes.
Mentions LF-tags or cross-account sharing as a way to scale grants.
Names the risk that direct S3 or default IAM access bypasses Lake Formation, or the added complexity of two permission layers.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present a requirement like column-level restriction or cross-account sharing and ask you to pick Lake Formation over bucket policies, so reasoning through scenarios builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: Amazon Athena lets you ask questions of files stored in Amazon S3, a cloud file store, by writing SQL, a standard language for querying tables, without setting up or running any database servers. Amazon QuickSight turns query results into charts and dashboards that people can share. Think of S3 as a huge filing cabinet. Athena is a librarian who reads the folders you point at and answers your question, charging you by how many pages she has to read. QuickSight is the person who turns her answers into a wall poster that the whole office can understand at a glance.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a query service charges you by how much data it reads, what two things could you do to your stored log files so that a question about one single day costs far less?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Athena is a serverless, interactive SQL query service. Serverless means AWS runs the compute and you never size or patch machines. Athena reads data where it already sits in Amazon S3, which is object storage. It uses schema-on-read: the table definition is applied when you query, not when you load. Those table definitions usually live in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, a shared list of tables, columns and file locations. Athena bills by the amount of data each query scans, so reading less data makes queries both cheaper and faster.

Three techniques shrink what gets scanned. Partitioning stores files in folders by a key such as date, so a filter on that key skips the other folders. Columnar formats such as Parquet or ORC store each column separately, so Athena reads only the columns you name. Compression makes every file smaller.

Here is a worked example. A team has 1 TB of raw CSV web logs in one folder and asks for yesterday's error count. First, with no partitions, Athena must open every file. Second, because CSV is row-based, it reads every column of every row, which is the full 1 TB. Now the team stores the logs as Parquet and partitions them by date. Third, the date filter limits the scan to one day's folder. Fourth, Parquet lets Athena read only the status column. The scan drops to a few gigabytes. The metric to watch is data scanned per query, alongside query run time.

Amazon QuickSight is a managed business-intelligence service, meaning a tool for building dashboards and reports. It can use Athena and many other services as data sources. Its SPICE engine is an in-memory store that holds a copy of the data, so dashboards load quickly and do not re-run an Athena scan each time someone views them.

A common mistake is treating Athena as the database behind an application. It is built for ad hoc analysis that takes seconds, not for many small, low-latency transactions. If you put it behind a busy web page, responses will be slow and you will pay a scan cost on every page load.

questions.prompt: A logistics company keeps 600 GB of uncompressed JSON shipment records in Amazon S3, all in one folder. Each record has 40 fields. Every week, analysts use Amazon Athena (a serverless SQL query service that bills by data scanned) to find the average delivery time for one warehouse in a single month. The team wants to cut cost and query time. Step 1: They reorganise the files into folders by month (partitioning), so a filter on month skips every other month's folder. Step 2: ??? Step 3: They compress the files so each one is smaller on disk. Result: the data scanned per query falls from 600 GB to well under 1 GB. Which action is the missing Step 2?
choices: Import the records into QuickSight SPICE so the analysts' Athena queries scan less
Register the records in the AWS Glue Data Catalog so Athena reads only the needed fields
Raise the Athena compute size so each query finishes scanning the 40 fields faster
Convert the files to Parquet so Athena reads only the warehouse and delivery-time columns
questions.why: Parquet is a columnar format, so Athena reads only the two columns the query names instead of all 40 fields in every row.

questions.prompt: Amazon Athena is described as using schema-on-read. What does schema-on-read mean?
choices: Data must be converted into a fixed table layout before it can be loaded into Athena
The schema is stored inside each S3 object, so no table definitions are needed anywhere
Athena reads the schema from the first row of each file and ignores the Glue Data Catalog
The table definition is applied when a query runs, and the data stays as it is in Amazon S3
questions.why: Schema-on-read means the table structure, usually kept in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, is applied at query time to files that stay where they are in S3, not when the data is loaded.

questions.prompt: A retailer has an Amazon QuickSight dashboard, a managed business-intelligence tool for dashboards and reports. The dashboard uses Amazon Athena as its data source. About 300 store managers open it each morning, and every view runs a new Athena query, so the Athena bill is climbing and the dashboard loads slowly. What change best addresses both problems?
choices: Switch the source files in Amazon S3 from Parquet to CSV
Ask managers to refresh the dashboard less often each day
Load the dataset into SPICE, QuickSight's in-memory store
Move the Athena tables into a new AWS Glue Data Catalog
questions.why: SPICE holds an in-memory copy of the data, so dashboard views load quickly and do not trigger a new Athena scan, and its scan cost, each time someone opens the dashboard.

questions.prompt: A startup plans to have its busy shopping website query Amazon Athena directly on every page load to fetch a single customer's cart. The cart data sits in Amazon S3. What is the most likely result?
choices: Pages respond slowly, and the company pays a data-scan charge on each page load
Pages respond quickly once the cart data is stored in a columnar format
Pages respond quickly because Athena is serverless and scales with web traffic
Athena caches each customer's cart, so only the first page load costs money
questions.why: Athena is built for ad hoc analysis that takes seconds, not many small low-latency lookups, so each page load is slow and incurs a scan cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would pick Athena plus QuickSight, how you would keep Athena fast and cheap, and one situation where it is the wrong choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Athena runs SQL directly against files in S3 with no servers to manage, and the table definitions come from the Glue Data Catalog. It suits ad hoc analysis of logs or data-lake files. QuickSight sits on top and turns the results into shareable dashboards. Its SPICE in-memory cache keeps those dashboards fast without re-scanning the data on every view. Athena charges by data scanned, so I would convert the files to a columnar format like Parquet, compress them, and partition them by a common filter such as date. Then each query reads only the folders and columns it needs. I would watch data scanned per query and query run time to confirm the change worked. The limit is that Athena is not a transactional database. For an application making many fast, small reads and writes, it would be too slow and too costly per query, and a purpose-built database is the right tool.
rubricPoints: Athena is serverless SQL over data stored in S3, with tables defined in a catalog such as Glue.
Athena cost and speed depend on the amount of data scanned.
Partitioning, columnar formats like Parquet, and compression reduce the data scanned.
QuickSight builds dashboards, and SPICE caches data in memory for fast viewing.
Data scanned per query and run time are the metrics to watch.
Athena is not suited to low-latency transactional application workloads.

suggested.rationale: The exam skill is spotting when serverless S3 querying and dashboards fit a requirement and which change cuts the data scanned, which is best practised by reasoning through scenario questions.

lessons.plain: Every system that collects data has doors where that data comes in: a place where phones upload photos, sensors send readings, or partners drop files. Securing those doors means deciding who is allowed to send data, making sure it travels encrypted, limiting where it can come from, and keeping it locked once it arrives. Think of a building's loading dock. You want a guest list, a sealed truck, a gate that only opens to known routes, and a locked storeroom. You do not want a dock that is wide open to anyone with a van.
lessons.guessPrompt: A mobile app needs to upload user photos straight into cloud storage. Would you put a permanent password for your storage account inside the app, or hand each user a short-lived pass for one upload? What could go wrong with the first choice?
lessons.teach:
An ingestion access point is any entry where data comes into your system. Examples include an upload path into Amazon S3 (object storage), a Kinesis data stream (a managed stream that accepts records in order), an Amazon API Gateway endpoint (a managed front door for HTTP APIs), or an SFTP endpoint from AWS Transfer Family (managed file transfer). Securing one means answering four questions: who may send, over what channel, from where, and how the data is protected once it lands.

Who: use IAM (Identity and Access Management, AWS's authorization service) with least privilege. Least privilege means granting only the exact action needed, such as writing records to one stream, with no permission to read or delete. Give callers temporary credentials, which are short-lived keys issued through a role, instead of long-term access keys. For outside users, use a presigned URL or an API Gateway authorizer. A presigned URL is a link signed with your credentials that permits one upload to one object name until it expires. An authorizer is a check that runs before a request is accepted, for example one backed by Amazon Cognito (a managed user sign-in service).

Channel: require TLS, which is encryption in transit. An S3 bucket policy is an authorization policy attached to the storage bucket itself, and it can deny any request that does not use a secure connection.

Where: for senders inside a VPC (your private virtual network), use a VPC endpoint. This is a private connection to the service, so the traffic never crosses the public internet. You can then limit the bucket policy to that endpoint.

At rest: turn on server-side encryption with AWS KMS (the managed key service).

Worked example: a photo app. First, the user signs in through Cognito. Second, the app calls your API, which checks the user's token and returns a presigned upload URL for uploads/user-123/photo.jpg that is valid for five minutes. Third, the app uploads directly to S3 over HTTPS. Fourth, the bucket policy rejects any request without TLS, and default KMS encryption applies to the stored file. Fifth, once the five minutes pass, the link no longer works.

Common mistake: putting long-term access keys inside the app, or allowing public write on the bucket. Anyone who extracts that key can upload or overwrite data without limit. That fills your storage, drives up cost, and corrupts downstream analytics. A further benefit of presigned uploads is performance: the data goes straight to S3 and skips your servers, so they carry less load.

questions.prompt: A medical testing lab runs an application on servers inside its VPC (its private virtual network). The application uploads finished test-result files to an S3 bucket under the prefix results/. The architect secures this ingestion point as follows. Who: the application uses a role, so it receives temporary credentials (short-lived keys) instead of long-term access keys, and [MISSING STEP]. Channel: the bucket policy denies any request that does not use TLS. Where: uploads travel through a VPC endpoint, and the bucket policy accepts writes only from that endpoint. At rest: default server-side encryption with AWS KMS is turned on. Which choice correctly fills the missing step?
choices: the role is allowed to read, write, and delete objects across the whole bucket so the application never hits a permissions error
the role is allowed only to write objects under results/, with no permission to read or delete them
the bucket allows public write so the role does not need any permissions of its own
the role is given a long-term access key as a backup in case the temporary credentials expire
questions.why: Least privilege means granting only the exact action the caller needs, which here is writing objects under results/ and nothing more.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company lets customers attach a scanned ID to their booking. The company's API, after checking the customer is signed in, hands back a link that allows the customer to upload one file named ids/booking-5521.png, and the link stops working after ten minutes. What is this link?
choices: An API Gateway authorizer
A bucket policy
A presigned URL
A VPC endpoint
questions.why: A presigned URL is a link signed with your credentials that permits one upload to one object name until it expires.

questions.prompt: A retailer's order-processing servers run inside its VPC and write records to a Kinesis data stream (a managed stream that accepts records in order). A new requirement says this traffic must never cross the public internet. Which change meets that requirement?
choices: Add an API Gateway authorizer backed by Amazon Cognito
Send the records through a VPC endpoint for the service
Turn on server-side encryption with AWS KMS for the stream
Give the servers temporary credentials through a role
questions.why: A VPC endpoint is a private connection to the service, so traffic from senders inside the VPC never crosses the public internet.

questions.prompt: A fitness startup ships a phone app that contains a long-term AWS access key with permission to write to its S3 bucket, so the app can upload workout logs. What is the most likely consequence for the running system?
choices: Uploads become slower because each one must be checked by an authorizer before it is accepted
Anyone who extracts the key can upload or overwrite data without limit, filling storage, raising cost, and corrupting downstream analytics
Stored workout logs stop being encrypted at rest because KMS cannot be used with access keys
The key expires after a few minutes, so uploads begin failing for all users
questions.why: A long-term key placed in an app can be pulled out and reused by anyone, letting them write or overwrite data with no limit, which drives up storage cost and damages data used downstream.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would secure the point where a mobile app or device sends data into AWS. Cover who can send, the channel, where it comes from, and storage. Name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I treat every ingestion point as a door and check four things. Who: callers get temporary, least-privilege credentials. For app users, that means signing in through Cognito, then getting a presigned URL that allows one upload to one object name for a few minutes. Internal producers get an IAM role that can only write to the specific stream or bucket. Channel: the bucket policy denies any request that is not over TLS. Where: producers inside our VPC use a VPC endpoint, and the policy only accepts traffic from it. At rest: KMS server-side encryption is on by default. I never ship long-term keys in an app, because anyone could extract them. The tradeoff is extra moving parts. We need a service to issue presigned URLs, we need to choose sensible expiry times, and KMS adds request cost and request-rate limits at very high volume.
rubricPoints: Uses least-privilege, temporary credentials such as roles, presigned URLs, or authorizers instead of long-term keys.
Requires encryption in transit with TLS, enforced by a policy.
Restricts network origin, for example with a VPC endpoint, for internal producers.
Enables encryption at rest with KMS.
Names the risk of embedded keys or public write access.
States a tradeoff, such as added complexity, expiry tuning, or KMS cost and limits.

suggested.rationale: Writing and testing policies that grant only write access, deny non-TLS requests, and limit traffic to one endpoint is the core skill, and an authorization policy evaluator would let the learner practise exactly that.

lessons.plain: Cloud storage comes in three main shapes, and each is billed differently. Object storage (Amazon S3) keeps whole files reached over the web and charges only for what you store. Block storage (Amazon EBS) acts like a hard drive attached to one server and charges for the size you reserve, full or empty. File storage (Amazon EFS, Amazon FSx) is a shared network drive many servers use at once, at a higher price per gigabyte. Picking the cheapest one is like choosing between a warehouse shelf, a desk drawer and a shared office cabinet. Match the shape to how the data is used.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have 2 TB of product photos that four web servers must all show to customers. Which is likely cheaper: giving each server its own 2 TB disk, or keeping one copy somewhere all four can read? Why?
lessons.teach:
Selecting the most cost-effective storage service means matching the access pattern to the cheapest storage type that still meets the requirement. There are three types. Object storage (Amazon S3) holds whole objects (files plus metadata) reached through an API over HTTP. You pay per gigabyte actually stored plus per request, and it has the lowest per-GB price. Block storage (Amazon EBS) is a virtual disk attached to one instance in one Availability Zone (a single data-center location). You pay for provisioned size, meaning the capacity you reserve, whether used or not. File storage is a shared file system that many instances mount at once: Amazon EFS for Linux, and Amazon FSx for Windows file shares or high-performance computing. You pay per GB stored, at the highest per-GB rate. Instance store is temporary disk that comes free with some instance types, but its data is lost when the instance stops.

This works as a selection rule because price follows capability. Shared, mountable, low-latency access costs more per GB. Simple object access costs least.

Worked example, using illustrative relative prices: object 1 unit per GB-month, block about 3.5, shared file about 13. You have 2 TB (2,000 GB) of images for four web servers. Option one is a 2 TB block disk on each server: 4 × 2,000 × 3.5 = 28,000 units. Option two is one shared file system: 2,000 × 13 = 26,000 units. Option three is S3, with servers or browsers fetching objects: 2,000 × 1 = 2,000 units plus small request charges. Because the images never need file-system semantics such as locking or in-place edits, S3 meets the requirement at a fraction of the cost.

A common mistake is choosing EFS because it is "elastic and shared" when the application only reads whole files. S3 would do the same job far more cheaply. The opposite mistake is putting a database on S3. Databases need block storage's low-latency random writes. In a running system, oversized EBS volumes and unneeded file systems keep billing every month, even for empty space.

questions.prompt:
A research lab keeps 800 GB of finished log archives. Five analysis servers each read whole archive files and never edit them in place or need file locking. Use these illustrative relative prices: object storage 1 unit per GB-month, block storage 3.5, shared file storage 13.

Step 1: A separate 800 GB block disk (EBS) on each server costs 5 × 800 × 3.5 = 14,000 units.
Step 2: One shared file system (EFS) costs 800 × 13 = 10,400 units.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The lab picks the cheapest option that still meets the requirement.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: S3 costs 800 × 1 = 800 units plus small request charges. Whole-file reads need no locking, so S3 meets the need.
Shared file storage at 10,400 units is required, because more than one server must reach the same files.
Instance store costs 0 units because it is free with some instance types, so the lab should keep the archives there.
S3 costs 5 × 800 × 1 = 4,000 units, because each of the five servers needs its own copy of the objects.
questions.why: One copy in object storage is billed per GB actually stored at the lowest rate, and every server can fetch the same objects over the API, so 800 units plus requests meets a read-whole-files requirement.

questions.prompt: A team creates a 1,000 GB Amazon EBS volume (a virtual block disk attached to one instance) but has written only 150 GB of data to it so far. For how much storage are they billed each month?
choices: 1,000 GB, because EBS charges for the provisioned size whether it is used or not
150 GB, because EBS charges only for data actually written
Nothing until the volume is more than half full
150 GB plus a per-request charge for each read and write
questions.why: Block storage is billed on the capacity you reserve, so the unused 850 GB keeps costing money every month.

questions.prompt: A startup runs a transactional database on one server. To save money, an engineer proposes moving the database's data files from Amazon EBS to Amazon S3, since S3 has the lowest per-GB price. What is the main problem with this plan?
choices: S3 cannot store files larger than a few gigabytes, so the database would not fit
S3 can only be reached by one instance at a time, which blocks database replicas
S3 charges per provisioned gigabyte, so it would actually cost more than EBS
A database needs low-latency random writes, which block storage provides and object storage over an HTTP API does not
questions.why: Price follows capability: S3 is cheap because it offers only whole-object access over an API, which does not suit a database's frequent small random writes.

questions.prompt: A company runs a Windows-based accounting application on six servers. All six must open the same files at the same time through a shared Windows file share. Which storage choice fits this requirement most directly?
choices: Amazon S3, because it has the lowest per-GB price of any storage type
One Amazon EBS volume on each server, kept in sync by copying files between them
Instance store on each server, because it comes free with some instance types
Amazon FSx for Windows, a managed shared file system that many Windows servers can mount at once
questions.why: The requirement is a shared, mountable Windows file share, which is what file storage such as FSx for Windows provides; the cheaper options cannot give all six servers one shared file system.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would pick the cheapest storage service for a new workload, and name one requirement that would force you off the cheapest option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with how the data is accessed, not with price. If the application reads and writes whole files through an API, such as images, logs, backups or uploads, I use S3. It is object storage with the lowest per-GB price, and I pay only for what I store. If one server needs a fast disk for random reads and writes, as a database or boot volume does, I use EBS block storage and size it carefully, because I pay for the provisioned capacity even when it is empty. Only if several servers must mount the same files with normal file-system behavior do I pay the higher per-GB rate of EFS, or FSx for Windows or HPC needs. The tradeoff is that S3 cannot be mounted as a low-latency disk. So a requirement for shared POSIX file access or database-style random writes pushes me to a more expensive service.
rubricPoints: Names the three storage types (object, block, file) and gives an example service for each.
States that S3 charges per GB stored at the lowest rate, while EBS charges for provisioned size.
Explains that shared file storage like EFS or FSx costs the most per GB and is justified only by shared mounting needs.
Chooses storage by access pattern first, then picks the cheapest type that meets it.
Names a limit, such as S3 not acting as a low-latency mountable disk or database volume.

suggested.rationale: Pricing the same dataset as object, block and file storage in fictional credits makes the learner feel the cost gap that drives this choice.

lessons.plain: Amazon S3 is a managed object store: you put files (called objects) into it and pay each month for the space they take. Not every file is touched equally. Fresh files get read often; old ones sit untouched for years. S3 offers storage tiers, called storage classes, that trade cheaper monthly storage for slower or costlier reading. A lifecycle rule is an automatic schedule that moves files to cheaper tiers as they age, or deletes them. Think of a kitchen: today's groceries go in the fridge, spare tins in the cupboard, and old paperwork in a box in the attic. The attic costs little, but fetching from it takes effort.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company keeps application logs that engineers read often in the first week, almost never after a month, and must keep for seven years for auditors who give a few days' notice. Where would you keep the logs at each age to pay the least, and what would you do with them after seven years?
lessons.teach:
A storage class is the price-and-access tier an S3 object lives in. S3 Standard has the highest storage price but no retrieval fee, so it suits data read often. Standard-Infrequent Access (Standard-IA) is cheaper to store but charges a per-gigabyte retrieval fee. One Zone-IA is cheaper again because it keeps data in a single Availability Zone, which is one isolated data center group, so losing that zone can lose the data. S3 Intelligent-Tiering watches each object's access and moves it between tiers for you, for a small monitoring fee per object. That fee makes it a good fit when access patterns are unknown.

The archival tiers are the Glacier classes. Glacier Instant Retrieval returns data in milliseconds and suits data read about once a quarter. Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours to restore. Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest of all, but a restore can take up to 12 hours or more.

The cheaper classes carry two hidden costs. The first is a minimum storage duration: you are billed for at least 30 days in the IA classes, 90 days in Glacier Instant and Flexible, and 180 days in Deep Archive, even if you delete the object sooner. The second is a minimum billable size of 128 KB in the IA classes, so tiny objects cost more than they should.

A lifecycle rule automates two kinds of action. A transition moves objects to another class after a set age. An expiration deletes them.

Here is a worked example for audit logs. Day 0: the logs land in Standard. Day 30: a transition moves them to Standard-IA. Day 90: they move to Deep Archive, because auditors give days of notice. Day 2555, about seven years: an expiration deletes them.

A common mistake is moving short-lived or tiny objects to IA or Glacier. The minimum duration and size charges then cost more than Standard would have. Another mistake is archiving data that an application must read instantly. Requests then stall for hours, and the running system effectively breaks.

questions.prompt: A property-listing website stores each listing's photos in S3. Here is its lifecycle plan, worked through. Day 0: new photos land in S3 Standard, because buyers view them many times a day while the listing is live. Day 60: the listing has usually closed, and a lifecycle transition moves the photos to a cheaper class. After that, an agent opens an old listing's photos about once a quarter. When they do, the photos must appear on screen in milliseconds, and the business requires that the photos survive the loss of a single Availability Zone (one isolated data center group). Day 1825, about five years: a lifecycle expiration deletes the photos. Which storage class should the Day 60 transition target?
choices: Glacier Instant Retrieval, because it returns data in milliseconds and suits data read about once a quarter
Glacier Flexible Retrieval, because it is cheaper than Instant Retrieval and quarterly reads are rare
One Zone-IA, because it is cheaper than Standard-IA and still returns data in milliseconds
Glacier Deep Archive, because it is the cheapest class and the photos are rarely read
questions.why: Glacier Instant Retrieval suits data read about once a quarter and still returns it in milliseconds, while One Zone-IA fails the zone-loss requirement and the other two Glacier classes take minutes to hours to restore.

questions.prompt: A research lab moves a large dataset straight into S3 Glacier Deep Archive. Forty days later, the lab realises the data is no longer needed and deletes it. For how many days of storage is the lab billed for that object?
choices: 40 days, because billing stops when the object is deleted
90 days, the minimum storage duration for the Glacier classes
30 days, the minimum storage duration for the cheaper classes
180 days, the minimum storage duration for Deep Archive
questions.why: Deep Archive has a 180-day minimum storage duration, so deleting the object after 40 days still incurs a charge for 180 days.

questions.prompt: A team is launching a new analytics product that stores large report files in S3. They have no idea yet which files customers will open often and which will sit untouched. They want the storage cost to adjust automatically without writing lifecycle rules. Which storage class fits best?
choices: S3 Standard, because it has no retrieval fee no matter how often files are read
One Zone-IA, because it is the cheapest class that still returns data quickly
S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which watches each object's access and moves it between tiers for a small per-object monitoring fee
Glacier Flexible Retrieval, because it is cheap and the files might rarely be read
questions.why: Intelligent-Tiering moves each object between tiers based on its observed access, which makes it a good fit when access patterns are unknown.

questions.prompt: A continuous-integration system writes thousands of 20 KB temporary build files to S3 every day and deletes each one after 5 days. To save money, an engineer adds a lifecycle transition that moves the files to Standard-IA after 1 day. What is the most likely result?
choices: Costs rise, because each file is billed as at least 128 KB and for at least 30 days
Nothing changes, because lifecycle transitions cannot apply to files younger than 30 days
Costs fall, because Standard-IA has a lower storage price than Standard
Builds stall for hours, because Standard-IA must be restored before files can be read
questions.why: Standard-IA has a 128 KB minimum billable size and a 30-day minimum storage duration, so tiny, short-lived files end up costing more than they would have in Standard.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use S3 storage classes and a lifecycle rule to cut the bill for data that cools over time, and name at least one tradeoff or trap that could make the cheaper tier cost more or break a requirement.
lessons.modelAnswer: S3 lets each object sit in a storage class. Standard is priced for frequent reads. The IA classes are cheaper to store but charge per retrieval.
