The Glacier classes are cheapest for archives. Instant Retrieval is fast, Flexible takes minutes to hours, and Deep Archive can take 12 hours or more. A lifecycle rule automates the moves: transition objects to IA after about 30 days, to Glacier or Deep Archive once nobody needs them quickly, and expire them when the retention period ends. The tradeoff is that cheaper storage means slower or paid access. The traps are minimum storage durations (30, 90 or 180 days) and the 128 KB minimum size in IA, so short-lived or tiny objects can cost more after a move. Archiving data an app reads live would also break its latency requirement. If access patterns are unknown, Intelligent-Tiering handles the moves for a small per-object fee.
rubricPoints: Defines a storage class as a tier trading lower storage price for retrieval cost or delay.
Places Standard, IA, and the Glacier archival tiers in order of cost and access speed.
Explains that a lifecycle rule transitions objects by age and can expire them.
Names minimum storage duration or minimum object size as a cost trap.
Notes that archive restore delays can violate an access or latency requirement.
Mentions Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access patterns.

suggested.rationale: Pricing a lifecycle schedule against minimum-duration and retrieval charges in fictional credits makes the learner feel when tiering saves money and when it backfires.

lessons.plain: Sizing storage means choosing how much disk space to reserve for a system. Some cloud storage works like a hotel room: you pay for the whole room you booked, even if you only use one bed. Other storage works like a taxi meter: you pay only for what you actually use. For the hotel-room kind, reserving too much wastes money every month, and reserving too little means the system can stop when the space runs out. Storage auto scaling is a setting that adds space automatically before you run out. You start small, keep a safety margin, and stop guessing at future growth.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database has 500 GB of disk reserved but only 120 GB in use, and it grows about 5 GB a month. If you pay for every reserved gigabyte, what would you change, and what would you be worried about after making that change?
lessons.teach:
Provisioned storage is space you allocate up front and pay for by size, whether it is full or empty. Amazon EBS (block volumes, which act like virtual hard drives attached to a server) and Amazon RDS (a managed relational database) both work this way. Elastic storage grows and shrinks with your data, and you pay only for the bytes you store. Amazon S3 (object storage) and Amazon EFS (a shared network file system) work this way, and so does Amazon Aurora's database storage. Sizing only matters for provisioned storage.

Right-sizing means allocating roughly what you need now plus sensible headroom (spare room for growth), instead of a large guess. Storage auto scaling, offered by RDS, watches free space. When free space falls low, roughly under 10 percent for several minutes, it increases the allocation on its own. It works up to a maximum threshold that you set. It waits several hours between increases, which is called a cooldown. It never shrinks storage.

Here is a worked example, using an illustrative price of 10 cents per GB-month. An RDS database has 500 GB allocated and 120 GB used, growing 5 GB a month, so it costs $50 a month. Step 1: allocate 150 GB, which is current use plus about six months of growth. Step 2: turn on storage auto scaling with a 400 GB maximum. Step 3: the cost becomes $15 a month, saving $35. Step 4: when usage nears 150 GB, auto scaling adds space with no human action.

Auto scaling is effectively required when growth is unpredictable, when nobody watches the disk, or when running out would stop the business. Without it, a full RDS disk blocks writes and the application fails.

A common mistake is over-allocating "to be safe" and planning to shrink later. RDS storage and EBS volumes can grow but cannot be shrunk in place. Reducing size means migrating the data to a new, smaller volume or database. The cooldown also means a sudden burst larger than your headroom can still fill the disk, so keep a real margin.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain runs its appointment system on an Amazon RDS database, a managed relational database where you pay for allocated storage. It has 1,000 GB allocated, 200 GB actually used, and the data grows about 10 GB a month. Use an illustrative price of 10 cents per GB-month. Step 1: the current cost is 1,000 GB x $0.10 = $100 a month. Step 2: right-size by moving the data to a new RDS database with 260 GB allocated, which is current use plus about six months of growth. A new database is needed because RDS storage cannot be shrunk in place. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: turn on storage auto scaling with a 700 GB maximum, so space is added automatically as usage approaches 260 GB. Which statement correctly completes Step 3?
choices: The cost becomes $20 a month, saving $80, because after right-sizing you pay only for the 200 GB actually used.
The cost becomes $70 a month, saving $30, because you are billed for the 700 GB auto scaling maximum.
The cost becomes $26 a month, saving $74, because you pay for the 260 GB allocated.
The cost becomes $6 a month, saving $94, because you pay only for the 60 GB of headroom.
questions.why: RDS is provisioned storage, billed on the allocated 260 GB (260 x $0.10 = $26), not on used bytes or the auto scaling maximum, so the saving is $100 - $26 = $74.

questions.prompt: A startup is reviewing its storage bill. Which of these is billed by the size you allocate up front, even if most of that space is empty?
choices: An Amazon EFS file system (a shared network file system)
An Amazon EBS volume (a block volume that acts like a virtual hard drive)
Amazon Aurora's database storage
An Amazon S3 bucket (object storage)
questions.why: EBS is provisioned storage, billed by allocated size, while S3, EFS and Aurora storage are elastic and bill only for the bytes stored.

questions.prompt: A delivery company keeps its order data in Amazon RDS. Growth is unpredictable because promotions cause sudden jumps. Nobody watches the database overnight, and if the disk fills, customers cannot place orders. The team wants to keep costs low. What is the best storage approach?
choices: Turn on storage auto scaling and rely on it to shrink storage again when the promotions end.
Right-size to current use plus a real margin, and turn on storage auto scaling with a sensible maximum threshold.
Allocate five times current usage to be safe, then shrink the volume in place after the busy season.
Allocate exactly the current usage with no headroom, and add space by hand when someone notices.
questions.why: Unpredictable growth, no one watching, and a business-stopping failure make auto scaling effectively required, and right-sizing with margin keeps cost down. RDS storage cannot shrink in place, and auto scaling never shrinks it.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site's RDS database has storage auto scaling enabled with a 2 TB maximum. One hour ago, auto scaling raised the allocation to 300 GB. Usage is now 285 GB, and a 40 GB bulk import is about to start. What is the main risk?
choices: None, because auto scaling adds space instantly whenever free space runs low, as long as usage stays under the 2 TB maximum.
Auto scaling is still in its cooldown period of several hours, so the disk can fill before more space is added, which blocks writes and makes the application fail.
The import will cause RDS to shrink other data to make room, which risks losing records.
RDS will switch the database to elastic storage for the import, which raises the monthly bill.
questions.why: Auto scaling waits several hours between increases. A burst larger than the remaining headroom (15 GB here) can fill the disk during the cooldown, and a full RDS disk blocks writes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you would shrink an over-provisioned database's storage and turn on storage auto scaling, and name at least one limit or risk of relying on auto scaling.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our database is on provisioned storage, so we pay for every gigabyte we allocate, not what we use. We have 500 GB allocated but only 120 GB used, so most of the bill is empty space. I'd allocate around 150 GB, which covers today's data plus a few months of growth, and enable storage auto scaling with a maximum cap. That way it grows on its own when free space gets low, and we don't pay for space we might need someday. The limits: auto scaling only grows storage and never shrinks it, and it waits hours between increases. A sudden burst bigger than our headroom could still fill the disk, and a full disk blocks writes. We also can't shrink an existing volume in place, so getting smaller means migrating. Storage like S3 or Aurora doesn't need any of this, because it already bills by use.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes provisioned storage (pay for allocation) from elastic storage (pay for usage).
Right-sizing means current need plus reasonable headroom, not a large guess.
Storage auto scaling grows allocation automatically up to a set maximum when free space runs low.
It is needed when growth is unpredictable or running out would cause an outage.
Names a limit: no automatic shrinking, a cooldown between increases, or burst growth outrunning headroom.
Running out of space blocks writes and breaks the application.

suggested.rationale: A cost model lets the learner compare over-provisioned, right-sized, and auto-scaled storage bills against growth and see the trade-off directly.

lessons.plain: A block storage volume is a virtual hard drive you attach to a cloud server; on AWS this is Amazon EBS (Elastic Block Store). You choose what kind of drive sits behind it. SSD (solid-state) types are fast at small, scattered reads and writes but cost more per gigabyte. HDD (spinning-disk) types are slow at scattered access but cheap, and they move large files in long, continuous streams well. Think of a sports car versus a freight train: the car is better for quick errands around town, while the train is cheaper for hauling bulk cargo in a straight line. Matching the drive to how the data is used is the saving.
lessons.guessPrompt: A nightly job reads 4 TB of log files from start to finish in big chunks, and nobody needs the results quickly. Would you pay for fast SSD storage or cheaper spinning-disk storage, and why?
lessons.teach:
EBS volume types fall into two families. SSD-backed volumes are priced for IOPS (input/output operations per second, meaning how many small reads or writes the volume can handle). gp3 is general-purpose SSD: it includes a baseline of 3,000 IOPS, and you can buy more IOPS or throughput separately. gp3 usually costs about 20% less per GB than the older gp2. io1 and io2 are provisioned-IOPS SSD for databases that need very high, steady IOPS, and you pay extra for every IOPS you reserve. HDD-backed volumes are priced for throughput (megabytes moved per second in long sequential runs). st1 (throughput optimized HDD) suits big sequential work such as log processing, data warehouses and streaming. sc1 (cold HDD) is the cheapest per GB and fits large data that is rarely read. HDD types cannot be boot volumes, they have a large minimum size, and their throughput grows with volume size.

The pricing works this way because spinning disks are slow to jump between scattered spots but steady once streaming, while flash handles random access well and costs more per GB.

Worked example: a log-analytics fleet uses 2 TB io1 volumes with 10,000 provisioned IOPS. First, check the access pattern: the jobs read whole files in large sequential chunks. Second, ask what limits the job: throughput matters here, IOPS does not. Third, change the volumes to st1. The IOPS charge goes away and the per-GB rate drops to well under half. If the data is only read monthly, sc1 cuts the cost further. The tradeoff is that random reads become very slow.

A common mistake is moving a transactional database or a boot disk to HDD to save money. Databases do many small random reads and writes, so latency jumps sharply. A running system then shows slow queries and timeouts, and the bill drops while the application stops meeting its requirements. A safe default is gp3, with HDD reserved for large, sequential, throughput-bound data.

questions.prompt: A video studio keeps a 12 TB archive of finished footage on gp2 SSD volumes. Editors restore a whole project about twice a year by copying large files from start to end. Step 1: the access pattern is large sequential reads, and the data is very rarely touched. Step 2: nothing about the job needs fast random access or a high IOPS rate, and it is not a boot volume. Step 3: ______. Step 4: accept the tradeoff that any random read from this volume will be very slow. Which choice best fills Step 3?
choices: Keep gp2, because HDD volumes cannot store files larger than 1 TB
Move the data to gp3 and buy extra IOPS so restores finish faster
Move the data to io2 so the reserved IOPS keep restore times steady
Move the data to sc1 (cold HDD), the cheapest per GB for large, rarely read data
questions.why: Large, sequential data read only a couple of times a year is exactly what cold HDD (sc1) is built and priced for, so it gives the lowest per-GB cost without breaking the requirement.

questions.prompt: In EBS pricing, what are HDD-backed volume types such as st1 and sc1 mainly priced and built for?
choices: Throughput: moving many megabytes per second in long sequential runs
Reserved IOPS that you pay for whether or not you use them
Low latency for boot disks and operating system files
IOPS: handling a high number of small random reads and writes
questions.why: Spinning disks are slow to jump between scattered spots but steady once streaming, so HDD types are priced for sequential throughput, not IOPS.

questions.prompt: A small company runs a web server whose 100 GB boot volume is io1 with 8,000 provisioned IOPS, but monitoring shows it rarely goes above 1,000 IOPS. They want to cut cost without risk. What is the best change?
choices: Change it to sc1, since cold HDD is the cheapest volume type
Change it to gp3, which includes 3,000 baseline IOPS at no extra IOPS charge
Keep io1 but raise provisioned IOPS so it never runs short
Change it to st1, since throughput HDD is cheaper per GB
questions.why: HDD types cannot be boot volumes, and gp3's included 3,000 IOPS covers this load while removing io1's charge for every reserved IOPS.

questions.prompt: To lower the bill, a team moves the volume holding their order-processing database from gp3 to st1. The database does many small random reads and writes. What is the most likely result in the running system?
choices: Nothing changes, because st1 automatically adds IOPS as the volume grows
The bill drops, but latency jumps and users see slow queries and timeouts
Queries get faster because st1 has higher throughput than gp3
The move fails because st1 has no minimum size and cannot hold a database
questions.why: HDD handles scattered small reads and writes poorly, so a transactional database on st1 costs less but stops meeting its performance requirements.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between an SSD volume (gp3 or io2) and an HDD volume (st1 or sc1) to cut storage cost, and name what you give up when you choose HDD.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the access pattern. If the workload does lots of small, random reads and writes, as a database, a boot disk or a busy app server does, it needs IOPS, so I use SSD. gp3 is the cheap default, and I only pay for io1 or io2 when I need very high, steady IOPS. If the workload streams big files in order, as log processing, ETL or a data warehouse does, throughput is what matters, and st1 gives it at a much lower per-GB price. If that data is large and rarely touched, sc1 is cheaper still. HDD has real costs, though. Random I/O is slow and latency is high, it can't be a boot volume, it has a large minimum size, and its throughput depends on volume size. So HDD only saves money when the workload is sequential and can tolerate the latency.
rubricPoints: Matches small random I/O to SSD and large sequential I/O to HDD.
Names gp3 as the cost-effective SSD default and io1/io2 as the option that charges for provisioned IOPS.
Distinguishes st1 for frequently streamed data from sc1 for rarely accessed data.
States that HDD cannot be a boot volume and gives poor random-access latency.
Notes that moving a database to HDD saves money but breaks performance requirements.

suggested.rationale: Pricing the same workload on io1, gp3, st1 and sc1 in fictional credits, then checking whether each choice still meets the performance requirement, trains exactly this tradeoff.

lessons.plain: Moving data into the cloud is like moving house: you can hire movers once, set up a mailbox that keeps receiving deliveries, or keep a small storeroom at home that is linked to a big warehouse. AWS offers a managed tool for each. AWS DataSync is the movers: it copies files across the network, once or on a schedule. AWS Transfer Family is the mailbox: an always-on file-upload door for partners. AWS Storage Gateway is the linked storeroom: an on-site appliance that keeps data in the cloud while local apps keep using it. The cheapest choice is whichever matches how the data actually moves.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company has a 40 TB file share in its own data center. It wants to copy everything to cloud storage once and then switch the old server off. Would you pay for a service that charges for every hour it is switched on, or one that charges only for each gigabyte copied? Why?
lessons.teach:
Three managed services move data into AWS storage, and each charges differently. AWS DataSync is an online transfer service. You install a small agent (a piece of software that reads your local storage) near the source, and it copies files from a file share or object store into Amazon S3 (object storage), Amazon EFS (a managed network file system) or Amazon FSx (managed file servers). You pay per gigabyte copied. It only copies changed files on later runs and checks data integrity, so it suits one-time migrations and scheduled syncs. AWS Transfer Family is a managed endpoint for file-transfer protocols such as SFTP (secure file transfer), FTPS and FTP, storing what arrives in S3 or EFS. You pay per hour for each enabled protocol endpoint, even when idle, plus per gigabyte. It suits outside partners who must keep using their existing SFTP scripts. AWS Storage Gateway is a hybrid appliance: a virtual machine or hardware box on site that presents a file share, a block disk (volumes) or virtual tapes to local servers, keeps a local cache of recent data, and stores the data in AWS. You pay for the gateway's storage and requests, and it suits ongoing on-site access, not one-off moves.

Why this ranking works: the cheapest service charges for the shape of your traffic. Worked example: 40 TB on an NFS share, move once, then decommission. Step one, the move is a single event, so an hourly endpoint is waste. Step two, no local apps need ongoing access, so a gateway and its cache are unnecessary. Step three, DataSync copies 40 TB, a final incremental run catches late changes, and billing stops once the copying stops. DataSync wins.

A common mistake is deploying Storage Gateway for a one-time migration, or leaving a Transfer Family endpoint enabled after partners stop uploading. In a running system both keep adding charges every month for capacity nobody uses.

questions.prompt: A design studio's branch office has 8 TB of drawing files. Staff there will keep opening and saving these files every day, and the studio wants the files stored durably in AWS while local reads stay quick. No outside partners send files in. The cheapest fit is worked out like this. Step one: access is ongoing, not a single move, so a service that only copies data from one place to another does not meet the need for continuing local access. Step two: [missing]. Step three: AWS Storage Gateway, an on-site virtual machine or hardware box, presents a file share to local servers, keeps a cache of recent files on site and stores the data in AWS. Storage Gateway wins. Which statement correctly fills step two?
choices: No partners need to keep using SFTP scripts, so a Transfer Family endpoint, billed per hour even when idle, would be paying for capacity nobody uses.
Transfer Family is cheapest for daily office access because its per-hour fee covers unlimited local reads of cached files.
Storage Gateway charges per gigabyte copied only, so it costs nothing once the files have been stored in AWS.
DataSync's agent keeps a local cache of recent files, so it can serve daily reads and should be used here instead.
questions.why: Transfer Family suits outside partners using file-transfer protocols and bills each enabled endpoint hourly even when idle, so with no partners it is pure waste.

questions.prompt: Which of these three services keeps charging for each enabled protocol endpoint every hour, even when nothing is being uploaded?
choices: AWS Transfer Family
AWS DataSync, because its agent stays installed near the source
None of them; all three charge only per gigabyte moved
AWS Storage Gateway, because it keeps a local cache
questions.why: Transfer Family bills per hour for each enabled endpoint, such as SFTP, whether or not files arrive, plus a per-gigabyte charge.

questions.prompt: A shipping company receives nightly manifest files from 30 carrier partners. The partners run existing SFTP (secure file transfer) scripts and will not rewrite them. The company wants the files to land in Amazon S3 with the least change for the partners. Which service fits?
choices: AWS DataSync, with an agent installed at each partner site
An S3 bucket alone, with partners asked to change their upload method
AWS Storage Gateway, presenting virtual tapes at each partner
AWS Transfer Family, providing a managed SFTP endpoint that stores files in S3
questions.why: Transfer Family offers a managed SFTP endpoint, so partners keep their existing scripts and the files are stored in S3.

questions.prompt: A retailer reviewing its bill sees a steady monthly charge for an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint. The supplier who used it stopped uploading four months ago, and no one else uses it. Which change cuts this cost without breaking any current requirement?
choices: Replace the endpoint with an AWS Storage Gateway appliance on site
Run an AWS DataSync task each month to keep the endpoint's data in sync
Keep the endpoint but compress future uploads to lower the per-gigabyte charge
Disable or remove the unused Transfer Family endpoint
questions.why: The endpoint is billed hourly even when idle, so removing it stops charges for capacity nobody uses, and no one depends on it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between DataSync, Transfer Family and Storage Gateway on cost, and name one tradeoff or limit of the cheapest-looking option.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by asking how the data moves. If it's a one-time migration or a scheduled copy from our own file shares, DataSync is usually cheapest because we pay per gigabyte copied and nothing when it's idle; it also only re-copies changed files. If outside partners push files over SFTP and can't change their tools, Transfer Family fits, but its endpoint bills every hour it's enabled, so we should switch off protocols nobody uses. If local servers must keep reading and writing a share while the data lives in AWS, Storage Gateway is the right fit, with a local cache for speed. The tradeoff: DataSync is cheap but doesn't give on-site apps ongoing local access, and it still needs enough network bandwidth to finish the copy in time. Picking a gateway or endpoint for a one-off move keeps costing money long after it's done.
rubricPoints: DataSync is per-gigabyte and suits one-time migration or scheduled sync.
Transfer Family provides SFTP/FTPS/FTP endpoints for partners and bills hourly per enabled endpoint.
Storage Gateway is a hybrid appliance for ongoing on-site access with a local cache.
Match the service to the traffic pattern rather than picking by features alone.
Names a limit, such as idle endpoint charges or DataSync needing bandwidth and giving no ongoing local access.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reading a scenario's traffic pattern and picking the transfer service whose billing model fits, which exam-style situations exercise best.

lessons.plain: Backups are spare copies kept in case something breaks. Archives are records you must keep for years but almost never open. Choosing one on cost means paying the least while still being able to get the data back as fast as your rules require. Think of a self-storage company. A unit by the front door costs more each month but is quick to reach. A warehouse out of town is cheap per month, but it charges a fee every time you collect something and takes a day to bring it to you. Old tax records belong in the warehouse. Your spare house key does not. The skill is matching each kind of data to the right shelf.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company must keep scanned contracts for ten years, expects to open one perhaps once a year, and is happy to wait a day when it does. Would you pay more per month for storage you can read instantly, or less per month for storage that takes hours to bring back? Why?
lessons.teach:
A backup is a copy kept so you can restore after loss. An archive is data kept for a long time, often for legal reasons, and read rarely. Selecting either on cost means choosing the cheapest storage that still meets two needs. The first is retrieval time: how fast data must come back, which is part of your recovery time objective (RTO), the longest outage you can accept. The second is how often you will read the data.

AWS cold storage trades a low monthly price per gigabyte against slower or pricier reads. Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval is an archive tier of S3, AWS's object store. It gives millisecond reads and cheap storage, but each gigabyte read costs a fee. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval is cheaper to store, and restores take minutes to hours. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the cheapest of all, and restores take up to about 12 hours, or longer for bulk restores. Cold tiers also have a minimum storage duration: you are billed for at least that long even if you delete early. It is 90 days for the first two Glacier tiers and 180 days for Deep Archive.

Other services work the same way. Amazon EBS snapshots are point-in-time copies of a virtual disk. They have an archive tier that is much cheaper for snapshots kept 90 days or more, but restoring one can take a day or more. AWS Backup, a managed service that runs backups for many services from one policy, can move recovery points to cold storage. Tape Gateway, part of AWS Storage Gateway, replaces physical tape libraries: existing backup software writes to virtual tapes, which are archived into Glacier tiers.

Worked example: auditors need seven years of records and give 48 hours' notice. Step one, reads are rare. Step two, a wait of hours is allowed. Step three, seven years is far beyond the 180-day minimum. So Deep Archive fits. If the records had to open instantly, Glacier Instant Retrieval would fit instead.

A common mistake is picking the lowest price per gigabyte and stopping there. Daily backups deleted after 30 days still pay 180 days in Deep Archive. Frequent restores pay retrieval fees that outweigh the savings. In a live incident, a restore that takes 12 hours can blow straight past the RTO.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic chain must keep X-ray images for 10 years. Vets open an old image only a few times a month, but when they do, the pet is on the table and the image must appear within a second. Step one: reads are rare, so a cold tier with a per-gigabyte read fee is affordable. Step two: [missing]. Step three: 10 years is far beyond the 90-day minimum storage duration, so early-deletion charges are not a concern. Conclusion: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval fits. Which statement correctly fills step two?
choices: Retrieval speed does not matter here, because rare reads mean retrieval fees are the only concern.
Images must come back in about a second, which rules out tiers whose restores take minutes to hours.
Every cold tier restores in hours, so the images must stay off cold storage entirely.
A wait of hours is allowed because reads are rare, so Deep Archive's lower price wins.
questions.why: The near-instant retrieval need rules out Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive, and Glacier Instant Retrieval is the cold tier that still gives millisecond reads.

questions.prompt: A small software company takes a database backup every night, keeps each one for 14 days, then deletes it. Restores happen a couple of times a year. An engineer proposes moving these backups to S3 Glacier Deep Archive because it has the lowest price per gigabyte. What is the main cost problem with this plan?
choices: Deep Archive cannot hold database backups, only tape images from Tape Gateway.
Deep Archive charges more per gigabyte to store than Glacier Instant Retrieval does.
Each backup is billed for Deep Archive's 180-day minimum even though it is deleted after 14 days.
Deep Archive bills a per-gigabyte fee every night that a new backup is written.
questions.why: Cold tiers bill a minimum storage duration, so 14-day backups in Deep Archive pay for 180 days each, which can wipe out the low per-gigabyte price.

questions.prompt: A regional broadcaster runs backup software in its own data centre that writes to a physical tape library. It wants to stop buying and handling tapes and store the archive in low-cost cloud storage, without replacing the backup software it already uses. Which option fits best?
choices: Use Tape Gateway so the software writes to virtual tapes archived into Glacier tiers.
Move the data to the EBS snapshot archive tier.
Write the backups directly to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.
Restore all tapes into EBS volumes and delete the library.
questions.why: Tape Gateway lets existing backup software keep writing to tapes, now virtual ones, which are then archived into low-cost Glacier tiers.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps monthly snapshots of a virtual disk (EBS snapshots) for 12 months for compliance. Its rule is that any restore from these snapshots must finish within 4 hours (its recovery time objective, or RTO). Someone suggests moving them to the EBS snapshot archive tier. What does that change trade away?
choices: It raises storage cost for snapshots kept longer than 90 days, but restores become faster.
It lowers storage cost, but snapshots are deleted automatically after 90 days.
It lowers storage cost and keeps restores instant, so nothing is given up.
It lowers storage cost, but a restore can take a day or more, which would break the 4-hour RTO.
questions.why: The snapshot archive tier is much cheaper for long-kept snapshots, but restores can take a day or more, far beyond a 4-hour RTO.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose the cheapest place to keep backups or archives on AWS. Use one example. Name at least one cost or limit that the 'lowest price per gigabyte' option hides.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from two requirements, not the price list. How fast must we get the data back, and how often will we read it? Cold tiers charge less to store but more, or more slowly, to read. Glacier Instant Retrieval reads in milliseconds but charges a retrieval fee. Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours. Deep Archive is the cheapest and can take around 12 hours. For seven-year audit records with two days' notice, Deep Archive wins. For a backup we might need back within the hour, it would break our recovery time objective. The cheapest tier also hides other costs. There are minimum storage durations: 90 days for the Glacier tiers and 180 days for Deep Archive. Short-lived backups get billed for time they never used, and frequent restores rack up retrieval fees. The same trade applies to EBS snapshot archive, AWS Backup cold storage, and Tape Gateway.
rubricPoints: Picks the tier from the required retrieval time and how often the data is read.
States that colder tiers lower storage cost but add retrieval fees or slower restores.
Mentions minimum storage duration charges that apply to early deletion.
Matches a long-retention, rarely read, hours-tolerant case to Deep Archive and an instant-access case to Instant Retrieval.
Notes that a slow restore can break the recovery time objective in a real incident.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests this through requirement-driven scenarios where the learner must weigh storage price against retrieval time, retrieval fees and minimum durations, so reasoning through situations teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Normally, whoever owns a storage bucket pays for everything that happens to it: keeping the files, every request to read them, and every byte sent out. A Requester Pays bucket in Amazon S3 (AWS's object storage service) changes who gets the bill. The owner still pays to store the data, but the person or company downloading it pays for their own requests and the data they pull out. Think of a library that keeps the books on its shelves for free but charges photocopy fees to whoever makes the copies. It suits large shared datasets that many outside parties read heavily.
lessons.guessPrompt: You host a huge public research dataset and partner companies download it constantly, so your bill keeps climbing. If you could make the people downloading the data pay part of the cost, which part of the cost would make sense to hand to them, and which part would you still have to keep paying yourself?
lessons.teach:
A Requester Pays bucket is an Amazon S3 bucket setting that moves request charges and data transfer charges from the bucket owner to the requester. Request charges are the small fees per read or list operation; data transfer charges are the fees for bytes leaving AWS or crossing Regions. The bucket owner keeps paying storage charges, the monthly cost of holding the data.

It works because every request carries an identity. The requester must be an authenticated AWS account (a signed-in identity AWS can bill), and each request must explicitly say it accepts the charges, using a request-payer flag or header. AWS then bills that account instead of the owner. Anonymous, unauthenticated requests are rejected, because there is nobody to bill.

Worked example: a genomics lab stores a 10 TB dataset. Three partner companies each download the full set every month, 30 TB out in total. Before the change, the lab pays storage for 10 TB plus transfer for 30 TB plus all requests. Step one, the lab enables Requester Pays. Step two, each partner updates its download tool to sign requests with its own AWS credentials and set the request-payer flag. Step three, at month end the lab pays only for 10 TB of storage, while each partner's own bill shows its 10 TB of transfer and its requests. The lab's largest cost line has moved to the people creating it.

A common mistake is choosing Requester Pays to shift costs onto anonymous public users, such as visitors to a public website. It cannot do that; unauthenticated access stops working. Another trap: if the requester assumes a role inside the owner's own account, the owner still pays, because the request comes from the owner's account.

In a running system, enabling the setting is a breaking change. Any existing client that does not send the request-payer flag starts receiving access-denied errors, so consumers must be told and updated before the switch.

questions.prompt: A satellite imaging firm keeps 6 TB of imagery in an Amazon S3 bucket. Four research institutes each download the full 6 TB every month, so 24 TB leaves AWS in total. Today the firm pays for storage, all 24 TB of transfer, and every request. Step 1: the firm turns on Requester Pays for the bucket. Step 2: ______. Step 3: at month end, the firm pays only for storing 6 TB. Each institute's own AWS bill shows its 6 TB of transfer and its requests. Which choice correctly fills Step 2?
choices: Each institute assumes a role inside the firm's AWS account and downloads through that role.
The firm makes the bucket publicly readable so the institutes can download without signing in.
Each institute updates its download tool to sign requests with its own AWS account credentials and set the request-payer flag.
The institutes keep their current tools unchanged, and AWS bills them based on where the downloads go.
questions.why: Requester Pays bills the authenticated account that sends the request, and only when that request explicitly accepts the charges with the request-payer flag.

questions.prompt: A media archive turns on Requester Pays for its Amazon S3 bucket. Which charge does the archive, as the bucket owner, still pay?
choices: Data transfer charges for bytes that requesters download out of AWS
No charges at all, because Requester Pays moves every cost to requesters
Request charges for the read and list operations that requesters make
Storage charges, the monthly cost of holding the data in the bucket
questions.why: Requester Pays moves request and data transfer charges to the requester, but the owner keeps paying storage.

questions.prompt: A recipe website serves its photos from an Amazon S3 bucket to anonymous visitors, and the transfer bill is growing. The team proposes enabling Requester Pays so that visitors cover the download cost. What actually happens if they do this?
choices: Each visitor's browser is charged a small fee for each photo it loads.
AWS splits the transfer cost evenly between the website and its visitors.
The photos stop loading, because unauthenticated requests are rejected when there is no account to bill.
The website's transfer costs fall to zero while the photos keep loading normally.
questions.why: Requester Pays needs an authenticated AWS account that accepts the charges, so anonymous public requests are refused rather than billed.

questions.prompt: A logistics company shares an Amazon S3 bucket with a partner. The partner runs nightly jobs that read files from the bucket using its own AWS credentials, but the jobs do not send a request-payer flag. The company enables Requester Pays on Monday without telling the partner. What happens to Monday night's jobs?
choices: They fail with access-denied errors, because their requests do not accept the charges.
They run normally, but the files they download arrive incomplete.
They run normally, and the company keeps paying until the partner opts in.
They run normally, and the partner is billed automatically from that night on.
questions.why: Enabling Requester Pays is a breaking change: any client that does not send the request-payer flag starts getting access-denied errors, so consumers must be told and updated first.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we don't just turn on Requester Pays for every bucket to cut our S3 bill. Explain in your own words what Requester Pays actually shifts, what it does not, and at least one limit that makes it the wrong choice for some buckets.
lessons.modelAnswer: Requester Pays moves only the cost of reading the data, meaning request fees and data transfer out, onto whoever makes the request. We still pay to store every byte, so if our bill is mostly storage, it barely helps. It also only works when the reader is an authenticated AWS account that explicitly accepts the charges on each request. That rules it out for public websites or anonymous downloads, which would simply be denied. It is also a breaking change: existing clients that don't send the request-payer flag start getting access-denied errors, so every consumer has to be updated first. And if someone reads through a role in our own account, we still pay. It fits best when outside organizations with their own AWS accounts download large shared datasets heavily, so the cost follows the people who cause it.
rubricPoints: The owner still pays storage; the requester pays request and data transfer charges.
Requesters must be authenticated AWS accounts, so anonymous or public access does not work.
Each request must explicitly accept the charges, or it is denied.
Enabling it breaks existing clients that do not send the request-payer flag.
Access through a role in the owner's account is still billed to the owner.
It fits large datasets downloaded heavily by external AWS customers.

suggested.rationale: Tracing which account is billed for storage, requests, and transfer before and after enabling Requester Pays is best learned by working through a cost model hands-on.

lessons.plain: An upload strategy is how you send data into cloud storage: one item at a time (individual uploads) or many items grouped together and sent as one larger piece (batch uploads). Storage services usually charge for each request as well as for the space used, so sending a million tiny files can cost far more in requests than in storage. Think of posting letters: mailing a thousand postcards separately costs a thousand stamps, while packing them into one box costs one shipment. Batching saves money and overhead, but the box takes longer to fill, and finding one postcard inside it takes extra work.
lessons.guessPrompt: A fleet of sensors writes ten million tiny readings a day into object storage, one file per reading. The storage space used is small. Where do you think most of the bill comes from, and what could you change to shrink it?
lessons.teach:
An individual upload sends each record as its own object in a single request. A batch upload collects many records into a buffer (a temporary holding area) and writes them as one larger object, or sends several items in one API call. This matters for cost because Amazon S3, AWS's object storage service, bills per request (for example, per thousand PUT requests) on top of per-gigabyte storage. Several other charges are also per object, not per byte. Lifecycle transitions, which move objects to a cheaper tier, are charged per object. Archive tiers add a small fixed metadata overhead to every object. Intelligent-Tiering, which moves objects between tiers automatically, charges a monitoring fee per object. Managed queues such as Amazon SQS charge per request, and one request can carry up to ten messages.

Worked example, using illustrative prices (always check current pricing). Ten million 2 KB readings a day are uploaded individually. That is 10,000,000 PUTs. At about $0.005 per thousand, that is roughly $50 a day, or about $1,500 a month in requests. The 20 GB of data costs well under a dollar to store. Now buffer readings into 5 MB files, for example with Amazon Data Firehose, a managed service that collects streaming records and writes them out in batches. That makes about 4,000 objects a day, roughly two cents in requests. Later tiering and archiving also get cheaper, because there are far fewer objects to move.

The opposite case is large files. A single big file is best sent with multipart upload, which splits it into parts sent in parallel and retries only the parts that fail.

A common mistake is assuming batching is free. It adds latency, because data waits until the buffer fills or a time limit passes. A batched record is also harder to read or delete on its own. And a failed batch must be retried or partly re-sent. Another mistake is leaving failed multipart uploads unfinished. Their parts are still billed as storage until a lifecycle rule aborts them.

questions.prompt:
A delivery company's mobile app sends 50 million small 1 KB location events a day to Amazon S3 (AWS's object storage service). Each event is uploaded individually, as its own object. Use an illustrative price of $0.004 per thousand PUT requests.

Step 1: Individual uploads make 50,000,000 PUTs a day. That is 50,000 thousands, so 50,000 x $0.004 = about $200 a day in request charges.

Step 2: The team switches to batching. A managed buffering service collects events and writes them as 10 MB files. The daily data is 50,000,000 KB, which is about 50 GB, or 50,000 MB.

Step 3: ???

Step 4: That is 5 thousands of PUTs, so 5 x $0.004 = about two cents a day in request charges.

Which statement correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: 50,000 MB divided by 10 MB per file gives about 50,000 objects a day
50,000 MB divided by 10 MB per file gives about 500 objects a day
50,000 MB is written as 1 KB objects, so the PUT count stays at 50,000,000 a day
50,000 MB divided by 10 MB per file gives about 5,000 objects, so about 5,000 PUTs a day
questions.why: Batching writes one object per 10 MB file, so 50,000 MB / 10 MB = about 5,000 objects and 5,000 PUTs, which matches the two-cent cost in Step 4.

questions.prompt: An order-processing service sends 900,000 messages a day to Amazon SQS, a managed message queue that charges per request. Today each message goes in its own request. If the service switches to sending the maximum number of messages allowed in one request, about how many send requests will it make per day?
choices: 9,000, because one request can carry up to one hundred messages
About 180, because messages are grouped into 5 MB batches like files
900,000, because the queue charges per message, not per request
90,000, because one request can carry up to ten messages
questions.why: SQS bills per request and one request can carry up to ten messages, so 900,000 messages need about 90,000 requests.

questions.prompt: A bank's fraud-detection system must react to each card transaction within one second. An engineer proposes buffering transactions into large batch files before writing them, to cut request costs. What is the main thing this change gives up?
choices: Nothing important, because batching only lowers cost and has no trade-offs
Low latency, because each transaction waits until the buffer fills or a time limit passes before it is written
Durability, because batched objects are not stored as safely as individual objects
Storage cost, because larger objects are billed at a higher per-gigabyte rate than small ones
questions.why: Batching holds data in a buffer until it fills or a time limit passes, which adds delay that a one-second requirement may not tolerate.

questions.prompt: A video studio uploads 40 GB raw footage files to Amazon S3 using multipart upload, which splits a large file into parts sent in parallel. Network drops often stop uploads partway, and nobody restarts or cleans them up. The monthly storage bill keeps rising even though the number of finished files is flat. What change best fixes this?
choices: Add a lifecycle rule that aborts incomplete multipart uploads, so their leftover parts stop being billed as storage
Switch to individual single-request uploads for the 40 GB files so no parts are ever created
Batch several 40 GB files together into one larger object before uploading
Turn on Intelligent-Tiering so the unfinished parts move to a cheaper tier automatically
questions.why: Parts of unfinished multipart uploads keep being billed as storage until a lifecycle rule aborts them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why switching from one-object-per-record uploads to batched uploads can cut an S3 bill sharply, and name what the system gives up in exchange.
lessons.modelAnswer: S3 charges for every request and for some per-object actions, not just for the bytes stored. If we write each small record as its own object, we pay a PUT for every record. With millions of tiny records, those request fees can dwarf the storage cost. Every one of those objects also costs extra later, when lifecycle rules move it or archive tiers add per-object overhead. If we buffer records, for example with Firehose, and write a few large files instead, the request count falls by orders of magnitude. Tiering and archiving get cheaper too. The trade-off is freshness: data waits in the buffer before it lands. Reading or deleting a single record means opening a bigger file, and a failed batch has to be retried as a unit. For very large single files we go the other way and use multipart upload, with a lifecycle rule that cleans up incomplete uploads.
rubricPoints: Object storage bills per request and some per-object actions, not only per gigabyte stored.
Many small individual uploads make request and per-object charges the dominant cost.
Batching small records into larger objects, for example with a buffering service, cuts request counts and later tiering costs.
Batching adds latency and makes single-record access and retries harder.
Large files suit multipart upload, and incomplete multipart uploads should be cleaned up by a lifecycle rule.

suggested.rationale: Modelling request counts and per-object charges for individual versus batched uploads in a cost model makes the size of the difference concrete in a way reading alone does not.

lessons.plain: When you rent servers in the cloud, you can pay for them in different ways, much like getting to work. On-Demand is a taxi: pay by the minute, no promises, full price. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans are a yearly transit pass: you promise to use a certain amount for one or three years and get a big discount, but you pay even on days you stay home. Spot Instances are standby seats: very cheap spare capacity, but the provider can take the seat back at short notice. Picking well means matching each part of your workload to the payment style that fits how it behaves.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app runs 4 servers all day, every day, adds 6 more during office hours, and has a nightly report job that can safely restart if stopped. Which part would you pay full price for, which part would you commit to long term, and which part would you run on cheap capacity that might be taken away?
lessons.teach:
A purchasing option is how you pay for the same virtual server (an EC2 instance). The server works the same way under every option. Only the price, the commitment and the risk of losing it change.

On-Demand means paying per second or per hour at full list price, with no commitment. It suits short, spiky or unpredictable usage. Spot Instances are AWS's unused spare capacity sold at a deep discount, often most of the list price off. AWS can reclaim a Spot Instance with about two minutes' warning, called an interruption. Spot suits work that is fault-tolerant: it is stateless or saves checkpoints, and it can stop and resume, such as batch jobs or rendering.

A Reserved Instance (RI) is a one- or three-year commitment to a particular instance configuration in a Region, in exchange for a large discount. Standard RIs give the deepest discount but are rigid. Convertible RIs let you exchange them for a different configuration in return for a smaller discount. A Savings Plan is a commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour for one or three years. A Compute Savings Plan applies across instance families, Regions, and even AWS Fargate and Lambda. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is locked to one instance family in one Region and discounts more. Paying all upfront instead of partial or nothing upfront deepens any commitment discount.

Worked example: 4 servers run all the time, 6 more run only during office hours, and a nightly report job can restart. Step 1: the constant 4 are a steady baseline, so cover them with a Savings Plan or RIs. Step 2: the extra 6 come and go, so leave them On-Demand. Step 3: the restartable nightly job goes on Spot.

A common mistake is putting stateful or must-not-stop work, such as a primary database, on Spot. An interruption then causes an outage or lost data. The opposite mistake is committing to peak capacity, which leaves you paying every hour for servers that sit idle.

questions.prompt: A data analytics startup runs 12 servers around the clock to serve its dashboards. Next year it plans to move these servers to a newer instance family, and to shift part of the work to AWS Lambda (run-on-demand functions that need no server to manage). It also has image-processing jobs that save checkpoints and can resume, plus unpredictable traffic bursts when customers launch campaigns. Worked so far: Step A, the image-processing jobs can stop and resume, so they go on Spot Instances (discounted spare capacity that AWS can reclaim). Step B, the campaign bursts are short and unpredictable, so they stay On-Demand (full price, no commitment). Step C, the missing step: which purchasing option best covers the 12 always-on servers?
choices: A three-year Standard Reserved Instance for the current instance configuration
Spot Instances, because the servers run all the time and Spot gives the deepest discount
A Compute Savings Plan, a fixed hourly spend commitment that also applies across families and Lambda
An EC2 Instance Savings Plan locked to the current instance family in the current Region
questions.why: The baseline is steady enough to commit to, but the planned family change and move to Lambda need the flexibility that only a Compute Savings Plan offers across instance families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda.

questions.prompt: A media company runs video encoding on Spot Instances (AWS's spare capacity sold at a deep discount). What does an interruption mean for these servers?
choices: AWS charges the full list price for any hour in which the server was running
AWS reclaims the server with about two minutes' warning, so the work must be able to stop and resume
AWS moves the server to On-Demand pricing for the rest of the hour without stopping it
AWS pauses the server for two minutes and then resumes it automatically on the same host
questions.why: An interruption is AWS taking back Spot capacity with roughly two minutes' notice, which is why Spot suits fault-tolerant work that saves checkpoints.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm runs one primary database server 24 hours a day on the same instance configuration in one Region. It has no plans to change that configuration for three years and wants the largest possible discount. Which purchasing option fits best?
choices: Spot Instances, because spare capacity is the cheapest way to pay
On-Demand, because a database must never be interrupted
A Convertible Reserved Instance with nothing upfront
A three-year Standard Reserved Instance paid all upfront
questions.why: A fixed, always-on configuration with no planned changes can accept the rigidity of a Standard RI, and a three-year term paid all upfront gives the deepest commitment discount; Spot would risk an outage for a must-not-stop database.

questions.prompt: A logistics company peaks at 50 servers for two days a month but averages about 15 servers the rest of the time. The team buys a one-year Savings Plan (a commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour) sized to cover all 50 servers. What is the most likely result?
choices: The company pays every hour for committed capacity that mostly sits unused
AWS lowers the hourly commitment automatically to match real usage
The extra committed spend is refunded at the end of the year
Peak days run on Spot, so the commitment is used only off-peak
questions.why: Committing to peak capacity means paying the fixed hourly amount all the time, even though most of that capacity is idle outside the short peaks; the better approach is to commit to the steady baseline and leave the peaks On-Demand.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between On-Demand, Spot, Reserved Instances and Savings Plans for a workload, and name what each discount option gives up in exchange for its lower price.
lessons.modelAnswer: All four options buy the same servers. They differ in price, commitment and risk. On-Demand is full price with no commitment, so I use it for unpredictable or short-lived load. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans give big discounts for a one- or three-year commitment. I use them only for the steady baseline I'm sure will keep running. RIs are tied to a configuration, while a Compute Savings Plan is a per-hour spend commitment that follows usage across instance families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda. The tradeoff is that I pay for the commitment even if usage drops, and the more flexible plans discount less. Spot is the cheapest because it's spare capacity AWS can reclaim with about two minutes' notice. I use it only for interruptible work like batch jobs and never for something like a primary database. A typical mix is commitments for the baseline, On-Demand for peaks and Spot for restartable jobs.
rubricPoints: States that the options change price and commitment, not how the server works.
Matches On-Demand to unpredictable or short-term usage at full price.
Matches Reserved Instances or Savings Plans to steady baseline usage over a one- or three-year commitment, and notes you pay even if usage drops.
Distinguishes RIs (tied to a configuration) from Savings Plans (hourly spend commitment, with Compute plans flexible across families and services).
Matches Spot to fault-tolerant, interruptible work, and notes it can be reclaimed with about two minutes' warning.
Warns against Spot for stateful critical work and against committing to peak capacity.

suggested.rationale: A cost model where the learner assigns baseline, peak and batch usage to different purchasing options and sees the bill change makes the tradeoffs concrete.

lessons.plain: Cloud servers come in families and sizes, like delivery vans sold in body styles and lengths. The family is the shape of the machine: balanced, extra processing power, extra memory, extra local disk, or special chips such as graphics processors. The size is how big that shape is, and each step up roughly doubles both resources and price. Choosing for cost means picking the family whose shape matches what your work actually uses, then the smallest size that still handles your busiest hour with some room to spare. Paying for a big van you never fill is the most common cloud waste.
lessons.guessPrompt: A server runs all day at about 20% processor use and uses about a third of its memory. What would you change to pay less, and what would you check before making that change?
lessons.teach:
An EC2 instance type is a virtual server's recipe, written as family, generation, optional attributes, then size. In m7g.xlarge, m is the family, 7 the generation, g means an AWS Graviton (ARM-based) processor, and xlarge the size. The main families are general purpose (M, a balanced ratio of about 4 GiB memory per vCPU), compute optimized (C, about 2 GiB per vCPU), memory optimized (R and X, 8 GiB or more per vCPU), storage optimized (I and D, fast local disks), accelerated (G and P, graphics chips), and burstable (T). A vCPU is one virtual processor thread. A burstable instance runs at a low baseline and earns CPU credits while idle, then spends them to burst. Within a family, each size step doubles vCPU, memory and price.

Right-sizing works because you pay for the whole box whether you use it or not. You match the resource that binds first (CPU, memory, disk or network) to the family's ratio, then shrink the size. Newer generations and Graviton usually cost less for the same work, provided your software runs on ARM. AWS Compute Optimizer reads utilization metrics and suggests a cheaper fit.

Worked example: an app runs on m5.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GiB). Over two weeks, peak CPU is 30% and peak memory is 10 GiB. Step one: 30% of 8 vCPU is about 2.4 vCPU in use. Step two: m5.xlarge has 4 vCPU and 16 GiB, so peak CPU would be about 60% and memory 10 of 16 GiB, which leaves headroom. Step three: the cost roughly halves. Step four: moving to m7g.xlarge, after testing on ARM, cuts cost further.

The common mistake is shrinking on CPU alone. If memory were the binding resource at 28 GiB, a smaller M size would run out of memory, swap to disk, and slow down or crash. A cheaper R size with fewer vCPU would fit that case instead. Another trap is picking T for steady high CPU. Once its credits run out, the server is throttled to baseline, or extra charges pile up in unlimited mode.

questions.prompt: A ticket-reporting service runs on c6i.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 32 GiB). In the C family each size step halves going down: c6i.2xlarge is 8 vCPU and 16 GiB, c6i.xlarge is 4 vCPU and 8 GiB, and c6i.large is 2 vCPU and 4 GiB. Over three weeks, peak CPU was 20% and peak memory was 6 GiB. Step one: 20% of 16 vCPU is about 3.2 vCPU in use at peak. Step two: [missing]. Step three: the bill for this server roughly halves. Step four: after testing the software on ARM, a Graviton version of the same size can cut cost further. Which choice is the missing step two?
choices: Choose c6i.xlarge: 3.2 of 4 vCPU is about 80% at peak and 6 of 8 GiB memory is used, which is the cheapest size that technically fits.
Choose an R size, because a memory-optimized family is always cheaper once memory use falls below half.
Choose c6i.2xlarge: 3.2 of 8 vCPU is about 40% at peak and 6 of 16 GiB memory is used, leaving headroom on both.
Choose c6i.large: 3.2 vCPU in use rounds down to the 2 vCPU this size provides, so it saves the most.
questions.why: c6i.2xlarge fits both peak CPU and peak memory with comfortable headroom, and one size step down roughly halves the price, which matches step three.

questions.prompt: A team is quoted the instance type c7g.large. Reading the name the way an EC2 instance type is built, what does it tell you?
choices: c is the compute-optimized family, 7 is the generation, g means burstable CPU credits, and large is the region.
c is the compute-optimized family (about 2 GiB per vCPU), 7 is the generation, g means a Graviton ARM-based processor, and large is the size.
c is the family, 7 is the number of vCPU, g means it has a graphics chip, and large is the size.
c is the generation, 7 is the family, g means general purpose, and large is the amount of memory in GiB.
questions.why: The name is family, generation, optional attributes, then size, and in this naming the letter g after the generation marks a Graviton (ARM-based) processor.

questions.prompt: An in-memory pricing cache runs on m6i.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 64 GiB). Over a month, peak CPU is 15% and peak memory is 58 GiB. The team wants to cut cost without hurting performance. Which change fits best?
choices: Move to m6i.2xlarge (8 vCPU, 32 GiB), because CPU use is so low that half the size is plenty.
Keep m6i.4xlarge, because there is no instance that offers 64 GiB of memory for less money.
Move to a burstable T instance, because low average CPU is exactly what burstable instances are for.
Move to a memory-optimized R size that still gives about 64 GiB but with fewer vCPU.
questions.why: Memory is the binding resource here, so a cheaper R size with 8 GiB or more per vCPU keeps the 58 GiB working set while dropping the unused vCPU, whereas shrinking the M size would cause swapping.

questions.prompt: A video transcoding worker keeps its CPU at about 85% around the clock. Someone moved it onto a burstable T instance to save money. What is the most likely result?
choices: Once its CPU credits are used up, it is throttled to the low baseline, or in unlimited mode extra charges keep piling up.
The instance automatically switches itself to a compute-optimized C family when credits run low.
It runs faster than a general-purpose instance, because burst mode is always above full speed.
Nothing changes, because burstable instances earn CPU credits faster when the CPU is busy.
questions.why: A burstable instance only earns credits while it sits near idle, so steady high CPU drains them. Then it either slows to baseline or, in unlimited mode, runs up extra cost.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose a cheaper instance family and size for an existing server, and name one risk or tradeoff of downsizing.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I look at real utilization over a representative period, including the busiest hours, for CPU, memory, disk and network. I find which resource runs out first and pick the family whose ratio matches it: C if it is CPU-heavy, R if it is memory-heavy, M if it is balanced, and T only if load is mostly idle with short spikes. Then I pick the smallest size that keeps the peak comfortably under capacity. Each size step down roughly halves the price. I also check whether a newer generation or a Graviton version is cheaper, which needs testing on ARM. The tradeoff is headroom: a tighter fit leaves less buffer for traffic spikes, and judging by CPU alone can starve memory. A burstable instance can be throttled once its credits run out. So I watch metrics after the change and pair it with scaling if load varies.
rubricPoints: Uses measured utilization at peak, not averages or guesses.
Identifies the binding resource and matches the family's CPU-to-memory ratio to it.
Picks the smallest size with headroom, knowing each size step roughly doubles price.
Mentions newer generations or Graviton as a cheaper option, with an ARM compatibility check.
Names a risk such as lost headroom, memory starvation, or burstable credit exhaustion.

suggested.rationale: Right-sizing is best learned by trying family and size swaps against utilization data and watching the cost and headroom change, which the planned cost model engine would let the learner do.

lessons.plain: Scaling to cut spend means paying for compute only while it is doing useful work. Instead of running enough servers for the busiest hour all day, you add servers when demand rises and remove or pause them when it falls. Think of a restaurant that calls in extra staff for the dinner rush and sends them home afterward, rather than paying a full crew all night. EC2 hibernation is the pause button for a single server: it saves the server's memory to disk and stops it, so you stop paying for the server while keeping everything it was working on, ready to resume quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: A team's test servers run 24 hours a day, every day, but engineers only use them about 50 hours a week. Roughly what share of that compute bill could they save by turning the servers off when nobody is using them?
lessons.teach:
An EC2 instance is a rented virtual server billed for the time it runs. Scaling to cut spend means matching the number of running instances to real demand. An Auto Scaling group is a managed set of identical instances that grows (scale out) or shrinks (scale in) between a minimum and maximum you set. A target tracking policy keeps a metric, such as average CPU, near a target by adding or removing instances. Scheduled scaling changes capacity at known times, such as 08:00 on weekdays. Predictive scaling forecasts recurring patterns and adds capacity before they arrive.

This saves money because you stop paying for idle peak capacity. Worked example: a web tier runs 10 instances all the time because peak needs 10. Traffic needs only 2 for 16 hours a day. With a group set to minimum 2, maximum 10, target 50 percent CPU: at night CPU drops, the policy removes instances down to 2; in the morning CPU climbs past 50 percent, it adds instances until average CPU returns near target. Instance-hours fall from 240 a day to roughly 2×16 + 10×8 = 112, a cut of over half.

For work that must pause rather than shrink, stop instances when idle. EC2 hibernation goes further: it writes the contents of memory (RAM) to the instance's root disk (an EBS volume, which must be encrypted and large enough to hold the RAM), then stops. You pay for that disk storage but not for compute. On start, memory is reloaded, so running programs and warmed caches resume without a slow startup. Hibernation only works on supported instance types, has a memory size limit, and must be enabled when the instance is launched.

A common mistake is setting the Auto Scaling minimum equal to peak, which looks safe but removes all savings. Another is forgetting that scaling in too aggressively can leave too little capacity during a sudden surge, slowing users while new instances boot.

questions.prompt: A news company runs its image-resizing tier on 8 EC2 instances (rented virtual servers billed for the time they run) all day, because its busiest period needs 8. Demand actually needs 8 instances for only 6 hours a day and just 3 for the other 18 hours. The team moves the tier into an Auto Scaling group (a managed set of identical instances that grows or shrinks between a minimum and a maximum) with minimum 3, maximum 8, and a target tracking policy (one that adds or removes instances to keep a metric such as average CPU near a target). Step 1: today's usage is 8 x 24 = 192 instance-hours a day. Step 2: when CPU falls in quiet hours, the policy scales in to the minimum of 3, and when CPU rises in the busy period it scales out to 8. Step 3: the new daily usage is ______. Step 4: comparing the two shows the saving comes from no longer paying for idle peak capacity. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: 8 x 24 = 192 instance-hours a day
3 x 24 = 72 instance-hours a day
8 x 18 + 3 x 6 = 162 instance-hours a day
3 x 18 + 8 x 6 = 102 instance-hours a day
questions.why: The group runs 3 instances for the 18 quiet hours and 8 for the 6 busy hours, so 54 + 48 = 102 instance-hours, down from 192.

questions.prompt: A data scientist keeps an EC2 instance (a rented virtual server) with a large in-memory dataset loaded. They want to pause it every night to save money and, in the morning, have their running programs and warmed memory come back without a slow reload. They plan to use EC2 hibernation, which saves the contents of memory (RAM) to disk and then stops the instance. Which statement about this plan is correct?
choices: Hibernation can be switched on at any time on an already running instance, and the instance keeps charging for compute while hibernated.
Hibernation works on every instance type and any memory size, as long as the instance belongs to an Auto Scaling group.
Hibernation needs no disk at all because memory is kept inside the stopped server, so the overnight cost is zero.

Hibernation must be enabled when the instance is launched, and the root EBS volume (its attached disk) must be encrypted and large enough to hold the RAM; while hibernated they pay for that disk but not for compute.
questions.why: Hibernation writes RAM to an encrypted root EBS volume big enough to hold it, must be enabled at launch, works only on supported types with a memory limit, and charges for disk storage but not compute while stopped.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking firm puts its 12-instance web tier into an Auto Scaling group (a managed set of identical instances that grows or shrinks between a minimum and a maximum). Peak demand needs 12 instances, but most of the day only 4 are needed. To feel safe, the team sets the minimum to 12 and the maximum to 12. What is the effect on cost?
choices: Costs fall slightly because a target tracking policy can still remove instances below the minimum.
Costs rise because the group adds a 13th instance whenever CPU passes the target.
There is no saving, because the group can never drop below 12, so they still pay for idle peak capacity all day.
Costs fall by about two thirds because the group now scales in automatically at quiet times.
questions.why: Setting the minimum equal to peak stops the group from ever scaling in, which removes all the savings scaling was meant to give.

questions.prompt: An online shop sets its Auto Scaling group (a managed set of identical instances that grows or shrinks between a minimum and a maximum) to scale in very aggressively, down to a minimum of 1 instance during quiet periods. A flash sale then sends a sudden surge of shoppers. What is the most likely problem?
choices: The single remaining instance automatically hibernates, so the site goes offline until someone restarts it.
The group exceeds its maximum and the bill becomes unlimited.
Too little capacity is running when the surge hits, so shoppers see slow pages while new instances boot.
Nothing changes, because instances added by scaling out are ready instantly with no startup time.
questions.why: Scaling in too far leaves little capacity for a sudden surge, and users are slowed during the time it takes new instances to start.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an Auto Scaling group and EC2 hibernation each cut compute spend, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: We pay for EC2 instances by the time they run, so the cheapest capacity is capacity that is off when unused. An Auto Scaling group keeps a fleet between a minimum and maximum and adds or removes instances to hold a metric like CPU near a target, or follows a schedule we know about. That stops us paying for peak capacity overnight. The tradeoff is that new instances take time to boot, so if we scale in too far a sudden spike can leave users waiting. Hibernation is for single servers we want to pause: it saves memory to an encrypted root disk and stops the instance, so we only pay for storage, and on start the apps resume with their warm state. The limit is that it must be enabled at launch, only works on supported instance types with a memory size cap, and the root volume must be big enough to hold RAM.
rubricPoints: States that EC2 compute is billed while running, so removing idle capacity saves money.
Explains an Auto Scaling group scaling out and in between a minimum and maximum using a policy such as target tracking or a schedule.
Explains hibernation saves RAM to an encrypted EBS root volume and stops compute charges while keeping state.
Names a scaling tradeoff such as boot delay during spikes or a minimum set too high.
Names a hibernation limit such as enabling at launch, supported types, memory cap, or paying for disk storage.

suggested.rationale: Tuning minimums, maximums and targets against a demand curve and seeing the resulting instance-hours is the fastest way to feel how scaling cuts spend and where it hurts.

lessons.plain: Every app needs somewhere to run, and AWS rents you that place in three main ways. Amazon EC2 is a rented virtual server: you pay for every hour it is switched on, busy or idle. AWS Lambda runs a small piece of code only when something triggers it, and you pay just for the moments it is running. AWS Fargate runs containers, which are packaged apps, without you managing the servers underneath, and bills for the time each container runs. Think of renting a car for a month, taking taxis, or using a car-share billed by the hour. Which is cheapest depends on how often you drive.
lessons.guessPrompt: A small report job runs for about one second, a few thousand times a day, and sits idle the rest of the time. Would you rather pay for a server that is on all day, or pay only for the seconds the job actually runs? Why?
lessons.teach:
The cheapest compute choice is the one whose billing model matches the workload's shape: how busy it is, how spiky it is, and how long each piece of work runs.

Amazon EC2 is a virtual server (a rented slice of a physical machine). You pay for the time it is running, whether it is working or idle, so it is cheapest when kept busy around the clock. AWS Lambda is a function service: you upload code, it runs when an event triggers it, and you pay per request plus per unit of memory multiplied by run time. Idle time costs nothing, but each busy second costs more than the same second on EC2, and one run cannot last longer than 15 minutes. AWS Fargate is a serverless container service: a container is an app packaged with everything it needs, and Fargate bills for the processor and memory each running container reserves, per second, with no servers to patch. It sits between the other two: no idle servers to manage, no 15-minute limit, but a container you leave running is billed like a server.

Worked example, in made-up credits. Suppose a small EC2 server costs 1 credit per hour, so 24 credits a day. Lambda costs about 3 times as much per busy second. A job runs 2,000 times a day for 1 second each, about 33 busy minutes. On Lambda that is roughly 0.55 hours × 3 = about 1.7 credits a day, against 24 on EC2. Now traffic grows until the work keeps a server busy all day. Lambda would cost about 24 × 3 = 72 credits, so EC2, or Fargate for a container, becomes cheaper.

A common mistake is assuming serverless is always cheaper. For steady, heavy load the per-second premium wins, and the monthly bill can end up several times higher than a right-sized server. The opposite mistake, a mostly idle EC2 server for spiky traffic, wastes money on unused hours.

questions.prompt: A ticket-scanning service at a concert venue is choosing between an EC2 server and Lambda. In made-up credits, the right-sized EC2 server costs 2 credits per hour, so 48 credits a day because it runs whether busy or idle. Lambda costs about 4 times as much per busy second as that server. Step 1: The scanning function runs 3,600 times a day for 2 seconds each, so it is busy 7,200 seconds, which is 2 hours a day. Step 2: [missing] Step 3: Compare the two. Lambda is far cheaper than 48 credits a day for EC2, because Lambda bills only for busy time and this workload is mostly idle. Which statement correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Lambda cost = 2 busy hours × 4 = about 8 credits a day.
Lambda cost = 48 credits × 4 = about 192 credits a day.
Lambda cost = 2 busy hours × 2 credits × 4 = about 16 credits a day.
Lambda cost = 2 busy hours × 2 credits = about 4 credits a day.
questions.why: Lambda bills only for busy time at the higher rate, so the cost is the 2 busy hours times the server's 2 credits per hour times the 4× premium, which gives 16 credits a day.

questions.prompt: How does AWS Fargate, a serverless container service, charge for the work it runs?
choices: Per hour for a virtual server, whether the server is working or idle.
Nothing while a container is running, only when it receives an event.
Per request, plus memory multiplied by run time, with each run capped at 15 minutes.
Per second, for the processor and memory each running container reserves, with no servers for you to patch.
questions.why: Fargate bills per second for the processor and memory a running container reserves. That is why a container left running is billed much like a server, even though there are no servers to manage.

questions.prompt: A small design agency renders client animations a few times a week. Each render job is packaged as a container and takes about 25 minutes. Between jobs, nothing runs. Which choice fits this workload at the lowest cost?
choices: Lambda, because idle time between jobs costs nothing.
Fargate, with a container left running all day so jobs start instantly.
Fargate, starting a container for each job and stopping it when the job finishes.
An EC2 server kept running around the clock so it is always ready.
questions.why: A 25-minute job breaks Lambda's 15-minute limit, and an always-on server or container would be billed for many idle hours. Running a Fargate container only for each job pays for busy time alone.

questions.prompt: A logistics company moved its order-tracking API from a right-sized EC2 server to Lambda, expecting savings. The API handles a heavy, steady stream of requests all day and night. The monthly compute bill roughly tripled. What best explains this?
choices: Under constant load, Lambda's higher price per busy second outweighs having no idle time, so a busy server is cheaper.
Lambda bills by processor and memory reserved per container, just like a server left running.
Lambda bills for idle time between requests, while EC2 does not.
