Each Lambda run was cut off at 15 minutes, so requests had to be retried.
questions.why: Lambda saves money only when work is spiky or idle. When the work keeps a server busy all day, the per-second premium makes Lambda several times more expensive than a right-sized EC2 server.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between Lambda, EC2 and Fargate for a new workload on cost alone, and name a limit or tradeoff of each choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with the workload's shape. If it is spiky or mostly idle and each piece of work is short, Lambda is usually cheapest because idle time is free. The tradeoff is a higher price per busy second and a 15-minute cap on each run. If the load is steady and heavy, an EC2 server I keep busy is usually cheapest per unit of work. The tradeoff is that I pay for idle hours and I have to patch and scale the servers myself. Fargate fits containerized apps that run longer or continuously when I don't want to manage servers. I pay for the processor and memory each container reserves, so it costs more than a well-used EC2 server but needs less operations work. Utilization is the deciding number.
rubricPoints: States that the cheapest choice depends on how busy and how spiky the workload is.
Explains that Lambda bills only for requests and run time, so idle time is free, but each busy second costs more.
Explains that EC2 bills for running time whether busy or idle, so it wins at steady high utilization.
Describes Fargate as billing per running container's reserved processor and memory, with no servers to manage.
Names at least one limit, such as Lambda's 15-minute run cap or EC2's idle cost and management burden.

suggested.rationale: Pricing the same workload under per-request, per-container and always-on billing in fictional credits shows the learner exactly where the break-even point between Lambda, Fargate and EC2 falls.

lessons.plain: An availability target is a promise about how much of the time a system must be up and usable, usually written as a percentage such as 99.9%. Production is the live system real customers depend on. Non-production covers development, testing and staging copies that only your own team uses. Each extra bit of uptime costs money, so production usually earns a high target and non-production a much lower one. It is like a hospital that keeps backup generators for its operating theatres but not for its staff training room: both matter, but only one would truly hurt people if the lights went out.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your company runs a customer-facing database spread across two data centres so it survives one failing, plus an identical setup for developers to test against. If you had to cut the bill without upsetting customers, which copy would you simplify first, and why?
lessons.teach:
An availability target is the share of time a workload must be working, often stated as a number of nines: 99.9% (three nines) or 99.99% (four nines). An SLA (service level agreement) is the target promised to someone outside the team. An error budget is the downtime the target still allows. A workload class is a group of systems with similar needs: production serves real users, while non-production (dev, test, staging) serves engineers.

Why it matters for cost: higher availability comes from redundancy, meaning duplicate resources that take over when one fails. On AWS that usually means running across several Availability Zones (separate data centres within a Region), for example a Multi-AZ database that keeps a standby copy. Redundancy roughly doubles what you pay for that component, so you buy it only where the target demands it.

Worked example. A 30-day month has 720 hours, or 43,200 minutes. At 99.9%, the error budget is 0.1% of that: 43.2 minutes. At 99.99% it is 4.32 minutes, too short for a human to fix anything by hand, which forces automatic failover and Multi-AZ. Now a dev environment used about 50 hours a week (roughly 217 hours a month). It needs no fixed target at all: run it in one Availability Zone, skip the standby database, use smaller instances, and stop it outside working hours. Stopping alone removes about 70% of its running hours (503 of 720).

A common mistake is cloning production's settings into every environment, so test databases quietly pay for Multi-AZ standbys nobody needs. The reverse mistake also appears in exam answers: trimming production redundancy to save money, which breaks a stated uptime requirement. One nuance: a staging environment used for failover or load testing may need to mirror production briefly, so scale it up for the test, then back down.

In a running system, matching the target to the class means production rides out a data-centre failure while non-production simply waits for someone to restart it, and the bill reflects only the uptime that actually protects users.

questions.prompt: A logistics company promises customers an SLA of 99.95% for its order-tracking API, measured over a 31-day month. The team works out the error budget and what it means for the design. Step 1: 31 days x 24 hours = 744 hours. Step 2: 744 hours x 60 = 44,640 minutes. Step 3: the share of time allowed to be down is 100% - 99.95% = 0.05%. Step 4: (missing). Step 5: the on-call team usually needs about 30 minutes to fix a failed database by hand, which is longer than the budget, so this production workload needs automatic failover across Availability Zones. Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: 0.5% x 44,640 minutes = about 223.2 minutes of allowed downtime
0.05% x 44,640 minutes = about 22.32 minutes of allowed downtime
99.95% x 44,640 minutes = about 44,617.7 minutes of allowed downtime
0.005% x 44,640 minutes = about 2.23 minutes of allowed downtime
questions.why: The error budget is the downtime share (0.05%, which is 0.0005 as a fraction) applied to the month's total minutes, giving about 22.32 minutes, which is shorter than the 30-minute manual fix.

questions.prompt: An online bookshop's monthly bill shows that its QA environment, which only engineers use to test new releases, runs a Multi-AZ database with a standby copy and large instances, all copied from production's settings. Production has a 99.9% uptime requirement for real shoppers. Which change cuts cost without breaking a stated requirement?
choices: Remove the Multi-AZ standby from production and keep it in QA, because QA is where failures are found
Keep QA identical to production at all times, because any difference makes the tests worthless
Run QA in a single Availability Zone without the standby database, use smaller instances, and stop it outside working hours
Move both production and QA to a single Availability Zone so their settings stay consistent
questions.why: QA is non-production with no fixed uptime target, so paying for redundancy there is waste, while production's 99.9% requirement is left untouched.

questions.prompt: A ticketing platform has a stated SLA of 99.99% for its checkout service, which allows about 4.3 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month. To lower the bill, someone proposes turning off the Multi-AZ standby on the checkout database and relying on an engineer to restore it by hand if it fails. What is the main problem with this proposal?
choices: A manual fix cannot fit inside a budget of a few minutes, so removing the standby breaks the stated uptime requirement
It saves almost nothing, because a standby copy costs very little compared with the main database
It is fine for a 99.99% target, since four nines allows several hours of downtime each month
It only matters for non-production workloads, which are the ones that need automatic failover
questions.why: Trimming production redundancy to save money is a classic mistake: a budget of about 4 minutes is too short for a human fix, so the requirement depends on automatic failover across Availability Zones.

questions.prompt: A small analytics team has a test environment that engineers use about 40 hours a week, which is roughly 173 hours in a 720-hour month. It currently runs all 720 hours. If the team schedules it to stop whenever nobody is working, about what share of its running hours does stopping remove?
choices: About 76%, because 547 of the 720 hours are no longer run
About 50%, because stopping overnight halves every day
About 40%, because the environment is used 40 hours a week
About 24%, because 173 of the 720 hours are no longer run
questions.why: Stopped hours are 720 - 173 = 547, and 547 / 720 is about 76% of the running hours removed; 173 hours is the time it still runs, not the time saved.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why production and non-production environments should have different availability targets, using numbers for the downtime each target allows, and name one risk or tradeoff of lowering the target for non-production.
lessons.modelAnswer: An availability target says how much downtime a workload can tolerate. Production serves real customers, so it often needs something like 99.99%, which allows only about 4.3 minutes of downtime a month. That is too short for manual fixes, so we pay for redundancy: Multi-AZ databases and instances spread across Availability Zones, roughly doubling those costs. Dev and test only serve us, so 99.9% (about 43 minutes a month) or no formal target is fine. There we run in one zone, drop standby databases, use smaller instances and stop everything outside working hours, which cuts around 70% of running hours. The tradeoff is that non-production no longer behaves exactly like production, so failover bugs or zone-failure behaviour can go untested. When we need that, we temporarily build a production-like staging copy for the test, then scale it back down.
rubricPoints: Defines an availability target as allowed uptime or downtime, expressed in nines.
Converts at least one target into concrete downtime per month.
Links higher availability to redundancy such as Multi-AZ, which raises cost.
Says production justifies the high target while non-production can run single-AZ, smaller and scheduled off.
Names a tradeoff, such as non-production no longer testing failover like production.
Warns against weakening production redundancy just to save money.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is reading a scenario's stated requirements and spotting which environment is over-paying for uptime it does not need, which an exam-style situation to reason through trains best.

lessons.plain: Most cloud computing happens in huge data centers far from you. Hybrid and edge options bring cloud-style servers closer: into your own building, into a nearby city, inside a mobile phone network, or onto a rugged box you can carry to a remote site. AWS Outposts is the main hybrid one. AWS installs and maintains a rack of its own hardware in your data center, and you use it the same way as the cloud. Think of it like a bank putting a cash machine inside your office. It is the same bank with the same card, but nearer. You pay for that convenience, so use it only when distance or data rules force it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A hospital wants to use the same cloud servers and tools its developers already know, but a law says patient scans may never leave the hospital building. Where would you put the computers that process those scans, and what do you think that choice costs compared with using the normal cloud?
lessons.teach:
Hybrid compute means running cloud-managed servers outside an AWS Region. A Region is the large group of data centers where most AWS services live. Edge compute means placing compute physically close to where data is created or where users are. AWS offers four main options.

AWS Outposts is a rack, or a smaller server, of AWS hardware installed in your own building. You run EC2 virtual servers, EBS block storage and some other services on it with the same tools as in the cloud, and AWS owns and maintains the hardware. You pay through a multi-year commitment for a fixed amount of capacity.

AWS Local Zones are small AWS-run sites in big cities that extend a Region. Nearby users get very low latency (latency is the round-trip delay). You pay as you go, usually a little more than in the Region.

AWS Wavelength places compute inside a mobile carrier's 5G network, for apps running on phones and connected devices.

The AWS Snow Family, for example Snowball Edge, is a set of rugged portable devices with compute and storage, for sites with poor or no network, like ships or field camps.

These options work because latency and data-location laws are physical. Moving compute to the data avoids slow trips and keeps regulated data in place, while you keep one set of tools.

Worked example: a factory must analyse camera images within 10 ms, and images may not leave the site. Step 1: the Region is 40 ms away, which fails. Step 2: a Local Zone is closer but off-site, which fails. Step 3: Snowball Edge works offline but suits temporary or disconnected jobs, not steady round-the-clock production. Step 4: Outposts is on-site, fast, and uses familiar tooling, so it wins, with a 3-year commitment accepted.

Common mistake: choosing Outposts to save money or to serve users spread across a country. Its capacity is fixed and prepaid, sized for peak, and it cannot burst. If the requirement is only low latency for city users, a Local Zone is cheaper and elastic.

In a running system, an Outpost still depends on its link to the parent Region for management. If that link fails, running instances continue, but changes and new launches become difficult, so plan spare capacity and redundant links.

questions.prompt: A video post-production studio in a large city has editors who need under 8 ms of delay to remote editing machines. Demand swings widely: busy for film deadlines, quiet for weeks in between. No law requires the footage to stay in the studio's own building. Step 1: the nearest Region is 30 ms away, so it fails the latency need. Step 2: AWS Outposts would be fast, but its capacity is fixed, prepaid over several years and sized for peak, so it cannot burst for deadlines and would sit idle in quiet weeks. That is a poor cost fit. Step 3: ??? Step 4: Snowball Edge is not needed, because the studio has a good network and runs ongoing work. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Use a Local Zone: an AWS-run site in the city that extends the Region, gives low latency, and is pay as you go, so capacity can grow and shrink with deadlines.
Stay in the Region and accept 30 ms, because no edge option can serve users who are not in the same building.
Use AWS Wavelength, because it puts compute inside a 5G carrier network, which gives the lowest delay for any office user in a city.
Use Outposts anyway, because keeping the hardware in-house is always the cheapest option over a multi-year term.
questions.why: A Local Zone gives city users low latency with elastic, pay-as-you-go capacity, which fits a varying workload with no on-site data rule.

questions.prompt: A polar research team spends five months at a remote camp with no network connection. They need to run analysis on sensor data at the camp and bring the data back afterwards. Which option fits best?
choices: AWS Outposts, because AWS installs and maintains a rack of its hardware in your own location
AWS Snow Family, such as Snowball Edge, because it is a rugged portable device with compute and storage for disconnected sites
AWS Wavelength, because it runs compute inside a mobile carrier's network
A Local Zone, because it places AWS compute close to users for low latency
questions.why: Snow Family devices are built for temporary jobs at sites with poor or no network, which is exactly this camp.

questions.prompt: A bank runs payment checks on an AWS Outpost in its own data center. The network link between the Outpost and its parent Region goes down for several hours. What is the most likely effect?
choices: All instances on the Outpost stop at once, because every request is processed in the Region
The Outpost automatically moves its workloads to a nearby Local Zone
Nothing changes, because an Outpost is fully independent of any Region
Running instances keep working, but making changes and launching new instances becomes difficult
questions.why: An Outpost relies on its Region link for management, so existing instances run on while changes and new launches suffer, which is why spare capacity and redundant links are planned.

questions.prompt: An online retailer proposes buying AWS Outposts racks to lower its compute bill and to serve shoppers spread across the whole country. Why is this a poor choice?
choices: Outposts capacity is fixed, prepaid and sized for peak, so it cannot burst, and it sits in one building rather than near users nationwide
Outposts is billed only per second of use, so costs are unpredictable
Outposts requires a 5G mobile network to reach users
Outposts cannot run EC2 virtual servers, only block storage
questions.why: Outposts is a multi-year commitment for fixed capacity in one location, so it neither saves money on varying demand nor brings compute close to users spread across a country.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would choose AWS Outposts over a Local Zone, Wavelength, Snow Family or just the normal Region, and name what Outposts costs you or gives up.
lessons.modelAnswer: Outposts is AWS hardware that AWS installs and manages inside our own data center, so we can run EC2 and EBS with the same tools as in the cloud. I would pick it only when the data must stay on our premises or needs very low latency to on-site systems. If the need is just low latency for users in one city, a Local Zone is cheaper and pay-as-you-go. For mobile 5G apps I would use Wavelength. For a disconnected or temporary site, a Snowball Edge device fits better. Otherwise the plain Region is the cheapest and most elastic choice. Outposts gives up elasticity: we commit to fixed capacity for years and must size it for peak. It also still relies on a network link to its parent Region for management, so we need redundant connectivity.
rubricPoints: Defines Outposts as AWS-managed hardware running in the customer's own facility with the same APIs.
Names the trigger for Outposts: data residency or very low latency to on-premises systems.
Distinguishes Local Zones (city users), Wavelength (5G mobile) and Snow Family (disconnected or remote sites).
States the cost tradeoff: a multi-year commitment to fixed capacity that cannot burst.
Notes the dependency on the link to the parent Region for management.

suggested.rationale: Exam questions present a scenario with latency, residency and connectivity constraints, and the skill is reasoning to the cheapest option that still meets them, which no current mission or planned engine exercises directly.

lessons.plain: A database is where an application stores data so it can find it again. Databases come in different shapes, each built for a certain job, and you pay for capacity in different ways. A serverless database grows and shrinks on its own and bills you for what you actually use, instead of renting a fixed-size machine around the clock. Purpose-built engines are specialists. A time-series database is built for streams of timestamped readings. A columnar database is built for big reports over millions of rows. Picking a database is like picking a vehicle: a delivery van, a sports car, or a bus each cost least only for the job they were built for.
lessons.guessPrompt: An internal admin tool is used for about two hours each weekday and sits idle the rest of the time. Would you rather pay for a database server that runs 24 hours a day, or for one that bills by actual use? Why?
lessons.teach:
Matching the database to the job has two parts: the pricing model and the engine type.

The pricing model first. Provisioned capacity means you choose a fixed size, such as a database instance on Amazon RDS (managed relational databases) or Amazon Aurora (AWS's cloud-built relational engine). You pay every hour whether the database is busy or not. Serverless means the service adds and removes capacity to follow demand and bills by use. Aurora Serverless v2 does this for relational data. Amazon DynamoDB, a managed key-value store that looks items up by a key, offers an on-demand mode that charges per request. Serverless wins when traffic is spiky or idle. Steady, heavy traffic usually costs less on provisioned capacity, especially with reserved pricing.

The engine type second. A relational database stores data as rows and is good at many small transactions. A time-series database, such as Amazon Timestream, stores timestamped measurements. It keeps recent data in fast memory and moves older data to cheaper storage automatically. A columnar database, such as the Amazon Redshift data warehouse, stores each column together. A report that averages one column reads only that column, not every full row, so it scans far less data.

Worked example: a logistics firm has 5,000 trucks, and each sends its position every 10 seconds. That is 500 writes per second, every second, always timestamped, so it belongs in a time-series store, where older readings age into cheap storage. The finance team wants monthly reports across a year of trips. That means scanning a few columns over billions of rows, which is a job for a columnar warehouse. The dispatch admin app is busy only during office hours, so serverless relational fits, because it shrinks to a small minimum overnight.

A common mistake is running heavy analytics on the production relational database. Teams then oversize the instance just to survive report queries, and they pay for that size all day while the reports also slow down live transactions.

questions.prompt: A regional weather service runs 2,000 stations, and each station reports temperature, humidity and wind every 60 seconds. Step 1: that is about 33 timestamped writes per second, all day, every day, so the readings go in a time-series database such as Amazon Timestream, where older readings move to cheaper storage automatically. Step 2: the climate team wants quarterly reports that average temperature and rainfall across five years of readings. Step 3: the staff rota app is used only on weekday mornings, so serverless relational (Aurora Serverless v2) fits, because it shrinks to a small minimum when nobody is using it. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Put the history in DynamoDB on-demand, because report queries arrive in bursts and per-request billing follows them.
Run the reports on the rota app's relational database and size it up so the report queries finish in time.
Keep the reports in the time-series store, because every reading carries a timestamp and that alone decides the engine.
Load the history into a columnar warehouse such as Amazon Redshift, because averaging a few columns over many rows reads only those columns.
questions.why: The reports scan a few columns across a huge number of rows, and a columnar warehouse reads only the columns a query needs, so it scans far less data than reading every full row.

questions.prompt: An online payments company runs an order-processing database that handles heavy, steady traffic around the clock, with no quiet periods. Which pricing model is most likely to cost the least?
choices: Aurora Serverless v2, because serverless always bills less than a fixed size
Provisioned capacity sized for the busiest hour, then switched off at night
DynamoDB on-demand, because charging per request is cheapest at high volume
Provisioned capacity with reserved pricing, because the load is steady and heavy
questions.why: Serverless pays off when traffic is spiky or idle. A database that is busy all the time gets full use of a fixed size, and reserved pricing lowers that hourly cost further.

questions.prompt: A retailer runs sales dashboards directly on its production Amazon RDS relational database. To keep the dashboards from timing out, the team moved to a much larger instance. What is the main cost and performance problem with this setup?
choices: Relational databases cannot store sales data, so the dashboards return incomplete results.
They pay for the large instance every hour, even when no reports run, and the reports still slow down live transactions.
RDS turns into a serverless service once it passes a certain size, so its capacity becomes unpredictable.
The larger instance switches to per-request billing, so the bill rises with every dashboard query.
questions.why: A provisioned instance is billed every hour whether it is busy or not, so oversizing it for occasional reports wastes money, and heavy analytics also competes with live transactions on the same database.

questions.prompt: An insurance company has a claims table with 40 columns and 2 billion rows. An analyst runs a query that averages only the claim_amount column. Why does a columnar database such as Amazon Redshift handle this more cheaply than a row-based relational database?
choices: It adds and removes capacity to follow demand, so it bills only for the seconds the query runs.
It keeps recent rows in fast memory and moves older rows to cheaper storage automatically.
It stores each column together, so it reads only claim_amount instead of all 40 columns in every row.
It looks each row up by a key, so it fetches 2 billion rows faster than a full table scan.
questions.why: Because a columnar database stores each column together, a query on one column reads only that column's data, so it scans far less than reading every full row.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a serverless and a provisioned database, and when a time-series or columnar engine would be cheaper than a general relational one. Name one case where serverless would cost more.
lessons.modelAnswer: I look at two things: the traffic shape and the query shape. For traffic, if load is spiky, unpredictable or idle for long stretches, serverless options like Aurora Serverless v2 or DynamoDB on-demand are cheaper because they bill by use and shrink when quiet. If load is steady and high all day, serverless costs more per unit of work, so a provisioned instance with reserved pricing wins. For queries, a relational row store is great for small transactions. Streams of timestamped sensor readings fit a time-series engine like Timestream, which moves older data to cheaper storage automatically. Big reports over a few columns fit a columnar warehouse like Redshift, which reads only those columns. The tradeoff is more services to run. And forcing analytics onto the production database usually means paying for an oversized instance all day.
rubricPoints: Serverless bills by use and suits spiky or idle workloads.
Steady heavy load is usually cheaper on provisioned capacity with reserved pricing.
A time-series engine suits timestamped streams and tiers old data to cheaper storage.
A columnar warehouse reads only the columns a report needs, which cuts scan cost for analytics.
Running analytics on the transactional database forces oversizing and slows live traffic.
Using purpose-built engines means more services to operate.

suggested.rationale: This objective is tested as scenario reasoning, where the learner matches traffic shape and query shape to a pricing model and engine, so working through exam-style situations builds the skill best.

lessons.plain: A backup policy answers three questions: how often you take a copy of your data, how long you keep each copy, and where the old copies live. It is like saving drafts of an important document. Saving every minute means you never lose much work, but your folder fills with thousands of drafts. A sensible person keeps recent drafts close, keeps one per day for a month, keeps one per month for the year, and moves the oldest to a cheap, slow drawer. On AWS the drafts are snapshots, and the folder is billed by the gigabyte each month.
lessons.guessPrompt: A database volume needs a copy at least every 4 hours. If you keep every one of those copies for a full year, roughly how many copies would you be paying to store, and does that sound necessary?
lessons.teach:
A snapshot is a point-in-time copy of a disk or database. On AWS, a block-storage (EBS) snapshot is incremental: the first one copies every used block, and each later one stores only the blocks that changed since the last. A retention policy says how long each snapshot is kept before deletion. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the most data, measured in time, the business can afford to lose. AWS Backup is a managed service that runs these schedules and deletes expired copies for you.

Frequency is set by the RPO: a 4-hour RPO needs a snapshot at least every 4 hours. Cost is driven mostly by retention, because each restore point you keep holds on to changed blocks that newer snapshots no longer need.

Worked example: a 500 GB volume, 4-hour RPO, and a rule to keep monthly copies for one year. Keeping every 4-hourly snapshot for a year means 6 per day times 365, about 2,190 restore points. A tiered policy instead keeps 4-hourly copies for 2 days (12), dailies for 30 days (30), and monthlies for 12 months (12): 54 restore points, same RPO, same yearly coverage. The monthlies can then move to an archive tier, which costs far less per gigabyte but stores each copy in full rather than incrementally, bills a minimum storage period, and takes hours to restore. So archive suits rarely-touched compliance copies, not recent ones.

Common mistake: snapshotting far more often than the RPO requires, or keeping everything forever because nobody set an expiry. Another is assuming deleting the first snapshot frees the full 500 GB; blocks still needed by later snapshots are kept. In a running system, unmanaged retention shows up as a storage bill that grows every month with no added protection, while too little frequency means a restore loses more data than the business agreed to.

questions.prompt: A clinic runs a 200 GB block-storage volume for patient scheduling. Its recovery point objective (RPO, the most data, measured in time, it can afford to lose) is 6 hours, and an auditor requires monthly copies kept for 2 years. Keeping every 6-hourly snapshot for 2 years would mean 4 per day times 730 days, about 2,920 restore points. The architect designs a tiered retention policy instead. Step 1: keep 6-hourly snapshots for 3 days, which is ___ restore points. Step 2: keep daily snapshots for 14 days, which is 14 restore points. Step 3: keep monthly snapshots for 24 months, which is 24 restore points. Step 4: add the tiers for the total, which still meets the 6-hour RPO and the 2-year audit rule. What number belongs in Step 1?
choices: 18 restore points, because there are 6 hours in each interval and 3 days
12 restore points, because 4 snapshots per day times 3 days is 12
3 restore points, one for each day kept
72 restore points, one for each hour in 3 days
questions.why: A 6-hour interval gives 24 / 6 = 4 snapshots per day, and 4 per day for 3 days is 12 restore points.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing company says it can lose at most 1 hour of order data if its database disk fails. That limit is its recovery point objective (RPO). Which snapshot schedule meets this requirement?
choices: One snapshot at least every hour
One snapshot per day, kept for 30 days
One snapshot every 2 hours, moved straight to an archive tier
One snapshot every 4 hours, with every copy kept for 5 years
questions.why: The RPO sets the snapshot frequency, so a 1-hour RPO needs a snapshot at least every hour, and keeping copies longer does not make up for gaps between them.

questions.prompt: A team has an 800 GB block-storage (EBS) volume with a chain of incremental snapshots, where each one stores only the blocks that changed since the one before it. To save money, they delete the oldest snapshot in the chain. What happens to storage?
choices: All 800 GB is freed, because the first snapshot held a full copy
Only blocks no longer needed by any later snapshot are freed, so the saving may be much less than 800 GB
The later snapshots become unusable, because they depended on the first one
Nothing can be freed until every snapshot in the chain is deleted
questions.why: Blocks that later snapshots still need are kept when an earlier snapshot is deleted, so the later snapshots still restore correctly and only the blocks nobody needs anymore are freed.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm keeps snapshots of its warehouse database. The firm can move some copies to an archive tier. That tier costs much less per gigabyte, but it stores each copy in full rather than incrementally, it bills a minimum storage period, and restores take hours. Which copies are the best fit for the archive tier?
choices: Every snapshot as soon as it is taken, so that all storage is billed at the lowest rate
Monthly compliance copies from 9 months ago that are kept only in case of an audit
Hourly snapshots from the last 2 days that operators use to undo mistakes
Daily snapshots from the past week that are often restored into test environments
questions.why: Archive suits old copies that are rarely restored, because recent copies are restored often and quickly and would pay for full copies, minimum storage periods and slow restores.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set snapshot frequency and retention for a production database to cut backup cost, and name what the cheaper choices give up.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start from the RPO: if we can lose at most 4 hours of data, we snapshot every 4 hours, not every 15 minutes, because extra frequency buys protection nobody asked for. Then I tier retention. Recent restore points are kept short, maybe two days, because they matter only for recent mistakes. Dailies stay for a month, and monthlies for a year if compliance needs them. That cuts thousands of restore points to a few dozen. I let a managed tool like AWS Backup expire copies automatically so nothing lingers. The oldest monthlies can go to an archive tier, which is much cheaper per gigabyte. The trade-offs: fewer kept copies means fewer points to roll back to; archived copies are stored in full, have a minimum billing period, and take hours to restore, so they are useless for a fast recovery.
rubricPoints: Snapshot frequency is set by the RPO, not by habit.
Retention, not frequency, is the main driver of snapshot storage cost.
A tiered schedule (short recent, longer daily, monthly) keeps coverage with far fewer restore points.
Automatic expiry, for example through AWS Backup, prevents copies piling up forever.
Archive tiers are cheaper per GB but store full copies, have minimum periods, and restore slowly.
Fewer retained copies means fewer points in time you can recover to.

suggested.rationale: A disaster-recovery planner would let the learner set RPO, snapshot frequency and retention tiers and see restore points and cost change, which is the exact trade-off this objective tests.

lessons.plain: Moving a database means two separate jobs. First you move its shape, called the schema: the tables, columns, data types and stored code that define how data is organized. Then you move the data itself. If the old and new databases use the same engine, the shape usually carries over unchanged. If they use different engines, the shape must be translated first, like converting a house's wiring before plugging in foreign appliances. AWS offers a managed copying service that moves data and keeps it in sync while the old system stays live. A separate conversion tool translates the schema between engines.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company wants to move a busy database to a different database engine without stopping its online store for a whole weekend. What do you think must happen besides copying the rows, and how could the store keep taking orders during the move?
lessons.teach:
A database migration moves a schema and its data from a source database to a target database. The schema is the structure: tables, column data types, indexes, views and stored procedures, which are programs saved inside the database. A homogeneous migration keeps the same engine, for example MySQL to MySQL. A heterogeneous migration changes engine, for example Oracle to PostgreSQL.

AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) is a managed replication service. You run a replication instance, which is a server DMS manages for you. You define a source endpoint and a target endpoint, which are the connection details for each database. A task then performs a full load, copying all existing rows. It can also run change data capture (CDC), which reads the source's change log and replays new inserts, updates and deletes on the target. Because CDC keeps the target in step, the application keeps running until a short cutover, when you point it at the new database. DMS copies data, not complex schema logic. For a heterogeneous move, the AWS Schema Conversion Tool (SCT), or the schema conversion feature inside DMS, translates the schema. It flags objects that need manual rewriting.

Worked example: a licensed commercial database moves to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL to drop license fees. Step one, the conversion tool translates the schema and reports two stored procedures it cannot convert, which engineers rewrite. Step two, the schema is applied to Aurora. Step three, a DMS task runs a full load, then CDC. Step four, once lag is near zero, writes stop briefly and the application is repointed. Step five, the replication instance is deleted.

A common mistake is assuming DMS alone handles a heterogeneous schema. Stored procedures then fail on the target. Another mistake is leaving the replication instance running after cutover. It bills by the hour, so the migration keeps costing money. For homogeneous moves, the engine's own native dump or replication tools are often simpler and cheaper.

questions.prompt:
A city library service is moving its 300 GB Oracle catalogue database to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, a managed PostgreSQL database. The catalogue website must stay online for borrowers during the move. Here is the plan, with one step missing.

Step 1: The schema conversion feature in DMS translates the tables, views and stored procedures (programs saved inside the database). It flags one view that it cannot translate, and an engineer rewrites that view by hand.
Step 2: The converted schema is applied to the RDS for PostgreSQL database.
Step 3: A DMS task copies all 300 GB of existing rows to the target (the full load).
Step 4: ____
Step 5: When the target is only seconds behind the source, writes are paused for a few minutes and the catalogue website is repointed to RDS.
Step 6: The DMS replication instance is deleted.

What belongs in Step 4?
choices: Take the catalogue website offline until the whole migration is finished, so that no new rows appear on the source.
Repeat the full load of all 300 GB every night until cutover day, so the target eventually catches up with the source.
Keep the DMS task running with change data capture (CDC), which reads Oracle's change log and replays new inserts, updates and deletes on RDS.
Run the stored procedures through DMS a second time so it can convert any schema logic that the first conversion step missed.
questions.why: CDC replays ongoing changes from the source's change log, which keeps the target in step while the website stays online until the short cutover in Step 5.

questions.prompt: Which of these moves is a heterogeneous migration, meaning one that changes the database engine?
choices: MySQL running on a virtual server moved to Amazon RDS for MySQL
PostgreSQL in one AWS Region moved to PostgreSQL in another Region
Oracle in an on-premises data centre moved to Oracle on Amazon RDS
Microsoft SQL Server in a data centre moved to Amazon Aurora MySQL
questions.why: Only SQL Server to Aurora MySQL changes the engine. The other three keep the same engine and change only the location, so they are homogeneous.

questions.prompt: An insurance company moves a Microsoft SQL Server database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The team creates a DMS source endpoint, a target endpoint and a task that runs a full load followed by CDC. They use no other tool. All the rows arrive correctly, but the application's calls to its stored procedures fail on Aurora. What is the most likely cause?
choices: CDC replays only inserts, so stored procedures that update or delete rows cannot run on the target until a second full load has completed.
Stored procedures can move only in a homogeneous migration, so the company has to stay on SQL Server and cannot move to Aurora.

DMS copies data, not complex schema logic. For an engine change, the schema should have been translated first with the Schema Conversion Tool or the DMS schema conversion feature, and any flagged objects rewritten by hand.
The replication instance was deleted too early, so the stored procedures were left only partly copied to the target.
questions.why: In a heterogeneous move, DMS alone does not translate schema logic such as stored procedures; a schema conversion tool must do that and flag objects that need manual rewriting.

questions.prompt: A media startup finished moving its database to Amazon Aurora three weeks ago. The application has used Aurora ever since, and the old source database is switched off. However, the monthly bill still shows an hourly charge for AWS DMS. What is the most likely reason, and what should the team do?
choices: CDC must keep running permanently after cutover to keep Aurora consistent, so the charge is expected and should be left as it is.
The source and target endpoints bill by the hour on their own, so the team should rerun the full load to close them.
The Schema Conversion Tool keeps billing until every flagged object has been rewritten, so the team should finish rewriting the stored procedures.
The DMS replication instance, the server DMS manages for the task, was left running after cutover. It bills by the hour, so the team should delete it.
questions.why: A replication instance bills by the hour until it is deleted. Once cutover is complete it is no longer needed, so leaving it running wastes money.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would move a production database from one engine to another with minimal downtime, which AWS tools do which part, and one limit or cost tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: There are two jobs: converting the schema and moving the data. Because we're changing engines, I'd first run the Schema Conversion Tool, or DMS's built-in schema conversion. It translates tables and data types and reports anything it can't convert, usually stored procedures, which we rewrite by hand. Then DMS moves the data. A replication instance does a full load of existing rows, then change data capture replays ongoing changes from the source's log, so the app keeps running. When lag is near zero, we pause writes briefly and repoint the app. That's the only downtime. The limit is that DMS doesn't translate complex database code, so the manual rewrite effort is real. On cost, the replication instance bills hourly, so we delete it right after cutover. If the engine stayed the same, native dump or replication tools might be cheaper.
rubricPoints: Separates schema conversion from data movement.
Names SCT or DMS schema conversion for heterogeneous schema translation and DMS for data.
Explains full load plus change data capture enabling a short cutover.
Notes that complex code like stored procedures may need manual rewriting.
Mentions a cost point such as deleting the replication instance or using native tools for same-engine moves.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between DMS, schema conversion and native tools is an exam-style judgment best practiced by reasoning through migration scenarios, and no current mission or planned engine performs it.

lessons.plain: A NAT gateway is a managed service that lets servers in a private part of your network reach the internet, for example to download updates, while the internet cannot start a connection back to them. Each one lives in a single Availability Zone (one data-center location in a region), and you pay for every hour it runs plus every gigabyte it handles. Think of it as a building's mailroom. One mailroom for the whole campus is cheaper, but staff walk across campus to use it, and if that building closes nobody can send mail. One mailroom per building costs more but is closer and keeps working.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your private servers are spread across three Availability Zones and all send internet traffic through a single NAT gateway in Zone A. What happens to the servers in Zones B and C if Zone A goes down, and what might they be paying extra for even on a normal day?
lessons.teach:
A NAT gateway (network address translation gateway) is a managed device that rewrites the private addresses of outbound traffic so servers in a private subnet, a network segment with no direct internet route, can reach the internet without being reachable from it. Each private subnet has a route table, a list of rules for where traffic goes; its default route points at a NAT gateway. A NAT gateway lives in one Availability Zone (AZ), an isolated data-center location inside a region. It is redundant within its own AZ, not across AZs.

You pay three things: an hourly charge per gateway, a per-gigabyte processing charge, and a cross-AZ data transfer charge when traffic leaves one AZ for another.

Worked example with illustrative numbers, not real prices: three AZs, gateway hourly cost about 32 credits a month each, cross-AZ transfer 0.02 credits per GB. Option one, a shared gateway in AZ A: 32 credits of hourly charge. AZs B and C each send 1,000 GB through it, so 2,000 GB crosses AZs, adding 40 credits. Total 72. Option two, one gateway per AZ, each AZ's route table pointing at its local gateway: 96 credits of hourly charge, zero cross-AZ transfer. Per-GB processing is the same in both options. At this traffic the shared design is cheaper; triple the traffic and cross-AZ charges reach 120 credits, so per-AZ wins on cost too.

The common mistake is assuming one NAT gateway is highly available across the region. It is not: if AZ A fails, private servers in B and C lose outbound internet, so a production system with a resilience requirement breaks even though its own servers are healthy.

The rule of thumb: one shared gateway suits non-production or low-traffic workloads that can tolerate an outage; one per AZ suits production workloads needing AZ-level resilience or moving heavy outbound traffic.

questions.prompt:
A media startup runs private servers in four Availability Zones (AZs), numbered 1 to 4. Illustrative numbers, not real prices: each NAT gateway (the managed device that lets private servers reach the internet without being reachable from it) costs 40 credits a month in hourly charges. Cross-AZ data transfer costs 0.01 credits per GB. Each AZ sends 2,000 GB of outbound traffic a month.

Option one is a single shared gateway in AZ 1. Step 1: the hourly charge is 40 credits. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the total is 100 credits.

Option two is one gateway per AZ, with each AZ's route table pointing at its local gateway. Step 1: the hourly charge is 4 × 40 = 160 credits. Step 2: there is no cross-AZ transfer. Step 3: the total is 160 credits.

Per-GB processing is the same in both options, so the shared design is cheaper at this traffic level. What is the missing Step 2 for option one?
choices: 2,000 GB crosses AZs, adding 20 credits
6,000 GB crosses AZs, adding 60 credits
Nothing is added, because all the traffic stays inside one region
8,000 GB crosses AZs, adding 80 credits
questions.why: Only the traffic from AZs 2, 3 and 4 has to travel to the gateway in AZ 1, so 3 × 2,000 = 6,000 GB crosses AZs, and at 0.01 credits per GB that adds 60 credits; AZ 1's own traffic never leaves its AZ.

questions.prompt: A retailer's production checkout service runs on private servers in three Availability Zones: X, Y and Z. To save money, all three private subnets have their default route pointing at a single NAT gateway in AZ X. A power failure takes AZ X offline. What happens to the healthy servers in AZs Y and Z?
choices: They automatically switch to a standby copy of the gateway in another AZ, because a NAT gateway is redundant across the region
They are unaffected, because a NAT gateway only handles inbound traffic from the internet
They keep running, but they lose outbound internet access, because their only NAT gateway was in AZ X
They lose all traffic, including traffic inside their own AZ, because the whole region shuts down
questions.why: A NAT gateway is redundant only within its own AZ, so when AZ X fails, servers elsewhere whose route tables point at it lose outbound internet even though the servers themselves are healthy.

questions.prompt: A university research lab runs a small test environment across two Availability Zones. It sends very little outbound internet traffic, and the team says a few hours without outbound internet during an AZ outage would be acceptable. Which NAT gateway design best fits these requirements at the lowest cost?
choices: One NAT gateway per AZ, because cross-AZ transfer charges always outweigh the hourly charge
No NAT gateway, with the servers kept in private subnets that have no route to the internet
One NAT gateway per AZ, because any multi-AZ environment needs AZ-level resilience
One shared NAT gateway in a single AZ, used by both AZs' private subnets
questions.why: Low traffic keeps cross-AZ charges small, and the workload can tolerate an outage, so paying the hourly charge for only one gateway is the cheapest design that still meets the requirements.

questions.prompt: An insurance firm uses two Availability Zones, A and B, with one shared NAT gateway in AZ A. Illustrative numbers, not real prices: each gateway costs 30 credits a month in hourly charges, and cross-AZ transfer costs 0.02 credits per GB. Per-GB processing is identical in both designs. Roughly how much monthly outbound traffic from AZ B makes adding a second gateway in AZ B break even on cost?
choices: About 1,500 GB, because the extra 30 credits for one more gateway equals 0.02 × 1,500 GB of avoided cross-AZ charges
Never, because adding a second gateway always increases the total cost
At any traffic level, because a per-AZ design also removes the per-GB processing charge
About 3,000 GB, because the full 60 credits for two gateways must be covered by cross-AZ savings
questions.why: Moving to per-AZ adds only one extra gateway (30 credits) and removes cross-AZ transfer, so the designs cost the same when 0.02 × GB = 30, which is 1,500 GB.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate whether we should run one NAT gateway for the whole VPC or one per Availability Zone, including what each choice costs and what it gives up.
lessons.modelAnswer: A NAT gateway lets our private servers make outbound internet connections, and each gateway sits in one Availability Zone. We pay per gateway per hour, per gigabyte processed, and extra whenever traffic crosses from one AZ to another. One shared gateway minimizes the hourly charge, but every server in the other AZs sends its traffic across zones, which adds a transfer charge, and if the gateway's AZ fails, servers in healthy AZs lose internet access. One gateway per AZ, with each AZ's route table pointing at its local gateway, costs more in hourly charges but removes cross-AZ transfer and keeps each zone independent. So for dev or test with light traffic, I'd share one and accept the outage risk. For production with a resilience requirement, or heavy outbound traffic where cross-AZ charges outweigh the extra gateways, I'd run one per AZ.
rubricPoints: States that a NAT gateway gives private subnets outbound-only internet access and lives in a single Availability Zone.
Names the cost components: hourly per gateway, per-GB processing, and cross-AZ data transfer.
Explains that a shared gateway saves hourly cost but adds cross-AZ transfer charges for other zones.
Explains that a shared gateway is a single point of failure for outbound access if its AZ fails.
Matches the choice to the requirement: shared for non-production or low traffic, per-AZ for production resilience or heavy traffic.

suggested.rationale: Comparing shared versus per-AZ gateway totals as traffic changes is best learned by adjusting a cost model in fictional credits and watching where the break-even point falls.

lessons.plain: Inside a cloud provider, moving data costs money depending on where it travels. Traffic that stays inside one data center building is usually free, crossing to another building in the same city costs a little, crossing to another region costs more, and passing through a paid middleman adds a fee per gigabyte. Cost-aware routing means choosing paths that avoid unnecessary crossings and middlemen. Think of shipping parcels: a hand-delivery down the corridor is free, a courier across town costs something, and paying a forwarding depot to relabel every parcel adds a charge on top. You pick the cheapest route that still delivers safely.
lessons.guessPrompt: Servers in a private network download several terabytes a month from cloud object storage, and today that traffic goes out through a paid address-translation device that charges for every gigabyte it handles. What might you change so the bill drops but the servers still never touch the public internet?
lessons.teach:
Data transfer cost is what AWS charges per gigabyte to move data. Its size depends on the path. An Availability Zone (AZ) is an isolated data center group inside a Region, which is a geographic area. Traffic over private addresses within one AZ is generally free; traffic between AZs is charged in each direction; traffic between Regions is charged at a higher rate.

A VPC (Virtual Private Cloud) is your private virtual network. A NAT gateway lets private servers reach outside services and charges per gigabyte it processes. A VPC endpoint is a private doorway from your VPC to an AWS service. Gateway endpoints, available for S3 (object storage) and DynamoDB (a key-value database), have no charge at all. Interface endpoints, built on AWS PrivateLink, cost an hourly fee plus a per-gigabyte fee, usually lower than NAT processing.

To connect VPCs to each other, VPC peering is a direct private link between two VPCs with no hourly fee; you pay only normal cross-AZ or cross-Region transfer. Peering is not transitive, so if A peers with B and B with C, A still cannot reach C, and many VPCs need many links. AWS Transit Gateway is a central hub router: every VPC attaches once, routing is simple at scale, but you pay per attachment per hour plus a per-gigabyte processing fee.

Worked example: private servers pull 10 TB a month from S3 through a NAT gateway. Step one, every gigabyte is billed as NAT processing. Step two, add an S3 gateway endpoint and a route-table entry pointing S3 traffic to it. Step three, traffic now bypasses the NAT, so that processing charge disappears, and the endpoint itself costs nothing.

Common mistake: putting two or three high-volume VPCs on Transit Gateway when peering would do, paying hub processing on every gigabyte. Another is spreading chatty services across AZs without need, so cross-AZ charges grow quietly. Each saving gives something up: keeping traffic in one AZ reduces resilience, and peering becomes hard to manage as VPC count grows.

questions.prompt:
A media company runs two VPCs in the same Region, with their servers in different Availability Zones. Every month 8 TB moves between them through AWS Transit Gateway, the central hub router. Nothing else is attached to the hub, and no more VPCs are planned.

Step one: each gigabyte is billed as Transit Gateway processing, and each of the two attachments is also billed per hour.

Step two: (missing)

Step three: the hub processing and attachment fees are gone. The only charge left is normal cross-AZ transfer, because the servers still sit in different AZs.

Which action is the missing step two?
choices: Replace the Transit Gateway with an interface endpoint in each VPC, so the traffic uses PrivateLink pricing instead.
Add a gateway endpoint in each VPC and point the route tables at it, so traffic between the VPCs moves for free.
Attach a third VPC to the Transit Gateway so the hourly fee is shared across more attachments.
Create a VPC peering connection between the two VPCs and update both route tables to send traffic over it, then detach them from the hub.
questions.why: VPC peering is a direct private link with no hourly fee, so moving the two VPCs onto peering removes the hub fees and leaves only normal transfer charges.

questions.prompt: A retailer has three VPCs. Ledger is peered with Orders, and Orders is peered with Inventory. There is no Transit Gateway. Can a server in Ledger reach a server in Inventory over these links?
choices: No. Peering is not transitive, so Ledger needs its own peering link to Inventory or a hub such as Transit Gateway.
No, because VPC peering only works between VPCs in different Regions.
Yes, but only if Ledger and Inventory are in the same Availability Zone.
Yes. Traffic passes through Orders automatically, because both links are in the same Region.
questions.why: Peering is not transitive, so a VPC cannot use one peered VPC as a stepping stone to reach another.

questions.prompt: An analytics app runs on private servers and reads about 6 TB a month from DynamoDB, a key-value database. Today that traffic goes out through a NAT gateway, which charges for every gigabyte it processes. Which change cuts this cost the most without exposing the servers publicly?
choices: Add an interface endpoint for DynamoDB, which has an hourly fee and a per-gigabyte fee.
Attach the VPC to Transit Gateway so the DynamoDB traffic goes through the hub.
Add a DynamoDB gateway endpoint and a route-table entry that points DynamoDB traffic to it.
Peer the VPC with a VPC that already has its own route to DynamoDB.
questions.why: A gateway endpoint for DynamoDB has no charge, and traffic sent to it skips the NAT gateway's per-gigabyte processing fee.

questions.prompt: A payments team notices that two very chatty services sit in different Availability Zones, and the cross-AZ transfer charges keep growing. They move both services into a single AZ. What do they give up in exchange for the lower bill?
choices: The ability to reach S3 through a gateway endpoint.
Resilience, because a failure of that one AZ now takes down both services.
Private addressing, because traffic inside one AZ has to use public IPs.
Nothing, because traffic inside one AZ is free and has no downside.
questions.why: Keeping traffic in one AZ removes the cross-AZ charges, but it also removes protection against the failure of that AZ.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would reduce data transfer charges in an architecture with private servers using S3, several VPCs that talk to each other, and services spread across AZs, and name one tradeoff each choice brings.
lessons.modelAnswer: First, private servers reaching S3 or DynamoDB through a NAT gateway pay NAT processing per gigabyte, so I would add a gateway endpoint, which is free and keeps traffic private. For other AWS services, an interface endpoint has an hourly and per-gigabyte fee but is usually cheaper than NAT. Second, for connecting VPCs, peering has no hourly fee and no hub processing charge, so for a few VPCs with heavy traffic it is cheapest; but it is not transitive, so with many VPCs the mesh becomes unmanageable and Transit Gateway's simplicity is worth its attachment and per-gigabyte fees. Third, cross-AZ and cross-Region traffic is billed per gigabyte, so I would keep chatty components in the same AZ where possible. The tradeoff there is resilience: concentrating in one AZ means an AZ failure hurts more, so production usually still spans AZs.
rubricPoints: Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB are free and remove NAT gateway processing charges.
Interface endpoints cost hourly plus per gigabyte but are often cheaper than routing through NAT.
VPC peering has no hourly or processing fee but is non-transitive and scales poorly to many VPCs.
Transit Gateway simplifies many-VPC routing but adds attachment and per-gigabyte processing fees.
Same-AZ private traffic is generally free, cross-AZ is charged, and cross-Region is charged more.
Reducing cross-AZ traffic can trade away resilience.

suggested.rationale: Pricing the same traffic through NAT, endpoints, peering and a transit hub in a cost model makes the per-gigabyte differences and their tradeoffs concrete.

lessons.plain: When an office or data centre needs to reach its systems in AWS, there are three common paths. The public internet is like posting letters: no setup, you just pay for what goes out. A VPN (virtual private network) is the same post with every letter locked in a tamper-proof envelope: cheap and quick, but just as fast or slow as the internet. AWS Direct Connect is like renting your own private road: it costs money every month whether you use it or not and takes weeks to build, but each trip is cheaper and more predictable. The cheapest choice depends mostly on how much data moves out of AWS.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company sends a small amount of data each month between its office and AWS, and it needs the link working by next week. Would you guess a private dedicated line or an encrypted tunnel over the internet is cheaper, and why?
lessons.teach:
Three options connect on-premises sites to AWS. The public internet carries traffic with no connection fee. You pay AWS's standard data transfer out rate, the per-gigabyte charge for data leaving AWS. Data coming into AWS is generally free, so outbound volume drives the bill. AWS Site-to-Site VPN is an encrypted tunnel over the internet, protected with a standard called IPsec. It adds a small hourly fee per connection, is ready in minutes, and still pays internet-rate egress, meaning outbound data. Its speed and delay vary because it rides the shared internet. AWS Direct Connect is a dedicated physical link from your network to AWS through a Direct Connect location, a building where AWS and carriers meet. You pay a fixed hourly port fee plus a telecom partner's circuit charge, but per-gigabyte egress is much lower. Setup takes weeks to months.

The pattern is that Direct Connect trades a fixed monthly cost for a cheaper per-gigabyte cost, so it wins only above a break-even volume. Here is a worked example using made-up rates, not real prices. Assume internet egress is 0.09 per GB, Direct Connect egress is 0.02, the VPN costs 36 a month, and Direct Connect port plus circuit costs 720 a month. At 50,000 GB out per month, the VPN path costs 36 + 4,500 = 4,536, and Direct Connect costs 720 + 1,000 = 1,720. Direct Connect wins. At 500 GB, the VPN costs 36 + 45 = 81, and Direct Connect costs 720 + 10 = 730. The VPN wins clearly.

A common mistake is picking Direct Connect for low or short-term traffic, or when the link is needed this week. You pay the fixed fee for capacity you never use, and the deadline is missed. Note also that Direct Connect is not encrypted by default. A cheap resilience pattern is a VPN kept as a backup path behind Direct Connect, so an outage of the dedicated line does not cut the site off.

questions.prompt: A media company in a regional office sends about 30,000 GB per month from AWS back to its on-premises servers. Using made-up rates: internet egress is 0.08 per GB, Direct Connect egress is 0.03 per GB, a Site-to-Site VPN costs 50 a month, and a Direct Connect port plus telecom circuit costs 1,050 a month. Step 1, the VPN path: 50 + (0.08 x 30,000) = 50 + 2,400 = 2,450 a month. Step 2, the Direct Connect path: missing. Step 3, compare the two totals and pick the cheaper option. What is the correct Step 2?
choices: 1,050 + 2,400 = 3,450 a month, so the VPN is cheaper
0.03 x 30,000 = 900 a month, so Direct Connect is cheaper
1,050 + 90 = 1,140 a month, so Direct Connect is cheaper
1,050 + 900 = 1,950 a month, so Direct Connect is cheaper
questions.why: Direct Connect costs its fixed monthly fee (1,050) plus its own lower egress rate times the volume (0.03 x 30,000 = 900), giving 1,950, which beats the VPN's 2,450.

questions.prompt: Why does AWS Direct Connect, a dedicated physical link to AWS, only save money above a certain monthly data volume?
choices: It is encrypted with IPsec by default, and the encryption overhead becomes cheaper per gigabyte at higher volumes
It has no fixed fee but a higher per-gigabyte rate, so it is only worth it when traffic is unpredictable
It swaps a fixed monthly port and circuit fee for a lower per-gigabyte egress rate, so the savings only cover that fee once enough data flows out
It charges for inbound data while the internet does not, so it only pays off when most traffic flows into AWS
questions.why: Direct Connect's savings come from cheaper outbound data, and those savings must exceed its fixed monthly cost before it beats the VPN or internet path.

questions.prompt: A small design agency needs to connect its single office to a new AWS environment by the end of this week. It expects only about 300 GB per month of outbound data and wants the traffic encrypted. Which option best fits the cost and timing requirements?
choices: AWS Direct Connect with a VPN backup, because a dedicated line is always required for encryption
The public internet with no tunnel, because it has no connection fee and is ready immediately
AWS Site-to-Site VPN, because it is encrypted, ready in minutes, and adds only a small hourly fee
AWS Direct Connect, because its per-gigabyte egress rate is the lowest of the three options
questions.why: At low volume the fixed Direct Connect fee would never be recovered and its weeks-to-months setup misses the deadline, while the VPN gives encryption cheaply and quickly.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm already sends large monthly volumes to on-premises over AWS Direct Connect. A review flags that a failure of the dedicated line would cut its warehouse off from AWS entirely. What is the low-cost way to address this risk?
choices: Move all traffic onto the public internet, because it has no connection fee
Order a second Direct Connect circuit and cancel the first one
Keep a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path behind Direct Connect
Rely on Direct Connect's built-in encryption to keep the link available
questions.why: A VPN backup costs only a small hourly fee yet keeps the site connected over the internet if the Direct Connect line goes down, while the main high-volume traffic still enjoys cheaper Direct Connect egress.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between the public internet, Site-to-Site VPN, and Direct Connect purely on cost, and name the tradeoff that comes with the cheapest per-gigabyte option.
lessons.modelAnswer: The bill is mostly driven by data leaving AWS, because inbound transfer is generally free. The public internet has no connection fee, and you pay standard egress per gigabyte. A Site-to-Site VPN adds a small hourly fee for an encrypted IPsec tunnel but still pays internet-rate egress. It is quick to set up, though its performance varies with the internet. Direct Connect is a dedicated line with a fixed monthly port fee plus a partner circuit charge, but much cheaper egress per gigabyte. So I'd estimate monthly outbound volume and compare fixed cost plus volume times rate for each option. Low or temporary volume points to a VPN. Sustained high volume points to Direct Connect. The tradeoff is that Direct Connect costs money even when idle, takes weeks to provision, and isn't encrypted by default. I'd often keep a VPN as a cheap backup path.
rubricPoints: Outbound data transfer from AWS is the main cost driver, and inbound is generally free.
A VPN adds a small hourly fee on top of internet-rate egress and is fast to set up.
Direct Connect has a fixed monthly port and circuit cost but a lower per-gigabyte egress rate.
The choice comes down to a break-even calculation of fixed cost versus volume times rate.
Direct Connect's downsides are idle cost, a long lead time, and no default encryption.
A VPN can serve as a low-cost backup path behind Direct Connect.

suggested.rationale: Computing the break-even between fixed connection fees and per-gigabyte egress for different traffic volumes is best learned by running the numbers in a cost model.

lessons.plain: A content delivery network (CDN) is a worldwide set of servers that keep copies of your files close to your users. Instead of every visitor reaching all the way back to your own server, called the origin, most of them get a nearby copy. Think of a bakery that stocks popular loaves in corner shops across town: the main bakery bakes once, the shops hand out the bread, and the bakery's ovens stay calm. Fewer trips to the origin means fewer origin servers to pay for and less data sent straight from them, so the bill drops and pages load faster.
lessons.guessPrompt: A website sends the same product photo to a million visitors a month. If a nearby copy of that photo could answer 9 out of every 10 requests, what do you think happens to the work and cost on the main server?
lessons.teach:
A CDN is a network of edge locations, which are servers placed in many cities, that cache content. To cache means to keep a stored copy so a later request can be answered without asking the source again. The origin is where the real content lives, such as an object storage bucket like Amazon S3 or a web server behind a load balancer. On AWS the CDN is Amazon CloudFront.

When a request reaches an edge location and a fresh copy is there, that is a cache hit. If not, it is a cache miss: the edge fetches the object from the origin, returns it, and stores it. How long the copy counts as fresh is the TTL, or time to live. The cache key is the set of request details (path, and optionally query strings, headers, cookies) used to decide whether two requests want the same object. The hit ratio is the share of requests answered from cache.

Why it saves money: origin cost scales with requests and bytes served. Every hit is a request your origin never processes and bytes it never sends. On AWS, transfer from an AWS origin to CloudFront is not charged, and CloudFront's own delivery rates are usually no higher than serving directly, so cost moves to the cheaper path.

Worked example: a site serves 10 TB of images a month directly from its origin. Add a CDN with a one-day TTL. A user in Frankfurt asks for logo.png: miss, the edge fetches it once and stores it. The next thousand Frankfurt users get hits. With a 90% hit ratio, the origin now sends about 1 TB instead of 10 TB and handles a tenth of the requests, so it can run on fewer, smaller servers.

Common mistake: putting cookies, every header, or random query strings in the cache key. Each request then looks unique, the hit ratio falls near zero, and the origin still takes full load while you pay for the CDN too. Personalized or fast-changing content is a poor fit, and long TTLs mean users may briefly see stale files unless you invalidate or version them.

questions.prompt: An online language school serves 40 TB of lesson audio files a month directly from an Amazon S3 bucket (object storage). It puts Amazon CloudFront (a CDN, a network of caching servers in many cities) in front of the bucket, with a TTL (how long a cached copy counts as fresh) of seven days. After a month the hit ratio (share of requests answered from the edge cache) is 75%. Step 1: 75% of requests are hits, answered by edge locations without contacting the bucket. Step 2: the other 25% are misses, where the edge fetches the file from the bucket, returns it, and stores it. Step 3: ______. Step 4: the bucket handles about a quarter of the requests it used to, and transfer from the AWS origin to CloudFront is not charged, so origin cost falls sharply. What is Step 3?
choices: The bucket now sends about 10 TB a month, because only the 25% of requests that miss reach the origin
The bucket now sends nothing at all, because after the first request every file is permanently stored at the edge
The bucket now sends about 30 TB a month, because 75% of the traffic still has to come from the origin
The bucket now sends 40 TB a month as before, because a CDN adds a cache but does not reduce origin traffic
questions.why: Only misses go back to the origin, so with a 75% hit ratio the bucket serves roughly 25% of 40 TB, which is about 10 TB.

questions.prompt: A news site places a CDN in front of its web servers. A reader in Tokyo requests a photo that the Tokyo edge location does not have a fresh copy of. What happens, and what is this called?
choices: A cache miss: the edge fetches the photo from the origin, returns it to the reader, and stores a copy
A cache hit: the edge answers from its stored copy and the origin is not contacted
A cache hit: the edge forwards every later request for the photo to the origin to keep it fresh
A cache miss: the request fails and the reader must retry until the edge finishes copying the photo
questions.why: When no fresh copy is at the edge it is a cache miss, so the edge fetches from the origin, serves the object, and stores it for later requests.

questions.prompt: A shoe retailer adds Amazon CloudFront in front of its product-image servers, but configures the cache key (the request details used to decide whether two requests want the same object) to include each visitor's session cookie. A month later the hit ratio is about 2% and the total bill went up. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The TTL was too long, so the edges kept stale images and had to refetch all of them
Transfer from an AWS origin to CloudFront is charged at a high rate, which raised the bill
Product images are personalized content, so they can never be cached by any CDN
Each visitor's cookie made every request look unique, so almost all were misses and the origin still took full load while the CDN added cost
questions.why: Putting a per-user cookie in the cache key makes requests for the same image look different, so the hit ratio collapses, the origin keeps its full load, and you pay for the CDN on top.

questions.prompt: A software company serves its website's stylesheet and script files through a CDN. To cut origin requests further, it raises the TTL on these files from one hour to 30 days. What does it give up in exchange for the lower origin cost?
choices: The hit ratio will drop, because longer TTLs cause more cache misses at the edge
The files can no longer be shared between users, since long TTLs make each copy user-specific
Each edge location must now ask the origin on every request whether the file has changed
After a file changes, users may keep getting the old cached copy unless the team invalidates it or uses a new versioned file name
questions.why: A longer TTL keeps cached copies counted as fresh for longer, which saves origin trips but means users can see stale files until they are invalidated or versioned.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, how putting a CDN in front of our origin lowers the bill, and name one limit or tradeoff they should know before turning it on.
lessons.modelAnswer: A CDN like CloudFront keeps copies of our files at edge locations near users. When a request hits a fresh cached copy, the edge answers it and our origin never sees it. Our origin costs grow with requests and bytes served, so if 90% of requests are hits, the origin serves roughly a tenth of the traffic and we can shrink the servers behind it. On AWS, transfer from our origin to CloudFront isn't charged, so the bytes shift onto a cheaper path. The savings depend on the hit ratio, which depends on the TTL and the cache key. If we include cookies or every query string in the key, nearly every request misses and we pay for the CDN without relieving the origin. The tradeoff is freshness: longer TTLs save more but users can see stale content until it expires, unless we version file names or invalidate. Personalized responses usually shouldn't be cached at all.
rubricPoints: Defines a CDN as edge locations that cache copies of origin content near users.
Explains that cache hits are requests and bytes the origin never serves, cutting origin compute and transfer cost.
Names hit ratio as the driver of savings, controlled by TTL and cache key.
Warns that an over-broad cache key (cookies, headers, random query strings) destroys the hit ratio.
States a tradeoff such as stale content from long TTLs or dynamic and personalized content not being cacheable.

suggested.rationale: Changing hit ratio and TTL in a credit-based cost model and watching origin requests and transfer cost fall makes the saving and its limits concrete.

lessons.plain: Throttling means deliberately capping how fast requests or data are allowed through, so one busy client, a sudden surge, or a runaway script cannot overwhelm a system or run up a huge bill. Bandwidth allocation is the same idea for network capacity: deciding how much of a connection a job may use, and when. Think of a motorway on-ramp with traffic lights: cars still get on, just at a steady pace, so the motorway keeps flowing and no one has to build extra lanes for the worst five minutes of the day. You trade a little waiting for not paying for capacity you rarely need.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your public API usually gets about 100 requests per second, but once a day a partner's buggy script sends 5,000 per second for a minute. If you could either buy enough backend capacity for the spike or cap that partner at a fixed rate, which is cheaper, and what would the partner notice?
lessons.teach:
A throttling strategy is a rule that limits the rate of incoming work. Most cloud services use a token bucket: a bucket holds tokens, each request spends one token, tokens refill at a steady rate (the rate limit), and the bucket size sets how many requests can arrive at once (the burst limit). When the bucket is empty, extra requests are rejected, usually with an HTTP 429 "too many requests" response, and the client is expected to retry later with backoff (waiting longer after each failure). In AWS, Amazon API Gateway, a managed front door for APIs, applies rate and burst limits per stage, per method, or per client through usage plans tied to API keys. AWS Lambda, a run-on-demand function service, can be capped with reserved concurrency, the maximum copies of a function running at once.

Why it cuts cost: every request that reaches the backend may trigger compute, database work and data transfer. Capping traffic means you size for the normal load plus a modest buffer, not for the worst spike, and a runaway client cannot generate an unlimited bill.

Worked example: rate 100 per second, burst 200. The bucket starts full at 200. A spike sends 500 requests in one second: 200 are served from the bucket, roughly 100 more as tokens refill, and about 200 get a 429. Next second the spike stops, the bucket refills, and normal traffic flows. The backend never saw more than about 300 in that second.

Bandwidth allocation applies the same thinking to transfers. AWS DataSync, a managed file-copy service, and AWS Storage Gateway, which links on-premises storage to the cloud, both let you cap upload bandwidth and schedule it, so a bulk copy runs overnight on an existing link instead of forcing you to buy a bigger one.
