The common mistake is setting limits without measuring normal peaks: limits too low reject paying customers, and clients without retry logic simply fail. Throttling saves money only when legitimate demand still fits under the cap.

questions.prompt: A ticketing startup puts a token bucket (a throttling rule where each request spends one token and tokens refill at a steady rate) in front of its booking API. The rate limit is 50 requests per second and the burst limit is 80. The bucket starts full. A flash sale sends 300 requests in a single second. Step 1: 80 requests are served at once from the full bucket. Step 2: roughly 50 more are served as tokens refill during that second. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: the next second the sale traffic drops, the bucket refills, and the backend never handled more than about 130 requests in the spike second. What is step 3?
choices: About 250 requests are rejected with a 429, because only the 50-per-second refill rate counts and the bucket size is ignored.
About 170 requests are rejected with a 429, and their clients should retry later with backoff.
The 170 extra requests wait inside the bucket and are served automatically the next second.
About 220 requests are rejected with a 429, because only the 80 tokens already in the bucket could ever be spent that second.
questions.why: 300 arrived, 80 were served from the full bucket and about 50 from refill, so roughly 300 - 130 = 170 are rejected with a 429 and must be retried by the client with backoff.

questions.prompt: In a token bucket throttling strategy, what does the size of the bucket control?
choices: The steady rate at which new tokens are added each second.
How many times a rejected client is allowed to retry.
How many requests can arrive at once before rejections start (the burst limit).
The maximum number of copies of a function that may run at the same time.
questions.why: The bucket size sets the burst limit, how many requests can be absorbed at once; the refill rate is the separate rate limit.

questions.prompt: A medical clinic must copy 40 TB of archived scans from its own data centre to AWS. Its existing internet link is busy with clinic work during business hours but almost idle at night. Which approach moves the data at the lowest cost without disrupting daytime work?
choices: Run the copy at full link speed during business hours so it finishes as soon as possible.
Pay to upgrade the link to a much faster one so the copy finishes in a single working day.
Use a managed file-copy service such as AWS DataSync with an upload bandwidth cap and a schedule that runs the copy overnight.
Put the copy behind an API Gateway usage plan with a low burst limit.
questions.why: Bandwidth allocation lets you cap and schedule the transfer so it uses the existing link when it is idle, avoiding the cost of a bigger link and the disruption of daytime saturation.

questions.prompt: An online shop sets an API Gateway rate limit of 20 requests per second on its checkout API based on a guess. Measurement later shows normal peak checkout traffic is 60 requests per second, and the shop's mobile app has no retry logic. What is the most likely result?
choices: Many paying customers get 429 errors and their checkouts simply fail, so the limit loses revenue instead of saving money.
The bill rises sharply because every rejected request is charged as backend compute.
Requests above 20 per second are held in a queue and completed a few seconds later.
The backend automatically scales up to serve all 60 requests per second, so nothing changes.
questions.why: A limit set below measured normal peaks rejects legitimate customers with 429 responses, and clients without retry logic just fail, so throttling only saves money when real demand fits under the cap.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use throttling and bandwidth limits to keep an architecture's costs down, including what users or jobs give up and how you would pick the limits.
lessons.modelAnswer: Throttling caps how fast work enters the system. With a token bucket, a refill rate sets the steady allowance and a burst size sets how much can arrive at once; anything over that gets a 429 and should retry with backoff. On AWS I'd set API Gateway rate and burst limits, per-client usage plans for partners, and reserved concurrency on Lambda so a spike can't fan out into unlimited compute and database load. For data transfers, I'd cap DataSync or Storage Gateway bandwidth and schedule bulk copies overnight so we keep our existing link instead of buying a bigger one. The tradeoff is latency or rejection: some requests wait or fail, and transfers take longer. So I'd set limits from measured normal peaks plus headroom, make sure clients retry, and watch 429 counts so we're not turning away real customers.
rubricPoints: Defines throttling as capping request rate, with a steady rate limit and a burst limit.
Explains the cost link: you size for normal load, and runaway clients can't drive unlimited backend spend.
Names concrete controls such as API Gateway limits or usage plans and Lambda reserved concurrency.
Describes bandwidth caps and scheduling for transfers to avoid buying a bigger link.
States the tradeoff: rejected or delayed requests and slower transfers.
Sets limits from measured peaks and requires clients to retry with backoff.

suggested.rationale: Working through a function throttling under a surge makes the learner see rate limits, concurrency caps and rejected requests in action, which is the core of choosing a throttling strategy.

lessons.plain: A load balancer is a front door that spreads incoming traffic across several servers so no single one is overwhelmed. AWS offers three main kinds. The Application Load Balancer reads web requests and routes by address or path. The Network Load Balancer passes raw connections through very fast without reading their content. The Gateway Load Balancer steers traffic through security appliances such as firewalls. Each one bills an hourly fee plus a usage fee. Choosing on cost is like choosing between a receptionist, a turnstile, and a security checkpoint: pick the cheapest door that still does the job, and share one door where you can.
lessons.guessPrompt: A company runs six small web services, and each one sits behind its own Application Load Balancer. All six use ordinary web traffic. Without changing what users see, how might they cut the load balancer bill?
lessons.teach:
A load balancer is a managed service that receives traffic and spreads it across a group of servers called targets. AWS has three current types, and all of them charge two things: a fixed hourly fee for each load balancer that exists, and a usage fee measured in capacity units. A capacity unit is a bundle of activity such as new connections, open connections, bytes processed and, for the Application type, routing rules checked. You pay for whichever of those you use most heavily.

The Application Load Balancer (ALB) works at the web request level (layer 7). It can read a hostname or URL path and send each request to a different target group. That means one ALB can front many services. The Network Load Balancer (NLB) works at the connection level (layer 4, TCP and UDP). It does not read requests, so it handles very high, simple traffic volumes efficiently and is often cheaper per unit there, but it cannot route by path. The Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) exists to pass traffic through third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls or inspection tools. Use it only when you actually need that inspection layer, because it adds its own hourly and usage charges plus endpoint charges.

Worked example, in fictional credits. Six services each have their own ALB at 20 credits a month in hourly fees, which comes to 120 credits. The architect replaces them with one ALB that has six path rules: /orders, /users, and so on. The usage fees stay roughly the same because the total traffic is unchanged. The fixed fee drops to 20 credits, a saving of 100 credits a month. The tradeoff is a shared blast radius, meaning a misconfigured rule or a deleted ALB now affects all six services. There is also a limit on how many rules one ALB can hold.

A common mistake is defaulting to one load balancer per service, or picking an ALB for plain high-volume TCP traffic that needs no content routing. In a running system, that means paying for capability nobody uses, month after month.

questions.prompt: A regional library network runs five separate web apps (catalog, events, room booking, e-books and donations). Each app has its own Application Load Balancer (ALB), a managed service that reads web requests and spreads them across servers. Each ALB costs 18 fictional credits a month in fixed hourly fees. Step 1: The current fixed cost is 5 x 18 = 90 credits a month. Step 2: The architect replaces the five ALBs with one ALB that has five hostname rules, such as catalog.library.example and events.library.example, each sending traffic to its own target group. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: The new fixed cost is 18 credits, a saving of 72 credits a month. Step 5: The tradeoff is a shared blast radius, so one bad rule or a deleted ALB affects all five apps. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Usage fees drop to about one fifth, because only one load balancer is now counting capacity units.
Usage fees stay roughly the same, because the total traffic across the five apps has not changed.
Usage fees disappear, because the shared ALB's fixed hourly fee now covers all traffic.
Usage fees rise about fivefold, because each request is now checked against five rules.
questions.why: Usage fees track the amount of activity, and consolidating does not change how much traffic the five apps receive in total, so only the fixed fee shrinks.

questions.prompt: An AWS load balancer charges a usage fee measured in capacity units. One month, a load balancer handles a modest number of new connections but processes a very large volume of bytes. How is its usage fee determined?
choices: By whichever activity dimension it uses most heavily, which here is bytes processed.
By the number of new connections only, since that is the main measure of load.
By a flat rate per target server registered behind it.
By adding together the charges for new connections, open connections, bytes and rules.
questions.why: A capacity unit bundles several kinds of activity, and you are billed on whichever of those you use most heavily, here bytes processed.

questions.prompt: A logistics company streams GPS readings from 200,000 trucks over plain TCP at very high volume. All readings go to one group of ingest servers, and nobody needs routing by URL path or hostname. Which load balancer type best fits on cost?
choices: One Application Load Balancer per region of trucks, so each region is isolated.
A Network Load Balancer, because it works at the connection level and handles simple, high-volume traffic efficiently.
An Application Load Balancer, because it can read each request and route it precisely.
A Gateway Load Balancer, because it is designed for very high traffic volumes.
questions.why: The Network Load Balancer handles plain high-volume TCP efficiently and is often cheaper per unit there, while an ALB's request-reading ability would be capability nobody uses.

questions.prompt: A startup adds a Gateway Load Balancer in front of its web tier "for future security", but it has no firewall or inspection appliance behind it and no plan to add one. What is the cost consequence in the running system?
choices: It pays nothing extra, because a Gateway Load Balancer is only billed once appliances are attached.
It pays the Gateway Load Balancer's hourly, usage and endpoint charges every month for an inspection layer it does not use.
It pays only a one-time setup fee, after which the Gateway Load Balancer runs free.
It saves money, because the Gateway Load Balancer replaces the need for an Application Load Balancer's path routing.
questions.why: A Gateway Load Balancer brings its own hourly and usage charges plus endpoint charges, so deploying one without a real inspection need wastes money month after month.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose between an Application, Network, or Gateway Load Balancer when cost matters, and name one thing you give up when you consolidate several services behind one load balancer.
lessons.modelAnswer: Every load balancer costs an hourly fee just for existing, plus a usage fee based on capacity units, which cover connections, bytes processed and, for the ALB, rule evaluations. So I start with the cheapest type that meets the requirement. If we need routing by hostname or path for web traffic, I use an Application Load Balancer, and I put several services behind one ALB with routing rules so we pay one hourly fee instead of many. If the traffic is plain TCP or UDP at high volume with no content routing, a Network Load Balancer is usually the better value. I only add a Gateway Load Balancer when we must send traffic through firewall or inspection appliances, because it adds its own charges. The tradeoff of consolidating is a shared blast radius: one bad rule change or outage hits every service on that load balancer, and there is a cap on how many rules it can hold.
rubricPoints: States that load balancers bill an hourly fee plus a usage-based capacity unit fee.
Matches ALB to request-level routing, NLB to high-volume connection-level traffic, and GWLB to appliance inspection.
Explains that one ALB with host or path rules can replace several load balancers and save hourly fees.
Notes that GWLB should be added only when inspection appliances are required.
Names a tradeoff of consolidation, such as shared blast radius or rule limits.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reading a requirement and picking the cheapest sufficient load balancer setup, which exam-style scenarios practise best, and no current mission or planned engine targets load balancer choice directly.

lessons.plain: Cost visibility means being able to see where your cloud money goes, and getting warned before it goes somewhere it shouldn't. Think of a household budget. One tool shows charts of past spending. Another tool is an alarm that rings when a category passes its limit. A third is the full itemised bank statement for detailed digging. Labels such as 'groceries' or 'kids' let you sort that spending by purpose. A family account lets one person pay for everyone and still see what each person spent. AWS offers each of these pieces for cloud bills, and you cannot cut a bill until you can see it clearly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your monthly cloud bill suddenly jumped 40%, and five teams share the company's AWS accounts. Before anyone touches a server, what two pieces of information would you want in order to find who caused the jump?
lessons.teach:
Cost visibility means knowing who spent what, on which service, and getting warned before spending runs away. AWS provides five pieces for this.

AWS Cost Explorer is a built-in chart-and-filter view of past spending, plus a short forecast. You can group spending by service, account, Region or tag. AWS Budgets lets you set a limit on cost or usage and sends an alert when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold you choose. By default it only alerts. Optional budget actions can apply a restricting permission policy. The AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) is the most detailed record available. It lists usage line by line, down to hourly, and delivers it as files into an S3 bucket (object storage), where you query it with SQL tools or load it into a dashboard. Cost allocation tags are key-value labels on resources, such as team=payments. Once you activate them in the billing console, they become fields you can group costs by. Multi-account billing uses AWS Organizations, a service for managing many accounts together. One management account pays for every member account, which is called consolidated billing. That account sees each member's costs, and the usage is pooled so that volume discounts and shared commitment discounts apply across all accounts.

This works because every charge is recorded against a resource and an account. Accounts and tags then give you two independent ways to slice the bill.

Worked example: finance asks who caused a 40% jump and wants a warning next time. Step 1: in Cost Explorer, group by account. The jump is in the analytics account. Step 2: group by tag. The extra cost is tagged team=ml. Step 3: group by service. The cause is large GPU instances. Step 4: create a budget for that account that alerts at 80% of forecast. Step 5: if finance wants its own per-resource chargeback, enable the CUR.

A common mistake is expecting tags to work backwards. Costs incurred before a tag was applied and activated are not grouped under it, and untagged resources show up as no-tag. Without these tools, a forgotten test cluster can run for months until the invoice arrives.

questions.prompt: A design agency runs everything in one AWS account. Its four departments (design, video, web, admin) share that account, and the finance lead wants to see each department's monthly cost. The engineer plans it like this. Step 1: on 1 March, add the key-value label dept=<department name> to every virtual server and storage bucket the agency owns. Step 2: ______. Step 3: at the end of March, open Cost Explorer and group March spending by the dept field. Step 4: create one AWS Budgets alert per department so each department lead hears early if their spend runs high. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Ask the CUR to rebuild February's files so the earlier spending is regrouped under the new dept label
Create a budget with a budget action for each department first, because Cost Explorer can only group spending that a budget is already tracking
Turn on consolidated billing in AWS Organizations, because labels on resources only appear in cost reports when several accounts share one bill
Activate dept as a cost allocation tag in the billing console so it becomes a field that costs can be grouped by
questions.why: A label on a resource only becomes a field you can group costs by after you activate it as a cost allocation tag in the billing console.

questions.prompt: A small company creates an AWS Budgets budget of $500 per month for its test account. It sets an alert at 100% of actual spend and does not configure any budget actions. A developer leaves a large database running, and the account's spend reaches $620 that month. What does AWS Budgets do?
choices: It stops the database once spend reaches $500, so the bill is capped at the limit
It does nothing, because a budget only reports at the end of the month and cannot alert during it
It automatically moves the test account under a management account so a volume discount absorbs the overspend
It sends the alert when spend crosses $500, and the database keeps running and adding cost
questions.why: By default a budget only sends alerts; restricting anything needs an optional budget action, and none was set up here.

questions.prompt: A retailer applies the label project=checkout to its order-processing servers on 15 June and activates it as a cost allocation tag the same day. In July, an analyst opens Cost Explorer and groups all of June's spending by the project tag. A few untagged log buckets were never labelled. What will the analyst see?
choices: No June data at all, because a tag only takes effect from the first day of the following month
Server spending from 15 June onward under project=checkout, with earlier server costs and the log buckets showing as no-tag
June's server and log bucket spending all under project=checkout, because untagged resources inherit the most common tag
All of June's server spending under project=checkout, because the tag is applied to the whole month once activated
questions.why: Tags do not work backwards, so costs before the tag was applied and activated, along with untagged resources, show up as no-tag.

questions.prompt: A hospital's finance team wants its own record of AWS charges, listed line by line down to the hour, so it can query the data with SQL and charge each ward for exactly what its resources used. Which AWS cost visibility tool best fits this need?
choices: The AWS Cost and Usage Report, which delivers detailed hourly line items as files into an S3 bucket
AWS Cost Explorer, which shows charts of past spending and a short forecast
AWS Budgets, which alerts when actual or forecast spend crosses a set threshold
Consolidated billing in AWS Organizations, which pools usage so discounts apply across accounts
questions.why: The CUR is the most detailed record available: it lists usage line by line, down to the hour, as files in S3 that you can query with SQL tools.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate asks why we need Cost Explorer, Budgets, the Cost and Usage Report and tags when the invoice already lists the total. Explain in your own words what each one is for, and name one limit, such as what Budgets does not do or what tags cannot show.
lessons.modelAnswer: The invoice tells us how much we spent, but not who spent it or why. Cost Explorer is for looking back. It charts spending and lets us group it by account, service or tag, so we can trace a spike to its source. Budgets look forward. We set a limit and get an alert when actual or forecast spend crosses it. By default a budget only warns us and does not stop resources. The Cost and Usage Report is the detailed raw data, delivered as files to S3. We use it when finance needs line-by-line queries or chargeback. Cost allocation tags such as team=ml let us split costs by owner, but only after they are applied and activated, and they don't cover earlier costs. If we use several accounts under AWS Organizations, we get one consolidated bill with per-account views and pooled discounts.
rubricPoints: Cost Explorer is for visualizing and filtering past spend, with a short forecast.
Budgets alert on actual or forecast thresholds, and by default do not stop spending.
The Cost and Usage Report is the most granular data, delivered to S3 for querying.
Cost allocation tags must be applied and activated, and they are not retroactive.
Organizations consolidated billing gives one bill, per-account visibility and pooled discounts.

suggested.rationale: The exam tests matching a stated need (explore trends, get alerts, run granular queries, see per-team costs, receive one bill) to the right tool, which is best practised by reasoning through scenarios.

scenarios.title: Tightening security at Larkspur Freight before an audit
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Freight is a small fictional shipping company that has just moved its booking website to AWS. You are the new junior engineer, and your manager has asked you to review the design before an external security audit next month. Here is what you find.

The founder signs in every day as the root user and has never turned on MFA. The root user is the single all-powerful identity created with the AWS account. It can do anything, including closing the account. MFA (multi-factor authentication) means signing in needs a second proof, such as a code from a phone app, as well as the password.

The website runs on EC2 instances, which are virtual servers. A PostgreSQL database runs on Amazon RDS, a managed database service, and it sits in a public subnet. A subnet is a slice of the company's VPC (virtual private cloud, its own private network inside AWS). A public subnet has a route to the internet. The database's security group, a virtual firewall attached to a resource that lists which traffic may come in, allows port 5432 from 0.0.0.0/0, which means from any address on the internet.

The database password is typed directly into a configuration file that is stored in the company's Git repository. Git is the version-control system where the developers keep their code, and all of them can read it.

Customer invoices, which contain names, addresses and bank details, are stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. S3 is object storage, and a bucket is a named container for files. Nobody has set up encryption for the bucket using keys the company controls, and nobody has decided who is allowed to use any keys.

For each problem below, name the missing control and the AWS service or feature that provides it. Describe the specific failure the control prevents. Then say whether the fix belongs in identity, network, or data.

1. The root user is used daily, with no MFA.
2. The database is in a public subnet, and its security group is open to the whole internet on port 5432.
3. The database password is hard-coded in a config file in Git.
4. The invoice bucket holds sensitive data, with no company-controlled encryption key or key access rules.
modelAnswer:
Layer: identity.

Missing control: root user protection.

The fix has two steps. First, turn on MFA for the root user, ideally with a hardware key or authenticator app kept somewhere safe. Second, stop using root for daily work. Create IAM users or federated sign-ins instead. IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the AWS service that decides who can do what. Put those identities in IAM groups with only the permissions each job needs. Keep the root user for the few tasks that truly need it.

Failure prevented: if the root password is phished, guessed or reused from another leaked site, an attacker gains unlimited control. They could delete everything, run up huge bills, or lock the company out. MFA blocks a stolen password on its own. Daily IAM identities limit the damage any one stolen login can do.

Common mistake: adding MFA but still using root every day. The broad exposure stays.

Layer: network.

Missing control: network segmentation and least-privilege firewall rules.

Move the RDS database into a private subnet. A private subnet has no route to an internet gateway, so nothing on the internet can reach it directly. Then change the database's security group. Remove the 0.0.0.0/0 rule. Allow port 5432 only from the security group attached to the web servers. That way, only the application tier can talk to the database. If the database later needs outbound internet access, for example to fetch updates, use a NAT gateway. A NAT gateway lets private resources start outbound connections while still blocking inbound ones.

Failure prevented: anyone on the internet can currently find the database and try passwords against it or exploit a flaw in it. That is a direct path to every booking record.

Common mistake: tightening only the security group but leaving the database in a public subnet with a public address. One wrong rule change later re-exposes it.

Layer: mainly identity. The fix changes how the application proves who it is, instead of relying on a shared secret in code. The secret itself is also protected as data, so naming data with that reasoning is also acceptable.

Missing control: centralised secret storage with rotation.

Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager. This is a managed service that keeps credentials encrypted, controls who can read them, and can change them on a schedule. Turn on automatic rotation. Give the EC2 instances an IAM role that is allowed to read only that one secret. The application then fetches the password when it runs. Remove the password from the config file. Also treat the old password as leaked and change it, because it stays in Git history even after the file is edited. Systems Manager Parameter Store, which stores configuration values and can encrypt them, is a cheaper option if built-in rotation is not needed.

Failure prevented: anyone with repository access, or anyone who gets a copy of the code, can read the password and log in to the database. Without rotation, a leaked password stays valid forever.

Layer: data.

Missing control: encryption at rest with a customer-controlled key, plus a key policy.

Use AWS KMS (Key Management Service), a managed service that creates and guards encryption keys. Create a customer managed key and set it as the bucket's default encryption. Then write a key policy, the rules attached to the key itself, that lets only the invoicing application's role and named administrators use the key to decrypt. Turn on automatic key rotation, and turn on S3 Block Public Access for the bucket.

Failure prevented: if someone gets access to the stored objects, they cannot read the invoices without permission to use the key. This could happen through a misconfigured bucket policy or an over-broad IAM permission. Every use of the key is also recorded, which gives the auditors evidence of who accessed the data.

Common mistake: writing a key policy so broad that any role in the account can decrypt. Encryption then exists on paper but stops nobody.
